Using surrounding context and expectation to interpret ambiguous input is top-down processing. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Bottom-up would rely only on the ambiguous marks themselves, which were illegible in isolation.
distractor_rationales.C: Rate coding is how intensity is signaled by firing frequency — unrelated.
distractor_rationales.D: A difference threshold is about telling two stimuli apart, not using context to read a word.

items.stem: Which statement about bottom-up and top-down processing is most accurate?

choices.text: Perception uses only one of the two at any time
Everyday perception usually combines both — sensory input (bottom-up) is interpreted using prior knowledge (top-down)
Bottom-up processing is immune to all perceptual error
Top-down processing ignores the actual stimulus entirely

items.explanation: Real perception is an interaction: bottom-up sensory data and top-down knowledge/expectation work together. Neither is used alone, and bottom-up isn't infallible. Takeaway: Everyday perception = bottom-up + top-down together. Bottom-up isn't error-proof; top-down doesn't ignore the stimulus. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Normal perception integrates both: raw sensory data and knowledge-driven interpretation operate together. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The two typically operate together, not in isolation.
distractor_rationales.C: Bottom-up processing can still be fooled by ambiguous or degraded stimuli — it isn't error-proof.
distractor_rationales.D: Top-down processing shapes interpretation of the stimulus but doesn't ignore it.

items.stem: Watching a basketball game on television, you perceive a fluid, meaningful game rather than a grid of individual colored pixels. This tendency to perceive organized wholes rather than isolated parts is the central idea of:
items.explanation: The Gestalt principles describe how the mind organizes sensory parts into meaningful wholes — 'the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.' Takeaway: Gestalt = we perceive organized wholes, not isolated parts. The grouping laws describe how. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gestalt psychology holds we perceive organized wholes — the whole is more than the sum of its parts. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Weber's law is about difference thresholds (JND), not perceptual grouping.
distractor_rationales.C: Signal detection theory concerns detecting a signal in noise, not organizing parts into wholes.
distractor_rationales.D: Sensory adaptation is reduced response to a constant stimulus, unrelated to grouping.

items.stem: A display of alternating columns of squares and circles is automatically seen as vertical columns rather than horizontal rows, because like items group together. This is the Gestalt principle of:
items.explanation: Similarity: we group elements that resemble one another (shape, color, size) — why like-columns are seen together. Takeaway: Similarity = group by looking alike. (Proximity = nearness; common fate = motion.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Grouping items that look alike (all squares, all circles) is similarity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Proximity groups items by nearness in space, not by appearance.
distractor_rationales.B: Closure is filling in missing parts of a figure, not grouping like items.
distractor_rationales.C: Common fate groups items by shared motion, not by appearance.

items.stem: Dots that are physically closer to one another are perceived as belonging to the same cluster, while dots farther apart seem to form separate groups. This is the principle of:
items.explanation: Proximity: elements that are close together are grouped into the same unit. Takeaway: Proximity = group by nearness in space. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Grouping elements by how near they are in space is proximity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Similarity groups by appearance, not distance.
distractor_rationales.B: Continuity concerns perceiving smooth continuous paths, not clustering by nearness.
distractor_rationales.C: Prägnanz is the preference for the simplest overall interpretation, not spatial clustering.

items.stem: Three angled shapes are arranged so that viewers 'see' a complete triangle even though no triangle is actually drawn — the mind fills in the missing edges. This is the Gestalt principle of:
items.explanation: Closure: the mind fills in gaps to perceive a complete, whole object — e.g., 'seeing' a triangle whose edges aren't drawn. Takeaway: Closure = fill in missing information to complete a figure (the illusory triangle). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Filling in missing information to perceive a complete figure is closure. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Continuity is perceiving lines as following the smoothest continuous path, not completing a figure.
distractor_rationales.B: Symmetry is perceiving balanced forms around a center, not filling gaps.
distractor_rationales.C: Proximity groups elements by nearness, not by completing an outline.

items.stem: When two lines cross, we perceive each as a single continuous line following the smoothest path, rather than as four separate segments meeting at a point. This is the principle of:
items.explanation: Continuity (good continuation): elements on a line or curve are perceived as following the smoothest, most continuous path. Takeaway: Continuity = perceive the smoothest continuous path (crossing lines seen as two flowing lines). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Perceiving elements as following the smoothest, most continuous path is continuity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Closure completes missing parts of a figure; here nothing is missing — it's about smooth flow.
distractor_rationales.C: Similarity groups by appearance, not by smooth continuation.
distractor_rationales.D: Common fate groups by shared motion, not by continuous line.

items.stem: Shown a pattern of overlapping shapes, the brain interprets the Olympic logo as five simple interlocking rings rather than a set of complex irregular figures. This preference for the simplest, most stable interpretation is the law of:
items.explanation: Prägnanz (law of good figure/simplicity): perception defaults to the simplest, most stable form — five clean rings rather than complex shapes. Takeaway: Prägnanz = we default to the simplest, most stable interpretation (Olympic rings). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The preference for the simplest, most orderly interpretation is Prägnanz. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Proximity groups by nearness, not by choosing the simplest interpretation.
distractor_rationales.B: Common fate groups by shared motion.
distractor_rationales.D: Past experience uses prior learning; here it's about defaulting to the simplest form.

items.stem: In a field of scattered, identical dots, those moving upward are perceived as one group and those moving downward as another. This grouping by shared motion is the law of:
items.explanation: Common fate: elements moving in the same direction are grouped together — even identical dots split into units by shared motion. Takeaway: Common fate = group by shared motion/direction. (Similarity = group by appearance.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Grouping elements that move together in the same direction is common fate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Similarity groups by appearance — but here the dots are identical; only motion differs.
distractor_rationales.B: Continuity concerns smooth continuous paths, not shared movement.
distractor_rationales.D: Closure is completing a figure, not grouping by motion.

items.stem: Two simple shapes placed side by side could be perceived as a single novel form or as two familiar letters; a fluent reader perceives the familiar letters. This influence of prior learning on grouping is the Gestalt law of:
items.explanation: Past experience: familiar patterns learned over time influence how we group and interpret stimuli — a reader sees letters where a non-reader sees shapes. Takeaway: Past experience = prior learning guides grouping/interpretation (seeing familiar letters). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. When prior learning shapes how elements are grouped, that's the law of past experience. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Prägnanz is about defaulting to the simplest form, not prior learning.
distractor_rationales.C: Proximity groups by spatial nearness, independent of experience.
distractor_rationales.D: Common fate groups by shared motion, not by learning.

items.stem: Looking at Rubin's famous image, a viewer sees either a white vase or two black faces in profile — but not both at once — depending on which region is taken as the object and which as the background. This is the Gestalt principle of:
items.explanation: Figure-ground organization separates a scene into a figure (the object) and the ground (background). Rubin's vase is reversible because either region can be taken as the figure. Takeaway: Figure-ground = separate the object (figure) from its background (ground). Rubin's vase = the classic reversible figure. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Segmenting a scene into a figure (object of focus) and a ground (background) is figure-ground; the vase/faces image is reversible because either region can be the figure. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Closure fills in missing parts of a figure, not object-vs-background segmentation.
distractor_rationales.C: Similarity groups items by appearance, not figure vs. ground.
distractor_rationales.D: Common fate groups by shared motion.

items.stem: Presented with a scattered set of brackets, viewers group them into symmetrical pairs balanced around a center, perceiving orderly units rather than random marks. This is the Gestalt principle of:
items.explanation: Symmetry: the mind perceives objects as symmetrical forms balanced around a center point, favoring orderly, balanced units. Takeaway: Symmetry = perceive balanced, symmetrical forms around a center. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Perceiving balanced, symmetrical forms organized around a center point is symmetry. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Proximity groups by nearness in space, not by symmetry.
distractor_rationales.B: Continuity concerns smooth continuous paths, not balanced pairing.
distractor_rationales.C: Past experience uses prior learning, not symmetrical organization.

items.stem: The ambiguous middle character in “A 13 C” is read as the letter “B,” but the identical mark in “12 13 14” is read as the number “13.” The surrounding items change how the same stimulus is perceived. This influence is best described as:

choices.text: A contextual effect on perceptual organization

items.explanation: Contextual effects: the surrounding context establishes how an ambiguous stimulus is organized — the same mark reads as 'B' among letters and '13' among numbers. Takeaway: Contextual effects = surrounding context determines how an ambiguous stimulus is organized/interpreted (B vs 13). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Context — the surrounding stimuli — determines how an ambiguous item is organized and interpreted. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The absolute threshold is about detecting a faint stimulus, not context-driven interpretation.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensory adaptation is reduced response to a constant stimulus.
distractor_rationales.D: Rate coding is how intensity is signaled by firing frequency.

items.stem: Trace the path of light entering the eye. In order, light passes through the:

choices.text: Lens → cornea → pupil → retina → vitreous humor
Cornea → aqueous humor → pupil → lens → vitreous humor → retina
Retina → lens → cornea → aqueous humor → pupil

items.explanation: Light path: cornea → aqueous humor → pupil → lens → vitreous humor → retina. Takeaway: Order of light: cornea → aqueous humor → pupil → lens → vitreous humor → retina. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Light enters the transparent cornea, crosses the aqueous humor, passes the pupil, is focused by the lens, traverses the vitreous humor, and lands on the retina. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The cornea — not the lens — is the first structure light reaches.
distractor_rationales.C: Light hits the cornea before the pupil, and the sclera is opaque (light doesn't pass through it).
distractor_rationales.D: This is reversed — the retina is the last structure, not the first.

items.stem: Which structure is the first to bend (refract) incoming light and provides most of the eye's focusing power?
items.explanation: The cornea is the first structure light reaches and does most of the eye's (fixed) refraction. The lens then fine-tunes the focus. Takeaway: Cornea = first to bend light and most of the fixed refraction. Lens fine-tunes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The transparent cornea is the first structure light hits and supplies most of the eye's fixed refractive power; the lens fine-tunes focus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The lens fine-tunes focus (accommodation) but provides less of the total bending than the cornea.
distractor_rationales.C: The retina detects light; it doesn't bend it.
distractor_rationales.D: The iris controls pupil size; it doesn't refract light.

items.stem: Unlike the cornea's fixed bending, the lens can change its focusing power to keep both near and far objects sharp. This adjustment is called:
items.explanation: Accommodation is the lens changing shape (via the ciliary muscle and suspensory ligaments) to focus on near vs. far objects. Takeaway: Accommodation = the lens changing shape to focus on near vs. far objects. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Accommodation is the lens changing shape to adjust focus for objects at different distances. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Adaptation is reduced sensory response to a constant stimulus, not focusing.
distractor_rationales.C: Convergence is the eyes rotating inward for near objects — a depth cue, not lens focusing.
distractor_rationales.D: Transduction is converting light into a neural signal, not adjusting focus.

items.stem: To focus on a nearby object, the ciliary muscle contracts, loosening the suspensory ligaments and allowing the lens to become:

choices.text: More rounded, increasing its focusing power

items.explanation: Near focus: the ciliary muscle contracts → suspensory ligaments loosen → the lens becomes rounder (more refractive power). Far focus is the reverse. Takeaway: Near: ciliary muscle CONTRACTS → ligaments loosen → lens ROUNDER (more power). Far: muscle relaxes, lens flattens. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. For near vision, ciliary contraction slackens the ligaments, so the elastic lens bulges rounder and more powerful. For distant objects the reverse occurs. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A flatter lens is for distant vision (ciliary muscle relaxed, ligaments taut).
distractor_rationales.C: The lens becoming opaque describes a cataract, not accommodation.
distractor_rationales.D: Pupil size is set by the iris, not by lens shape.

items.stem: In bright light the pupil narrows; in dim light it widens. This change in pupil size is produced by:

choices.text: The iris — a muscle that constricts or dilates the pupil

items.explanation: The iris is the muscle (and the source of eye color) that constricts or dilates the pupil, regulating how much light enters. Bright = constrict, dim = dilate. Takeaway: Iris (muscle) sets pupil size → controls light entering. Bright = constrict, dim = dilate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The iris is the pigmented muscle (which also gives eye color) that constricts or dilates to set pupil size and regulate light entry. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Lens shape change is accommodation (focus), not pupil size.
distractor_rationales.B: The cornea's shape is fixed; it doesn't regulate light entry by thickening.
distractor_rationales.C: Retinal adaptation adjusts sensitivity, but the pupil's size is set by the iris muscle.

items.stem: At the retina, incoming light is converted into electrochemical (neural) signals the brain can interpret. This conversion of a physical stimulus into a neural signal is called:
items.explanation: The retina's photoreceptors perform transduction — converting light (a physical stimulus) into electrochemical neural signals. Takeaway: Transduction = converting a physical stimulus (light) into a neural signal, at the retina's photoreceptors. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Transduction is converting a physical stimulus (light) into an electrochemical neural signal — done by the retina's photoreceptors. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Accommodation is the lens focusing; it doesn't create the neural signal.
distractor_rationales.B: Refraction is bending light (cornea/lens), not converting it to a signal.
distractor_rationales.C: Adaptation is a change in responsiveness, not the initial conversion of light to signal.

items.stem: A person entering a dark room relies mainly on receptors that are highly sensitive to dim light but cannot distinguish color. These are the:
items.explanation: Rods are highly sensitive to dim light and drive night vision, but give no color and low detail. Cones handle color and fine detail in bright light. Takeaway: Rods = dim light/night, no color, high sensitivity. Cones = color + fine detail in bright light. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rods are highly light-sensitive and mediate dim-light (night) vision but don't detect color. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Cones handle color and fine detail in bright light — they're poor in the dark.
distractor_rationales.B: Ganglion cells carry output to the optic nerve; they aren't the dim-light photoreceptors.
distractor_rationales.D: Bipolar cells relay signals within the retina; they aren't photoreceptors.

items.stem: Which region of the retina contains only cones (no rods) and provides the sharpest, most detailed central vision?
items.explanation: The fovea (center of the macula) is all cones, no rods, giving the sharpest central/detail vision. The periphery is rod-rich. Takeaway: Fovea = all cones, no rods → sharpest central/detail vision. Periphery = rod-rich (dim light, motion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The fovea, at the center of the macula, is packed exclusively with cones (no rods), giving the highest visual acuity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The optic disc has no photoreceptors at all — it's the blind spot where the optic nerve exits.
distractor_rationales.B: The choroid is a vascular/pigmented layer, not a photoreceptor region.
distractor_rationales.C: The peripheral retina is rod-dominated — good for dim light and motion, poor for detail.

items.stem: The choroid is a pigmented, blood-vessel-rich layer behind the retina. Its two main functions are to:

choices.text: Nourish the retina and absorb stray light to prevent internal reflection

items.explanation: The choroid nourishes the outer retina (blood vessels) and its dark pigment absorbs stray light to prevent scattering. Some nocturnal animals instead have a reflective layer for better night vision. Takeaway: Choroid = blood supply to retina + absorbs stray light (dark pigment). Reflective in some night animals. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The choroid supplies blood to the outer retina, and its dark pigment absorbs stray light, preventing internal scattering. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Focusing is done by the cornea and lens, not the choroid.
distractor_rationales.C: Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body, not the choroid.
distractor_rationales.D: Transduction is the photoreceptors' job, not the choroid's.

items.stem: Which correctly describes the two fluids of the eye?

choices.text: Aqueous humor fills the main cavity; vitreous humor sits just in front of the lens
Aqueous humor (watery, front chambers, nourishes cornea/lens); vitreous humor (jelly-like, main cavity, maintains eyeball shape)
Both are jelly-like and fill the same chamber
Aqueous humor transduces light; vitreous humor bends light

items.explanation: Aqueous humor: watery, in the front chambers, nourishes cornea/lens and maintains pressure. Vitreous humor: jelly-like, fills the large rear cavity, maintains the eyeball's shape. Takeaway: Aqueous = watery, front, nourishes cornea/lens. Vitreous = jelly, back, maintains eyeball shape. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Aqueous humor is the watery fluid in the front chambers that nourishes the avascular cornea and lens; vitreous humor is the jelly-like fluid in the large rear cavity that maintains eyeball shape. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the vitreous (jelly) fills the main rear cavity; the aqueous (watery) is in front.
distractor_rationales.C: They differ: aqueous is watery (front), vitreous is jelly-like (rear).
distractor_rationales.D: Neither fluid transduces or focuses light — those are the retina and cornea/lens.

items.stem: After light is transduced in the retina, the neural signal flows through the retina in which order before leaving the eye?

choices.text: Ganglion cell → bipolar cell → photoreceptor → optic nerve
Bipolar cell → photoreceptor → ganglion cell → optic nerve
Photoreceptor → ganglion cell → bipolar cell → optic nerve
Photoreceptor (rod/cone) → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve

items.explanation: Retinal signal flow: photoreceptor → bipolar cell → ganglion cell → optic nerve → brain. Takeaway: Signal flow in the retina: photoreceptor → bipolar → ganglion → optic nerve → brain. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Signals begin in the photoreceptors, pass to bipolar cells, then to ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — signals start in photoreceptors, not ganglion cells.
distractor_rationales.B: Bipolar cells are the middle relay, not the starting point.
distractor_rationales.C: Bipolar cells come before ganglion cells, not after.

items.stem: Counterintuitively, when light strikes a rod, the rod's immediate response is to:

choices.text: Depolarize and fire an action potential
Release more neurotransmitter than in darkness
Hyperpolarize — effectively turning 'off' and reducing its signaling

items.explanation: The counterintuitive core of phototransduction: in the dark the photoreceptor is depolarized ('on'); light hyperpolarizes it, turning it 'off' and reducing its signal. Takeaway: Light turns photoreceptors OFF (hyperpolarizes them); in the DARK they're 'on.' The famous counterintuitive fact. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In the dark a rod is depolarized ('on'); light hyperpolarizes it, turning it 'off' and decreasing its neurotransmitter release. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Photoreceptors don't fire classic action potentials; light hyperpolarizes them rather than depolarizing.
distractor_rationales.B: Light decreases neurotransmitter release — rods release more in the dark, not in light.
distractor_rationales.C: Photoreceptors don't divide in response to light.

items.stem: Which retinal cells relay signals from the photoreceptors onward to the ganglion cells?
items.explanation: Bipolar cells are the middle relay of the retina: they carry the photoreceptor signal to the ganglion cells. Takeaway: Bipolar cells = the middle relay: photoreceptor → BIPOLAR → ganglion. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Bipolar cells sit between the photoreceptors and ganglion cells, passing the signal along. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Ganglion cells are the next stage after bipolar cells, not the relay from photoreceptors.
distractor_rationales.C: The choroid is a vascular/pigment layer, not part of the signal relay.
distractor_rationales.D: The cornea is a light-bending structure at the front of the eye, not a retinal relay.

items.stem: The optic nerve that carries visual information to the brain is formed by the axons of which retinal cells?
items.explanation: The ganglion cells' axons converge and leave the eye as the optic nerve (exiting at the blind spot). Takeaway: Ganglion cell axons = the optic nerve. They exit at the optic disc (blind spot). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ganglion cell axons bundle together and exit the back of the eye as the optic nerve. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Bipolar cells relay within the retina; their processes don't form the optic nerve.
distractor_rationales.C: Rods are photoreceptors, not the source of the optic nerve's axons.
distractor_rationales.D: Cones are photoreceptors, not the source of the optic nerve's axons.

items.stem: The point where the optic nerve exits the retina contains no photoreceptors, producing a gap in the visual field called the:
items.explanation: The optic disc — where the optic nerve exits — has no photoreceptors, creating the blind spot. Takeaway: Optic disc = blind spot: no photoreceptors where the optic nerve exits. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no rods or cones — the blind spot (optic disc). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The fovea is the cone-packed region of sharpest vision, not a gap.
distractor_rationales.B: The macula is the cone-rich central retina, not the optic-nerve exit.
distractor_rationales.C: The choroid is the vascular layer behind the retina, not the blind spot.

items.stem: The human retina contains roughly 120 million of one photoreceptor and 6–7 million of the other. These are, respectively:
items.explanation: There are about 120 million rods (dim light, periphery) and 6–7 million cones (color, fovea). Takeaway: ~120 million rods (dim light) vs. ~6–7 million cones (color). Rods massively outnumber cones. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rods (~120 million) vastly outnumber cones (~6–7 million), fitting their role in dim-light peripheral vision. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — rods are the ~120 million; cones are the ~6–7 million.
distractor_rationales.C: These are the photoreceptors' counts, not bipolar/ganglion cells.
distractor_rationales.D: The second figure refers to cones, not ganglion cells.

items.stem: To read fine print or find Waldo in a crowded picture, you rely on the region of the retina where cones are most densely concentrated: the:
items.explanation: Cones are concentrated in the fovea, providing the acuity for detail (reading, finding Waldo). The periphery is rod-dominated. Takeaway: Cones cluster in the fovea → detail/acuity. Periphery = rods (dim light, motion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cones pack into the fovea, giving the high acuity needed for detail tasks; the periphery is rod-dominated. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The peripheral retina is rod-rich — good for dim light and motion, poor for fine detail.
distractor_rationales.C: The optic disc has no photoreceptors at all (the blind spot).
distractor_rationales.D: The choroid is a vascular layer, not a photoreceptor region.

items.stem: In the eye, the conversion of light energy into an electrical (neural) signal by a photoreceptor is an example of:
items.explanation: Transduction = converting a physical stimulus (light) into a neural signal. (Transmission = neuron→neuron; perception = the conscious experience.) Takeaway: Transduction = physical stimulus → neural signal. Transmission = neuron→neuron. Perception = conscious experience. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Transduction transforms a physical stimulus (light) into a neural signal — performed here by the photoreceptors. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transmission is one neuron electrically activating another, not converting light to a signal.
distractor_rationales.C: Perception is the conscious experience of the processed signal, not the initial conversion.
distractor_rationales.D: Accommodation is the lens changing shape to focus, not signal conversion.

items.stem: Visible light is electromagnetic radiation, and the color (hue) we perceive corresponds most directly to the light's:
items.explanation: Wavelength → hue (color); amplitude → brightness. Visible light spans roughly 400–700 nm. Takeaway: Wavelength = color/hue; amplitude = brightness. Visible range ~400–700 nm. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hue corresponds to wavelength (~400 nm violet/blue to ~700 nm red); amplitude corresponds to brightness. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Amplitude corresponds to brightness/intensity, not hue.
distractor_rationales.B: Light's speed is essentially constant in a given medium and doesn't set color.
distractor_rationales.D: Phase doesn't determine the perceived hue.

items.stem: Within the visible spectrum, which pairing of wavelength and color is correct?

choices.text: ~400 nm = violet/blue (short wavelength); ~700 nm = red (long wavelength)
Wavelength has no relationship to color

items.explanation: Short λ (~400 nm) = violet/blue; long λ (~700 nm) = red. ROYGBV runs from longest (red) to shortest (violet) wavelength. Takeaway: Short λ ~400nm = violet/blue; long λ ~700nm = red. Red = longest visible wavelength, violet = shortest. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Short wavelengths (~400 nm) look violet/blue; long wavelengths (~700 nm) look red. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — red is the long-wavelength (~700 nm) end, violet the short (~400 nm).
distractor_rationales.C: Green sits in the middle of the spectrum, not at 400 nm; blue isn't at 700 nm.
distractor_rationales.D: Wavelength directly determines perceived hue.

items.stem: The trichromatic (Young–Helmholtz) theory explains color vision by proposing that:

choices.text: There are four cone types arranged in opposing pairs
There are three cone types (roughly red, green, and blue), and their combined activation yields all perceived colors
Each distinct color has its own dedicated photoreceptor

items.explanation: Trichromatic theory: three cone types (red/green/blue) whose combined firing produces all colors. It operates at the receptor (cone) level. Takeaway: Trichromatic = 3 cone types (R/G/B); their combined firing makes all colors. Receptor-level. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Three cone types tuned to long (red), medium (green), and short (blue) wavelengths combine to produce every perceived color. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Opposing pairs describe opponent-process theory; trichromatic theory posits three cone types.
distractor_rationales.C: Cones — not rods — detect color; rods handle dim-light vision.
distractor_rationales.D: Colors arise from combinations of just three cone types, not one receptor per color.

items.stem: After staring at a green image and then looking at a white wall, you briefly see a red afterimage. This is best explained by:

choices.text: Opponent-process theory — color is coded in opposing pairs (red–green, blue–yellow, black–white)

items.explanation: Opponent-process theory: colors are processed in opposing pairs. A green afterimage's complement (red) appears once the green response fatigues — which trichromatic theory can't explain. Takeaway: Opponent-process = color in opposing pairs (red–green, blue–yellow, black–white). Explains afterimages. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fatiguing the 'green' side of the red–green channel leaves the red response unopposed, producing a red afterimage. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Trichromatic theory explains color mixing but not afterimages.
distractor_rationales.C: Dark adaptation is regaining sensitivity in dim light, unrelated to color afterimages.
distractor_rationales.D: The blind spot is a gap with no photoreceptors, not the cause of afterimages.

items.stem: According to opponent-process theory, why can a color be described as 'bluish-green' but never as 'reddish-green'?

choices.text: Red and green are opponents in the same channel, so only one can be signaled at a time
Green is always brighter than red
The eye contains no green cones
Red and green have identical wavelengths

items.explanation: Red–green is a single opponent channel, so the two can't be signaled together (no 'reddish-green'); blue and green are different channels, so 'bluish-green' is fine. Takeaway: Opponent pairs (red–green, blue–yellow) can't co-occur → no 'reddish-green.' Cross-channel blends (bluish-green) are fine. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Red and green form one opponent channel — signaling one suppresses the other — so reddish-green can't be perceived, while blue and green (different channels) can blend. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Relative brightness isn't why reddish-green is impossible.
distractor_rationales.C: The eye does have green-sensitive (medium-wavelength) cones.
distractor_rationales.D: Red and green have different wavelengths.

items.stem: Trichromatic theory neatly explains color mixing but struggles with color afterimages. Which theory accounts for those?
items.explanation: Trichromatic theory explains mixing; opponent-process explains afterimages and the absence of reddish-green — each covers what the other can't. Takeaway: Trichromatic explains mixing; opponent-process explains afterimages. They're complementary. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Afterimages (and the impossibility of reddish-green) are explained by opponent-process theory. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Signal detection theory is about detecting signals in noise, not color coding.
distractor_rationales.C: Place theory concerns pitch perception in hearing, not color.
distractor_rationales.D: Gestalt theory concerns perceptual grouping, not color afterimages.

items.stem: Modern vision science regards the trichromatic and opponent-process theories as:

choices.text: Mutually exclusive, with only one being true
Both correct, operating at different stages — trichromatic at the cones, opponent-process in later neural processing
Identical restatements of the same idea

items.explanation: Not either/or: trichromatic processing happens at the cones, opponent-process coding happens in later neural stages. Together they explain color vision. Takeaway: Trichromatic (at the cones) + opponent-process (later neural stages) together explain color vision. Both are right. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Trichromatic processing occurs at the cone (receptor) level; opponent-process coding occurs downstream in ganglion cells and the brain. Together they explain color vision. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: They're complementary, not mutually exclusive.
distractor_rationales.C: Both remain well-supported, describing different stages.
distractor_rationales.D: They describe different mechanisms at different stages, not the same idea.

items.stem: When a photon strikes rhodopsin in a rod, the retinal molecule it contains switches from its 11-cis (bent) form to its all-trans (straight) form. This conformational change:

choices.text: Activates rhodopsin and triggers the phototransduction cascade
Directly opens the rod's sodium channels
Immediately releases neurotransmitter from the rod

items.explanation: Light isomerizes 11-cis retinal → all-trans retinal, changing rhodopsin's shape and kicking off the phototransduction cascade. Takeaway: Light bends retinal from 11-cis to all-trans → activates rhodopsin → starts the cascade. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Light isomerizes 11-cis retinal to all-trans, changing rhodopsin's shape and starting the cascade (activating transducin). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The channels are gated by cGMP downstream, not opened directly by retinal's shape change.
distractor_rationales.C: Light actually decreases neurotransmitter release; it isn't the immediate result of isomerization.
distractor_rationales.D: Regeneration of rhodopsin happens later, during recovery, not at activation.

items.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the phototransduction cascade after light activates rhodopsin?

choices.text: cGMP broken down → PDE → transducin → rhodopsin
Rhodopsin → transducin (G protein) → phosphodiesterase (PDE) → cGMP broken down

items.explanation: Cascade order: rhodopsin → transducin → PDE → cGMP hydrolyzed (cGMP levels fall). Takeaway: Rhodopsin → transducin (G protein) → PDE → cGMP broken down. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Activated rhodopsin activates transducin, whose alpha subunit activates PDE, which hydrolyzes (breaks down) cGMP. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: This is reversed — rhodopsin is the start, cGMP breakdown the end.
distractor_rationales.B: Transducin comes before PDE, and cGMP is broken down (not made).
distractor_rationales.C: Rhodopsin is activated first, before transducin.

items.stem: In the dark, cGMP levels inside a rod are high. What does this cGMP do?

choices.text: Closes the Na⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing the rod
Keeps cGMP-gated Na⁺ channels open, so the rod stays depolarized ('on')

items.explanation: In the dark: high cGMP holds Na⁺ channels open → rod depolarized ('on'), releasing glutamate (the 'dark current'). Takeaway: Dark = high cGMP → Na⁺ channels OPEN → rod depolarized ('on'), releasing glutamate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. High cGMP holds the Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx → the rod is depolarized ('dark current'), releasing glutamate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Closing channels/hyperpolarization happens in the light, when cGMP falls — the opposite.
distractor_rationales.C: Retinal isomerization is triggered by light, not by cGMP.
distractor_rationales.D: cGMP doesn't regenerate rhodopsin.

items.stem: When light activates the cascade and PDE lowers cGMP, the rod responds by:

choices.text: Closing its Na⁺ channels, hyperpolarizing, and turning 'off'
Opening more Na⁺ channels and depolarizing
Releasing more glutamate than in the dark

items.explanation: Light → PDE lowers cGMP → Na⁺ channels close → rod hyperpolarizes ('off') → less glutamate. Takeaway: Light → cGMP falls → Na⁺ channels close → hyperpolarize ('off'). Dark is the reverse. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Less cGMP → Na⁺ channels close → less Na⁺ enters → the rod hyperpolarizes ('off') and releases less glutamate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Channels close (not open) as cGMP falls; the rod hyperpolarizes.
distractor_rationales.C: Photoreceptors don't fire classic action potentials; they hyperpolarize gradually.
distractor_rationales.D: Light decreases glutamate release — more is released in the dark.

items.stem: Transducin, which links activated rhodopsin to PDE in the cascade, is a:

choices.text: An ion channel that lets Na⁺ into the rod
A neurotransmitter released onto bipolar cells
G protein made of alpha, beta, and gamma subunits, whose alpha subunit activates PDE

items.explanation: Transducin is the G protein (alpha/beta/gamma) coupling rhodopsin to PDE — its alpha subunit activates PDE. Takeaway: Transducin = G protein (alpha/beta/gamma). Its alpha subunit activates PDE. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Transducin is a heterotrimeric G protein; light-activated rhodopsin frees its alpha subunit to activate PDE. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transducin is a signaling G protein, not an ion channel.
distractor_rationales.B: It's an intracellular G protein, not a neurotransmitter.
distractor_rationales.D: The photopigment is rhodopsin; transducin is downstream of it.

items.stem: Rhodopsin, the light-sensitive pigment of rods, is the protein opsin bound to retinal. The analogous pigment in cones is called:
items.explanation: Rods = rhodopsin; cones = photopsin (three types). Both are opsin + retinal. Takeaway: Rods use rhodopsin; cones use photopsin (3 types for color). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rods use rhodopsin; cones use photopsins (three types, for color). Both are opsin + retinal. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transducin is the G protein in the cascade, not the cone pigment.
distractor_rationales.C: cGMP is the second messenger, not a photopigment.
distractor_rationales.D: Melanin is a pigment in the choroid/iris, not the cone photopigment.

items.stem: Vision in very low light (e.g., a moonless night), mediated mainly by rods, is termed:
items.explanation: Scotopic = very low light (rods); photopic = bright (cones); mesopic = dawn/dusk (both). Takeaway: Scotopic = dim (rods), photopic = bright (cones), mesopic = dawn/dusk (both). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Scotopic = very low light (rods); photopic = bright light (cones); mesopic = intermediate (dawn/dusk, both). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Photopic vision is bright-light, cone-driven vision.
distractor_rationales.C: Mesopic vision is dawn/dusk light, using both rods and cones.
distractor_rationales.D: Myopic means nearsighted — unrelated to light level.

items.stem: Because light turns a photoreceptor 'off' (hyperpolarizes it), light causes the photoreceptor to release:

choices.text: The same amount regardless of light
Less neurotransmitter (glutamate) than it does in darkness

items.explanation: Light hyperpolarizes the photoreceptor → less glutamate. In the dark it's depolarized → more glutamate. Takeaway: Light → hyperpolarize → LESS glutamate. Dark → depolarized → MORE glutamate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Photoreceptors release glutamate steadily in the dark; light hyperpolarizes them, reducing release — the signal the retina reads. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Light decreases, not increases, glutamate release.
distractor_rationales.B: Release changes with light — more in dark, less in light.
distractor_rationales.C: Glutamate is released most in the dark, not in bright light.

items.stem: The human retina has roughly 20 times more of one photoreceptor than the other. Which is more numerous, and what does it suit?

choices.text: Cones (~120 million) — suited to color and fine detail
Rods (~120 million) — suited to dim-light, peripheral, black-and-white vision
They are present in equal numbers
Rods (~120 million) — suited to color vision

items.explanation: ~120 million rods (dim light, periphery, B/W) vs. ~6 million cones (color, detail, fovea) — about 20:1. Takeaway: ~120M rods (dim/periphery/B&W) vs. ~6M cones (color/detail/fovea). Rods win ~20:1. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rods (~120 million) vastly outnumber cones (~6 million), fitting dim-light peripheral (black-and-white) vision. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Rods, not cones, are the ~120 million; cones number ~6 million.
distractor_rationales.C: They are not equal — rods outnumber cones ~20:1.
distractor_rationales.D: Rods handle dim-light black-and-white vision, not color.

items.stem: Rods are roughly 1000× more sensitive to light than cones. This makes rods most important for:

choices.text: Detecting whether any light is present, especially in dim conditions

items.explanation: Rods are ~1000× more light-sensitive than cones → best for detecting faint light / dim-condition vision. Cones = color + detail. Takeaway: Rods ~1000× more sensitive → detect faint light (night, B&W). Cones = color + fine detail. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rods' extreme sensitivity makes them the receptors for detecting faint light and dim-condition (night) vision. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Rods can't distinguish color — that's the cones' job.
distractor_rationales.B: Fine detail (acuity) is a cone strength, tied to the fovea.
distractor_rationales.C: Bright daylight is cone (photopic) vision; rods saturate in bright light.

items.stem: Rods and cones use different photopigments. Rods contain rhodopsin; cones contain:
items.explanation: Rods = rhodopsin; cones = photopsin (three types for color). Both are opsin + retinal. Takeaway: Rods = rhodopsin. Cones = photopsin (3 types). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rods use rhodopsin; cones use photopsins (three types), each opsin bound to retinal. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Rhodopsin is specifically the rod pigment; cones use photopsin.
distractor_rationales.C: Transducin is the cascade G protein, not a photopigment.
distractor_rationales.D: Cone pigments are opsin (photopsin) bound to retinal, not retinal alone.

items.stem: After a bright flash, one photoreceptor type recovers and can fire again quickly, while the other is slow to reactivate. Which recovers faster?

choices.text: Rods recover fast; cones recover slowly
Cones recover fast; rods recover slowly

items.explanation: Cones recover fast (rapid re-firing, quick adaptation); rods recover slowly (need reactivation). Takeaway: Cones = fast recovery (bright, detail, motion). Rods = slow recovery. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cones adapt and recover quickly (firing frequently); rods are slow to reactivate — part of why cones handle fast, bright, detailed vision. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — cones are the fast ones; rods are slow to recover.
distractor_rationales.B: They differ markedly: cones fast, rods slow.
distractor_rationales.D: Both recover; they just do so at very different rates.

items.stem: Human color vision uses three cone types. Their approximate proportions in the retina are:
items.explanation: Three cone types: ~60% red, ~30% green, ~10% blue. Red-sensitive cones are most numerous, blue least. Takeaway: Cone proportions: ~60% red, ~30% green, ~10% blue. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The three cone types are unevenly distributed — roughly 60% red, 30% green, 10% blue. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The three types are not equal in number.
distractor_rationales.C: Reversed — red cones are the most common, blue the least.
distractor_rationales.D: Blue cones are the least common (~10%), not the majority.

items.stem: Across the retina, rods and cones are distributed such that:

choices.text: Cones are concentrated in the fovea; rods dominate the periphery
Rods are concentrated in the fovea; cones dominate the periphery
Rods are found only in the fovea

items.explanation: Cones → concentrated in the fovea (detail/color). Rods → dominate the periphery (dim light, motion). Takeaway: Cones = fovea (detail/color). Rods = periphery (dim light, motion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cones pack into the fovea (detail/color); rods dominate the periphery (dim light, motion). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — cones are foveal, rods peripheral.
distractor_rationales.C: Distribution is uneven, not uniform.
distractor_rationales.D: Rods are found mostly in the periphery, not the fovea.

items.stem: The fovea gives the sharpest vision partly because light there reaches the photoreceptors directly rather than passing through overlying neural layers. This is because the fovea is:

choices.text: A pit (dimple) where the overlying cells and axons are displaced, so light hits the cones directly
Covered by an extra-thick layer of axons
Packed with rods rather than cones
The point where the optic nerve exits

items.explanation: The fovea is a pit where overlying cells/axons are pushed aside, so light hits the cone-packed floor directly → sharpest vision. (At the periphery, light passes through axon layers first.) Takeaway: Fovea = a dimple where light hits cones directly (no overlying axons) → highest acuity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The fovea is a depression where inner retinal layers are pushed aside, so light strikes the densely packed cones with minimal scattering — maximal acuity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The opposite — overlying layers are displaced at the fovea, not thickened.
distractor_rationales.C: The fovea is cone-packed, not rod-packed.
distractor_rationales.D: That describes the optic disc (blind spot), not the fovea.

items.stem: An astronomer sees a very faint star more easily when looking slightly to the side of it rather than directly at it. This 'averted vision' works because:

choices.text: The fovea is the most light-sensitive region
Cones detect dim light better than rods
It moves the image onto the blind spot
Looking to the side places the star's image on the rod-rich periphery, which is far more light-sensitive than the cone-packed fovea

items.explanation: Averted vision: looking slightly away images a faint object on the rod-rich, highly sensitive periphery — the cone-packed fovea is poor in dim light. Takeaway: Averted vision: look slightly away to use the rod-rich periphery for faint objects. Fovea (cones) is weak in dim light. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The fovea (cones) is poor in dim light; shifting the faint image onto the sensitive peripheral rods makes it easier to detect. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The fovea (cones) is actually poor in dim light — that's why you look away from it.
distractor_rationales.B: Rods, not cones, are the dim-light detectors.
distractor_rationales.C: Imaging onto the blind spot would make the star vanish, not appear.

items.stem: Visual information from your right visual field is ultimately processed in which hemisphere of your brain?

choices.text: Neither — it stays in the eye

items.explanation: Each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere: right field → left brain, left field → right brain. Takeaway: Right visual field → LEFT brain; left visual field → RIGHT brain (contralateral). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The right visual field projects to the left hemisphere (and the left field to the right hemisphere). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The right field goes to the LEFT hemisphere, not the right.
distractor_rationales.C: Each visual field is routed to one (contralateral) hemisphere, not both equally.
distractor_rationales.D: Visual information is processed in the brain, not the eye.

items.stem: The structure where the optic nerves meet and some of their fibers cross to the opposite side of the brain is the:
items.explanation: The optic chiasm is where the optic nerves partially cross en route to the brain. Takeaway: Optic chiasm = where optic nerve fibers partially cross. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The optic chiasm is where the optic nerves partially cross (decussate). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The optic disc is the blind spot where the nerve exits one eye, not the crossover.
distractor_rationales.C: The fovea is the cone-rich region of sharpest vision, not a crossing point.
distractor_rationales.D: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, but isn't the visual crossover.

items.stem: At the optic chiasm, which retinal fibers cross to the opposite side of the brain?

choices.text: The temporal fibers cross; the nasal fibers do not
The nasal fibers cross; the temporal fibers do not

items.explanation: At the chiasm, nasal fibers cross, temporal fibers stay — routing each visual field to the contralateral hemisphere. Takeaway: Optic chiasm: nasal fibers CROSS, temporal fibers DON'T. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Nasal (medial) retinal fibers decussate at the chiasm; temporal (lateral) fibers stay on the same side. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — nasal fibers cross, temporal fibers stay ipsilateral.
distractor_rationales.C: Only the nasal fibers cross; the temporal ones don't.
distractor_rationales.D: The nasal fibers do cross — that's what routes each field to the opposite hemisphere.

items.stem: Light from the left visual field falls on which parts of the two retinas?

choices.text: The temporal retina of the left eye and the nasal retina of the right eye
The nasal retina of both eyes
The nasal retina of the left eye and the temporal retina of the right eye
The temporal retina of both eyes

items.explanation: The inverting lens sends the left visual field to the nasal retina of the left eye and the temporal retina of the right eye — both then routed to the right hemisphere. Takeaway: Left field → nasal retina (left eye) + temporal retina (right eye) → right hemisphere. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Because the lens inverts the image, the left field projects to the nasal half of the left eye and the temporal half of the right eye. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed for each eye — the left field hits nasal-left and temporal-right.
distractor_rationales.B: It hits nasal on the left eye but temporal (not nasal) on the right eye.
distractor_rationales.D: It hits temporal on the right eye but nasal (not temporal) on the left eye.

items.stem: A pituitary tumor presses on the center of the optic chiasm, damaging the crossing fibers. The patient will most likely lose:

choices.text: Peripheral (temporal) vision in both eyes — bitemporal vision loss
All vision in the left eye only

items.explanation: Midline chiasm damage hits the crossing nasal fibers, which carry the temporal (peripheral) fields → bitemporal hemianopia ('tunnel vision'). Classic pituitary tumor sign. Takeaway: Midline chiasm lesion (pituitary tumor) → crossing nasal fibers hit → loss of both TEMPORAL fields (bitemporal hemianopia). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The crossing (nasal) fibers carry the temporal visual fields; midline chiasm damage produces bitemporal hemianopia — the classic pituitary-tumor finding. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: A single-eye total loss points to an optic-nerve lesion (before the chiasm), not the midline chiasm.
distractor_rationales.C: Central vision loss isn't the chiasm pattern; the crossing fibers carry peripheral (temporal) fields.
distractor_rationales.D: Damaging the crossing fibers does cause a specific field loss.

items.stem: The routing of each visual field to the opposite hemisphere is one example of the nervous system's general pattern of:

choices.text: Ipsilateral organization — each hemisphere handles the same side
Contralateral organization — each hemisphere handles the opposite side
Random wiring with no side preference

items.explanation: Vision (like motor control) is contralateral: each hemisphere handles the opposite side / opposite visual field. Takeaway: Contralateral organization: each hemisphere handles the opposite side (vision, movement). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Like motor and much of somatosensation, vision is organized contralaterally — each hemisphere serves the opposite side. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ipsilateral (same-side) is the opposite of how vision and motor control are organized.
distractor_rationales.C: The wiring is highly organized, not random.
distractor_rationales.D: Each field goes to one hemisphere, not duplicated to both.

items.stem: After the partial crossing at the optic chiasm, the fibers continue as the optic tracts. Each optic tract therefore carries:

choices.text: One entire visual field — e.g., the left tract carries the right visual field from both eyes

items.explanation: After the chiasm, each optic tract carries the complete contralateral visual field (combining fibers from both eyes). Takeaway: Post-chiasm: each optic tract = one whole (opposite) visual field, from both eyes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Post-chiasm, each tract combines the right fibers from both eyes to carry the full contralateral visual field to that hemisphere. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Each tract carries input from both eyes (one visual field), not one eye.
distractor_rationales.C: Each tract carries one visual field (the contralateral one), not both.
distractor_rationales.D: The tracts carry the visual information onward to the brain.

items.stem: In feature detection, the visual system breaks an object down into which three key features to make sense of it?
items.explanation: Feature detection breaks an object into three features: color, form, and motion. Takeaway: Feature detection = color + form (shape) + motion. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The visual system analyzes color, form (shape/boundaries), and motion. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Size and distance are depth cues, not the three feature-detection channels.
distractor_rationales.C: These are all attributes of light/color, not the three feature channels.
distractor_rationales.D: Smell and sound aren't visual features.

items.stem: The parvocellular pathway has high spatial resolution and detects fine detail, shape/boundaries, and color, but cannot detect motion well. It is specialized for:
items.explanation: Parvocellular = form, shape/boundaries, and color; high spatial resolution, poor motion. (Mnemonic: Pink Pyramid → Parvo/form.) Takeaway: Parvocellular = form + color, high SPATIAL resolution (detail), poor at motion. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The parvocellular ('P') pathway handles form/shape, boundaries, and color with high spatial resolution — but poor motion (temporal) resolution. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Motion is the magnocellular pathway's specialty, not parvocellular.
distractor_rationales.C: Dim-light detection is a rod/scotopic function, not the parvocellular pathway's role.
distractor_rationales.D: Sound is auditory, not visual.

items.stem: The magnocellular pathway has high temporal resolution but poor spatial resolution and no color. It is specialized for detecting:
items.explanation: Magnocellular = motion; high temporal resolution, poor spatial resolution, no color. (Mnemonic: Motion → Magno.) Takeaway: Magnocellular = motion, high TEMPORAL resolution, poor spatial detail, no color. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The magnocellular ('M') pathway detects motion with high temporal resolution, but is colorblind and low in spatial detail. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Color is handled by the parvocellular pathway.
distractor_rationales.C: Fine detail is a parvocellular (high spatial resolution) strength.
distractor_rationales.D: Static form is parvocellular; magnocellular is tuned to change/motion.

items.stem: Which correctly contrasts the two feature-detection pathways?

choices.text: Parvocellular = motion; magnocellular = color and detail
Parvocellular = high spatial resolution (detail, color); magnocellular = high temporal resolution (motion)

items.explanation: Parvo = high spatial resolution (detail + color). Magno = high temporal resolution (motion). Takeaway: Parvo = SPATIAL (form/color/detail). Magno = TEMPORAL (motion). Pink Pyramid = Parvo; Motion = Magno. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Parvocellular = spatial detail and color; magnocellular = temporal resolution and motion. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — parvo does detail/color, magno does motion.
distractor_rationales.C: Only parvocellular has high spatial resolution; magno is poor at it.
distractor_rationales.D: Only magnocellular is specialized for motion; parvo is for static detail.

items.stem: The brain analyzes an object's color, form, and motion simultaneously rather than one at a time. This simultaneous analysis is called:
items.explanation: Parallel processing: the brain analyzes color, form, and motion at the same time (not one after another). Takeaway: Parallel processing = color, form, and motion analyzed simultaneously. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Parallel processing is analyzing multiple features (color, form, motion) at the same time. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Serial processing would handle features one at a time — the opposite.
distractor_rationales.C: Bottom-up processing describes building perception from the stimulus, not simultaneity of feature channels.
distractor_rationales.D: Transduction is converting light into a neural signal, not simultaneous feature analysis.

items.stem: A goalkeeper tracking a fast-moving soccer ball relies most heavily on which visual pathway?

choices.text: The magnocellular pathway (motion, high temporal resolution)

items.explanation: Tracking fast motion → magnocellular pathway (high temporal resolution). Takeaway: Fast motion → magnocellular pathway. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fast motion is the magnocellular pathway's job — high temporal resolution. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The parvocellular pathway handles static detail and color, not fast motion.
distractor_rationales.B: Tracking motion clearly uses a visual pathway — the magnocellular one.
distractor_rationales.D: Color detection isn't what's needed to track a moving ball's motion.

items.stem: Reading small print and distinguishing the precise shapes of letters relies most on which pathway?

choices.text: The parvocellular pathway (fine detail, form, high spatial resolution)

items.explanation: Fine detail and letter shape → parvocellular pathway (high spatial resolution). Takeaway: Fine detail/shape → parvocellular pathway. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fine spatial detail and form are parvocellular — high spatial resolution. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The magnocellular pathway is for motion, not fine static detail.
distractor_rationales.B: Reading fine print in normal light uses cones/parvocellular detail, not the dim-light rod system.
distractor_rationales.C: Reading recruits the parvocellular detail pathway.

items.stem: Sound waves first reach the outer ear at which structure, which funnels them inward toward the auditory canal?
items.explanation: Sound enters at the pinna, which funnels it into the auditory canal toward the eardrum. Takeaway: Sound path starts at the pinna (outer ear) → auditory canal → eardrum. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The pinna is the visible outer ear that funnels sound into the auditory canal. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The tympanic membrane (eardrum) is reached after the auditory canal, not first.
distractor_rationales.B: The cochlea is deep in the inner ear — the last stop, not the first.
distractor_rationales.D: The oval window is inside the middle/inner ear boundary, not the outer entry.

items.stem: After the eardrum vibrates, three tiny bones transmit the vibration in which order?
items.explanation: The ossicles vibrate in order: malleus → incus → stapes (MIS). Takeaway: Ossicle order: Malleus → Incus → Stapes (MIS). The 3 smallest bones. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Malleus (hammer) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup) — mnemonic MIS. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the malleus (attached to the eardrum) comes first, stapes last.
distractor_rationales.B: The malleus is first, not the incus.
distractor_rationales.C: The incus sits between the malleus and stapes, not last.

items.stem: The malleus, incus, and stapes — the three smallest bones in the body — are collectively called the ossicles and make up the:
items.explanation: The three ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) are the middle ear. Takeaway: Ossicles = middle ear. Outer = pinna→eardrum; inner = cochlea + semicircular canals. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) constitute the middle ear. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The outer ear runs from the pinna to the eardrum — no ossicles.
distractor_rationales.B: The inner ear is the cochlea and semicircular canals, not the ossicles.
distractor_rationales.D: The cochlea is an inner-ear structure, not the ossicles.

items.stem: Sound funneled through the auditory canal strikes and vibrates which structure, setting the ossicles in motion?
items.explanation: The tympanic membrane (eardrum) vibrates from incoming sound and drives the ossicles. Takeaway: Auditory canal → tympanic membrane (eardrum) vibrates → ossicles. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The tympanic membrane (eardrum) vibrates when sound reaches it, driving the malleus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The oval window is driven later, by the stapes, not directly by the canal.
distractor_rationales.C: The basilar membrane is inside the cochlea, far downstream.
distractor_rationales.D: The pinna is the outer funnel, reached before the canal.

items.stem: The stapes transmits vibration into the fluid-filled cochlea by pushing on which membrane-covered opening?
items.explanation: The stapes vibrates the oval window, launching pressure waves through the cochlear fluid. Takeaway: Stapes → oval window → pressure waves in cochlear fluid. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The stapes presses on the oval window, sending pressure waves into the cochlear fluid. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The round window bulges out to relieve pressure; the stapes pushes the oval window.
distractor_rationales.C: The tympanic membrane is the eardrum, upstream of the ossicles.
distractor_rationales.D: The tectorial membrane is inside the organ of Corti, not where the stapes pushes.

items.stem: As pressure waves travel through the cochlea, the round window bulges outward. Its role is to:

choices.text: Transduce sound into a neural signal
Relieve the pressure of the (incompressible) cochlear fluid, allowing the fluid to move

items.explanation: The round window flexes outward to relieve pressure, allowing the incompressible cochlear fluid to move. Takeaway: Round window = pressure-relief valve so the incompressible cochlear fluid can move. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Since the cochlear fluid can't compress, the round window bulges out to accommodate the wave, letting fluid move. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transduction is done by hair cells, not the round window.
distractor_rationales.B: Amplification is done by the ossicles/eardrum, not the round window.
distractor_rationales.C: The ossicles are anchored in the middle ear, not by the round window.

items.stem: Within the cochlea, the sound receptors that convert fluid vibration into neural signals are the hair cells of the:

choices.text: Organ of Corti (on the basilar membrane)

items.explanation: The organ of Corti (on the basilar membrane) contains the hair cells that transduce sound into neural signals. Takeaway: Hearing receptors = hair cells of the organ of Corti (on the basilar membrane). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The organ of Corti, sitting on the basilar membrane, holds the hair cells that transduce sound. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The semicircular canals are for balance (rotation), not hearing.
distractor_rationales.B: The oval window is a pressure entry point, not the receptor organ.
distractor_rationales.C: The tectorial membrane is one part of the organ of Corti, not the receptor by itself.

items.stem: Which correctly matches an ear division to its components?

choices.text: Middle ear = pinna and auditory canal
Inner ear = cochlea and semicircular canals

items.explanation: Outer = pinna→eardrum; middle = ossicles; inner = cochlea + semicircular canals. Takeaway: Outer ear = pinna→eardrum. Middle = ossicles. Inner = cochlea + semicircular canals. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The inner ear comprises the cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The pinna and canal are the OUTER ear, not the middle.
distractor_rationales.B: The ossicles are the MIDDLE ear, not the outer.
distractor_rationales.D: The eardrum is the boundary of the outer/middle ear, not the inner ear.

items.stem: In a cochlear hair cell, the fine projections (stereocilia) are joined near their tips by filaments called tip links. When the stereocilia bend, the tip links:

choices.text: Release neurotransmitter directly onto the nerve
Stretch and pull open mechanically-gated ion channels

items.explanation: Bending stereocilia stretches the tip links, mechanically opening ion channels — the first step of hearing transduction. Takeaway: Stereocilia bend → tip links stretch → mechanically-gated channels open. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Bending stretches the tip links, which mechanically pull open ion channels on the stereocilia. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Neurotransmitter release happens later, after depolarization — not directly by tip links.
distractor_rationales.C: Tip links don't regenerate the cell; they gate channels.
distractor_rationales.D: They open (not block) the channels when stretched.

items.stem: Cochlear hair cells sit in endolymph, an unusual fluid rich in K⁺. When the channels open, K⁺:

choices.text: Flows INTO the hair cell, depolarizing it
Flows out of the cell, hyperpolarizing it

items.explanation: The K⁺-rich endolymph drives K⁺ into the hair cell when channels open, depolarizing it — unusual compared with typical neurons. Takeaway: Hair cells: endolymph is K⁺-rich → K⁺ flows IN → depolarization (opposite of most neurons). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Because endolymph is K⁺-rich, opening the channels lets K⁺ flow INTO the cell, depolarizing it — opposite of a typical neuron. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: In most neurons K⁺ leaving repolarizes/hyperpolarizes; here the unusual gradient drives K⁺ IN.
distractor_rationales.C: K⁺ is the key ion here, entering from the K⁺-rich endolymph.
distractor_rationales.D: The channels let K⁺ in; it isn't pumped out during transduction.

items.stem: After K⁺ entry depolarizes the hair cell, what happens next to trigger neurotransmitter release?

choices.text: K⁺ is pumped back out first
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ enters the cell
The cell hyperpolarizes and shuts down

items.explanation: Depolarization → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ influx → neurotransmitter release. Takeaway: K⁺ in → depolarize → Ca²⁺ in → neurotransmitter release. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx triggers neurotransmitter release. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Neurotransmitter release depends on Ca²⁺ entry, not K⁺ being pumped out first.
distractor_rationales.B: Rhodopsin is a visual pigment — irrelevant to hair cells.
distractor_rationales.D: Depolarization (not hyperpolarization) is what opens the Ca²⁺ channels.

items.stem: The hair cell's Ca²⁺-triggered neurotransmitter release activates which neuron, whose axons form the auditory nerve?

choices.text: A bipolar cell of the retina

items.explanation: Hair cells activate spiral ganglion neurons → their axons form the auditory nerve → brain. Takeaway: Hair cell → spiral ganglion cell → auditory nerve → brain. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hair cells synapse onto spiral ganglion neurons, whose axons make up the auditory (cochlear) nerve. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Retinal ganglion cells are in the eye, forming the optic nerve.
distractor_rationales.C: Retinal bipolar cells are in vision, not hearing.
distractor_rationales.D: Golgi tendon organs are proprioceptors in tendons, unrelated to hearing.

items.stem: Put the cochlear transduction steps in order: (1) Ca²⁺ influx, (2) stereocilia bend, (3) K⁺ influx / depolarization, (4) neurotransmitter release to the auditory nerve.
items.explanation: Order: bend → K⁺ in (depolarize) → Ca²⁺ in → neurotransmitter release. Takeaway: Hearing transduction: stereocilia bend → K⁺ in → Ca²⁺ in → transmitter release. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Stereocilia bend → K⁺ enters (depolarize) → Ca²⁺ enters → neurotransmitter release. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The stereocilia must bend before K⁺ can enter.
distractor_rationales.C: K⁺ entry/depolarization precedes Ca²⁺ entry, not the reverse.
distractor_rationales.D: Neurotransmitter release is the last step, not the first.

items.stem: The hair cells that transduce sound sit within the organ of Corti, between which two structures?

choices.text: The oval window and the round window
The basilar membrane and the tectorial membrane

items.explanation: Hair cells sit between the basilar membrane (below) and tectorial membrane (above); their relative motion bends the stereocilia. Takeaway: Organ of Corti: hair cells between basilar (below) and tectorial (above) membranes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hair cells sit on the basilar membrane with their stereocilia contacting the tectorial membrane; relative movement bends them. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The oval and round windows are pressure ports, not where hair cells sit.
distractor_rationales.B: The ossicles are middle-ear bones, not part of the organ of Corti.
distractor_rationales.C: The pinna and eardrum are outer/middle-ear structures.

items.stem: Why is hair-cell depolarization by K⁺ influx considered unusual compared with a typical neuron?

choices.text: In most neurons K⁺ leaving the cell repolarizes/hyperpolarizes it; here K⁺ enters and depolarizes
K⁺ never moves across neuronal membranes
It is exactly the same as in a typical neuron
Hair cells use only Na⁺, never K⁺

items.explanation: Unusual: the K⁺-rich endolymph makes K⁺ flow IN to depolarize the hair cell, whereas in most neurons K⁺ flowing OUT repolarizes. Takeaway: Hair cells depolarize via K⁺ IN (K⁺-rich endolymph) — opposite of the usual K⁺-out repolarization. The keyed choice holds because: Correct.
