Normally K⁺ efflux repolarizes a neuron; the K⁺-rich endolymph reverses the gradient so K⁺ influx depolarizes the hair cell. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: K⁺ moves readily across neuronal membranes — that's central to signaling.
distractor_rationales.C: It's the opposite of a typical neuron, not the same.
distractor_rationales.D: Hair cells depend on K⁺ influx here, not Na⁺ only.

items.stem: High-frequency sounds maximally vibrate the basilar membrane at one end of the cochlea, low-frequency sounds at the other. Which is correct?

choices.text: High frequencies at the apex; low frequencies at the base
High frequencies at the base (near the oval window); low frequencies at the apex

items.explanation: Base (stiff, narrow) = high frequencies; apex (wide, floppy) = low frequencies. Takeaway: Cochlea tonotopy: base = high frequency, apex = low frequency. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The stiff, narrow base responds to high frequencies; the floppy, wide apex responds to low frequencies (long-wavelength sounds travel farther to the apex). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the base handles high frequencies, the apex low.
distractor_rationales.C: High and low frequencies peak at different places, not both at the base.
distractor_rationales.D: They peak at different places, not both at the apex.

items.stem: The idea that we perceive a sound's pitch based on WHERE along the basilar membrane vibration peaks is called:
items.explanation: Place theory: pitch is coded by the place of peak vibration on the basilar membrane. Best for high frequencies. Takeaway: Place theory = pitch by LOCATION of peak basilar-membrane vibration. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Place theory: pitch corresponds to the location of maximal basilar-membrane vibration. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Frequency theory codes pitch by firing RATE, not location.
distractor_rationales.C: Opponent-process theory is about color vision.
distractor_rationales.D: Signal detection theory is about detecting signals in noise.

items.stem: The orderly mapping of sound frequencies to specific locations — along the basilar membrane and up into the auditory cortex — is called:
items.explanation: Tonotopic organization: an orderly frequency-to-place map, preserved from the basilar membrane to the auditory cortex. Takeaway: Tonotopy = orderly frequency→place map, cochlea to cortex. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Tonotopy is the frequency-to-place mapping preserved from cochlea to cortex. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Somatotopic maps the body surface (touch), not sound frequency.
distractor_rationales.B: Retinotopic maps the visual field, not sound.
distractor_rationales.C: The mapping is highly orderly, not random.

items.stem: The primary auditory cortex, which receives this tonotopic input, is located in the:
items.explanation: The primary auditory cortex is in the temporal lobe. Takeaway: Primary auditory cortex = temporal lobe ('hear Time'). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The primary auditory cortex sits in the temporal lobe (mnemonic: 'hear Time' → Temporal). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The parietal lobe houses somatosensory cortex, not auditory.
distractor_rationales.B: The occipital lobe is visual cortex.
distractor_rationales.D: The frontal lobe handles motor/executive function, not primary hearing.

items.stem: Place theory explains high-frequency pitch well but struggles with very low frequencies. The theory that low-frequency pitch is coded by the RATE of neural firing matching the sound's frequency is:
items.explanation: Frequency (temporal) theory: pitch coded by firing RATE — best for low frequencies. Place theory covers high frequencies; together they span the range. Takeaway: Place theory (WHERE) = high freq; frequency theory (firing RATE) = low freq. Complementary. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Frequency (temporal) theory codes low-frequency pitch by firing rate matching the sound frequency; place theory covers high frequencies. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Place theory codes by location and struggles at low frequencies — the gap being filled here.
distractor_rationales.C: Trichromatic theory is about color vision, not pitch.
distractor_rationales.D: The volley principle helps mid-range frequencies but isn't the named low-frequency rate theory.

items.stem: A cochlear implant restores some hearing in sensorineural loss by:

choices.text: Amplifying sound into the ear canal like a hearing aid
Bypassing damaged hair cells and directly stimulating the auditory nerve

items.explanation: A cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells and stimulates the auditory nerve directly (requires an intact nerve). A hearing aid, by contrast, just amplifies sound. Takeaway: Cochlear implant = bypass damaged hair cells, stimulate the auditory nerve directly. (Hearing aid = amplify sound.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Unlike a hearing aid (which amplifies sound), a cochlear implant bypasses damaged hair cells and electrically stimulates the auditory nerve directly. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That describes a hearing aid; an implant bypasses the hair cells entirely.
distractor_rationales.B: Implants don't replace the eardrum; they stimulate the nerve.
distractor_rationales.D: Implants don't regrow hair cells; they substitute for them electrically.

items.stem: In a cochlear implant, the external microphone and speech processor pass information to an external transmitter, which sends it to an internal receiver/stimulator that then:

choices.text: Moves the eardrum back and forth
Amplifies air pressure in the canal
Sends electrical signals to electrodes in the cochlea, stimulating the auditory nerve

items.explanation: Implant chain: mic → speech processor → transmitter (outside) → receiver/stimulator (inside) → electrodes in cochlea → auditory nerve. Takeaway: Cochlear implant: mic → processor → transmitter → receiver/stimulator → cochlear electrodes → auditory nerve. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The internal stimulator drives electrodes threaded into the cochlea, electrically stimulating the auditory nerve. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The implant bypasses the ossicles rather than vibrating them.
distractor_rationales.B: It bypasses the eardrum entirely.
distractor_rationales.C: It doesn't amplify air pressure; it stimulates the nerve electrically.

items.stem: Humans hear roughly 20–20,000 Hz. Distinguishing a low-pitched drum from a high-pitched whistle depends most on:

choices.text: All frequencies activating the same spot on the membrane
Different frequencies activating hair cells at different places along the basilar membrane

items.explanation: We distinguish pitches because different frequencies peak at different places on the basilar membrane (tonotopy), preserved to the cortex. Takeaway: Pitch discrimination relies on tonotopy: frequency → place on the basilar membrane. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Tonotopy — different frequencies peaking at different basilar-membrane locations — lets the brain distinguish pitches. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Different frequencies peak at different places, not the same spot.
distractor_rationales.B: The pinna funnels sound; it doesn't sort pitch.
distractor_rationales.D: The ossicle count is fixed and doesn't encode pitch.

items.stem: The 'sensory homunculus' refers to:

choices.text: A gland that secretes touch hormones
A single type of touch receptor
A topographic map of the body's surface represented across the somatosensory cortex
A reflex arc in the spinal cord

items.explanation: The sensory homunculus is a topographic map of the body's surface across the somatosensory cortex. Takeaway: Sensory homunculus = a body map across the somatosensory cortex. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The sensory homunculus is a distorted body map laid out across the somatosensory cortex. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It's a cortical map, not a gland.
distractor_rationales.B: It's a whole cortical map, not one receptor type.
distractor_rationales.D: It's in the cortex, not a spinal reflex arc.

items.stem: The somatosensory cortex containing the sensory homunculus is located in the:
items.explanation: The somatosensory cortex (sensory homunculus) is in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe. Takeaway: Sensory homunculus = postcentral gyrus, parietal lobe. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The somatosensory cortex sits in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The temporal lobe houses auditory cortex.
distractor_rationales.C: The occipital lobe is visual cortex.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement/balance, not the somatosensory map.

items.stem: The sensory homunculus is drawn with enormous hands and lips but a tiny torso. This distortion reflects that:

choices.text: Body areas with more sensory receptors (greater sensitivity) occupy proportionally more cortex
Physically larger body parts always get more cortex
The map is drawn to true physical scale
Sensitivity is uniform across the body

items.explanation: The homunculus is distorted because cortical space tracks receptor density/sensitivity, not body size — hands, lips, and face are magnified. Takeaway: Homunculus distortion: more cortex for more sensitive areas (hands, lips, face), not bigger body parts. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cortical area is allotted by receptor density/sensitivity, so hands, lips, and face dominate the map. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: It's sensitivity/receptor density, not physical size, that determines cortical area.
distractor_rationales.C: The map is deliberately distorted, not to scale.
distractor_rationales.D: Sensitivity varies widely — that's why the map is distorted.

items.stem: Adjacent regions of the body tend to map to adjacent regions of the sensory cortex. This orderly body-to-cortex mapping is described as:
items.explanation: Somatotopic organization: the body surface maps in an orderly way onto the sensory cortex. Takeaway: Somatotopy = orderly body→cortex map (touch). (Tonotopy = sound; retinotopy = vision.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Somatotopy is the orderly body-surface-to-cortex mapping. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Tonotopic maps sound frequency, not body surface.
distractor_rationales.B: Retinotopic maps the visual field.
distractor_rationales.D: The mapping is orderly, not random.

items.stem: The sensory homunculus lies in the postcentral gyrus (parietal lobe). A parallel MOTOR homunculus lies just across the central sulcus in the:

choices.text: Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe

items.explanation: Sensory homunculus = postcentral gyrus (parietal); motor homunculus = precentral gyrus (frontal), across the central sulcus. Takeaway: Sensory = postcentral gyrus (parietal). Motor = precentral gyrus (frontal). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The motor homunculus occupies the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, just anterior to the sensory strip. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The occipital lobe is visual, with no motor homunculus.
distractor_rationales.B: The temporal lobe is auditory, not motor.
distractor_rationales.D: The motor map is in the precentral gyrus, not the postcentral (sensory) one.

items.stem: Walking across a dark room and touching your nose with your eyes closed relies on your sense of body position, called:
items.explanation: Proprioception = the sense of where the body/limbs are positioned in space (works with eyes closed). Takeaway: Proprioception = sense of body POSITION in space. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Proprioception is the sense of the body's position in space. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Kinesthesia is the sense of body movement, more than static position.
distractor_rationales.C: Nociception is pain.
distractor_rationales.D: Audition is hearing.

items.stem: Proprioceptive signals about muscle stretch and length come largely from receptors called:
items.explanation: Muscle spindles (stretch receptors in muscle) supply proprioceptive information about muscle length. Takeaway: Muscle spindles = stretch receptors in muscle → proprioception (limb position). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Muscle spindles are stretch receptors within muscle that report length/stretch for proprioception. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Cochlear hair cells are for hearing.
distractor_rationales.C: Rods are photoreceptors for dim-light vision.
distractor_rationales.D: Pacinian corpuscles detect skin pressure/vibration, not muscle stretch.

items.stem: The sense concerned specifically with the MOVEMENT of the body and limbs — more behavioral, refined through learning — is:
items.explanation: Kinesthesia = the sense of body/limb movement — more behavioral and learned than proprioception. Takeaway: Kinesthesia = sense of body MOVEMENT (learned, behavioral). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Kinesthesia is the sense of body/limb movement (mnemonic: Kinetics = movement). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Proprioception emphasizes position; kinesthesia emphasizes movement.
distractor_rationales.B: Equilibrioception is the sense of balance (vestibular).
distractor_rationales.C: Gustation is taste.

items.stem: Which best distinguishes proprioception from kinesthesia?

choices.text: Proprioception is a form of hearing
Proprioception = sense of body POSITION (cognitive/subconscious); kinesthesia = sense of MOVEMENT (behavioral)

items.explanation: Proprioception = position (cognitive); kinesthesia = movement (behavioral). Both track the body in space. Takeaway: Proprioception = POSITION (cognitive). Kinesthesia = MOVEMENT (behavioral). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Proprioception emphasizes static position (cognitive), kinesthesia emphasizes movement (behavioral) — both tell you where your body is in space. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — proprioception is position, kinesthesia is movement.
distractor_rationales.B: They overlap but aren't identical: position vs. movement.
distractor_rationales.C: Proprioception is a body-position sense, not hearing.

items.stem: A gymnast holding a still, balanced pose with eyes closed is relying most on:
items.explanation: Holding a still pose = knowing where your body is = proprioception. Takeaway: Static balanced pose → proprioception (position). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A static, balanced pose is about knowing body position — proprioception. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Kinesthesia is about movement; the pose is held still.
distractor_rationales.B: Audition is hearing, not body position.
distractor_rationales.D: Place theory concerns pitch perception in hearing.

items.stem: A batter adjusting the path of a swing to connect with a pitch — 'if I move this way, I'll hit it' — draws on:

choices.text: Kinesthesia (the learned sense of body movement)

items.explanation: Refining a learned movement toward a goal = kinesthesia (behavioral movement sense). Takeaway: Adjusting a learned movement to hit a target → kinesthesia (movement). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Refining a learned movement to accomplish a task is kinesthesia — the behavioral movement sense. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Static position sense (proprioception) doesn't capture the learned, adjusted movement.
distractor_rationales.C: Nociception is pain, unrelated.
distractor_rationales.D: The otoliths sense head linear acceleration, not a learned swing.

items.stem: The ability to sense pain and the ability to sense temperature are called, respectively:
items.explanation: Nociception = pain; thermoception = temperature. Both are comparatively slow. Takeaway: Pain = nociception; temperature = thermoception (both slow). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pain = nociception; temperature = thermoception. Both are relatively slow senses. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — pain is nociception, temperature is thermoception.
distractor_rationales.B: Proprioception is body position, not pain.
distractor_rationales.D: Mechanoreception is pressure/touch, not temperature.

items.stem: Which receptor detects heat and is also activated by painful stimuli and by capsaicin (the compound in chili peppers)?
items.explanation: TrpV1 detects heat and painful stimuli; capsaicin binds it (why chili feels hot). Heat causes a conformational change that activates the cell. Takeaway: TrpV1 = heat + pain receptor; capsaicin binds it (why peppers feel hot). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. TrpV1 senses heat and noxious stimuli, and capsaicin binds it — which is why chili peppers feel 'hot.' Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: TrkB is a neurotrophin receptor (BDNF), unrelated to heat/pain sensing.
distractor_rationales.B: Muscle spindles sense stretch (proprioception), not heat/pain.
distractor_rationales.D: Pacinian corpuscles sense pressure/vibration, not heat.

items.stem: Capsaicin from chili peppers makes your mouth feel like it is burning because it:

choices.text: Physically raises the temperature of your tongue
Binds the TrpV1 receptor and triggers the same response as actual heat

items.explanation: Capsaicin binds TrpV1 and triggers the heat/pain response without any real temperature change — the tongue only feels like it's burning. Takeaway: Capsaicin binds TrpV1 (the heat receptor) → 'burning' feeling with no real heat. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Capsaicin binds TrpV1 — the heat receptor — so the brain interprets it as burning heat, though no real temperature change occurs. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Capsaicin doesn't actually heat the tissue; it hijacks the heat receptor.
distractor_rationales.B: It creates a burning sensation via TrpV1, not by damaging taste buds.
distractor_rationales.C: It activates the heat receptor (TrpV1), not cold receptors.

items.stem: Pain and temperature travel on three fiber types. Which correctly ranks conduction speed?

choices.text: All three conduct at the same speed
A-beta (fast, thick, myelinated) > A-delta (medium) > C (slow, unmyelinated)

items.explanation: Speed: A-beta > A-delta > C. Thicker + more myelin = faster conduction. Takeaway: Fiber speed: A-beta (fast, myelinated) > A-delta > C (slow, unmyelinated). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A-beta fibers are thick and myelinated (fastest); A-delta are thinner with less myelin; C fibers are thin and unmyelinated (slowest). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — unmyelinated C fibers are slowest, not fastest.
distractor_rationales.B: A-beta (thick, myelinated) is faster than A-delta.
distractor_rationales.C: They differ greatly in speed based on diameter and myelination.

items.stem: The slow, lingering, dull quality of pain that persists after an injury is carried mainly by:
items.explanation: C fibers (unmyelinated, slow) carry the dull, lingering pain that lingers after the initial sharp sensation. Takeaway: C fibers = slow, unmyelinated → dull, lingering pain. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Unmyelinated C fibers conduct slowly, producing the dull, lingering 'second' pain. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: A-beta fibers are fast and carry touch/pressure, not lingering pain.
distractor_rationales.C: Muscle spindles are proprioceptors, not pain fibers.
distractor_rationales.D: Cochlear hair cells are for hearing.

items.stem: A-beta fibers conduct faster than C fibers largely because A-beta fibers are:

choices.text: Thicker and myelinated, giving less resistance and higher conduction velocity

items.explanation: Myelination + larger diameter → faster conduction. A-beta (thick, myelinated) beats C (thin, unmyelinated). Takeaway: More myelin + bigger diameter = faster conduction (A-beta fast, C slow). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Myelination and larger diameter speed conduction (saltatory conduction, lower resistance). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That describes C fibers — the slow ones.
distractor_rationales.C: These are peripheral sensory fibers, not brain-only.
distractor_rationales.D: Nerve conduction is electrical; myelin speeds it.

items.stem: Rubbing a bumped elbow makes the pain feel better. The gate control theory of pain explains this by proposing that:

choices.text: Non-painful input can 'close the gate,' blocking pain signals from reaching the brain
Pain signals travel faster than touch signals
The brain cannot process two sensations at once

items.explanation: Gate control theory (Melzack & Wall): non-painful input closes the 'gate' to pain signals in the spinal cord — 'fast blocks slow' (why rubbing helps). Takeaway: Gate control theory: non-painful input closes the gate to pain ('fast blocks slow'). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Melzack and Wall's gate control theory: large-fiber (non-painful) input closes the spinal 'gate' to small-fiber pain input — 'fast blocks slow.' Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Rubbing doesn't remove the injury; it modulates the pain signal.
distractor_rationales.C: Fast touch (A-beta) input is what closes the gate to slower pain — but the mechanism is gating, not a race the pain wins.
distractor_rationales.D: The brain can process multiple sensations; the effect is spinal gating.

items.stem: Pain has two components: one describing its intensity and location, the other its emotional unpleasantness. These are, respectively:

choices.text: The affective component and the sensory component
The sensory component and the affective component
The nociceptive and the proprioceptive components

items.explanation: Pain's sensory component = intensity/location; affective component = the emotional unpleasantness. Takeaway: Pain: sensory component (intensity) + affective component (emotion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The sensory component encodes intensity/location; the affective component is the emotional experience of pain. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — sensory = intensity, affective = emotion.
distractor_rationales.C: Proprioception is body position, unrelated to pain's emotional aspect.
distractor_rationales.D: Fast/slow refer to fiber conduction, not the sensory vs. emotional split.

items.stem: The smell receptors (olfactory sensory neurons) that detect odor molecules are located in the:

choices.text: Olfactory epithelium, high in the nasal cavity

items.explanation: Smell receptors are the olfactory sensory neurons of the olfactory epithelium in the upper nose. Takeaway: Smell receptors = olfactory sensory neurons in the olfactory epithelium (upper nose). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Olfactory sensory neurons sit in the olfactory epithelium lining the upper nasal cavity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The basilar membrane is for hearing.
distractor_rationales.C: Taste buds are for gustation, not smell.
distractor_rationales.D: The retina is for vision.

items.stem: The thin bone (perforated by small holes) that separates the olfactory epithelium from the brain and lets olfactory axons pass through is the:
items.explanation: The cribriform plate is the perforated bone through which olfactory axons pass to the olfactory bulb. Takeaway: Cribriform plate = perforated bone; olfactory axons pass through it to the olfactory bulb. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Olfactory neuron axons pass through the holes in the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The tectorial membrane is in the cochlea (hearing).
distractor_rationales.B: The basilar membrane is in the cochlea (hearing).
distractor_rationales.C: The oval window is in the middle/inner ear (hearing).

items.stem: In the olfactory bulb, all olfactory neurons carrying the SAME receptor type converge onto a single structure called a:
items.explanation: A glomerulus pools all olfactory neurons of one receptor type, synapsing onto mitral/tufted cells — organizing smell before it reaches the brain. Takeaway: Glomerulus = convergence point for olfactory neurons of the same receptor type → mitral/tufted cells. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A glomerulus is the convergence point where neurons sensitive to the same odorant meet and synapse onto mitral/tufted cells. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Papillae are tongue structures for taste.
distractor_rationales.C: The cochlea is for hearing.
distractor_rationales.D: Semicircular canals are for balance.

items.stem: A key feature of olfactory coding is that each olfactory sensory neuron:

choices.text: Expresses one receptor type, so it responds to essentially one class of molecule
Expresses all receptor types at once

items.explanation: Each olfactory neuron expresses one receptor type; combinations across glomeruli encode different smells. Takeaway: One receptor type per olfactory neuron; the population pattern codes the odor. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Each olfactory neuron carries one receptor type; the pattern across many neurons/glomeruli encodes the smell. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Each neuron expresses one receptor type, not all of them.
distractor_rationales.C: Olfactory neurons detect odor molecules, not color.
distractor_rationales.D: They fire in response to odorants, not tied to sleep.

items.stem: When an odor molecule binds an olfactory receptor, the receptor acts as a GPCR: a G protein dissociates and triggers a cascade that:

choices.text: Opens ion channels, depolarizing the neuron and generating an action potential
Hyperpolarizes the neuron to silence it

items.explanation: Olfactory transduction: odorant → GPCR → G-protein cascade → ion channels open → depolarization → AP. Takeaway: Smell transduction = odorant → GPCR → cascade → depolarization → AP. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Odorant → GPCR → G-protein cascade → ion channels open → depolarization → action potential to the olfactory bulb. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Stereocilia bending is hair-cell (hearing/balance) transduction, not smell.
distractor_rationales.C: Olfactory transduction depolarizes (excites) the neuron, not silences it.
distractor_rationales.D: Rhodopsin is a visual pigment, unrelated to smell.

items.stem: Unlike vision, hearing, and touch, the sense of smell is unusual in that its signals:

choices.text: Must pass through the thalamus first
Reach the cortex and amygdala without first synapsing in the thalamus (and are largely ipsilateral)

items.explanation: Smell is the exception: it bypasses the thalamus, going straight to piriform cortex and the amygdala, and is largely ipsilateral (vision/hearing/touch are contralateral). Takeaway: Olfaction bypasses the thalamus (direct to cortex/amygdala) and is ipsilateral — a classic distinctive fact. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Olfaction is the classic exception: it bypasses the thalamus, projecting directly to olfactory (piriform) cortex and the amygdala, and is largely ipsilateral. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Vision/hearing/touch are contralateral; smell is largely ipsilateral — the opposite.
distractor_rationales.B: Smell famously does NOT relay through the thalamus first.
distractor_rationales.D: Olfactory signals do reach the cortex — just without a thalamic relay.

items.stem: From the olfactory bulb, smell information travels next to the amygdala and which cortical area, before reaching the orbitofrontal cortex?
items.explanation: Olfactory pathway: bulb → piriform cortex + amygdala → orbitofrontal cortex. Takeaway: Smell pathway: olfactory bulb → piriform cortex + amygdala → orbitofrontal cortex. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The pathway runs olfactory bulb → piriform cortex + amygdala → orbitofrontal cortex. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The visual cortex processes sight, not smell.
distractor_rationales.C: The basilar membrane is a cochlear (hearing) structure.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not olfactory processing.

items.stem: The theory that odor molecules are recognized because their SHAPE fits a receptor like a lock and key is the:
items.explanation: Steric/shape theory = odorants fit receptors by shape (lock-and-key). Vibrational theory = odor from vibrational frequency; labeled-line = each receptor wired to a specific odor. Takeaway: Steric/shape theory = lock-and-key by molecular shape. (Vibrational = by frequency.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Steric/shape theory: odorants fit receptors by molecular shape (lock-and-key). The vibrational theory instead attributes odor to a molecule's vibrational frequency. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Vibrational theory attributes odor to vibrational frequency, not shape.
distractor_rationales.B: Place theory is about pitch perception in hearing.
distractor_rationales.C: Gate control theory is about pain.

items.stem: A person who has completely lost the ability to smell (for example, after a head injury damaging the olfactory nerves) has:
items.explanation: Anosmia = inability to smell (aNOSEmia). It also blunts flavor, since smell contributes to taste. Takeaway: Anosmia = loss of smell (aNOSEmia). Also why a cold dulls flavor. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Anosmia is the inability to perceive smell (mnemonic: aNOSEmia). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ageusia is loss of taste, not smell.
distractor_rationales.B: Presbyopia is age-related farsightedness (vision).
distractor_rationales.C: Tinnitus is ringing in the ears (hearing).

items.stem: The five basic taste qualities the gustatory system detects are:

choices.text: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and spicy
Sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and cold
Sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami
Sweet, salty, bitter, spicy, and metallic

items.explanation: Five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami. (Spicy is pain/heat, not a taste.) Takeaway: Five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami. Spicy = pain (TrpV1), not a taste. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The five basic tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami (savory/glutamate). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: 'Spicy' is a pain/heat sensation (TrpV1), not a basic taste.
distractor_rationales.B: 'Cold' is temperature, not a taste; umami is the fifth taste.
distractor_rationales.D: Spicy and metallic aren't among the five basic tastes; umami is.

items.stem: The fifth basic taste, umami, corresponds to the detection of:
items.explanation: Umami = the savory taste of glutamate. Takeaway: Umami = glutamate (savory). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Umami is the savory taste of glutamate (e.g., in meats, broth, MSG). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Sugar is sweet, not umami.
distractor_rationales.C: Hydrogen ions produce sour taste.
distractor_rationales.D: Fat is not one of the five basic taste qualities.

items.stem: Taste receptor cells are clustered into taste buds, which are housed within bumps on the tongue called:
items.explanation: Taste buds are housed in papillae — fungiform (tip/sides), foliate (sides/back), circumvallate (back). Takeaway: Taste buds live in papillae (fungiform, foliate, circumvallate). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Taste buds sit within papillae (fungiform, foliate, circumvallate). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glomeruli are olfactory bulb structures.
distractor_rationales.B: Ossicles are middle-ear bones.
distractor_rationales.C: Dermatomes are skin regions mapped to spinal nerves.

items.stem: One type of papilla covers much of the tongue's center but contains NO taste buds — which is why the tongue's center tastes little. These are the:
items.explanation: Filiform papillae have NO taste buds (texture only) — why the tongue's center tastes little. Takeaway: Filiform papillae = no taste buds (texture). The other three types carry taste buds. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Filiform papillae provide texture/grip but have no taste buds; the tongue's center has mainly these. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Circumvallate papillae (back) do contain taste buds.
distractor_rationales.B: Fungiform papillae (tip/sides) contain taste buds.
distractor_rationales.D: Foliate papillae (sides/back) contain taste buds.

items.stem: The old idea that specific tastes are confined to separate zones of the tongue (a 'tongue map') is:

choices.text: A myth — each taste can be detected across the whole tongue wherever taste buds exist

items.explanation: The tongue map is a myth: taste buds throughout the tongue can detect all five tastes. Takeaway: Tongue map = myth. Any taste bud can detect all five tastes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Each taste bud can detect all five tastes; the tongue-map of exclusive zones is a debunked myth. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: It's a debunked myth, not established fact.
distractor_rationales.C: All tastes can be detected wherever taste buds are, not just bitter in one zone.
distractor_rationales.D: The whole-tongue detection holds generally, not just for infants.

items.stem: Sweet, bitter, and umami tastes are transduced through metabotropic receptors — specifically:

choices.text: GPCRs (which activate the G protein gustducin)

items.explanation: Sweet, bitter, umami → GPCRs (via gustducin). Salty and sour → ion channels. Takeaway: Sweet/bitter/umami = GPCR (gustducin). Salty/sour = ion channels. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sweet, bitter, and umami use GPCRs coupled to gustducin; salty and sour instead use ion channels. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Na⁺ channels transduce salty taste, not sweet/bitter/umami.
distractor_rationales.C: Tip-link channels are for hearing (hair cells).
distractor_rationales.D: Rhodopsin is a visual pigment.

items.stem: Salty and sour tastes are transduced not by GPCRs but by ion channels. Specifically, salty is sensed when:

choices.text: Na⁺ ions enter the cell through channels, depolarizing it
K⁺ leaves the cell to hyperpolarize it

items.explanation: Salty = Na⁺ entering through channels → depolarization; sour = H⁺ acting on channels. Both use ion channels, not GPCRs. Takeaway: Salty = Na⁺ in (channel); sour = H⁺ (channel). GPCR tastes = sweet/bitter/umami. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Salt (NaCl) provides Na⁺ that flows through channels into the taste cell, depolarizing it. Sour is sensed via H⁺ acting on channels. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glutamate/GPCR is umami, not salty.
distractor_rationales.C: Retinal isomerization is vision.
distractor_rationales.D: Salty depolarizes via Na⁺ entry, not K⁺-driven hyperpolarization.

items.stem: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by which cranial nerve (via the chorda tympani)?
items.explanation: Anterior 2/3 taste → facial nerve (VII) via chorda tympani; posterior 1/3 → glossopharyngeal (IX); throat → vagus (X). Takeaway: Taste nerves: anterior 2/3 = facial (VII); posterior 1/3 = glossopharyngeal (IX); throat = vagus (X). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Anterior 2/3 taste → facial nerve (VII, chorda tympani); posterior 1/3 → glossopharyngeal (IX); throat/epiglottis → vagus (X). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The glossopharyngeal (IX) carries the posterior 1/3, not the anterior 2/3.
distractor_rationales.C: The optic nerve is for vision.
distractor_rationales.D: The vagus (X) carries taste from the throat region, not the anterior tongue.

items.stem: The G protein that mediates sweet, bitter, and umami taste transduction is called:
items.explanation: Gustducin = the taste G protein for sweet/bitter/umami (the gustatory analog of vision's transducin). Takeaway: Gustducin = taste G protein (sweet/bitter/umami GPCRs). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gustducin is the taste G protein (analogous to transducin in vision), coupling sweet/bitter/umami GPCRs to their cascade. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transducin is the visual G protein (phototransduction).
distractor_rationales.C: Rhodopsin is the rod photopigment.
distractor_rationales.D: There are no hair cells in taste; that's hearing/balance.

items.stem: A pheromone is best defined as:

choices.text: A chemical signal released by one member of a species that triggers an innate response in another member of the SAME species
A chemical released to communicate with a different species
A hormone that acts only inside one's own body

items.explanation: A pheromone is a chemical signal released by one animal that triggers an innate response in another member of the same species. Takeaway: Pheromone = within-species chemical signal → innate response (mating, aggression, communication). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pheromones are chemical signals used for communication within a species, eliciting innate (unlearned) responses. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Pheromones act within a species, not between different species.
distractor_rationales.C: Pheromones are released externally to signal others, unlike internal hormones.
distractor_rationales.D: The response is innate, not a learned association.

items.stem: In many animals, pheromones are detected by a specialized structure separate from the main olfactory epithelium, called the:
items.explanation: The vomeronasal organ (accessory olfactory system) detects pheromones, separate from the main smell pathway. Takeaway: Pheromones → vomeronasal organ (accessory olfactory system). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The vomeronasal organ, part of the accessory olfactory system, detects pheromones. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The cochlea is for hearing.
distractor_rationales.C: The organ of Corti is the hearing receptor organ.
distractor_rationales.D: The fovea is the high-acuity spot of the retina.

items.stem: In the accessory olfactory system, pheromone signals pass from the accessory olfactory bulb, via mitral/tufted cells, to which emotion-related brain region?
items.explanation: Pheromone signals reach the amygdala (emotion, aggression, mating) — fitting pheromones' role in innate social behavior. Takeaway: Pheromone pathway → accessory olfactory bulb → amygdala (emotion/mating/aggression). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pheromone signals project to the amygdala, which handles emotion, aggression, and mating behavior. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The cerebellum coordinates movement.
distractor_rationales.B: The occipital cortex processes vision.
distractor_rationales.D: The cochlear nucleus is an auditory relay.

items.stem: Pheromone-triggered behaviors (e.g., mating or territorial responses in animals) are described as innate, meaning they are:

choices.text: Unlearned and automatic, not acquired through experience

items.explanation: Pheromone responses are innate — unlearned, automatic, species-typical behaviors. Takeaway: Pheromone responses = innate (unlearned, automatic). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Innate responses are hardwired and automatic rather than learned. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Innate means unlearned — the opposite of carefully learned.
distractor_rationales.C: Innate pheromone responses are largely automatic, not deliberate.
distractor_rationales.D: They're species-typical, not unique to each individual.

items.stem: Compared with many animals, humans rely very little on pheromones. A key anatomical reason is that humans:

choices.text: Lack any olfactory system at all
Have far more pheromone receptors than other animals
Have a vestigial vomeronasal organ but no functional accessory olfactory bulb

items.explanation: Humans have a vestigial vomeronasal organ but no functional accessory olfactory bulb — so we rely very little on pheromones. Takeaway: Humans: vomeronasal organ present but no functional accessory olfactory bulb → minimal pheromone reliance. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Humans have a (vestigial) vomeronasal organ but lack a functional accessory olfactory bulb, so pheromone signaling is minimal. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Humans have a full main olfactory system for ordinary smell.
distractor_rationales.B: Humans have fewer, not more, functional pheromone structures.
distractor_rationales.C: The cochlea is for hearing, not chemical signals.

items.stem: Like ordinary smell, pheromone detection in the vomeronasal system works by a molecule binding a receptor that is a:

choices.text: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channel opened by light
GPCR, whose activation depolarizes the cell and sends a signal to the brain

items.explanation: Pheromone transduction uses a GPCR → depolarization → signal to the brain, like ordinary olfaction. Takeaway: Pheromone detection = GPCR → depolarization → brain (via accessory olfactory bulb). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pheromone binding activates a GPCR → cascade → depolarization → signal to the brain (via the accessory olfactory bulb). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Light-gated channels are for vision, not chemical signals.
distractor_rationales.C: Mechanical gating is for hearing/balance hair cells.
distractor_rationales.D: Photopigment bleaching is a visual process.

items.stem: In psychology, consciousness is best described as:

choices.text: The complete absence of brain activity
A single fixed state that never varies
Awareness of oneself and one's environment

items.explanation: Consciousness = awareness of self and environment, spanning levels from full alertness to sleep. Takeaway: Consciousness = awareness of self + environment, at varying levels. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Consciousness is awareness of self and environment, and it exists at varying levels (alertness → sleep). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Consciousness involves active awareness, not absence of brain activity.
distractor_rationales.B: It ranges across levels (alertness, drowsiness, sleep), not a single fixed state.
distractor_rationales.C: Dreaming is one altered state; consciousness is broader.

items.stem: A person who is awake, alert, and actively concentrating shows which EEG wave, the fastest of the four?
items.explanation: Beta (12–30 Hz, fastest) = awake and concentrating. Too much sustained beta → stress/anxiety. Takeaway: Beta = fastest, awake + concentrating. (Alpha=relaxed, theta=drowsy/light sleep, delta=deep sleep.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Beta waves (highest frequency) dominate alert, concentrated wakefulness. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Alpha waves appear in relaxed/daydreaming wakefulness, slower than beta.
distractor_rationales.C: Theta waves appear in drowsiness/light sleep.
distractor_rationales.D: Delta waves appear in deep sleep.

items.stem: When you are awake but relaxed — daydreaming or with eyes closed — your EEG shows mostly:
items.explanation: Alpha (8–13 Hz) = awake but relaxed / daydreaming. Slower than beta. Takeaway: Alpha = relaxed, awake, daydreaming (slower than beta). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alpha waves mark a relaxed, awake (daydreaming) state — slower than beta. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Beta is for active concentration, not relaxed daydreaming.
distractor_rationales.B: Delta is deep sleep, not relaxed wakefulness.
distractor_rationales.C: The brain always produces measurable activity when alive.

items.stem: The slowest, highest-amplitude EEG waves, seen in deep (slow-wave) sleep and coma, are:
items.explanation: Delta (0.5–3 Hz, slowest) = deep (slow-wave) sleep and coma. Takeaway: Delta = slowest waves, deep sleep/coma. Ordering (fast→slow): beta > alpha > theta > delta. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Delta waves (slowest) dominate deep sleep (N3) and coma. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Theta waves appear in drowsiness and light sleep (N1), faster than delta.
distractor_rationales.B: Alpha is relaxed wakefulness.
distractor_rationales.D: Beta is alert concentration.

items.stem: Ordered from HIGHEST to LOWEST frequency, the four main EEG waves are:
items.explanation: Frequency order (fast→slow): Beta > Alpha > Theta > Delta — mapping alert → relaxed → drowsy → deep sleep. Takeaway: Fast→slow: Beta > Alpha > Theta > Delta (alert→relaxed→drowsy→deep sleep). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Beta (fastest, alert) > alpha (relaxed) > theta (drowsy/light sleep) > delta (deep sleep). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That's lowest-to-highest — reversed.
distractor_rationales.C: Beta is faster than alpha; delta is slower than theta.
distractor_rationales.D: This ordering is scrambled.

items.stem: Right as you drift off to sleep or during light sleep and drowsiness, the EEG is dominated by:
items.explanation: Theta (4–7 Hz) = drowsiness and light sleep (N1) — slower than alpha, faster than delta. Takeaway: Theta = drowsy / light sleep (N1). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Theta waves mark drowsiness and light sleep (Stage N1). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Beta is alert concentration, not drowsiness.
distractor_rationales.C: Delta is deep sleep, slower than theta.
distractor_rationales.D: Alpha is relaxed wakefulness; drifting into sleep shifts toward theta.

items.stem: Sleep is divided into two broad types. The three stages N1, N2, and N3 are categorized as:
items.explanation: Sleep stages: NREM (N1, N2, N3) plus REM. N1–N3 are the non-REM stages. Takeaway: N1–N3 = NREM; REM is the separate stage (most dreaming). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. N1–N3 are the non-REM stages; REM is the separate fourth stage. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: REM is the distinct stage where most dreaming occurs, separate from N1–N3.
distractor_rationales.B: Paradoxical sleep is another name for REM, not N1–N3.
distractor_rationales.D: These are sleep stages, not wakefulness.

items.stem: The lightest stage of sleep, N1, is dominated by which EEG waves and may include hypnagogic hallucinations and hypnic jerks?
items.explanation: N1 = lightest sleep, theta waves; hypnagogic hallucinations and hypnic jerks occur here. Takeaway: N1 = light sleep, theta waves (hypnagogic hallucinations, hypnic jerks). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. N1 (light sleep) shows theta waves, with hypnagogic hallucinations and hypnic (falling) jerks. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Delta waves characterize N3 (deep sleep), not N1.
distractor_rationales.B: Beta waves are alert wakefulness.
distractor_rationales.D: Sleep spindles are a hallmark of N2, not N1.

items.stem: Stage N2 sleep is specifically identified on an EEG by two features:
items.explanation: N2 is marked by sleep spindles (help maintain sleep through noise) and K-complexes (memory consolidation, suppress arousal). Takeaway: N2 = sleep spindles + K-complexes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. N2 shows sleep spindles (bursts of activity) and K-complexes, important for memory consolidation and staying asleep. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Delta waves define N3; REM bursts define REM.
distractor_rationales.C: Beta and eye movements aren't the N2 signature.
distractor_rationales.D: Alpha is relaxed wakefulness; hypnic jerks are N1.

items.stem: The deepest, hardest-to-wake stage — slow-wave sleep, important for declarative memory consolidation — is:
items.explanation: N3 = deepest, slow-wave sleep, delta waves; hardest to wake; declarative memory consolidation. Takeaway: N3 = deep slow-wave sleep, delta waves, declarative memory. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. N3 (slow-wave sleep) shows delta waves; it's the deepest stage and key for declarative memory consolidation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: N1 is the lightest stage (theta), not the deepest.
distractor_rationales.B: REM has beta-like activity but the body is paralyzed — not slow-wave deep sleep.
distractor_rationales.D: N2 has spindles but isn't the deepest slow-wave stage.

items.stem: REM sleep is called 'paradoxical sleep' because:

choices.text: The body is active while the brain is silent
Both brain and body are completely inactive
The brain is active (awake-like waves) while the body's voluntary muscles are paralyzed
It only occurs during daytime naps

items.explanation: REM = paradoxical sleep: active, awake-like brain but paralyzed muscles. Most vivid dreaming and episodic-memory formation occur here. Takeaway: REM = paradoxical sleep: brain active, body paralyzed. Most dreaming + episodic memory. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In REM the brain shows active, awake-like activity, yet the skeletal muscles are paralyzed (atonia) — hence 'paradoxical.' Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It's the reverse — brain active, body paralyzed.
distractor_rationales.B: The brain is highly active in REM, not inactive.
distractor_rationales.D: REM occurs in normal nighttime sleep cycles, not only naps.

items.stem: REM sleep is especially associated with:

choices.text: Declarative memory consolidation only (a slow-wave role)
Formation of episodic memories and processing of emotional experiences

items.explanation: REM — episodic memory formation and emotional processing. (Slow-wave N3 — declarative memory.) Takeaway: REM = episodic memory + emotional processing. N3 = declarative memory. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. REM is linked to episodic memory formation and emotional processing (N3/slow-wave is more tied to declarative consolidation). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Declarative consolidation is more a slow-wave (N3) function.
distractor_rationales.B: REM brain activity is high, not absent.
distractor_rationales.C: REM's cognitive/emotional roles are the emphasis here, not physical repair.

items.stem: A full sleep cycle repeats roughly every 90 minutes, 4–5 times a night. Early in the night, the progression through the cycle goes:
items.explanation: Each ~90-min cycle: N1 → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM, repeating 4–5 times. N3 dominates early night; REM lengthens toward morning. Takeaway: Cycle (~90 min): N1→N2→N3→N2→REM, x4–5/night. More N3 early, more REM later. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A cycle descends N1→N2→N3, ascends back to N2, then enters REM, about every 90 minutes. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's roughly reversed — you start in light N1, not REM.
distractor_rationales.C: You begin in light sleep (N1), then deepen — not start at N3.
distractor_rationales.D: REM comes after the NREM descent/ascent, not right after N1.

items.stem: The roughly 24-hour internal cycle that governs sleepiness, alertness, body temperature, and other functions is called the:
items.explanation: The circadian rhythm is the ~24-hour cycle regulating sleep/wake, temperature, and alertness. Takeaway: Circadian rhythm = ~24-hour internal clock (sleep/wake, temperature). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The circadian rhythm is the ~24-hour internal biological clock. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ultradian rhythms are shorter than 24 hours (e.g., the ~90-min sleep cycle).
distractor_rationales.B: Sleep spindles are an N2 EEG feature, not a rhythm.
distractor_rationales.C: The refractory period is a neuron's recovery phase.

items.stem: The hormone that rises in darkness to promote sleepiness and helps regulate the circadian rhythm is:
items.explanation: Melatonin (from the pineal gland) rises in darkness to promote sleep and regulate the circadian clock. Takeaway: Melatonin = sleep hormone from the pineal gland; rises in darkness. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Melatonin, secreted by the pineal gland, rises in darkness and signals sleep. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Cortisol rises with stress and in the morning to promote wakefulness.
distractor_rationales.C: Ghrelin is the hunger hormone.
distractor_rationales.D: Gustducin is a taste G protein.

items.stem: Melatonin is produced and released by which structure?
items.explanation: The pineal gland produces melatonin. Takeaway: Melatonin comes from the pineal gland. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The pineal gland secretes melatonin. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy. Neighbouring options fail because they name a different relation, drop a required conversion, or contradict a number given in the stem. Those traps are not a second live key. This row stays unverified and is not an official percentile item.

distractor_rationales.B: The pituitary secretes many hormones but not melatonin.
distractor_rationales.C: The adrenal cortex secretes cortisol and aldosterone.
distractor_rationales.D: The cochlea is a hearing organ.

items.stem: The most powerful external cue that entrains (resets) the circadian rhythm each day is:
items.explanation: Light is the dominant external cue (zeitgeber) that resets the circadian clock daily — even artificial light shifts it. Takeaway: Light = the master cue that resets the circadian clock (even artificial light). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Light is the dominant zeitgeber ('time-giver') that synchronizes the circadian clock; even artificial light affects it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Temperature has minor effects; light is the master cue.
distractor_rationales.B: Meals can weakly influence rhythms but aren't the dominant cue.
distractor_rationales.C: Blood pressure is a downstream physiological variable, not the entraining cue.

items.stem: Your notes mention that sleep timing shifts with age. Which pattern is typical?

choices.text: Everyone's timing is identical regardless of age
Older adults become extreme night owls
Timing is set permanently at birth and never changes
Younger people tend toward 'night owl' timing; older adults tend to sleep and wake earlier

items.explanation: Chronotype shifts with age: teens/young adults skew late ('night owls'); older adults shift earlier. Takeaway: Age shifts sleep timing: young = night owls; older adults = earlier to bed/rise. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Adolescents/young adults skew later ('night owls'); older adults tend to shift earlier. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Chronotype varies systematically with age, not identical for all.
distractor_rationales.B: Older adults trend earlier, not toward extreme late nights.
distractor_rationales.C: Circadian timing shifts across the lifespan; it isn't fixed at birth.

items.stem: The vivid, memorable dreams people usually recall occur mostly during:
items.explanation: Vivid, memorable dreams occur mainly in REM sleep; NREM dreams are less memorable. Takeaway: Vivid/memorable dreams = REM sleep. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Most vivid, memorable dreaming occurs in REM (NREM dreams are typically less memorable). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: N3 dreams, if any, are less vivid and rarely recalled.
distractor_rationales.C: N1 has brief hypnagogic imagery, not full memorable dreams.
distractor_rationales.D: Dreaming is a sleep phenomenon, not wakefulness.

items.stem: Dreams often defy logic partly because, during REM sleep, activity in the ______ is decreased.
items.explanation: Decreased prefrontal cortex activity in REM reduces logical checking — why dreams can defy logic and still feel normal. Takeaway: REM: prefrontal (logic) activity down → dreams defy logic yet feel normal. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Reduced prefrontal activity during REM lessens logical monitoring, so dreams can seem bizarre yet feel normal. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The amygdala is often quite active in REM, adding emotional intensity.
distractor_rationales.C: Visual imagery in dreams involves visual areas, not reduced logic.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not dream logic.

items.stem: In Freud's theory of dreams, the literal storyline you remember is the ______, while the hidden symbolic meaning is the ______.
items.explanation: Freud: manifest content = the remembered surface story; latent content = the hidden symbolic meaning (unconscious wishes). Takeaway: Freud: manifest = surface story; latent = hidden meaning. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Manifest content = the surface story; latent content = the hidden wishes/meaning Freud believed underlie it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — manifest is the surface story, latent is the hidden meaning.
distractor_rationales.C: Activation/synthesis belong to a different (neurobiological) theory.
distractor_rationales.D: Those are sleep-stage terms, not Freud's dream constructs.

items.stem: The Activation-Synthesis hypothesis proposes that dreams are:

choices.text: Encoded messages from the unconscious that must be decoded
Accurate rehearsals of the next day's events
Produced only when the brainstem is inactive
The cortex's attempt to make sense ('synthesis') of random neural signals ('activation') from the brainstem

items.explanation: Activation-synthesis: brainstem activation (random signals) + cortical synthesis (making a story) — dreams may lack hidden meaning. Takeaway: Activation-synthesis: brainstem = activation (random signals); cortex = synthesis (story). Maybe no hidden meaning. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Brainstem activation generates random signals; the cortex synthesizes them into a narrative — so dreams may have no hidden meaning. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's Freud's view; activation-synthesis instead sees dreams as arising from random signals.
distractor_rationales.B: The hypothesis doesn't claim dreams predict future events.
distractor_rationales.C: It requires brainstem ACTIVATION, not inactivity.

items.stem: Which is an example of an evolutionary/biological account of why we dream?

choices.text: Dreams are random noise with no function
Threat simulation — rehearsing responses to danger to prepare for the real world
Dreams replay the exact day's events verbatim

items.explanation: Evolutionary accounts: dreams may serve adaptive functions like threat simulation and problem solving. Takeaway: Evolutionary view: dreams = threat simulation / problem solving (adaptive rehearsal). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Evolutionary accounts propose adaptive functions such as threat simulation and problem solving. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's Freud's psychodynamic view, not an evolutionary one.
distractor_rationales.B: 'Random noise' is the activation-synthesis stance, not an adaptive evolutionary claim.
distractor_rationales.D: Verbatim replay isn't the evolutionary threat-simulation idea.

items.stem: A widely supported cognitive account of sleep and dreaming is that it helps:

choices.text: Erase all memories formed that day
Consolidate memories and integrate new learning
Prevent the brain from ever forming memories
Replace long-term memory with short-term memory

items.explanation: A well-supported role of sleep/dreaming is memory consolidation — learners who sleep retain more. Takeaway: Sleep/dreaming consolidates memory (sleep after learning → better retention). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sleep (and associated dreaming) supports memory consolidation — people who sleep after learning retain more. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Sleep consolidates rather than erases memories.
distractor_rationales.C: Sleep supports, not prevents, memory formation.
distractor_rationales.D: It strengthens long-term storage, not replaces it with short-term.

items.stem: Persistent difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep defines:
items.explanation: Insomnia = persistent trouble falling or staying asleep. (Overusing sleep meds → tolerance/dependence.) Takeaway: Insomnia = chronic trouble falling/staying asleep. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Insomnia is chronic trouble initiating or maintaining sleep. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Narcolepsy is uncontrollable sleep attacks, not trouble sleeping.
distractor_rationales.B: Sleep apnea is breathing interruptions during sleep.
distractor_rationales.D: Somnambulism is sleepwalking.

items.stem: A disorder marked by uncontrollable sleep attacks — sometimes going straight into REM — linked to loss of an alertness neurotransmitter, is:
items.explanation: Narcolepsy = sudden uncontrollable sleep attacks (often into REM), linked to loss of an alertness neurotransmitter (orexin). Takeaway: Narcolepsy = uncontrollable sleep attacks, often straight into REM. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Narcolepsy causes sudden, uncontrollable sleep episodes, often entering REM directly; linked to loss of orexin/hypocretin. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Insomnia is the opposite — too little sleep, not sudden sleep attacks.
distractor_rationales.B: Sleep apnea involves breathing stoppages, not sleep attacks.
distractor_rationales.C: Night terrors are arousal episodes in deep sleep, not sleep attacks.

items.stem: A person who repeatedly stops breathing during sleep, briefly wakes to gasp, and often feels unrefreshed (with loud snoring) likely has:
items.explanation: Sleep apnea = repeated breathing stoppages during sleep → gasping arousals, snoring, daytime fatigue (often reducing deep N3 sleep). Takeaway: Sleep apnea = repeated breathing stops in sleep → gasping, snoring, fatigue. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sleep apnea involves repeated breathing stoppages and micro-awakenings; snoring and daytime fatigue are common signs. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Narcolepsy is sleep attacks, not breathing stoppages.
distractor_rationales.C: Insomnia is difficulty sleeping, not breathing interruptions.
distractor_rationales.D: RBD involves acting out dreams, not breathing stoppages.

items.stem: Sleepwalking and sleep-talking (somnambulism) occur mostly during which stage — which is also why they're more common in children?
items.explanation: Sleepwalking/talking occur in N3 (deep slow-wave) sleep — more common in children (more N3). In REM, muscle paralysis prevents it. Takeaway: Sleepwalking = N3 (slow-wave), not REM. More common in kids (more N3). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sleepwalking/talking arise from N3 (slow-wave) sleep; children have more N3, so it's more common in them. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: In REM the body is paralyzed, so complex walking generally can't occur.
distractor_rationales.B: N1 is light sleep, not where sleepwalking typically originates.
distractor_rationales.C: By definition it happens during sleep, not wakefulness.

items.stem: Chronic sleep deprivation is associated with all of the following EXCEPT:

choices.text: Increased obesity risk (raised cortisol and ghrelin)
Improved reaction time and sharper attention

items.explanation: Sleep deprivation impairs attention, memory, and mood, and raises accident and obesity risk — it does not improve performance. Takeaway: Sleep deprivation → worse attention/memory/mood, more accidents, obesity risk. 'Sleep debt' can be partly repaid. The keyed choice holds because: Correct — as the EXCEPTION. Sleep deprivation WORSENS reaction time and attention; it doesn't improve them. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Deprivation increases accidents and impairs attention — a true effect.
distractor_rationales.B: It raises cortisol and hunger hormones, increasing obesity risk — true.
distractor_rationales.D: It worsens memory and mood — true.

items.stem: Hypnosis is best described as:

choices.text: A form of deep sleep with delta waves
An induced state of heightened suggestibility and focused, relaxed attention
A naturally occurring state that arises without any induction
A permanent alteration of the brain

items.explanation: Hypnosis = an induced state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility (awake but relaxed; more alpha waves). Takeaway: Hypnosis = induced state, focused attention + high suggestibility (alpha waves). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hypnosis is an induced state of focused attention and increased suggestibility (more alpha waves — awake but relaxed). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Hypnotized people are awake and relaxed (alpha), not in delta-wave deep sleep.
distractor_rationales.C: It's an INDUCED state, not spontaneous.
distractor_rationales.D: Its effects are temporary, not permanent.

items.stem: A documented risk of using hypnosis to 'retrieve' memories is that it can:

choices.text: Perfectly restore forgotten memories with total accuracy
Replace alpha waves with delta waves
Create false memories that incorporate the hypnotist's expectations

items.explanation: Hypnosis makes memory malleable — it can create false memories shaped by the hypnotist's expectations, so it's unreliable for recall. Takeaway: Hypnosis can implant FALSE memories (memory is malleable under suggestion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Under hypnosis memory is malleable; suggestion can implant false memories shaped by the hypnotist's cues. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Hypnosis does not reliably recover accurate memories — that's the danger.
distractor_rationales.B: It doesn't erase all autobiographical memory.
distractor_rationales.C: Hypnosis is associated with alpha (relaxed wakefulness), not a shift to delta.

items.stem: Two competing explanations of hypnosis are dissociation theory and social influence theory. Social influence theory holds that hypnotized people:

choices.text: Act out the social role expected of them, like absorbed actors
Undergo a genuine split in consciousness

items.explanation: Social influence theory: hypnotized people enact an expected social role. Dissociation theory: hypnosis is a genuine split (extreme divided consciousness). Takeaway: Hypnosis theories: dissociation (split consciousness) vs. social influence (playing a role). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Social influence theory: hypnotic behavior reflects playing an expected social role. (Dissociation theory instead posits a real split in awareness.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That describes dissociation theory, the competing account.
distractor_rationales.C: Hypnosis is awake/relaxed (alpha), not delta deep sleep.
distractor_rationales.D: Brain activity continues normally under hypnosis.

items.stem: Meditation is best described as:

choices.text: A disorder that prevents focused attention
Training to self-regulate attention and awareness

items.explanation: Meditation = training to self-regulate attention and awareness (focused or open-monitoring). Takeaway: Meditation = deliberate training of attention/awareness. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Meditation is deliberate training of attention/awareness — focused (e.g., on breathing) or open/unfocused. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It enhances, rather than prevents, attentional control.
distractor_rationales.B: Meditation is a waking practice, not a sleep stage.
distractor_rationales.D: It's a deliberate practice, not an involuntary reflex.

items.stem: Light meditation and relaxed hypnosis share an EEG signature of an awake-but-relaxed state, namely increased:

choices.text: Beta waves of intense concentration only
Alpha waves (with more theta in deep meditation by experts)

items.explanation: Light meditation/hypnosis → more alpha (awake but relaxed); deep meditation in experts → more theta. Takeaway: Meditation/hypnosis = more alpha (relaxed-awake); deep meditation (experts) = more theta. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Light meditation and hypnosis show increased alpha (awake, relaxed); experienced meditators show more theta in deep meditation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Delta marks deep sleep, not relaxed meditation.
distractor_rationales.B: Beta is intense concentration; meditation is relaxed alpha (deep: theta).
distractor_rationales.C: There is a measurable shift toward alpha/theta, not 'no change.'

items.stem: Psychoactive drugs are commonly grouped into three main categories:
items.explanation: Three main psychoactive categories: depressants, stimulants, hallucinogens (opiates/opioids often a separate class). Takeaway: Psychoactive drug categories: depressants, stimulants, hallucinogens. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The three main categories of psychoactive drugs are depressants, stimulants, and hallucinogens (with opiates/opioids often treated as a distinct related class). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Vitamins aren't a psychoactive drug category.
distractor_rationales.B: Antibiotics aren't psychoactive drugs.
distractor_rationales.C: Antibiotics and steroids aren't the psychoactive categories.

items.stem: Depressants (like alcohol) affect the CNS by:

choices.text: Increasing arousal, heart rate, and alertness
Causing vivid hallucinations as their primary effect
Lowering CNS activity — decreasing arousal, heart rate, BP, and reaction/processing time
Having no effect on the nervous system

items.explanation: Depressants lower CNS activity → decreased arousal, heart rate, BP, and reaction/processing time (you act and think slowly). Takeaway: Depressants = lower CNS activity (slower HR/BP/processing). Alcohol is the most common. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Depressants slow the CNS: reduced arousal, heart rate, blood pressure, and processing speed. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That describes stimulants, the opposite of depressants.
distractor_rationales.B: Distorted perception is the hallmark of hallucinogens, not depressants.
distractor_rationales.D: Depressants clearly act on the CNS.

items.stem: Alcohol has a dose-dependent effect on blood vessels. At low doses it acts as a ______, and at high doses as a ______.
items.explanation: Alcohol: vasodilate at low dose, vasoconstrict at high dose — and it's a CNS depressant throughout. Takeaway: Alcohol: low dose = vasodilate; high dose = vasoconstrict (and always a depressant). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alcohol vasodilates at low doses and vasoconstricts at high doses. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — low dose dilates, high dose constricts.
distractor_rationales.C: Alcohol is a depressant, not a stimulant/hallucinogen.
distractor_rationales.D: Alcohol is a depressant at all doses; the vessel effect is dilate→constrict.

items.stem: Most depressants — including alcohol, barbiturates, and benzodiazepines — calm the CNS largely by enhancing the activity of which inhibitory neurotransmitter?
items.explanation: Depressants enhance GABA (inhibitory): opening Cl⁻ channels hyperpolarizes neurons, calming the CNS. Takeaway: Depressants work by boosting GABA (inhibitory) → Cl⁻ in → neurons less likely to fire. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Depressants boost GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, opening Cl⁻ channels and making neurons more negative (less likely to fire). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Dopamine is tied to reward/stimulants, not the inhibitory depressant mechanism.
distractor_rationales.B: Glutamate is the main EXCITATORY transmitter — the opposite of what depressants enhance.
distractor_rationales.D: Acetylcholine is where nicotine acts, not the general depressant mechanism.

items.stem: Compared with barbiturates, benzodiazepines ('benzos') are far more commonly prescribed today mainly because they:

choices.text: Have a safer side-effect profile (barbiturates carry high overdose risk, worse with alcohol)
Do not affect GABA at all

items.explanation: Barbiturates and benzos both enhance GABA, but barbiturates are far more dangerous (overdose, lethal with alcohol) — so benzos are now preferred. Takeaway: Benzos preferred over barbiturates: same GABA action, but barbiturates are far more dangerous (overdose, deadly with alcohol). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Both enhance GABA, but barbiturates have a narrow safety margin (overdose, deadly with alcohol), so benzodiazepines largely replaced them. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Both are depressants, not stimulants.
distractor_rationales.C: Both act on the GABA system.
distractor_rationales.D: Both are sedating depressants, not hallucinogens.

items.stem: One documented effect of alcohol on sleep is that it:

choices.text: Increases REM sleep and improves memory
Disrupts the REM cycle, reducing REM sleep (impairing memory/new synapse formation)
Has no effect on sleep architecture
Eliminates deep slow-wave sleep entirely and nothing else
