items.explanation: Autobiographical memory = your life story, combining episodic (events) and semantic (self-knowledge) memory. Takeaway: Autobiographical memory = life story (episodic events + semantic self-knowledge). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Autobiographical memory blends episodic (specific events) and semantic (general self-knowledge) components into a coherent life narrative. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Procedural memory is for skills, not one's life story.
distractor_rationales.B: Iconic memory is a brief visual sensory trace.
distractor_rationales.C: Working memory is temporary online storage, not the life narrative.

items.stem: Encoding refers to:

choices.text: Retrieving a stored memory back into awareness
The brief holding of raw sensory input
Transferring information from working memory into long-term storage
The gradual weakening of a memory over time

items.explanation: Encoding = transferring information from working memory into long-term storage. Takeaway: Encoding = getting information INTO long-term memory. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Encoding is the process of getting information into long-term memory (often requiring active effort). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's retrieval, not encoding.
distractor_rationales.B: That's sensory memory, not encoding.
distractor_rationales.D: That's decay/forgetting, not encoding.

items.stem: Simply repeating someone's name over and over to remember it is:

choices.text: Elaborative encoding — the most effective strategy
Rote rehearsal — the least effective encoding strategy (little cognitive effort)

items.explanation: Rote rehearsal = plain repetition, minimal effort, least effective. Deeper strategies (elaboration, chunking) work better. Takeaway: Rote rehearsal = repetition, least effective (shallow processing). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rote rehearsal is plain repetition; it requires little deep processing and is the least effective for durable memory. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Elaborative encoding (linking to existing knowledge) is more effective, and different from rote repetition.
distractor_rationales.B: Chunking groups items meaningfully; rote rehearsal doesn't.
distractor_rationales.C: Mnemonics link material to existing memory; rote repetition doesn't.

items.stem: Grouping a long string of items into meaningful categories you already know (fruits, grains, proteins) to remember them better is:
items.explanation: Chunking = grouping items into meaningful categories/units, making them easier to hold and recall. Takeaway: Chunking = organize into meaningful groups → remember more. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Chunking organizes information into meaningful groups, expanding how much fits in memory. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Rote rehearsal is plain repetition, not grouping into meaningful units.
distractor_rationales.C: The method of loci ties items to spatial locations, not category grouping.
distractor_rationales.D: State-dependent memory concerns internal state at encoding/retrieval.

items.stem: Remembering a list in order by mentally 'placing' each item at successive spots along a familiar route (your house, a street) uses the:
items.explanation: Method of loci = tie items to locations along a familiar route — strong for remembering things in order. Takeaway: Method of loci = place items along a familiar route (ordered recall). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The method of loci links items to well-known physical locations, good for ordered recall. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The peg-word system pairs items with number-rhyme pegs, not spatial locations.
distractor_rationales.C: Self-referencing relates material to yourself, not to locations.
distractor_rationales.D: Rote rehearsal is plain repetition.

items.stem: Remembering new information better by relating it to your own life and experiences is called:
items.explanation: Self-referencing = relate new information to yourself → deeper processing → better memory. Takeaway: Self-referencing = link material to yourself (deep processing). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Self-referencing links new material to yourself, producing deep processing and better retention. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The peg-word system uses number-rhyme anchors, not personal relevance.
distractor_rationales.C: Rote rehearsal is shallow repetition, not personal linking.
distractor_rationales.D: Decay is a forgetting mechanism, not an encoding strategy.

items.stem: Spreading study out across several shorter sessions over time, rather than cramming it all at once, improves long-term retention. This is the:
items.explanation: Spacing effect: distributed study over time beats cramming for long-term retention. Takeaway: Spacing effect = spread study out (distributed) → better long-term memory than cramming. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The spacing effect: distributed practice beats massed practice (cramming) for durable learning. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The serial position effect is about recall of list positions.
distractor_rationales.C: Encoding specificity is about matching cues at encoding and retrieval.
distractor_rationales.D: Rote rehearsal is a shallow repetition strategy, not spacing.

items.stem: Encoding specificity is the principle that memory is best when:

choices.text: Information is repeated the maximum number of times
The material is completely novel and unrelated to anything
Retrieval conditions (cues, context) match the conditions present during encoding

items.explanation: Encoding specificity: memory is best when retrieval cues/context match those at encoding. Takeaway: Encoding specificity = match retrieval cues to encoding conditions. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Encoding specificity: retrieval improves when cues at recall match those present when the memory was formed. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Repetition alone (rote) isn't the encoding-specificity principle.
distractor_rationales.B: Relating to existing knowledge helps; total novelty doesn't aid encoding specificity.
distractor_rationales.C: Cues are central to encoding specificity, not absent.

items.stem: Retrieval is best defined as:

choices.text: Getting new information into long-term storage
The brief sensory trace of a stimulus
Bringing information from long-term memory back into conscious (working) memory

items.explanation: Retrieval = bringing stored information from long-term memory back into conscious awareness (cue-dependent). Takeaway: Retrieval = pulling a stored memory back into awareness (needs cues). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Retrieval is accessing stored information and bringing it back into awareness; it depends on effective cues. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's encoding, not retrieval.
distractor_rationales.B: That's sensory memory, not retrieval.
distractor_rationales.D: That's LTP (a storage mechanism), not the act of retrieval.

items.stem: Scuba divers who learned words underwater recalled them better when tested underwater than on land. This is:
items.explanation: Context-dependent memory: matching the external environment (place) at encoding and retrieval improves recall. Takeaway: Context-dependent memory = same external environment at encoding & retrieval aids recall. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Context-dependent memory: recall improves when the external environment at retrieval matches the environment at encoding. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: State-dependent memory concerns internal state (mood, intoxication), not external setting.
distractor_rationales.B: Priming is implicit facilitation by a prior stimulus.
distractor_rationales.D: The spacing effect concerns distributed practice.

items.stem: Information learned while in a particular internal state (e.g., a certain mood, or intoxicated) is best recalled in that same internal state. This is:
items.explanation: State-dependent memory: your internal state (mood, intoxication) is a cue — matching it at retrieval aids recall. Takeaway: State-dependent memory = same internal state (mood/substance) at encoding & retrieval aids recall. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. State-dependent memory: internal state (mood, intoxication) serves as a retrieval cue; matching it at recall aids memory. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Context-dependent memory concerns the external environment, not internal state.
distractor_rationales.C: This is an application of encoding specificity, not a failure of it.
distractor_rationales.D: Source monitoring is tracking where a memory came from.

items.stem: Reading a story about rabbits makes you more likely to later interpret the spoken word 'hair/hare' as 'hare.' This retrieval-related facilitation is:
items.explanation: Priming = prior activation of associated nodes makes related information easier to retrieve (often unconsciously). Takeaway: Priming = a prior stimulus activates associations → related info easier to retrieve. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Priming is the (often unconscious) activation of associations that makes related information easier to retrieve. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Context-dependent memory involves matching external environment, not associative activation.
distractor_rationales.B: Rote rehearsal is a repetition encoding strategy.
distractor_rationales.C: Proactive interference is old memories disrupting new learning.

items.stem: Ordered from MOST difficult to EASIEST, the three types of retrieval tasks are:
items.explanation: Retrieval difficulty: free recall (hardest) → cued recall → recognition (easiest) — more cues make it easier. Takeaway: Hard→easy: free recall → cued recall → recognition. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Free recall (no cues) is hardest; cued recall (with hints) is easier; recognition (choose from options) is easiest. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's easiest-to-hardest — reversed.
distractor_rationales.C: Free recall is harder than cued recall, not easier.
distractor_rationales.D: Free recall is harder than recognition; this ordering is scrambled.

items.stem: Being asked to list everything you can remember from a lecture, with no hints provided, is an example of:
items.explanation: Free recall = retrieve with no cues (hardest). You generate everything yourself. Takeaway: Free recall = no cues, generate it all yourself (hardest). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Free recall provides no cues — you must generate the information yourself, making it the hardest task. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Cued recall provides hints or partial cues.
distractor_rationales.B: Recognition provides options to choose from.
distractor_rationales.C: Priming is an implicit facilitation, not a recall task type.

items.stem: Being given the hint 'it starts with pl___' to recall the word 'planet' is an example of:
items.explanation: Cued recall = hints/partial cues help you produce the answer (easier than free recall, harder than recognition). Takeaway: Cued recall = hints help you produce the answer. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cued recall provides retrieval cues that make recall easier than free recall but still require producing the answer. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Free recall gives no cues.
distractor_rationales.C: Recognition presents the answer among options to select.
distractor_rationales.D: The recency effect concerns list-position recall.

items.stem: A multiple-choice question, where you select which option you saw before, is a test of:
items.explanation: Recognition = identify the correct item from presented options (easiest retrieval; multiple choice). Takeaway: Recognition = pick the right answer from options (easiest). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Recognition presents options and asks you to identify the correct one — the easiest form of retrieval. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Free recall requires generating the answer with no options.
distractor_rationales.C: Reconstruction is rebuilding a memory, not selecting from options.
distractor_rationales.D: Decay is a forgetting mechanism.

items.stem: The tendency to recall the first items (primacy) and last items (recency) of a list better than the middle produces the:
items.explanation: Serial position curve: primacy (first items, rehearsed to LTM) + recency (last items, in working memory) → U-shape; middle recalled worst. Takeaway: Serial position curve = primacy + recency, middle worst (U-shape). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The serial position (U-shaped) curve shows good recall for early (primacy) and late (recency) items, poor for the middle. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The forgetting curve (Ebbinghaus) plots memory loss over time, not list position.
distractor_rationales.B: There is no standard 'encoding-specificity curve.'
distractor_rationales.C: The Yerkes-Dodson curve relates arousal to performance.

items.stem: The finding that memory is not a perfect recording but is rebuilt each time — and can be altered by goals, mood, and new information — is called:
items.explanation: Reconstructive memory: recall rebuilds a memory from fragments/schemas each time, so it can be altered — not a video recording. Takeaway: Memory is reconstructive (rebuilt each time), not a perfect recording. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Memory is reconstructive: we rebuild it from fragments and schemas, so it can be distorted rather than replayed verbatim. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Memory is not a perfect photographic recording — that's the point being refuted.
distractor_rationales.B: Sensory memory is a brief raw trace, not the reconstruction of past events.
distractor_rationales.D: Procedural memory is for skills, not event reconstruction.

items.stem: When you fill gaps in a memory using general knowledge of how things usually go (a mental blueprint of the world), you are relying on a:
items.explanation: A schema = mental blueprint of how things usually are; it aids interpretation but can distort memory by filling gaps. Takeaway: Schema = mental framework of the world; fills gaps (can cause distortion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A schema is an organized mental framework; it helps interpretation but can also introduce distortions when it fills gaps. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A flashbulb memory is a vivid emotional memory, not a general knowledge framework.
distractor_rationales.C: A retrieval cue triggers recall; a schema organizes/interprets information.
distractor_rationales.D: A peg-word is a mnemonic device.

items.stem: After watching a car crash, people asked how fast cars were going when they 'smashed' later recall more broken glass than those asked about 'hit.' This is the:
items.explanation: Misinformation effect: misleading information after an event (e.g., 'smashed' vs. 'hit') distorts the memory — why leading questions are problematic. Takeaway: Misinformation effect = misleading post-event info distorts memory (Loftus). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Loftus's misinformation effect: misleading post-event information (word choice) distorts the memory, so leading questions are risky. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A flashbulb memory is a vivid emotional memory, not memory distortion by wording.
distractor_rationales.B: The spacing effect concerns distributed practice.
distractor_rationales.D: Encoding specificity concerns matching cues at encoding/retrieval.

items.stem: Recalling a fact but misremembering WHERE you learned it — e.g., 'remembering' a detail from a movie as something you witnessed — is a:
items.explanation: Source-monitoring error = remembering information but misattributing where/when/how you learned it (vs. source amnesia = no memory of the source). Takeaway: Source-monitoring error = right info, wrong source. (Source amnesia = no memory of source at all.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Source-monitoring errors occur when you retain information but misattribute its origin (source amnesia is the inability to recall the source at all). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: A flashbulb memory is a vivid emotional memory, not a source confusion.
distractor_rationales.C: Proactive interference is old learning disrupting new learning.
distractor_rationales.D: Chunking is an encoding strategy, unrelated to source confusion.

items.stem: A vivid, emotionally charged memory of learning shocking news (e.g., where you were during 9/11) that feels as real as life is a:
items.explanation: Flashbulb memory = vivid, emotionally intense memory of a shocking event; feels accurate but is still reconstructive and error-prone. Takeaway: Flashbulb memory = vivid emotional 'snapshot' memory (still error-prone despite feeling real). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Flashbulb memories (Brown & Kulik) are vivid emotional memories — but, despite feeling perfectly accurate, they're still susceptible to reconstruction/error. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Procedural memory is for skills, not vivid emotional events.
distractor_rationales.C: Iconic memory is a brief visual sensory trace.
distractor_rationales.D: A chunk is a unit of grouped information.

items.stem: The strengthening of a synaptic connection that results from repeated, high-frequency stimulation — a leading physical basis of learning — is:
items.explanation: Long-term potentiation (LTP) = lasting synaptic strengthening from repeated stimulation — a physical basis of learning/memory. Takeaway: LTP = synapses strengthen with repeated stimulation (basis of learning). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. LTP is the lasting strengthening of synapses following repeated stimulation, thought to underlie learning and memory (synaptic plasticity). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: LTP is strengthening; long-term depression is the weakening counterpart.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensory adaptation is reduced receptor response, unrelated to synaptic strengthening.
distractor_rationales.D: Rote rehearsal is a behavioral study strategy, not a synaptic mechanism.

items.stem: The broader capacity of synapses to strengthen or weaken over time, changing the brain's structure and function with experience, is called:
items.explanation: Synaptic/neural plasticity = experience-driven changes in synaptic strength and brain structure (LTP is one instance). Takeaway: Synaptic plasticity = experience changes synaptic strength/brain structure. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Synaptic/neural plasticity is the experience-driven change in synaptic strength and brain structure; LTP is one example. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Homeostasis is maintaining internal stability, not changing synaptic strength with learning.
distractor_rationales.B: Refractoriness is a neuron's brief inability to fire again, not plasticity.
distractor_rationales.C: Myelination speeds conduction but isn't the definition of plasticity.

items.stem: In LTP, repeated presynaptic stimulation leads to a stronger postsynaptic response mainly because:

choices.text: Myelin is stripped from the axon
More receptors/ion channels open in the postsynaptic neuron, facilitating future firing

items.explanation: In LTP, repeated stimulation increases postsynaptic responsiveness (more channels open) → easier future firing → stronger memory. Takeaway: LTP: repeated stimulation → more postsynaptic channels open → stronger, easier future response. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. LTP involves increased postsynaptic responsiveness (more open channels/receptors), so the same input more easily triggers firing later — facilitated recall. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Neither neuron is destroyed; the connection is strengthened.
distractor_rationales.B: Myelin isn't stripped; the synapse is potentiated.
distractor_rationales.D: Silencing a synapse is the opposite of potentiation.

items.stem: Forgetting because a memory trace fades over time when it is not used or retrieved is explained by:
items.explanation: Decay: memory traces fade over time with disuse (the pathway weakens). Takeaway: Decay = memory fades over time from disuse. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Decay: an unused memory trace weakens over time, making the neurons harder to re-activate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Retroactive interference is new learning disrupting old memory, not passive fading.
distractor_rationales.C: Proactive interference is old learning disrupting new, not passive fading.
distractor_rationales.D: Encoding specificity concerns cue matching, not fading.

items.stem: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, measured with nonsense syllables, showed that:

choices.text: Forgetting is slow at first, then accelerates
Forgetting is fastest right after learning, then levels off over time

items.explanation: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve: rapid initial forgetting that then levels off — most loss happens soon after learning. Takeaway: Ebbinghaus curve = fast forgetting at first, then it levels off. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The forgetting curve drops steeply soon after learning, then flattens — most forgetting happens early. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It's the reverse — forgetting is fastest early, then slows.
distractor_rationales.B: A great deal is forgotten, especially early on.
distractor_rationales.D: Memory declines (not improves) without review.

items.stem: Even when you can't recall something, relearning it is faster than the first time. Ebbinghaus called this measurable benefit:
items.explanation: Savings = relearning is faster than first learning — evidence a memory trace persists even when recall fails. Takeaway: Savings = relearning is faster than original learning (a trace remains). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Savings: relearning takes less time than original learning, showing some trace remains even when recall fails. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Interference is memories disrupting each other, not the relearning benefit.
distractor_rationales.B: Decay is the fading of memory, not the relearning savings.
distractor_rationales.C: Priming is implicit facilitation by a prior stimulus, a different phenomenon.

items.stem: Getting a new phone number makes it hard to recall your OLD number. New learning disrupting an older memory is:
items.explanation: Retroactive interference: NEW learning disrupts recall of OLDER memories (new number → forget old). Takeaway: Retroactive interference = new info disrupts OLD memory. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Retroactive interference: newer information interferes with the recall of older information. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Proactive interference is the reverse — OLD learning disrupting NEW.
distractor_rationales.B: Decay is passive fading, not interference from other learning.
distractor_rationales.D: State-dependent forgetting concerns mismatched internal states.

items.stem: Your OLD password keeps interfering with learning your NEW one. Older learning disrupting NEW learning is:
items.explanation: Proactive interference: OLD learning disrupts NEW learning/recall (old password → hard to learn new one). Takeaway: Proactive interference = old info disrupts NEW learning. (Pro = prior/forward.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Proactive interference: previously learned information interferes with acquiring or recalling new information. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Retroactive interference is the reverse — NEW disrupting OLD.
distractor_rationales.B: Savings is faster relearning, not interference.
distractor_rationales.C: Chunking is an encoding strategy.

items.stem: With normal aging, which memory abilities tend to remain relatively STABLE?
items.explanation: With aging: implicit/procedural memory and recognition stay stable; recall, episodic formation, processing speed, and divided attention decline. Takeaway: Aging stable: procedural memory + recognition. Declines: recall, new episodic, speed, divided attention. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Implicit/procedural memory (e.g., riding a bike) and recognition tend to hold up with age. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Processing speed and divided attention typically DECLINE with age.
distractor_rationales.B: Forming new episodic memories tends to decline.
distractor_rationales.C: Prospective memory typically declines with age.

items.stem: Which cognitive ability tends to IMPROVE (or peak later) with age?

choices.text: Semantic memory and crystallized intelligence (accumulated knowledge/vocabulary)

items.explanation: With aging, semantic memory and crystallized intelligence (knowledge, vocabulary) improve, even as speed and fluid abilities decline. Takeaway: Aging improves: semantic memory + crystallized IQ (knowledge/vocab). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Semantic memory (facts, vocabulary) and crystallized intelligence often improve into older adulthood; fluid abilities/speed decline. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Processing speed declines with age.
distractor_rationales.B: Divided attention declines with age.
distractor_rationales.D: New episodic memory formation declines with age.

items.stem: Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia, is characterized by progressive memory loss and, in the brain, a buildup of:
items.explanation: Alzheimer's disease = progressive dementia with amyloid plaques and cortical shrinkage; earliest signs are trouble with recent memories. Takeaway: Alzheimer's = amyloid plaques + progressive memory loss (recent memories first). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alzheimer's involves amyloid plaques (and tau tangles), progressive neuron death, and cerebral cortex shrinkage; early symptoms are trouble retrieving recent memories. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Dopamine loss in the striatum characterizes Parkinson's, not Alzheimer's plaques.
distractor_rationales.B: Thiamine deficiency characterizes Korsakoff's, not Alzheimer's.
distractor_rationales.C: Alzheimer's involves neurodegeneration, not myelin overgrowth.

items.stem: Korsakoff's syndrome, marked by severe memory loss and confabulation (filling gaps with invented memories), is caused by a deficiency of:

choices.text: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) — often from chronic alcoholism

items.explanation: Korsakoff's syndrome = thiamine (B1) deficiency (often from alcoholism) → severe memory loss + confabulation. Wernicke's encephalopathy is the acute precursor. Takeaway: Korsakoff's = thiamine (B1) deficiency (alcoholism) → memory loss + confabulation. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Korsakoff's results from thiamine (B1) deficiency, commonly due to alcoholism; confabulation is a hallmark. (Wernicke's encephalopathy is the acute precursor.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Dopamine loss relates to Parkinson's, not Korsakoff's.
distractor_rationales.B: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not Korsakoff's.
distractor_rationales.C: Amyloid buildup characterizes Alzheimer's, not Korsakoff's.

items.stem: After brain damage, a patient can recall their childhood but cannot form any NEW long-term memories. This is:
items.explanation: Anterograde amnesia = can't form NEW memories after injury (past intact). Retrograde amnesia = lost memories from BEFORE the injury. Takeaway: Anterograde = no NEW memories after injury. Retrograde = lost OLD memories before injury. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form NEW memories after the injury (old memories are intact). Retrograde amnesia is loss of memories from BEFORE the injury. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Retrograde amnesia is loss of PRE-injury memories, but here childhood memory is intact.
distractor_rationales.B: Source amnesia is forgetting where information was learned, not an inability to form new memories.
distractor_rationales.C: Proactive interference is old learning disrupting new, not an amnesia from brain damage.

items.stem: Dementia is best defined as:

choices.text: A normal, expected part of healthy aging
A decline in memory and other cognitive functions severe enough to interfere with daily life
A brief, fully reversible memory lapse
A deficiency of vitamin B1 specifically

items.explanation: Dementia = cognitive decline (memory + other functions) severe enough to disrupt daily life — not normal aging. Takeaway: Dementia = cognitive decline disrupting daily life (not normal aging). Most common cause: Alzheimer's. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Dementia is a significant cognitive decline (memory plus other domains) that disrupts daily functioning — beyond normal aging; Alzheimer's is the most common cause. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Dementia is not a normal part of aging — it's pathological.
distractor_rationales.C: Dementia is progressive and impairing, not a brief reversible lapse.
distractor_rationales.D: B1 deficiency causes Korsakoff's; dementia has many causes, most commonly Alzheimer's.

items.stem: A semantic network models how concepts are stored in the mind as:

choices.text: A single unstructured list with no connections
Interconnected nodes, with closely related ideas linked more tightly
Separate isolated facts with no links

items.explanation: A semantic network stores concepts as interconnected nodes; closer-related ideas are more tightly linked. Takeaway: Semantic network = concepts as connected nodes (closer ideas = stronger links). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In a semantic network, concepts are represented as nodes connected by links; closely related ideas have shorter/stronger links. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A semantic network is highly interconnected, not an unstructured list.
distractor_rationales.B: Sensory traces are a memory-store concept, not the semantic network structure.
distractor_rationales.D: The whole point is that concepts are linked, not isolated.

items.stem: The FIRST semantic-network model proposed that concepts are organized:

choices.text: Hierarchically — from higher-order (broad) categories down to lower-order (specific) ones

items.explanation: The first model was hierarchical: broad categories at higher nodes, specifics below; shared traits stored at the highest level (cognitive economy). Takeaway: Hierarchical model = concepts from broad (top) to specific (bottom). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The hierarchical model organizes concepts from broad superordinate categories to specific ones, storing shared traits at the highest applicable node. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The hierarchical model is highly organized, not random.
distractor_rationales.C: It organizes by category level, not emotion.
distractor_rationales.D: It's a multi-level hierarchy, not a flat list.

items.stem: Storing a shared property like 'can breathe' only once at the highest node ('animal') rather than repeating it for every specific animal reflects the:
items.explanation: Cognitive economy: store a shared property once at the highest applicable node (efficient, non-redundant storage). Takeaway: Cognitive economy = store shared traits at the highest node (no redundancy). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cognitive economy stores properties at the highest applicable level to avoid redundancy — making storage efficient. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Spreading activation is about activation flowing across links, not efficient storage.
distractor_rationales.C: The availability heuristic is a decision-making shortcut, unrelated.
distractor_rationales.D: The serial position effect concerns list-position recall.

items.stem: Evidence for the hierarchical model comes from the finding that verifying 'a canary is an animal' takes LONGER than 'a canary is a bird' because:

choices.text: More nodes/links must be traversed for the more distant category
Animals are less common than birds

items.explanation: Verification time rises with semantic distance: more nodes to traverse (canary→bird→animal) = slower verification. Takeaway: More links between concepts → longer verification time (hierarchical model evidence). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Greater semantic distance (more links to traverse) means longer verification time — the hierarchical model's key prediction. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Frequency of the category isn't the model's explanation; distance is.
distractor_rationales.C: Word length isn't the mechanism.
distractor_rationales.D: Preference is irrelevant to verification time.

items.stem: A problem for the strict hierarchical model is that people verify 'a pig is an animal' FASTER than 'a pig is a mammal,' which the model can't explain. This helped motivate the:

choices.text: Modified (non-hierarchical) semantic network with spreading activation

items.explanation: The pig-animal/pig-mammal reversal breaks strict hierarchy → the modified spreading-activation network (link strength by experience) fits better. Takeaway: Hierarchy fails for some pairs (pig→animal faster than pig→mammal) → modified spreading-activation model. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Such reversals (and individual differences) led to the modified spreading-activation network, where link strength varies by experience rather than strict hierarchy. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Cognitive economy is part of the hierarchical model being challenged, not the fix.
distractor_rationales.C: The serial position curve concerns list recall, not category verification.
distractor_rationales.D: The method of loci is a mnemonic device.

items.stem: Thinking of 'fire engine' automatically makes 'truck,' 'red,' and 'fire' easier to retrieve, because activating one node activates connected ones. This is:
items.explanation: Spreading activation: activating one node spreads to connected nodes, making related concepts easier to retrieve (and can cause related-memory errors). Takeaway: Spreading activation = activating one concept primes connected ones. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Spreading activation: activating one concept spreads to linked concepts, easing their retrieval (and it can explain false/related-memory errors). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Cognitive economy concerns efficient storage, not activation spreading.
distractor_rationales.C: Proactive interference is old learning disrupting new.
distractor_rationales.D: Chunking is grouping items to expand memory.

items.stem: In a spreading-activation network, the strength of the link between two nodes is largely a function of:

choices.text: Exposure — more experience strengthens the link (and speeds processing)
The alphabetical order of the words
The number of letters in each word

items.explanation: Node link strength grows with exposure/experience; stronger links speed processing — which is why learning reduces retrieval time. Takeaway: Link strength grows with exposure → stronger links = faster processing (learning speeds retrieval). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Repeated exposure strengthens node links; stronger links transmit more activation and reduce processing time (learning speeds retrieval). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Alphabetical order doesn't set associative strength.
distractor_rationales.C: Links are shaped by experience, not fixed randomly at birth.
distractor_rationales.D: Word length doesn't determine link strength.

items.stem: In Piaget's first stage, a hallmark achievement is object permanence — understanding that objects still exist when out of sight. This stage is:
items.explanation: Sensorimotor (0–2): learning via senses/motor action; key milestone = object permanence. Takeaway: Sensorimotor (0–2) = senses/motor; object permanence develops here. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In the sensorimotor stage, infants learn through senses/motor action and develop object permanence (why peek-a-boo works before it's mastered). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Preoperational children already have object permanence; it develops earlier.
distractor_rationales.B: Concrete operational is far later; object permanence is achieved by then.
distractor_rationales.C: Formal operational is adolescence — well past object permanence.

items.stem: A 4-year-old assumes you can see exactly what she sees and can't take another's viewpoint. This egocentrism (and symbolic thinking) is characteristic of the:
items.explanation: Preoperational (2–7): symbolic thought, but egocentrism (can't take another's perspective) and magical thinking. Takeaway: Preoperational (2–7) = symbols + egocentrism (no perspective-taking). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Preoperational children use symbols/language and show egocentrism (can't take others' perspectives) and magical thinking. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Sensorimotor is the infant sensory/motor stage, before symbolic egocentrism.
distractor_rationales.B: Concrete operational children have overcome egocentrism.
distractor_rationales.C: Formal operational is abstract adolescent reasoning.

items.stem: A child now understands that pouring water into a taller, thinner glass doesn't change the amount — grasping conservation. This marks the:
items.explanation: Concrete operational (7–11): logical reasoning about concrete things; masters conservation and reversibility. Takeaway: Concrete operational (7–11) = conservation + logical thinking about concrete objects. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Concrete operational children master conservation (and reversibility) and can reason logically about concrete objects. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Preoperational children typically FAIL conservation tasks.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensorimotor is infancy, far before conservation.
distractor_rationales.D: Formal operational adds abstract reasoning beyond concrete conservation.

items.stem: The ability to reason abstractly and hypothetically, consider consequences, and engage in moral reasoning emerges in Piaget's final stage, the:
items.explanation: Formal operational (12+): abstract and hypothetical reasoning, consequences, and moral reasoning. Takeaway: Formal operational (12+) = abstract/hypothetical + moral reasoning. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Formal operational thought (adolescence onward) enables abstract, hypothetical, and moral reasoning. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Concrete operational reasoning is tied to concrete objects, not abstract hypotheticals.
distractor_rationales.B: Preoperational thought is pre-logical and egocentric.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensorimotor is infancy.

items.stem: Piaget's four stages, in the correct developmental order, are:

choices.text: Sensorimotor → preoperational → concrete operational → formal operational
Preoperational → sensorimotor → formal operational → concrete operational
Sensorimotor → concrete operational → preoperational → formal operational
Formal operational → concrete operational → preoperational → sensorimotor

items.explanation: Piaget's order: sensorimotor → preoperational → concrete operational → formal operational. Takeaway: Piaget order: sensorimotor → preoperational → concrete operational → formal operational. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The order is sensorimotor → preoperational → concrete operational → formal operational. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Sensorimotor comes first, not preoperational.
distractor_rationales.C: Preoperational precedes concrete operational, not the reverse.
distractor_rationales.D: That's the reverse order.

items.stem: Later research modified Piaget's theory by showing that:

choices.text: The stages occur in reverse order
Children don't always develop these abilities in a rigid, predictable timeline (some abilities appear earlier)

items.explanation: Modern view: Piaget's stages aren't as rigid/fixed in timing as proposed — some abilities appear earlier, development is more continuous. Takeaway: Critique: development is less rigidly staged/timed than Piaget claimed (but framework is foundational). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Development is less rigidly staged than Piaget claimed; some abilities emerge earlier and progress is more continuous — though his framework remains foundational. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The stages don't reverse; the critique is about timing/rigidity.
distractor_rationales.B: Cognitive development clearly occurs; the critique is about its pace/rigidity.
distractor_rationales.C: Children have schemas too — that's central to Piaget.

items.stem: In Piaget's theory, a schema is:

choices.text: A mental framework used to organize and interpret new information

items.explanation: A schema = a mental framework for organizing and interpreting information; development is the growth/change of schemas. Takeaway: Schema = mental framework to organize/interpret information. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A schema is a cognitive framework/model that organizes knowledge and guides interpretation of new experiences. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A raw sensory trace is sensory memory, not a schema.
distractor_rationales.B: A schema is a cognitive structure, not an anatomical region.
distractor_rationales.C: A schema is a framework for understanding, not a forgetting mechanism.

items.stem: Fitting a new experience into an existing schema without changing the schema — e.g., a child calling a new small dog 'doggie' — is:
items.explanation: Assimilation = fit new info into an existing schema (no change). Mnemonic: 'ss' = Same Schema. Takeaway: Assimilation = fit new info into existing schema (same schema, 'ss'). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Assimilation interprets new information using current schemas (mnemonic: assimilation has 'ss' = same schema). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Accommodation changes the schema; assimilation keeps it the same.
distractor_rationales.C: Conservation is understanding quantity is unchanged despite appearance.
distractor_rationales.D: Equilibrium is the balanced end-state, not the process of fitting in new info.

items.stem: Adjusting or creating a new schema because new information doesn't fit existing ones — e.g., learning a whale is not a fish — is:
items.explanation: Accommodation = change or create a schema to fit new info. Mnemonic: 'cc' = Change/Create. Takeaway: Accommodation = change/create a schema for new info ('cc' = change/create). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Accommodation changes or creates schemas to fit new information (mnemonic: 'cc' = change/create). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Assimilation fits info into an existing schema without change — the opposite.
distractor_rationales.B: Egocentrism is failing to take another's perspective.
distractor_rationales.C: Object permanence is knowing objects exist unseen.

items.stem: In Piaget's model, when new information can be assimilated smoothly, the child returns to a balanced cognitive state called:
items.explanation: Equilibrium = the balanced cognitive state reached by assimilating/accommodating new information (equilibration drives development). Takeaway: Equilibrium = balanced state after assimilating/accommodating new info. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Development moves through equilibrium: assimilate/accommodate new info to restore a balanced state (equilibration). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Disequilibrium is the temporary imbalance that drives accommodation, not the resolved state.
distractor_rationales.B: Egocentrism is a preoperational limitation, not the balanced state.
distractor_rationales.C: Fixation is getting stuck on a wrong problem-solving approach.

items.stem: A problem with a clear starting point and clear criteria for success (e.g., 'turn on the light') is ______; one with an ambiguous goal (e.g., 'live a happy life') is ______.
items.explanation: Well-defined = clear start, end, and success criteria. Ill-defined = ambiguous goal or missing information. Takeaway: Well-defined = clear goal/criteria. Ill-defined = ambiguous goal. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Well-defined problems have clear start/end and success criteria; ill-defined problems have ambiguous goals or lack information. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — clear criteria = well-defined.
distractor_rationales.C: Algorithm/heuristic are solution METHODS, not the problem-clarity distinction.
distractor_rationales.D: Trial-and-error/insight are approaches, not the definition of the problem.

items.stem: A step-by-step procedure that systematically tries options and is guaranteed to eventually find the correct solution (though possibly slow) is a(n):
items.explanation: An algorithm = a systematic step-by-step method guaranteed to find the solution (but can be slow). Takeaway: Algorithm = systematic, guaranteed, but can be slow. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. An algorithm is a methodical, exhaustive procedure that guarantees a solution but can be inefficient. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A heuristic is a shortcut that's faster but not guaranteed.
distractor_rationales.B: Insight is a sudden solution, not a systematic procedure.
distractor_rationales.D: Fixation is getting stuck on a wrong approach.

items.stem: A mental shortcut that reduces the number of options considered — faster than an algorithm but not guaranteed to find the correct answer — is a(n):
items.explanation: A heuristic = a mental shortcut: faster than an algorithm but not guaranteed correct. Takeaway: Heuristic = shortcut (fast, not guaranteed). Algorithm = exhaustive (guaranteed, slow). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A heuristic trims the search space for speed, trading the algorithm's guarantee for efficiency. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: An algorithm is exhaustive and guaranteed, not a shortcut.
distractor_rationales.B: Conservation is a Piagetian concept, unrelated to problem-solving shortcuts.
distractor_rationales.C: Confabulation is filling memory gaps with invented information.

items.stem: Breaking a big problem into subgoals and repeatedly reducing the difference between your current state and the goal state is the heuristic called:
items.explanation: Means-end analysis: break the problem into subgoals, reducing the difference between current and goal states (current → goal). Takeaway: Means-end analysis = reduce the gap between current state and goal (via subgoals). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Means-end analysis reduces the gap between the current and goal states step by step (current state → goal state). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Working backwards starts from the goal and reasons toward the current state — the reverse direction.
distractor_rationales.B: Trial and error tries options at random, without subgoal structure.
distractor_rationales.D: Fixation is getting stuck on a wrong approach.

items.stem: Starting from the goal and reasoning back toward the current state — common in math proofs and mazes — is the heuristic called:
items.explanation: Working backwards: start at the goal and reason back to the current state (goal → current). Useful in proofs and mazes. Takeaway: Working backwards = start at the goal, reason back to the start. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Working backwards begins at the goal and finds connections back to the starting point (goal state → current state). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Means-end analysis works forward from the current state toward the goal.
distractor_rationales.B: Trial and error tries options without a directional strategy.
distractor_rationales.C: Insight is a sudden realization, not a stepwise strategy.

items.stem: Getting stuck approaching a problem the wrong way is fixation; the sudden 'aha!' realization that often breaks it is:
items.explanation: Fixation = stuck on a wrong approach; insight = sudden 'aha' solution (may follow incubation). Takeaway: Fixation = stuck; insight = sudden 'aha' solution (may follow incubation). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fixation is being stuck on an unproductive approach; insight is the sudden solution that overcomes it (sometimes after incubation). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: An algorithm is a systematic procedure, not a sudden realization.
distractor_rationales.C: Assimilation is a Piagetian schema process.
distractor_rationales.D: The recency effect concerns list recall.

items.stem: In decision terms, a Type I error is a ______ and a Type II error is a ______.
items.explanation: Type I error = false positive; Type II error = false negative. Takeaway: Type I = false positive. Type II = false negative. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Type I = false positive (detecting something that isn't there); Type II = false negative (missing something that is there). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — Type I is a false positive.
distractor_rationales.C: Those are correct outcomes, not errors.
distractor_rationales.D: Algorithm/heuristic are problem-solving methods, not error types.

items.stem: After seeing news coverage of shark attacks, people overestimate their risk (though firework accidents kill more). Judging probability by how easily examples come to mind is the:
items.explanation: Availability heuristic: judge probability by how easily examples come to mind (vivid/publicized events seem more likely). Takeaway: Availability heuristic = judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The availability heuristic estimates likelihood by how easily instances are recalled — so vivid, publicized events feel more probable than they are. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The representativeness heuristic judges by similarity to a prototype, not ease of recall.
distractor_rationales.C: Anchoring adjusts from an initial reference value.
distractor_rationales.D: Confirmation bias is seeking confirming evidence, not estimating frequency.

items.stem: Judging that 'Linda' is more likely a feminist bank teller than a bank teller, because she matches a prototype, illustrates the:
items.explanation: Representativeness heuristic: judge probability by resemblance to a prototype (can override actual base rates). Takeaway: Representativeness heuristic = judge by match to a prototype (ignores base rates). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The representativeness heuristic judges probability by how well something matches a prototype — here overriding base rates. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The availability heuristic uses ease of recall, not prototype match.
distractor_rationales.C: Anchoring adjusts from a starting value.
distractor_rationales.D: Framing concerns how options are worded.

items.stem: Believing 'Linda is a bank teller AND a feminist' is more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller' alone is the:
items.explanation: Conjunction fallacy: judging two conditions together as MORE likely than one alone (impossible) — a product of representativeness. Takeaway: Conjunction fallacy = thinking A+B is more likely than A alone (impossible). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The conjunction fallacy: thinking two conditions together are more likely than one alone — statistically impossible — driven by representativeness. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The availability heuristic concerns ease of recall, not this probability error.
distractor_rationales.C: Framing concerns wording of options.
distractor_rationales.D: Belief perseverance is clinging to beliefs despite disconfirmation.

items.stem: When negotiating, the first number mentioned strongly shapes the final figure because people adjust from that reference point. This is the:
items.explanation: Anchoring-and-adjustment: an initial anchor value biases later judgments, which are adjusted (often too little) from it. Takeaway: Anchoring = an initial value biases later estimates (adjust from the anchor). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Anchoring: an initial value (anchor) biases subsequent estimates, which are adjusted — usually insufficiently — from it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The availability heuristic uses ease of recall, not a reference anchor.
distractor_rationales.B: Representativeness uses prototype match, not an anchor value.
distractor_rationales.C: Framing concerns how options are described.

items.stem: Only reading news stories that support your preferred candidate, while avoiding critical ones, is:
items.explanation: Confirmation bias = actively seeking/favoring information that confirms what you already believe. Takeaway: Confirmation bias = seek only confirming evidence. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Confirmation bias is actively seeking (and favoring) information that confirms existing beliefs. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Belief perseverance is clinging to a belief after it's been disconfirmed, not seeking confirming info.
distractor_rationales.B: Overconfidence is overestimating the accuracy of one's judgments.
distractor_rationales.D: Framing concerns how choices are worded.

items.stem: Continuing to hold a belief even after the evidence supporting it has been discredited is:
items.explanation: Belief perseverance: holding onto a belief even after its supporting evidence is discredited. Takeaway: Belief perseverance = keep a belief after evidence is discredited. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Belief perseverance is maintaining a belief despite contradicting/discrediting evidence (rationalizing or ignoring it). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Confirmation bias is seeking confirming info; belief perseverance is clinging after disconfirmation.
distractor_rationales.C: The availability heuristic estimates frequency by recall ease.
distractor_rationales.D: Anchoring biases estimates from a reference value.

items.stem: People choose differently between 'save 200 of 600' and 'let 400 of 600 die' even though the outcomes are identical. This is the:
items.explanation: Framing effect: wording (gain vs. loss framing) changes decisions even when outcomes are identical (risk-averse for gains, risk-seeking for losses). Takeaway: Framing effect = how a choice is worded changes decisions (same outcome). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The framing effect: how options are worded (gains vs. losses) changes choices even when the underlying outcomes are the same — people are risk-averse for gains, risk-seeking for losses. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The availability heuristic concerns ease of recall.
distractor_rationales.B: The conjunction fallacy is a probability error about combined events.
distractor_rationales.C: Anchoring biases estimates from a reference value.

items.stem: Walking into a test sure you know the material — partly because it felt easy to study — only to overestimate your actual ability, is:
items.explanation: Overconfidence = overestimating the accuracy of your own knowledge/judgments (fluency can inflate it). Takeaway: Overconfidence = overestimating your own accuracy/ability. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Overconfidence is overestimating the accuracy of one's knowledge or judgments (sometimes fueled by fluency during study). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Belief perseverance is clinging to a discredited belief.
distractor_rationales.B: Confirmation bias is seeking confirming evidence.
distractor_rationales.D: Anchoring biases numeric estimates from a reference.

items.stem: Spearman used factor analysis to argue that a single underlying factor accounts for people doing well across many mental tasks. This is:
items.explanation: Spearman's g factor = a single general intelligence underlying performance across many domains (found via factor analysis). Takeaway: Spearman = general intelligence (g factor): one factor across domains. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Spearman's g factor is a single general intelligence underlying performance across diverse cognitive tasks (people strong in one area tend to be strong in others). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Emotional intelligence is perceiving/managing emotions, not Spearman's general factor.
distractor_rationales.C: Crystallized intelligence is one type (accumulated knowledge), not the overarching g.
distractor_rationales.D: The representativeness heuristic is a decision-making shortcut, unrelated.

items.stem: Sternberg proposed three types of intelligence: analytical (academic problem-solving), creative (novel ideas/adapting), and:
items.explanation: Sternberg's triarchic theory: analytical (academic), creative (novel/adaptive), practical (everyday problem-solving). Takeaway: Sternberg = analytical + creative + practical intelligence (triarchic). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sternberg's triarchic theory: analytical, creative, and practical ('street smarts') intelligence. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Emotional intelligence is Goleman/Salovey-Mayer's construct, not part of Sternberg's triarchic theory.
distractor_rationales.B: Crystallized intelligence is from the Cattell fluid/crystallized distinction.
distractor_rationales.D: Fluid intelligence is also from Cattell, not Sternberg's three types.

items.stem: Howard Gardner argued that intelligence isn't a single 'book smarts' but several independent intelligences (musical, bodily-kinesthetic, interpersonal, etc.). A common criticism is that:

choices.text: It has been definitively proven by research
It reduces all intelligence to one g factor
It denies that any mental abilities exist
It's hard to test empirically, and some 'intelligences' may be better called talents/abilities

items.explanation: Gardner's multiple intelligences: several independent intelligences — but hard to test, and some may be talents rather than intelligences. Takeaway: Gardner = multiple independent intelligences (criticized as untestable / talents). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gardner's multiple intelligences expanded the concept, but critics note it's difficult to test and may relabel talents as intelligences. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It is criticized precisely because it lacks strong empirical support.
distractor_rationales.B: Gardner argues AGAINST a single g factor, positing many independent intelligences.
distractor_rationales.C: It affirms many abilities — it doesn't deny them.

items.stem: The ability to perceive, understand, manage, and use emotions in oneself and interactions with others is:
items.explanation: Emotional intelligence = perceiving, understanding, managing, and using emotions (in self and others). Takeaway: Emotional intelligence = perceive/understand/manage emotions. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Emotional intelligence is the capacity to perceive, understand, and manage emotions. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fluid intelligence is abstract reasoning with novel problems, not emotion management.
distractor_rationales.B: The g factor is general cognitive ability, not emotional skill.
distractor_rationales.C: Analytical intelligence is academic problem-solving in Sternberg's theory.

items.stem: Reasoning quickly and abstractly to solve a brand-new logic problem, independent of prior knowledge, draws on:
items.explanation: Fluid intelligence = fast, abstract reasoning on novel problems (independent of experience); declines with age. Takeaway: Fluid intelligence = novel abstract reasoning (declines with age). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fluid intelligence (Cattell) is on-the-spot abstract reasoning with novel problems; it tends to decline with age. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge/vocabulary, not novel reasoning.
distractor_rationales.B: Practical intelligence is everyday 'street smarts' in Sternberg's theory.
distractor_rationales.D: Fluid/crystallized is a distinct framework from Spearman's g.

items.stem: Accumulated knowledge, facts, and vocabulary — which tends to grow or stay stable into older adulthood — is:
items.explanation: Crystallized intelligence = accumulated knowledge/vocabulary; grows or stays stable with age (unlike fluid, which declines). Takeaway: Crystallized intelligence = accumulated knowledge/vocab (stable/improves with age). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Crystallized intelligence (Cattell) is accumulated knowledge and verbal skill; it increases or holds steady with age. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fluid intelligence is novel reasoning that declines with age — the opposite trend.
distractor_rationales.B: Creative intelligence (Sternberg) is generating novel ideas, not accumulated knowledge.
distractor_rationales.C: Emotional intelligence concerns emotions, not accumulated facts.

items.stem: On standardized IQ tests, scores are scaled so that the average (mean) is ____ and the standard deviation is ____.
items.explanation: IQ scores: mean = 100, standard deviation = 15. A score reflects your position relative to the population. Takeaway: IQ: mean = 100, SD = 15. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. IQ tests are standardized to a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The mean is 100 and SD is 15, not 50/10.
distractor_rationales.B: That's a z-score scale, not the IQ scale.
distractor_rationales.D: The SD is 15, not 30.

items.stem: Binet's concept of 'mental age' referred to:

choices.text: The child's actual age in years
The age at which the brain stops growing
The chronological age that matches a child's level of intellectual performance

items.explanation: Binet's mental age = the age level of a child's intellectual performance (vs. average for that age). Takeaway: Mental age = performance level expressed as an age (Binet). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Mental age is the age level at which a child is performing intellectually, compared with average performance for that age. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Mental age is about performance level, not literal chronological age.
distractor_rationales.B: It isn't about physical brain-growth cutoff.
distractor_rationales.D: It concerns cognitive, not emotional, performance.

items.stem: Alfred Binet developed the first intelligence test (to identify French schoolchildren needing help). Lewis Terman's revision, standardized for U.S. use and extended to adults, became the:
items.explanation: Binet made the first intelligence test; Terman's revision = the Stanford-Binet (standardized for the U.S., includes adults). Takeaway: Binet = first test; Terman's revision = Stanford-Binet. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Terman (Stanford) revised Binet's test into the Stanford-Binet, incorporating teens and adults. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The WAIS is a separate Wechsler test, not Terman's revision of Binet.
distractor_rationales.C: The MMPI is a personality inventory, not an intelligence test.
distractor_rationales.D: The Rorschach is a projective personality test.

items.stem: Twin and adoption studies of intelligence find the strongest IQ correlation for:

choices.text: Identical twins raised together — with identical twins raised apart still more similar than fraternal twins
Adoptive parents and their adopted children

items.explanation: IQ correlations are highest for identical twins (raised together), and identical-apart > fraternal-together — pointing to strong genetic influence plus some environmental. Takeaway: Twin studies: identical twins most similar in IQ (genetic component) + some environmental influence. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Identical twins (especially raised together) show the highest IQ correlations; identical twins raised apart still correlate more than fraternal twins — evidence of a genetic component, with some environmental influence. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fraternal twins share only ~50% of genes and correlate less than identical twins.
distractor_rationales.C: Unrelated children raised together share environment but not genes, correlating less.
distractor_rationales.D: Adoptive relationships show weaker IQ correlations than genetic ones.

items.stem: Regarding environment's effect on intelligence, the evidence best supports which statement?

choices.text: There is a proven recipe to raise any child to genius
Deprived environments can impair intellectual development, though enrichment beyond adequate levels doesn't reliably create genius
Environment has no effect on intelligence at all
Only genes matter; exposure is irrelevant

items.explanation: Deprived environments impair intelligence, but enrichment beyond adequate levels doesn't reliably create genius — nature AND nurture both contribute. Takeaway: Environment: deprivation harms intelligence; no recipe guarantees genius. Nature + nurture. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Impoverished/deprived environments harm cognitive development, but there's no reliable formula to manufacture genius — both nature and nurture contribute. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: No such reliable 'recipe' for genius exists.
distractor_rationales.C: Environment clearly affects development (e.g., deprivation impairs it).
distractor_rationales.D: Both genes and environment contribute; exposure matters.

items.stem: A student who believes intelligence can improve with effort and learning has a ______ mindset, which is associated with greater achievement over time.
items.explanation: Growth mindset: intelligence is changeable with effort (linked to achievement). Fixed mindset: intelligence is innate/unchangeable. Takeaway: Growth mindset = ability improves with effort. Fixed mindset = ability is innate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A growth mindset (Dweck) treats intelligence as changeable with effort; a fixed mindset treats it as innate and unchangeable. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A fixed mindset sees intelligence as innate/unchangeable — the opposite.
distractor_rationales.B: Convergent thinking is a problem-solving style, not a mindset about ability.
distractor_rationales.D: Egocentric refers to Piaget's perspective-taking limitation.

items.stem: Damage to Broca's area (frontal lobe) produces an aphasia in which the person understands language but struggles to produce fluent speech — speaking in broken, halting words. This is:
items.explanation: Broca's aphasia (frontal): non-fluent/expressive — comprehension intact, but broken, effortful speech. 'Broca's = Broken.' Takeaway: Broca's aphasia = broken/non-fluent speech, comprehension intact (frontal lobe). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Broca's aphasia is non-fluent: comprehension is relatively intact but speech production is effortful and broken. Mnemonic: Broca's = Broken speech. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Wernicke's aphasia is fluent but meaningless, with impaired comprehension — the opposite pattern.
distractor_rationales.C: Conduction aphasia impairs repetition, from arcuate fasciculus damage.
distractor_rationales.D: Global aphasia impairs both production and comprehension (both areas damaged).

items.stem: Damage to Wernicke's area (temporal lobe) produces an aphasia in which the person speaks fluently and grammatically but the speech is meaningless, and comprehension is impaired. This is:
items.explanation: Wernicke's aphasia (temporal): fluent but meaningless speech + impaired comprehension. 'Wernicke's = What?' (comprehension wrecked). Takeaway: Wernicke's aphasia = fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension (temporal lobe). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Wernicke's aphasia is fluent but nonsensical, with poor comprehension (mnemonic: Wernicke's = 'What?' — comprehension is wrecked). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Broca's aphasia is non-fluent with intact comprehension — the reverse.
distractor_rationales.B: Global aphasia impairs both production and comprehension.
distractor_rationales.D: Conduction aphasia specifically impairs repetition.

items.stem: Damage to the arcuate fasciculus, which connects Broca's and Wernicke's areas, produces an aphasia mainly characterized by:

choices.text: Total loss of both comprehension and production
Impaired repetition, despite relatively intact comprehension and fluent speech
Inability to see written words only

items.explanation: Conduction aphasia = arcuate fasciculus damage disconnecting Broca's and Wernicke's → impaired repetition (comprehension/fluency relatively intact). Takeaway: Conduction aphasia = arcuate fasciculus damage → can't repeat (comprehension/fluency intact). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Conduction aphasia results from disconnecting Broca's and Wernicke's areas (arcuate fasciculus), impairing the ability to repeat while comprehension and fluency are relatively preserved. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: There is a deficit — specifically in repetition.
distractor_rationales.B: That's global aphasia (both areas damaged), not conduction.
distractor_rationales.D: That describes a visual/reading deficit, not conduction aphasia.

items.stem: In split-brain patients, the structure that has been severed (often to treat severe epilepsy), preventing the two hemispheres from communicating, is the:
items.explanation: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres; severing it (for epilepsy) produces split-brain phenomena. Takeaway: Split-brain = severed corpus callosum (hemispheres can't communicate). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The corpus callosum is the large bundle of fibers connecting the hemispheres; cutting it produces split-brain effects. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The arcuate fasciculus connects language areas within a hemisphere, not the two hemispheres broadly.
distractor_rationales.B: Broca's area is a language-production region, not the interhemispheric bridge.
distractor_rationales.D: The optic chiasm is where optic nerves partially cross.

items.stem: For most people, language is predominantly processed in the:
items.explanation: Language is predominantly left-hemisphere (dominant for ~90%+). The right hemisphere handles more spatial/emotional-prosody aspects. Takeaway: Language = left hemisphere (dominant in most people). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In about 90%+ of people (especially right-handers), language is left-hemisphere dominant. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The right hemisphere is more associated with spatial/holistic and emotional prosody, not core language.
distractor_rationales.C: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not language.
distractor_rationales.D: Language is typically left-lateralized, not equally split.

items.stem: Because vision is contralateral, in a split-brain patient an object shown ONLY in the LEFT visual field is processed by the right hemisphere — which usually cannot ______, so the patient can't name it aloud.

choices.text: Produce language (the language centers are in the left hemisphere)

items.explanation: Split-brain: left visual field → right hemisphere, but language is in the LEFT hemisphere → the patient sees but can't name the object aloud. Takeaway: Split-brain: left-field object → right hemisphere → can't name it (language is left-hemisphere). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere, but language is left-lateralized — so a split-brain patient sees the object but can't verbally name it (though the left hand can point to it). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The right hemisphere does perceive the object; it just can't verbalize it.
distractor_rationales.C: This concerns naming, not loss of touch in the left hand.
distractor_rationales.D: Breathing control is a brainstem function, unrelated.

items.stem: The view that humans are born with an innate, biological capacity for language — including a 'language acquisition device' (LAD) and universal grammar — is associated with:
items.explanation: Nativist theory (Chomsky): an innate language acquisition device (LAD) and universal grammar make language capacity biological. Takeaway: Nativist = Chomsky: innate LAD + universal grammar. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Chomsky's nativist theory posits an innate LAD and universal grammar underlying all human languages. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Skinner's behaviorist theory says language is learned via operant conditioning, not innate.
