distractor_rationales.B: Vygotsky is linked to the interactionist/social view, not the pure nativist LAD.
distractor_rationales.C: Piaget tied language to cognitive development, not an innate LAD.

items.stem: The view that children acquire language purely through operant conditioning — reinforcement and imitation — is associated with:
items.explanation: Behaviorist theory (Skinner): language is learned via operant conditioning (reinforcement/imitation) — but struggles to explain novel sentences. Takeaway: Behaviorist = Skinner: language learned by conditioning/reinforcement. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Skinner's behaviorist theory: language is learned through reinforcement (e.g., praising 'mama'). A key criticism is it can't easily explain novel, never-heard sentences. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Chomsky's nativist view opposes the purely learned account.
distractor_rationales.C: Vygotsky emphasized social interaction (interactionist), not pure conditioning.
distractor_rationales.D: The critical period is a nativist concept, not the behaviorist mechanism.

items.stem: The view that biological readiness AND social interaction together drive language — children's desire to communicate with others motivates learning — is associated with:
items.explanation: Interactionist theory (Vygotsky): biology + social interaction together — the drive to communicate motivates language learning. Takeaway: Interactionist = Vygotsky: biology + social interaction drive language. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The interactionist approach (Vygotsky) blends biological and social factors: social interaction motivates and shapes language learning. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Skinner's is the pure behaviorist account, not the interactionist blend.
distractor_rationales.C: Chomsky's nativist view emphasizes innate mechanisms, not the social-interaction blend.
distractor_rationales.D: Binet developed intelligence testing, unrelated to language theory.

items.stem: The idea that there is an early window (roughly up to about age 8–9) during which language is most easily acquired, after which it becomes much harder, is the:
items.explanation: Critical (sensitive) period: an early window (up to ~8–9) when language is most readily acquired; harder afterward. Takeaway: Critical period = early window (~to age 8–9) for easiest language learning. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The critical/sensitive period is an early window when the LAD is most effective for language acquisition. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The refractory period is a neuron's brief recovery phase, unrelated to language.
distractor_rationales.C: The serial position effect concerns list recall.
distractor_rationales.D: Object permanence is a Piagetian infant milestone.

items.stem: Which correctly matches a typical language-development milestone?

choices.text: Babbling around 9–12 months; first words around 12–18 months; word combinations by ~18–20 months
First words at 5 years, babbling at 4 years

items.explanation: Timeline: babbling ~9–12 mo → first words ~12–18 mo → word 'explosion'/combining ~18–20 mo → sentences 2–3 yr → rules mastered ~5 yr. Takeaway: Language timeline: babble (~9–12mo) → first words (~12–18mo) → combine (~18–20mo) → rules by ~5yr. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The rough timeline: babbling ~9–12 months, ~one word/month at 12–18 months, a word 'explosion'/combining by ~18–20 months, longer sentences by 2–3 years, rules largely mastered by ~5 years. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Grammar is not mastered at birth; it develops over years.
distractor_rationales.C: Babbling precedes first words and both occur in infancy, not at 4–5 years.
distractor_rationales.D: Language milestones begin in infancy, not at age 10.

items.stem: The strong linguistic-determinism view (the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis) claims that:

choices.text: Language determines thought — you can only think in ways your language allows
Language and thought are entirely unrelated

items.explanation: Strong linguistic determinism (Sapir-Whorf): language determines thought — you can only think what your language allows. Takeaway: Strong Whorf = language DETERMINES thought. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Strong linguistic determinism (Sapir-Whorf) holds that the structure of one's language determines/shapes what one can think. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's the universalist view (thought → language), the opposite direction.
distractor_rationales.C: Whorf argued language strongly influences thought, not that they're unrelated.
distractor_rationales.D: Thought isn't limited to infants; that's unrelated.

items.stem: The weaker, more widely accepted version of the Whorfian idea holds that:

choices.text: Language has no effect on thought
Language influences (but does not fully determine) thought

items.explanation: Weak linguistic relativism: language influences thought (but doesn't fully determine it) — the more accepted version. Takeaway: Weak Whorf/relativism = language INFLUENCES thought (doesn't fully determine). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Weak linguistic relativism: language influences habitual thought without rigidly determining it — the more supported version. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The weak version says language does influence thought, not that it has no effect.
distractor_rationales.B: That's the universalist direction, not linguistic relativism.
distractor_rationales.C: Language and cognition are related but not identical.

items.stem: The view that thought shapes language — human cognition comes first and language is built from universal semantic distinctions — is:
items.explanation: Universalism: thought determines language — cognition comes first, language built from universal semantic distinctions. Takeaway: Universalism = thought DETERMINES language (reverse of Whorf). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Universalism reverses Whorf: underlying thought/cognition determines language, which is built from universal conceptual distinctions. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Strong determinism is the opposite claim (language → thought).
distractor_rationales.B: Behaviorism concerns learning via conditioning, not the thought/language direction.
distractor_rationales.D: The critical period concerns timing of acquisition, not the thought/language relationship.

items.stem: On the language–thought relationship, Piaget and Vygotsky differed in that:

choices.text: Both said language is entirely innate from birth
Piaget said cognitive development drives language (thought first); Vygotsky said social interaction and language converge with development
Both denied any link between language and thought
Piaget said language determines all thought

items.explanation: Piaget: cognition drives language (thought first). Vygotsky: language + thought converge through social interaction. Takeaway: Piaget = thought drives language. Vygotsky = social interaction converges language & thought. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Piaget: thought/cognitive development leads, and language reflects it. Vygotsky: language and thought develop through social interaction and eventually converge. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Neither claimed language is fully innate from birth (that's closer to Chomsky).
distractor_rationales.C: Both saw a link between language and thought.
distractor_rationales.D: Piaget emphasized thought driving language, not language determining thought.

items.stem: The smallest distinct units of SOUND in a language (English has about 40) are called:
items.explanation: Phonemes = smallest units of sound (English ~40). Mnemonic: Phone = sound. Takeaway: Phonemes = smallest sound units (~40 in English). Phone = sound. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Phonemes are the smallest units of sound (mnemonic: Phone = sound). Categorical perception lets us distinguish them. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Morphemes are the smallest units of MEANING, not sound.
distractor_rationales.C: 'Lexeme' refers to a vocabulary item, not a sound unit.
distractor_rationales.D: Syntax concerns sentence structure, not individual sound units.

items.stem: The smallest units of MEANING in a language (e.g., 'cat,' 're-,' '-s') are called:
items.explanation: Morphemes = smallest units of meaning (word stems, prefixes, suffixes); morphology studies their combination. Takeaway: Morphemes = smallest MEANING units. (Phonemes = smallest SOUND units.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Morphemes are the smallest meaningful units; morphology studies how they combine into words. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Phonemes are the smallest units of sound, not meaning.
distractor_rationales.B: Prosody is the rhythm/intonation of speech, not a meaning unit.
distractor_rationales.D: A semantic field is a group of related meanings, not the smallest meaning unit.

items.stem: The component of language concerned with the MEANING of words, phrases, and sentences is:
items.explanation: Semantics = the meaning of words/phrases/sentences (meaning violations → N400 response). Takeaway: Semantics = meaning. (Meaning violation → N400.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Semantics is the study of meaning; violations of meaning produce an N400 brain response. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Syntax concerns grammatical structure/word order, not meaning per se.
distractor_rationales.C: Phonology concerns the sound system.
distractor_rationales.D: Pragmatics concerns language use in context.

items.stem: The component of language governing how words are arranged into grammatically correct sentences is:
items.explanation: Syntax = rules for arranging words into grammatical sentences (grammar violations → P600 response). Takeaway: Syntax = word arrangement/grammar. (Grammar violation → P600.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Syntax is the set of rules for arranging words into sentences; syntactic (grammatical) violations produce a P600 brain response. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Semantics concerns meaning, not word-order rules.
distractor_rationales.B: Phonology concerns the sound system.
distractor_rationales.C: Prosody is intonation/rhythm, not grammatical structure.

items.stem: The component of language dealing with how context and pre-existing knowledge affect meaning — including tone, sarcasm, and social use — is:
items.explanation: Pragmatics = how context and prior knowledge shape meaning (tone, sarcasm, social use); affected by prosody. Takeaway: Pragmatics = language in context (tone, sarcasm, social use). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pragmatics concerns language use in context (and is affected by prosody — rhythm, cadence, intonation). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Phonology is the sound system, not contextual use.
distractor_rationales.C: Morphology concerns units of meaning within words.
distractor_rationales.D: Syntax concerns grammatical arrangement, not contextual/social meaning.

items.stem: The rhythm, stress, cadence, and intonation of speech — which can change meaning (e.g., signaling sarcasm or a question) — is called:
items.explanation: Prosody = the rhythm, stress, and intonation of speech (conveys emphasis, emotion, sarcasm) — shapes pragmatic meaning. Takeaway: Prosody = speech rhythm/intonation (conveys emphasis, emotion, sarcasm). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Prosody is the melodic/rhythmic quality of speech that conveys emphasis, emotion, and intent, shaping pragmatic meaning. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: 'Phonics' refers to sound-letter relationships in reading, not speech melody.
distractor_rationales.C: Syntax is grammatical structure, not intonation.
distractor_rationales.D: A morpheme is a unit of meaning, not the rhythm/intonation of speech.

items.stem: The limbic system's core structures can be recalled with 'HAT Hippo.' These are the:
items.explanation: Limbic system ('HAT Hippo'): Hypothalamus, Amygdala, Thalamus, Hippocampus — emotion and memory. Takeaway: Limbic system = Hypothalamus, Amygdala, Thalamus, Hippocampus (HAT Hippo). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. 'HAT Hippo' = Hypothalamus, Amygdala, Thalamus, Hippocampus — the key limbic structures for emotion and memory. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The adrenal gland is an endocrine organ, not a limbic brain structure.
distractor_rationales.C: The auditory cortex/tectum aren't the limbic core.
distractor_rationales.D: The hindbrain/tegmentum aren't the HAT-Hippo structures.

items.stem: Stimulating the amygdala produces anger, aggression, and fear/anxiety; destroying it produces a 'mellowing' effect. The amygdala is best described as the:
items.explanation: The amygdala = aggression/fear center. Stimulation → anger/fear; bilateral destruction → mellowing (Kluver-Bucy). Takeaway: Amygdala = fear/aggression center. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The amygdala drives aggression and fear responses; bilateral damage produces Kluver-Bucy syndrome (docility, hyperorality, hypersexuality). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The thalamus is the sensory relay station, not the amygdala.
distractor_rationales.C: The hippocampus forms new memories.
distractor_rationales.D: The hypothalamus regulates hunger/thirst.

items.stem: Bilateral destruction of the amygdala can produce a syndrome of hyperorality, hypersexuality, and disinhibited behavior, called:
items.explanation: Kluver-Bucy syndrome = bilateral amygdala destruction → hyperorality, hypersexuality, disinhibition (a 'mellowing'). Takeaway: Kluver-Bucy = bilateral amygdala damage → hyperorality + hypersexuality + disinhibition. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Kluver-Bucy syndrome results from bilateral amygdala damage: hyperorality, hypersexuality, disinhibition, and docility. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Korsakoff's is thiamine-deficiency amnesia, not amygdala damage.
distractor_rationales.B: Wernicke's aphasia is a fluent language disorder.
distractor_rationales.D: Broca's aphasia is non-fluent speech.

items.stem: Within the limbic/sensory system, the structure that acts as a relay station — routing incoming sensory information to the appropriate cortical areas — is the:
items.explanation: The thalamus = sensory relay station (all senses except smell, which bypasses it). Takeaway: Thalamus = sensory relay (all senses but smell bypasses it). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The thalamus is the sensory relay station for all senses except smell (which bypasses it and goes toward the amygdala). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The amygdala processes fear/aggression, not general sensory relay.
distractor_rationales.B: The hippocampus forms new memories.
distractor_rationales.D: The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and the ANS.

items.stem: The limbic structure essential for converting short-term memories into long-term memories — whose destruction causes anterograde amnesia — is the:
items.explanation: The hippocampus converts short-term → long-term memory; damage → anterograde amnesia (can't form new memories). Takeaway: Hippocampus = STM → LTM consolidation; damage → anterograde amnesia. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The hippocampus consolidates new long-term memories; its destruction leaves old memories intact but prevents forming new ones (anterograde amnesia). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The amygdala handles emotional processing, not memory consolidation broadly.
distractor_rationales.C: The thalamus relays sensory information.
distractor_rationales.D: The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis/ANS.

items.stem: The tiny structure below the thalamus that regulates the autonomic nervous system, triggers hormone release, and controls hunger, thirst, sleep, and sex is the:
items.explanation: The hypothalamus regulates the ANS and endocrine system — hunger, thirst, sleep, sex (homeostasis). Takeaway: Hypothalamus = regulates ANS + hormones (hunger, thirst, sleep, sex). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The hypothalamus regulates the ANS and endocrine system (hunger, thirst, sleep, sex, temperature) — the 'homeostasis' hub. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The hippocampus forms new memories.
distractor_rationales.C: The amygdala is the fear/aggression center.
distractor_rationales.D: The thalamus relays sensory information.

items.stem: EEG studies find that positive, joyful emotions are associated with increased activity in which hemisphere?
items.explanation: Positive emotions → more left-hemisphere activity; negative emotions → more right-hemisphere activity. Takeaway: Positive emotion = left hemisphere; negative emotion = right hemisphere. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Positive emotions (joy, enthusiasm) show more left-hemisphere activity; negative emotions show more right-hemisphere activity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The right hemisphere is linked to negative emotions (fear, sadness).
distractor_rationales.C: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not emotional valence.
distractor_rationales.D: Emotional valence does show lateralization in EEG studies.

items.stem: Timid, fearful, and depressed states, and negative emotions, are associated with increased activity in:
items.explanation: Negative emotions (fear, sadness) → more right-hemisphere activity. Takeaway: Negative emotion = right hemisphere activity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Negative emotions correspond to greater right-hemisphere activity (positive emotions to the left). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The left hemisphere is linked to positive emotions.
distractor_rationales.B: Emotional valence involves cortical hemispheres, not just the brainstem.
distractor_rationales.C: The occipital lobe processes vision, not emotional valence.

items.stem: The cortical region responsible for executive control — higher-order planning, decision-making, and appropriate social behavior — is the:
items.explanation: The prefrontal cortex = executive control (planning, decisions, social behavior); undergoes prolonged development. Takeaway: Prefrontal cortex = executive function + social/emotional regulation. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The prefrontal cortex handles executive function and social/emotional regulation; it undergoes the most development from birth. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The occipital cortex processes vision.
distractor_rationales.B: The auditory cortex processes sound.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement.

items.stem: The famous case of Phineas Gage — who became rude and behaved inappropriately after a rod penetrated his brain — demonstrated the role of the ______ in personality and social behavior.
items.explanation: Phineas Gage's prefrontal-cortex injury → personality/social-behavior changes — classic evidence of PFC's role. Takeaway: Phineas Gage = prefrontal cortex damage → personality/social change. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gage's prefrontal damage altered his personality/social conduct, illustrating that region's role in behavior regulation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The hippocampus is for memory, not the personality change Gage showed.
distractor_rationales.B: The cerebellum coordinates movement.
distractor_rationales.D: The occipital lobe processes vision.

items.stem: The autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary responses, has two branches:

choices.text: Sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest)

items.explanation: The ANS has two branches: sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest). Takeaway: ANS: sympathetic (fight/flight) + parasympathetic (rest/digest). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The ANS divides into the sympathetic (fight-or-flight) and parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) branches, with opposing effects. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Somatic/central refer to other nervous-system divisions, not the ANS branches.
distractor_rationales.B: Sensory/motor describe neuron types, not ANS branches.
distractor_rationales.D: Broca's/Wernicke's are language areas.

items.stem: Which set of changes is produced by the SYMPATHETIC (fight-or-flight) response?

choices.text: Pupils constrict, heart rate down, digestion up
Pupils dilate, heart rate up, respiration up, digestion down, adrenaline up
Salivation up, heart rate down, glucose stored
Pupils constrict, adrenaline down, digestion up

items.explanation: Sympathetic: pupils DILATE, ↑heart rate, ↑respiration, ↑adrenaline/glucose, ↓digestion/salivation (get ready to act). Takeaway: Sympathetic (fight/flight): pupils dilate, HR/respiration up, digestion down, adrenaline up. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sympathetic activation dilates pupils, raises heart/respiration rate, releases glucose and adrenaline, and suppresses digestion/salivation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Those are parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) effects.
distractor_rationales.C: Increased salivation and glucose storage are parasympathetic.
distractor_rationales.D: Pupil constriction and increased digestion are parasympathetic.

items.stem: Which set of changes is produced by the PARASYMPATHETIC (rest-and-digest) response?

choices.text: Pupils dilate, heart rate up, digestion down
Adrenaline up, respiration up, glucose released
Pupils dilate, salivation down, heart rate up
Pupils constrict, heart rate down, salivation up, digestion up

items.explanation: Parasympathetic: pupils CONSTRICT, ↓heart rate, ↑salivation, ↑digestion, ↓adrenaline (return to rest). Takeaway: Parasympathetic (rest/digest): pupils constrict, HR down, digestion up, adrenaline down. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Parasympathetic activation constricts pupils, slows the heart, and increases salivation/digestion (returning to calm). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Those are sympathetic (fight-or-flight) effects.
distractor_rationales.B: Increased adrenaline/glucose release is sympathetic.
distractor_rationales.C: Pupil dilation and raised heart rate are sympathetic.

items.stem: The ANS is distinguished from the somatic nervous system because the ANS controls:

choices.text: Involuntary responses (heart rate, digestion, pupil size) not under conscious control

items.explanation: The ANS controls involuntary responses (heart rate, digestion, pupils) — the somatic system controls voluntary movement. Takeaway: ANS = involuntary responses (not conscious control). Somatic = voluntary movement. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The ANS governs involuntary physiological responses; the somatic system controls voluntary movement. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Voluntary skeletal movement is the somatic nervous system's job.
distractor_rationales.C: Conscious decision-making is a cortical/executive function.
distractor_rationales.D: Language production involves Broca's area, not the ANS.

items.stem: Emotion is composed of three interrelated components:
items.explanation: Emotion = physiological (arousal) + behavioral (expression) + cognitive (appraisal) components. Takeaway: Emotion components: physiological + behavioral + cognitive. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Emotion has a physiological component (bodily arousal), a behavioral component (expressions), and a cognitive component (appraisal/interpretation). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Sensory/motor/reflexive describe nervous-system functions, not emotion's components.
distractor_rationales.B: Those are Freudian levels of consciousness, not emotion components.
distractor_rationales.D: Those are nervous-system divisions, not emotion components.

items.stem: The component of emotion involving your interpretation, appraisal, and thoughts about a situation is the:
items.explanation: The cognitive component = your appraisal/interpretation and thoughts about the situation. Takeaway: Cognitive component = appraisal/interpretation of the situation. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The cognitive component is the mental appraisal/interpretation of the situation (and it varies person to person). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The physiological component is bodily arousal (heart rate, muscle tension).
distractor_rationales.B: The behavioral component is outward expression (facial/body language).
distractor_rationales.C: 'Reflexive' isn't one of the three emotion components.

items.stem: How do emotions differ from moods?

choices.text: Emotions last for weeks; moods are instantaneous
Emotions are relatively brief and often have a clear trigger; moods last much longer and are more diffuse
Only moods can be positive or negative

items.explanation: Emotions = brief, often triggered; moods = longer-lasting and diffuse. Takeaway: Emotions = brief/triggered. Moods = long-lasting/diffuse. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Emotions are temporary responses (often to a specific cause); moods are longer-lasting, less targeted affective states. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — emotions are brief, moods are prolonged.
distractor_rationales.C: They are distinct in duration and specificity.
distractor_rationales.D: Both emotions and moods can be positive or negative.

items.stem: Paul Ekman identified six basic emotions with facial expressions recognizable across all cultures. They are:

choices.text: Love, hate, joy, envy, pride, and shame
Trust, anticipation, boredom, awe, guilt, and hope
Happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, anger, and surprise

items.explanation: Ekman's six universal emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, anger, surprise (FAHDSS) — recognized across cultures. Takeaway: Ekman's 6 universal emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, disgust, anger, surprise (FAHDSS). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ekman's six universal emotions (FAHDSS): fear, anger, happiness, disgust, sadness, surprise — with consistent cross-cultural facial expressions. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Those are complex/social emotions, not Ekman's six universal ones.
distractor_rationales.B: Those aren't Ekman's six basic universal emotions.
distractor_rationales.C: Ekman identified six, not two.

items.stem: Darwin's explanation for why basic emotional expressions are recognized worldwide is that:

choices.text: They are entirely learned from one's culture
They are innate and adaptive — they gave a survival advantage (newborns and blind individuals show them too)
They are unique to each individual

items.explanation: Basic emotional expressions are innate and adaptive (Darwin) — shown even by newborns and congenitally blind people. Takeaway: Universal emotions = innate/adaptive (Darwin); shown by newborns + blind individuals. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Darwin argued emotional expression is an innate, adaptive ability aiding survival — supported by newborns and congenitally blind people showing the same expressions. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Their cross-cultural universality argues for innateness, not pure learning.
distractor_rationales.C: Newborns show them, so they aren't adulthood-only.
distractor_rationales.D: They're species-typical and universal, not individually unique.

items.stem: The James-Lange theory of emotion proposes that:

choices.text: Emotion and physiological response occur simultaneously and independently
A stimulus triggers a physiological response first, and our interpretation of that bodily response IS the emotion
We consciously label our arousal to produce emotion
The situation must be cognitively appraised before any arousal

items.explanation: James-Lange: event → physiological response → emotion (you feel afraid because your heart is already racing). Takeaway: James-Lange: arousal FIRST, then emotion (feel afraid because heart races). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. James-Lange: event → physiological arousal → emotion (we feel afraid BECAUSE our heart races). Emotion follows from the bodily reaction. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Simultaneous-and-independent is Cannon-Bard, not James-Lange.
distractor_rationales.C: Labeling arousal is Schachter-Singer's two-factor theory.
distractor_rationales.D: Appraisal-first is Lazarus's theory.

items.stem: The Cannon-Bard theory of emotion proposes that:

choices.text: The emotion is simply an interpretation of bodily arousal
The physiological response and the emotional experience occur at the same time, independently

items.explanation: Cannon-Bard: event → physiological response AND emotion at the same time (simultaneous, independent). Takeaway: Cannon-Bard: arousal and emotion happen SIMULTANEOUSLY (independently). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cannon-Bard: a stimulus triggers physiological arousal AND the conscious emotion simultaneously and independently. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Arousal-then-interpretation is James-Lange.
distractor_rationales.B: Appraisal-first is Lazarus.
distractor_rationales.D: Labeling arousal is Schachter-Singer.

items.stem: The Schachter-Singer (two-factor) theory proposes that emotion results from:

choices.text: Physiological arousal alone, with no cognition
A cognitive appraisal with no bodily arousal
Simultaneous but independent arousal and emotion
Physiological arousal PLUS a cognitive label identifying the reason for the arousal

items.explanation: Schachter-Singer (two-factor): emotion = physiological arousal + a cognitive LABEL for its cause. Takeaway: Schachter-Singer: emotion = arousal + cognitive label (reason for the arousal). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Two-factor theory: you experience arousal, then cognitively label its cause, and the label determines the specific emotion. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Arousal alone (no label) isn't sufficient in two-factor theory.
distractor_rationales.B: Two-factor theory requires physiological arousal, not appraisal alone.
distractor_rationales.C: Simultaneous-and-independent is Cannon-Bard.

items.stem: The Lazarus theory of emotion holds that the FIRST step in an emotional response is:

choices.text: An automatic physiological response with no thought
A facial expression that creates the feeling
A cognitive appraisal (labeling) of the situation, which then triggers both the emotion and the physiological response
Simultaneous arousal and emotion with no appraisal

items.explanation: Lazarus: cognitive appraisal comes FIRST → then emotion + physiological response together. Takeaway: Lazarus: appraisal FIRST → then emotion + physiological response. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lazarus: appraisal comes first — you label the event, and that appraisal produces both the emotion and the bodily response. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A thoughtless physiological-first response is James-Lange.
distractor_rationales.B: Facial-feedback isn't the core Lazarus claim.
distractor_rationales.D: No-appraisal simultaneity is Cannon-Bard.

items.stem: The Yerkes-Dodson law describes the relationship between arousal and performance as:

choices.text: Linear — more arousal always improves performance
Flat — arousal has no effect on performance
An inverted-U — performance peaks at moderate arousal and declines when arousal is too low or too high
U-shaped — performance is best at the extremes

items.explanation: Yerkes-Dodson law: inverted-U — moderate arousal maximizes performance; too little or too much impairs it. Takeaway: Yerkes-Dodson = inverted-U: moderate arousal is best for performance. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Yerkes-Dodson: an inverted-U — moderate arousal is optimal; too little or too much impairs performance (and hard tasks need lower optimal arousal). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Performance doesn't rise indefinitely with arousal — too much hurts.
distractor_rationales.B: Arousal does affect performance (the inverted-U).
distractor_rationales.D: It's an inverted-U (best in the middle), not best at the extremes.

items.stem: The threatening or challenging EVENT itself is the ______; the body's subsequent physical and emotional response is the ______.
items.explanation: Stressor = the threatening event; stress reaction = the body's response to it. Takeaway: Stressor = the event. Stress reaction = the body's response. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The stressor is the triggering event; the stress reaction is the physical/emotional response to it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the event is the stressor, the response is the reaction.
distractor_rationales.C: Appraisal is the interpretation, not the event itself.
distractor_rationales.D: Coping is how one manages stress, not the event.

items.stem: Lazarus's appraisal theory of stress holds that stress arises less from events themselves and more from:

choices.text: Our cognitive appraisal (interpretation) of those events
The physical intensity of the event alone

items.explanation: Lazarus: stress comes from our appraisal of events, in primary and secondary stages — not the events alone. Takeaway: Lazarus appraisal theory: stress depends on how you INTERPRET the event. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lazarus: stress depends on how we appraise/interpret an event, in two stages (primary and secondary appraisal). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The event's physical intensity matters less than its appraisal, per Lazarus.
distractor_rationales.C: Genetics isn't the core of Lazarus's appraisal theory.
distractor_rationales.D: Appraisal, not chance, drives the stress response.

items.stem: In Lazarus's model, primary appraisal is:

choices.text: Deciding whether an event is irrelevant, benign/positive, or stressful/negative
Evaluating your resources and ability to cope
The long-term health consequence of stress

items.explanation: Primary appraisal = judging whether an event is irrelevant, benign/positive, or stressful/negative. Takeaway: Primary appraisal = is it irrelevant, benign, or stressful? The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Primary appraisal assesses the situation (irrelevant, benign/positive, or stressful); if stressful, one proceeds to secondary appraisal. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Assessing coping ability is SECONDARY appraisal.
distractor_rationales.C: Primary appraisal is a cognitive judgment, not the physiological response.
distractor_rationales.D: Health consequences follow the stress response, not the appraisal step.

items.stem: Secondary appraisal (following a stressful primary appraisal) evaluates:

choices.text: Whether the event is relevant at all
The exact cortisol level in the blood
Your ability and resources to cope — appraising harm, threat, and challenge

items.explanation: Secondary appraisal = evaluating your resources/ability to cope (harm, threat, challenge). Takeaway: Secondary appraisal = can I cope? (harm/threat/challenge). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Secondary appraisal assesses one's capacity to cope — harm already done, potential threat, and the challenge of overcoming it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Judging relevance is primary appraisal.
distractor_rationales.B: Cortisol level is a physiological measure, not the appraisal.
distractor_rationales.C: Muscle relaxation is a coping technique, not the appraisal step.

items.stem: Which correctly identifies a category of stressor and an example?

choices.text: Ambient stressors — a single major life change like marriage
Significant life changes — background pollution and noise
Daily hassles — minor recurring irritations (traffic, spam, lost keys), often considered a major source of stress

items.explanation: Four stressor types: significant life changes, catastrophic events, daily hassles (minor recurring), and ambient stressors (pollution/noise/crowding). Takeaway: Stressors: life changes, catastrophes, daily hassles, ambient stressors. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Daily hassles are minor recurring irritations; many researchers consider them a major source of chronic stress. (Others: significant life changes, catastrophic events, ambient stressors.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Catastrophic events are large-scale disasters, not minor annoyances.
distractor_rationales.B: Ambient stressors are background environmental factors (pollution/noise), not a single life change.
distractor_rationales.C: Significant life changes are major personal events, not background pollution.

items.stem: Walter Cannon's term for the sympathetic-nervous-system response to a threat — raising heart rate and respiration and diverting blood to vital organs — is:
items.explanation: Fight-or-flight (Cannon) = acute sympathetic response: ↑heart rate, ↑respiration, blood to vital organs, digestion/immune down. Takeaway: Fight-or-flight (Cannon) = sympathetic threat response (HR/respiration up, blood to core). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cannon's fight-or-flight is the acute sympathetic response mobilizing the body to confront or flee a threat. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Tend-and-befriend is an alternative social response, not the sympathetic mobilization itself.
distractor_rationales.C: GAS (Selye) is the three-phase stress model, not this acute term.
distractor_rationales.D: Homeostasis is the balanced baseline the response departs from.

items.stem: In the endocrine stress response, the adrenal MEDULLA releases catecholamines — namely:
items.explanation: Adrenal medulla → catecholamines: epinephrine + norepinephrine (fast stress response). Takeaway: Adrenal medulla = epinephrine + norepinephrine (catecholamines). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine (catecholamines, tyrosine derivatives) in the fast stress response. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Cortisol/aldosterone come from the adrenal CORTEX, not the medulla.
distractor_rationales.C: Insulin/glucagon are pancreatic hormones.
distractor_rationales.D: Melatonin (pineal) and oxytocin (posterior pituitary) aren't adrenal catecholamines.

items.stem: The adrenal CORTEX releases a glucocorticoid steroid hormone that redistributes glucose and suppresses the immune system during stress. This is:
items.explanation: Adrenal cortex → cortisol (glucocorticoid): raises glucose, suppresses immunity. 'COTisol from the CORTex.' Takeaway: Adrenal cortex = cortisol (glucocorticoid; raises glucose, suppresses immunity). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cortisol is the glucocorticoid from the adrenal cortex (mnemonic: COTisol from the CORTex); it raises available glucose and suppresses immunity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Epinephrine is a catecholamine from the medulla, not the cortex.
distractor_rationales.B: Norepinephrine is a catecholamine from the medulla.
distractor_rationales.C: Oxytocin is a bonding hormone, not an adrenal glucocorticoid.

items.stem: An alternative stress response — seeking social support and bonding — linked to oxytocin and often stronger in women, is:
items.explanation: Tend-and-befriend = coping by seeking social support/bonding (oxytocin-linked; often stronger in women). Takeaway: Tend-and-befriend = social-support stress response (oxytocin, often stronger in women). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Tend-and-befriend involves nurturing and social bonding (oxytocin-linked); oxytocin ties to estrogen, which may explain the stronger effect in women. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fight-or-flight is the confront/flee sympathetic response, not social bonding.
distractor_rationales.C: GAS is the three-phase physiological model.
distractor_rationales.D: The alarm phase is the first stage of GAS, not the social-support response.

items.stem: Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes the body's response to prolonged stress in three phases, in order:
items.explanation: Selye's GAS: alarm → resistance → exhaustion (mobilize → sustained coping → depletion/illness). Takeaway: GAS (Selye): alarm → resistance → exhaustion. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. GAS: alarm (mobilize for fight-or-flight) → resistance (sustained coping, high cortisol) → exhaustion (resources depleted, illness risk). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Alarm comes first (the initial reaction), not resistance.
distractor_rationales.B: That's reversed — alarm is first, exhaustion last.
distractor_rationales.D: Resistance precedes exhaustion, not the reverse.

items.stem: A key documented effect of chronic stress on the immune system is that it:

choices.text: Suppresses immune function, making a person more susceptible to illness (e.g., slower wound healing)
Has no effect on the immune system

items.explanation: Chronic stress suppresses immunity (via cortisol) → slower healing, more infections. (Acute stress can transiently overactivate/inflame.) Takeaway: Chronic stress suppresses immunity → slower healing, more illness. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Chronic stress (via sustained cortisol) suppresses immune function — studies show slower wound healing and greater susceptibility to infection. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Chronic stress weakens, not strengthens, immunity.
distractor_rationales.C: It clearly affects immunity (suppression).
distractor_rationales.D: Stress doesn't cure infections; it raises susceptibility.

items.stem: The two brain areas with the highest density of glucocorticoid (cortisol) receptors — and thus most vulnerable to stress-induced atrophy — are the:
items.explanation: Cortisol receptors are densest in the hippocampus (memory) and frontal cortex (judgment/planning) — both atrophy with chronic stress. Takeaway: Most glucocorticoid receptors: hippocampus + frontal cortex (both atrophy under chronic stress). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The hippocampus (memory/learning) and frontal cortex (impulse control, judgment, planning) are dense in cortisol receptors and show atrophy under chronic stress. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The cerebellum and pons aren't the main glucocorticoid-receptor sites.
distractor_rationales.C: These aren't the highest-density cortisol-receptor regions.
distractor_rationales.D: The adrenal glands release cortisol; they aren't the brain targets that atrophy.

items.stem: A major emotional effect of chronic stress is depression, whose core feature — the inability to experience pleasure — is called:
items.explanation: Anhedonia = inability to experience pleasure — a core feature of stress-related depression. Takeaway: Anhedonia = can't feel pleasure (core of depression). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Anhedonia (loss of pleasure) is central to depression; it can make a person perceive even more events as stressors. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Anosmia is loss of smell.
distractor_rationales.C: Alexithymia is difficulty identifying/describing emotions, not loss of pleasure.
distractor_rationales.D: Anhidrosis is the inability to sweat.

items.stem: Part of the biological backing for stress-related depression is that, under chronic stress, the anterior cingulate cortex:
items.explanation: Under stress, the anterior cingulate cortex stops responding normally to serotonin — a biological link to depression. Takeaway: Chronic stress → anterior cingulate stops responding to serotonin → depression link. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The anterior cingulate (anterior frontal cortex) reduces its serotonin responsiveness under stress, contributing to depression. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The mechanism described is reduced serotonin responsiveness, not dopamine overproduction.
distractor_rationales.C: It becomes LESS, not more, responsive to serotonin.
distractor_rationales.D: It doesn't shut down sensory input; the issue is serotonin signaling.

items.stem: After repeatedly experiencing uncontrollable stress, a person comes to believe they have no control and stops trying to cope — spiraling toward depression. This is:
items.explanation: Learned helplessness: repeated uncontrollable stress → belief that nothing can be done → loss of coping → depression. Takeaway: Learned helplessness = learning you have no control → stop coping → depression (Seligman). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Learned helplessness (Seligman): repeated loss of control teaches the belief that outcomes are uncontrollable, eroding coping and driving depression. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Proactive coping is anticipating and preparing for stressors — the opposite.
distractor_rationales.C: Cognitive flexibility is reappraising a stressor adaptively.
distractor_rationales.D: Tend-and-befriend is a social stress response.

items.stem: Beyond depression, your notes group the emotional/behavioral effects of stress as three A's:
items.explanation: Stress's three A's: anger, anxiety, addiction. Takeaway: Three A's of stress: Anger, Anxiety, Addiction. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The 'three A's' of stress responses: anger, anxiety, and addiction. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Those aren't the three stress A's.
distractor_rationales.B: Aggression relates to anger, but the trio is anger/anxiety/addiction.
distractor_rationales.D: Those are unrelated clinical terms, not the stress trio.

items.stem: Friedman and Rosenman linked heart disease to a personality type. The type at higher risk — competitive, easily angered, and hostile — is:
items.explanation: Type A (competitive, hostile, easily angered) → higher heart-disease risk (Friedman & Rosenman); the toxic ingredient is hostility. Anger accompanies the 'fight' response. Takeaway: Type A (hostile/competitive) = heart-disease risk; toxic part = hostility. Type B = easygoing. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Type A (competitive, hostile, easily angered) was linked to greater heart-disease risk; the toxic component is specifically hostility/anger. Type B is easygoing. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Type B is easygoing and at lower risk.
distractor_rationales.B: 'Type C' isn't the Friedman-Rosenman category tied to heart disease here.
distractor_rationales.C: Type D isn't the pair studied by Friedman and Rosenman.

items.stem: Among the stress responses, anxiety centers on which brain structure — the one handling fears and phobias?
items.explanation: Anxiety centers on the amygdala (fears/phobias) and accompanies the 'flight' aspect of the stress response. Takeaway: Anxiety = amygdala (fear/phobia); accompanies flight. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Anxiety is centered on the amygdala (fears/phobias); it accompanies the 'flight' aspect of the sympathetic response. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not fear/anxiety.
distractor_rationales.C: The hippocampus handles memory, not the fear center.
distractor_rationales.D: The pons is a hindbrain relay, not the fear center.

items.stem: Your notes explain that stress raises addiction risk partly because impaired functioning of the ______ worsens judgment and coping choices.
items.explanation: Stress impairs the frontal cortex (reasoning) → worse judgment → higher risk of addictive/maladaptive coping. Takeaway: Stress impairs frontal cortex (reasoning) → poor coping choices → addiction risk. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Stress impairs the frontal cortex (reasoning/judgment), so a person is more likely to choose maladaptive coping like alcohol or tobacco. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not judgment.
distractor_rationales.B: The occipital cortex processes vision.
distractor_rationales.C: The cochlea is a hearing organ.

items.stem: A robust finding (Sapolsky's baboons, the Whitehall studies) is that a major buffer against stress is:

choices.text: A complete lack of any responsibility
A sense of perceived control over one's situation

items.explanation: Perceived control buffers stress — low control/status is tied to higher stress (Sapolsky, Whitehall). Takeaway: Perceived control lowers stress; low control (low status) raises it. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Greater perceived control is associated with lower stress; low control (low rank/status) is linked to higher stress. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Lack of control raises, not lowers, stress.
distractor_rationales.B: Higher arousal is part of the stress response, not a buffer.
distractor_rationales.C: Isolation tends to worsen stress; social support buffers it.

items.stem: Confiding in others, feeling understood, and belonging to a supportive community reduces stress. This coping resource is:
items.explanation: Social support = confiding in and belonging to others → lower stress and healthier habits. Takeaway: Social support = sharing/belonging → lower stress. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Social support lets us share difficult feelings and feel less alone, and is linked to healthier eating/sleep/exercise and lower stress. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Proactive coping is anticipating a future stressor, a different mechanism.
distractor_rationales.B: Overcompensation is a maladaptive coping category.
distractor_rationales.D: Learned helplessness is a route into depression, not a coping resource.

items.stem: Coping that targets the stressor itself — acting to master, minimize, or eliminate it — is ______ coping; coping that manages the emotional reaction instead is ______ coping.
items.explanation: Problem-focused coping changes the stressor; emotion-focused coping manages your reaction to it. Takeaway: Problem-focused = fix the stressor. Emotion-focused = manage the feelings. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Problem-focused coping addresses the stressor; emotion-focused coping manages the feelings it produces. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — problem-focused targets the stressor.
distractor_rationales.C: Proactive/reactive describe timing, not the problem-vs-emotion target.
distractor_rationales.D: Both problem- and emotion-focused coping can be adaptive.

items.stem: Anticipating a difficult upcoming challenge and preparing for how you'll handle it BEFORE it happens is:
items.explanation: Proactive coping = anticipate a future stressor and prepare before it arrives (reduces its impact). Takeaway: Proactive coping = anticipate + prepare before the stressor hits. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Proactive coping reduces a stressor's impact by anticipating and preparing for it in advance. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reactive coping responds after the stressor has already hit.
distractor_rationales.B: Avoidance coping evades the stressor rather than preparing for it.
distractor_rationales.D: Emotion-focused coping manages feelings, not advance preparation.

items.stem: Coping by finding personal significance or growth in a stressful experience — drawing meaning from it — is:
items.explanation: Meaning-focused coping = deriving meaning/growth from the stressful experience. Takeaway: Meaning-focused coping = find meaning in the stressor. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Meaning-focused coping concentrates on deriving meaning from the stressful experience. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor itself, not its meaning.
distractor_rationales.B: Overcompensation is a maladaptive category.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensitization is a maladaptive rehearsal of fearful events.

items.stem: Changing how you interpret a stressful situation — reappraising it so it feels less threatening — draws on:
items.explanation: Cognitive flexibility = reappraising a stressor so it feels less threatening (perception shapes stress). Takeaway: Cognitive flexibility = reframe the stressor (perception drives stress). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cognitive flexibility lets you reframe a stressor; perception of the situation strongly shapes how stressful it is. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Learned helplessness is the opposite — rigid belief in no control.
distractor_rationales.B: Anhedonia is loss of pleasure, not reappraisal.
distractor_rationales.D: Fasciculation is a muscle twitch, unrelated.

items.stem: Regular exercise and meditation reduce stress in part through measurable physiological changes, including:

choices.text: Lower heart rate and blood pressure (and, for exercise, neurogenesis)

items.explanation: Exercise and meditation lower heart rate/BP (exercise also drives neurogenesis) → less stress, lower cardiovascular risk. Takeaway: Exercise/meditation → lower HR/BP (exercise: neurogenesis) → less stress. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Exercise and meditation lower heart rate/BP (and exercise promotes neurogenesis), reducing stress and cardiovascular risk. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: They lower, not raise, stress hormones over time.
distractor_rationales.B: They lower blood pressure.
distractor_rationales.C: They support, rather than reduce, healthy immune function.

items.stem: Using humor — finding things to laugh about — to master a painful situation and reduce its sting is a form of:
items.explanation: Humor is a positive, adaptive coping method — mastering a painful situation by finding lightness in it. Takeaway: Humor = adaptive coping (master pain by finding the funny). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Humor is one of the most positive coping methods — it helps you master painful situations by turning them into something bearable. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Humor here is constructive, not avoidance.
distractor_rationales.B: Overcompensation is a maladaptive category (e.g., aggression, dominance).
distractor_rationales.D: Surrender is a maladaptive category (compliance, dependence).

items.stem: The key difference between adaptive and maladaptive coping is that maladaptive coping:

choices.text: Reduces symptoms short-term but maintains the disorder long-term (stress often stays or rises)
Reliably lowers stress and resolves the problem
Is always more effective than adaptive coping
Only occurs in people without any stress

items.explanation: Maladaptive coping eases symptoms short-term but maintains the disorder long-term; adaptive coping genuinely reduces stress. Takeaway: Maladaptive coping = short-term relief, long-term problem persists. Adaptive = truly reduces stress. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Maladaptive coping can relieve symptoms briefly but sustains the underlying problem; adaptive/constructive coping actually reduces stress. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That describes adaptive coping, not maladaptive.
distractor_rationales.C: Maladaptive coping is generally less effective long-term.
distractor_rationales.D: Maladaptive coping is a response to stress, not an absence of it.

items.stem: Your notes group maladaptive coping into three broad categories:
items.explanation: Maladaptive coping categories: overcompensation, surrender, avoidance. Takeaway: Maladaptive coping: overcompensation, surrender, avoidance. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Maladaptive coping falls into overcompensation, surrender, and avoidance. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Alarm/resistance/exhaustion are the GAS phases, not coping categories.
distractor_rationales.B: Those are appraisal stages, not maladaptive-coping categories.
distractor_rationales.D: Fight/flight/freeze are acute stress responses, not the coping categories.

items.stem: Coping with a threat by counterattacking — aggression, dominance, manipulation, or excessive status-seeking — is the maladaptive category of:
items.explanation: Overcompensation = counterattacking the threat: aggression, dominance, manipulation, status-seeking. Takeaway: Overcompensation = counterattack (aggression, dominance, manipulation). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Overcompensation fights the threat through aggression, control, dominance, recognition-seeking, or manipulation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Surrender is giving in — compliance and dependence.
distractor_rationales.C: Avoidance is withdrawing or escaping, not counterattacking.
distractor_rationales.D: Proactive coping is an adaptive, anticipatory strategy.

items.stem: Coping by giving in to the threat — excessive compliance, dependence, clinging, and people-pleasing — is the maladaptive category of:
items.explanation: Surrender = giving in: compliance, dependence, clinging, people-pleasing. Takeaway: Surrender = give in (compliance, dependence, people-pleasing). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Surrender means submitting to the threat through compliance and dependence. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Overcompensation counterattacks the threat, the opposite of giving in.
distractor_rationales.C: Avoidance evades rather than submits.
distractor_rationales.D: Meaning-focused coping is an adaptive strategy.

items.stem: Coping by escaping the threat — social withdrawal, compulsive distraction, addictive self-soothing, or retreating into fantasy — is the maladaptive category of:
items.explanation: Avoidance = escaping the threat: withdrawal, compulsive distraction, addictive self-soothing, fantasy. Takeaway: Avoidance = escape (withdrawal, distraction, self-soothing, fantasy). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Avoidance evades the threat via withdrawal, compulsive stimulation-seeking, addictive self-soothing, or psychological escape (dissociation, fantasy). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Overcompensation counterattacks; it doesn't evade.
distractor_rationales.B: Surrender submits to the threat rather than escaping it.
distractor_rationales.C: Cognitive flexibility is an adaptive reappraisal strategy.

items.stem: A maladaptive avoidance strategy in which the mind separates or compartmentalizes thoughts, memories, and emotions — often associated with post-traumatic stress — is:
items.explanation: Dissociation = mentally separating/compartmentalizing thoughts and emotions; often linked to PTSD. Takeaway: Dissociation = compartmentalize thoughts/emotions (linked to PTSD). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Dissociation compartmentalizes distressing thoughts/emotions and is often associated with PTSD. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Sensitization is rehearsing/anticipating fearful events, not compartmentalizing.
distractor_rationales.C: Overcompensation is counterattacking, not mental separation.
distractor_rationales.D: Proactive coping is an adaptive strategy.

items.stem: The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) consists of:

choices.text: Everything else — the nerves and ganglia outside the brain and spinal cord

items.explanation: CNS = brain + spinal cord. PNS = everything else (nerves, ganglia; 12 cranial + 31 spinal nerve pairs). Takeaway: CNS = brain + spinal cord. PNS = nerves/ganglia outside it. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = all the nerves and ganglia outside it (afferent + efferent neurons; 12 cranial + 31 spinal nerve pairs). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The cerebral hemispheres are part of the CNS (brain).
distractor_rationales.C: The spinal cord is part of the CNS.
distractor_rationales.D: The brain and cerebellum are CNS structures.

items.stem: Neurons that carry sensory information TOWARD the central nervous system are ______; neurons that carry motor commands AWAY from it are ______.
items.explanation: Afferent = sensory, toward CNS (Approach); Efferent = motor, away from CNS (Exit). Takeaway: Afferent = toward CNS (sensory). Efferent = away (motor). A=approach, E=exit. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Afferent = sensory, toward the CNS ('Approach'); efferent = motor, away from the CNS ('Exit'). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — afferent is toward, efferent is away.
distractor_rationales.B: Sympathetic/parasympathetic are autonomic branches, not the afferent/efferent distinction.
distractor_rationales.C: Upper/lower describe motor neurons, not the sensory/motor direction.

items.stem: The developing brain is organized into three primary divisions:

choices.text: Left brain, right brain, and brainstem

items.explanation: Three primary brain divisions: forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain. Takeaway: Brain divisions: forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The three primary divisions are forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The spinal cord isn't one of the three brain divisions.
distractor_rationales.C: These are individual structures, not the three primary divisions.
distractor_rationales.D: Hemispheres and brainstem aren't the three developmental divisions.

items.stem: The forebrain develops into the ______, which includes the cerebral hemispheres and handles higher functions like cognition and emotion.
items.explanation: Forebrain → cerebrum (cerebral hemispheres): higher functions — cognition, emotion. Takeaway: Forebrain → cerebrum (higher functions). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The forebrain becomes the cerebrum (cerebral hemispheres) — cognition, emotion, voluntary action. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The pons develops from the hindbrain.
distractor_rationales.C: The medulla develops from the hindbrain.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum develops from the hindbrain.

items.stem: The hindbrain develops into which set of structures?
items.explanation: Hindbrain → pons, medulla, cerebellum (vital autonomic functions + movement coordination). Takeaway: Hindbrain → pons + medulla + cerebellum. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The hindbrain becomes the pons, medulla, and cerebellum (vital functions and movement coordination). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The cerebrum and thalamus are forebrain-derived.
distractor_rationales.C: The cerebral hemispheres come from the forebrain.
distractor_rationales.D: The hypothalamus and amygdala are forebrain structures.

items.stem: The peripheral nervous system includes how many pairs of cranial nerves and spinal nerves?
items.explanation: PNS: 12 cranial + 31 spinal nerve pairs. Takeaway: 12 cranial nerve pairs, 31 spinal nerve pairs. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — 12 cranial, 31 spinal.
distractor_rationales.B: These counts are incorrect.
distractor_rationales.D: These counts are incorrect.

items.stem: A motor unit is defined as:

choices.text: A single motor neuron together with all the skeletal muscle fibers it innervates
A single muscle fiber and all neurons touching it
The brain region that plans movement
A cluster of sensory receptors in muscle

items.explanation: A motor unit = one motor neuron + all the muscle fibers it innervates. Takeaway: Motor unit = one motor neuron + all fibers it controls. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A motor unit = one motor neuron plus every muscle fiber it controls — the functional unit of muscle contraction. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: It's one neuron to many fibers, not one fiber to many neurons.
distractor_rationales.C: The motor unit is peripheral, not a brain planning region.
distractor_rationales.D: Those would be proprioceptors (e.g., muscle spindles), not a motor unit.

items.stem: A lower motor neuron (LMN) is the efferent neuron that:

choices.text: Carries sensory information from the skin to the brain
Synapses directly on skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction
Connects two regions of the cerebral cortex
Relays pain signals to the thalamus

items.explanation: A lower motor neuron (LMN) is the efferent neuron that synapses on skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction. Takeaway: LMN = efferent neuron → skeletal muscle at the NMJ. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The LMN is the final efferent neuron, contacting skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) to trigger contraction. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That describes an afferent (sensory) neuron.
distractor_rationales.C: That describes cortical association fibers, not an LMN.
distractor_rationales.D: That describes a sensory pain pathway, not the motor LMN.

items.stem: The synapse where a motor neuron meets and signals a skeletal muscle fiber is the:
items.explanation: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) = the motor neuron–skeletal muscle synapse (acetylcholine). Takeaway: NMJ = motor neuron ↔ muscle synapse. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The neuromuscular junction is the motor neuron–muscle synapse (using acetylcholine). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A node of Ranvier is a gap in myelin along an axon, not a neuron–muscle synapse.
distractor_rationales.C: A glomerulus is an olfactory bulb structure.
distractor_rationales.D: The optic chiasm is where optic nerves cross.

items.stem: Damage to a lower motor neuron produces a characteristic set of signs. Which set is correct?

choices.text: Increased muscle tone and brisk reflexes

items.explanation: LMN signs: atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia (everything DOWN/loose). UMN signs are the opposite (hypertonia, hyperreflexia). Takeaway: LMN damage = atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia (all 'down'). UMN = 'up' (hyper). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. LMN lesions cause muscle atrophy, fasciculations (involuntary twitches), hypotonia (low tone), and hyporeflexia (reduced reflexes). (Upper motor neuron lesions instead cause hypertonia/hyperreflexia.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and spasticity are UPPER motor neuron signs.
distractor_rationales.B: Increased tone and brisk reflexes are upper motor neuron signs.
distractor_rationales.C: LMN damage clearly produces motor changes (weakness, atrophy).

items.stem: The small, involuntary muscle twitches seen with lower motor neuron damage are called:
items.explanation: Fasciculations = involuntary skeletal-muscle twitches — a hallmark lower-motor-neuron sign. Takeaway: Fasciculations = involuntary muscle twitches (LMN sign). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fasciculations are visible involuntary twitches of skeletal muscle, a hallmark LMN sign. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Retinal fibrillations aren't a thing; fasciculations are muscle twitches.
distractor_rationales.C: Saccades are rapid eye movements, not muscle twitches from LMN damage.
distractor_rationales.D: Tonic-clonic seizures are a generalized seizure type, not LMN twitches.

items.stem: The fast-adapting mechanoreceptor in the superficial skin that detects light touch and flutter with a small receptive field is the:
items.explanation: Meissner's corpuscle = fast-adapting, superficial, light touch/flutter, small receptive field. Takeaway: Meissner = fast-adapting, light touch/flutter, small field (superficial). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Meissner's corpuscles are fast-adapting, superficial receptors for light touch/flutter with small receptive fields (fine spatial detail, velocity). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Pacinian corpuscles are deep, fast-adapting receptors for vibration, with large receptive fields.
distractor_rationales.B: Ruffini endings are slow-adapting stretch receptors.
distractor_rationales.C: Merkel discs are slow-adapting fine-touch/pressure receptors.

items.stem: The slow-adapting mechanoreceptor that senses sustained fine touch, pressure, and edges/detail with a small receptive field is the:
items.explanation: Merkel disc = slow-adapting, sustained fine touch/pressure, small receptive field (detail). Takeaway: Merkel = slow-adapting, fine touch/pressure/detail (sustained). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Merkel discs are slow-adapting receptors for sustained fine touch/pressure and fine spatial detail. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Pacinian corpuscles are fast-adapting vibration receptors.
distractor_rationales.B: Meissner's corpuscles are fast-adapting flutter receptors.
distractor_rationales.D: Ruffini endings sense skin stretch (slow-adapting, large field).

items.stem: The deep, fast-adapting mechanoreceptor that detects vibration and deep pressure (responding to acceleration) with a large receptive field is the:
items.explanation: Pacinian corpuscle = deep, fast-adapting, vibration/deep pressure, large field. Mnemonic: 'Phone vibrates.' Takeaway: Pacinian = deep, fast-adapting, vibration (Phone vibrates). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pacinian corpuscles are deep, fast-adapting receptors for vibration/deep pressure with large receptive fields (mnemonic: Pacinian = Phone vibrates). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Merkel discs are slow-adapting fine-touch receptors.
distractor_rationales.C: Meissner's corpuscles are superficial flutter receptors with small fields.
distractor_rationales.D: Ruffini endings are slow-adapting stretch receptors.

items.stem: The slow-adapting mechanoreceptor in the deeper dermis that detects skin stretch, with a large receptive field, is the:
items.explanation: Ruffini ending = slow-adapting, skin stretch, large field. Mnemonic: Ruffini = stRetch. Takeaway: Ruffini = slow-adapting, skin stRetch, large field. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ruffini endings are slow-adapting receptors for skin stretch (mnemonic: Ruffini = stRetch), with large receptive fields. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Meissner's corpuscles sense flutter (fast-adapting, small field).
distractor_rationales.C: Pacinian corpuscles sense vibration (fast-adapting).
distractor_rationales.D: Merkel discs sense fine touch/pressure, not stretch.

items.stem: Sorted by adaptation, which pairing is correct?

choices.text: Fast-adapting: Meissner & Pacinian (detect change/vibration); slow-adapting: Merkel & Ruffini (detect sustained pressure/stretch)
Fast-adapting: Merkel & Ruffini; slow-adapting: Meissner & Pacinian

items.explanation: Fast-adapting = Meissner + Pacinian (change/vibration); slow-adapting = Merkel + Ruffini (sustained pressure/stretch). Takeaway: Fast-adapting: Meissner + Pacinian. Slow-adapting: Merkel + Ruffini. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fast-adapting (Meissner, Pacinian) signal change and vibration; slow-adapting (Merkel, Ruffini) signal sustained pressure and stretch. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — Merkel and Ruffini are the slow-adapting pair.
distractor_rationales.C: Merkel and Ruffini are slow-adapting, not fast.
distractor_rationales.D: Meissner and Pacinian are fast-adapting, not slow.

items.stem: Mechanoreceptors sense pressure/vibration/touch, nociceptors sense pain, and thermoreceptors sense temperature. Which stimulus–receptor pairing is correct?
items.explanation: Receptor classes: mechano (touch/pressure/vibration), noci (pain), thermo (temperature), photo (light), chemo (chemicals). Takeaway: Mechano=touch, noci=pain, thermo=temp, photo=light, chemo=chemicals. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Photoreceptors (rods/cones) detect light. Mechanoreceptors = pressure/touch/vibration; nociceptors = pain; thermoreceptors = temperature; chemoreceptors = chemicals (taste/smell, blood pH/CO₂). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Chemoreceptors detect chemicals, not light.
distractor_rationales.B: Mechanoreceptors detect pressure/touch; thermoreceptors detect temperature.
distractor_rationales.D: Nociceptors detect pain/noxious stimuli, not sound.

items.stem: Every reflex has two parts: an afferent limb and an efferent limb. These carry, respectively:

choices.text: The motor response and the sensory stimulus
The sensory stimulus (afferent) and the motor response (efferent)

items.explanation: A reflex = afferent (sensory stimulus in) + efferent (motor response out). Takeaway: Reflex = afferent (stimulus in) + efferent (response out). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The afferent limb carries the sensory stimulus into the CNS; the efferent limb carries the motor response back out. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — afferent is sensory (in), efferent is motor (out).
distractor_rationales.B: A reflex arc has one sensory and one motor limb, not two sensory.
distractor_rationales.D: It has one sensory and one motor limb, not two motor.

items.stem: The knee-jerk reflex — a muscle contracting after it's stretched, as a protective response — is the:
