items.explanation: The muscle stretch reflex (knee-jerk) is ipsilateral and monosynaptic — a stretched muscle contracts protectively. Takeaway: Muscle stretch reflex = stretched muscle contracts (ipsilateral, monosynaptic). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The muscle stretch (myotatic) reflex causes a stretched muscle to contract; afferent and efferent limbs are on the SAME side (ipsilateral), and it's monosynaptic. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The withdrawal reflex pulls a limb away from a painful stimulus, a different reflex.
distractor_rationales.C: The corneal reflex is the blink to eye stimulation.
distractor_rationales.D: The startle reflex is a whole-body response to a sudden stimulus.

items.stem: The sensory receptors within a muscle that detect stretch and initiate the stretch reflex are the:
items.explanation: Muscle spindles detect stretch and send afferent signals that trigger the stretch reflex. Takeaway: Muscle spindles = stretch sensors that trigger the reflex. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Muscle spindles are the stretch-sensing proprioceptors whose afferent (somatosensory) neurons trigger the reflex. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Pacinian corpuscles are skin vibration receptors, not muscle stretch sensors.
distractor_rationales.B: Merkel discs sense fine touch in skin, not muscle stretch.
distractor_rationales.C: Cochlear hair cells are for hearing.

items.stem: For the stretch reflex to work, when the stretched muscle is excited to contract, the opposing (antagonist) muscle on the other side is:
items.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition: the antagonist muscle is inhibited while the agonist contracts — required for the reflex to move the limb. Takeaway: Reciprocal inhibition = antagonist muscle inhibited so the reflex can move the limb. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Reciprocal inhibition: the antagonist muscle is inhibited so the reflex movement isn't opposed — necessary for the reflex to occur. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: If the antagonist also contracted, the limb couldn't move — it must be inhibited.
distractor_rationales.C: The antagonist is inhibited, not destroyed.
distractor_rationales.D: It must be actively inhibited, not left unaffected.

items.stem: In the autonomic nervous system, the sympathetic (fight-or-flight) division has a characteristic ganglionic pattern of:

choices.text: A long preganglionic then a short postganglionic axon
A single axon straight to the target
A short preganglionic axon (ganglia near the spine) then a long postganglionic axon

items.explanation: Sympathetic = short preganglionic (ganglia near spine) → long postganglionic. Parasympathetic = long then short. Takeaway: Sympathetic = short-then-long. Parasympathetic = long-then-short. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sympathetic: SHORT preganglionic (ganglia sit close to the spinal cord) → LONG postganglionic to the target. Parasympathetic is the reverse. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's the parasympathetic pattern (long then short).
distractor_rationales.B: The autonomic pathway is a two-neuron chain with a ganglion, not one axon.
distractor_rationales.D: There is a ganglionic synapse; both divisions have ganglia.

items.stem: The sympathetic division originates from the middle of the spinal cord (thoracolumbar), while the parasympathetic division originates from:

choices.text: The middle of the spinal cord as well
The brainstem and the bottom of the spinal cord (craniosacral)

items.explanation: Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (middle cord); parasympathetic = craniosacral (brainstem + sacral cord). Takeaway: Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (middle). Parasympathetic = craniosacral (brainstem + sacral). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (middle); parasympathetic = craniosacral (brainstem + sacral cord). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's the sympathetic origin; parasympathetic is craniosacral.
distractor_rationales.C: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not autonomic outflow origin.
distractor_rationales.D: Free nerve endings are sensory receptors, not autonomic origins.

items.stem: In the CNS, gray matter and white matter are distinguished by their contents:

choices.text: Gray matter = myelinated axons; white matter = somas
Gray matter = neuron cell bodies (somas); white matter = myelinated axons

items.explanation: Gray matter = neuron cell bodies; white matter = myelinated axons (myelin = white). Takeaway: Gray matter = somas. White matter = myelinated axons. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gray matter holds most neuron somas; white matter is made of myelinated axon tracts (myelin gives the white color). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — gray = somas, white = myelinated axons.
distractor_rationales.C: Gray matter contains cell bodies, not only axons.
distractor_rationales.D: White matter is axons, not cell bodies.

items.stem: The arrangement of gray and white matter differs between the spinal cord and the brain:

choices.text: In the spinal cord gray is inside and white outside; in the brain white is inside and gray (cortex) outside
Both have gray outside and white inside
Both have gray inside and white outside
The brain has no gray matter

items.explanation: Spinal cord: gray inside, white outside. Brain: white inside, gray (cortex) outside. Takeaway: Cord: gray in / white out. Brain: white in / gray out. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Spinal cord: gray inside (butterfly), white outside. Brain: gray outside (cortex), white inside (tracts). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The spinal cord has gray INSIDE, not outside.
distractor_rationales.C: The brain has gray OUTSIDE (cortex), not inside.
distractor_rationales.D: The brain's cortex is gray matter.

items.stem: Somatosensory information travels in two broad tract categories. One carries position sense, vibration, and fine touch; the other carries:

choices.text: Pain, temperature, and gross (less precise) touch

items.explanation: Somatosensory tracts: (1) position/vibration/fine touch and (2) pain/temperature/gross touch. Takeaway: Somatosensory tracts: fine touch/vibration/proprioception vs. pain/temp/gross touch. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The two categories are (1) fine touch/vibration/proprioception and (2) pain/temperature/crude touch. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Vision and hearing aren't somatosensory tracts.
distractor_rationales.B: These are sensory tracts, not motor.
distractor_rationales.D: These carry somatosensation, not autonomic outflow.

items.stem: Somatosensory pathways cross to the opposite side of the body (decussate). A key consequence is that:

choices.text: Each side of the brain serves the same side of the body
Injury to one side of the brain often impairs sensation on the opposite side of the body
Both sides of the brain serve only the left side

items.explanation: Somatosensory pathways decussate (cross) → one hemisphere represents the opposite side of the body (contralateral). Takeaway: Sensory tracts cross → brain represents the opposite side of the body (contralateral). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Because the pathways cross (decussate), one side of the brain represents the opposite side of the body — so a lesion affects the contralateral side. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Sensory/motor representation is contralateral, not ipsilateral, due to crossing.
distractor_rationales.B: Sensation does reach the brain via these tracts.
distractor_rationales.D: Each hemisphere serves the contralateral side, not both to one side.

items.stem: Which sensations are carried by the dorsal-column (position/vibration/fine-touch) pathway?

choices.text: Proprioception (position sense), vibration, and fine discriminative touch

items.explanation: The dorsal-column pathway = fine touch + vibration + proprioception. Pain/temperature = the spinothalamic pathway. Takeaway: Dorsal column = fine touch, vibration, proprioception. Spinothalamic = pain, temperature. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The dorsal-column pathway carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception; pain/temperature travel in the separate spinothalamic pathway. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic (not dorsal-column) pathway.
distractor_rationales.B: Crude touch travels with pain/temperature, not the fine-touch pathway.
distractor_rationales.D: Hearing and balance are separate senses, not somatosensory tracts.

items.stem: An upper motor neuron (UMN) is a neuron that:

choices.text: Synapses directly on skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction
Carries sensory information from skin to brain
Originates in the cerebral cortex and synapses on lower motor neurons in the brainstem or spinal cord
Regulates hormone release from the pituitary

items.explanation: Upper motor neurons start in the cerebral cortex and command lower motor neurons; LMNs then drive the muscle. Takeaway: UMN = cortex → controls LMNs (which drive muscle). UMN controls LMN. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. UMNs live in the cerebral cortex and control LMNs (in the brainstem/cord); the LMNs are the ones that contact muscle directly. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's a LOWER motor neuron — the LMN contacts muscle at the NMJ.
distractor_rationales.B: That describes an afferent (sensory) neuron.
distractor_rationales.D: That describes hypothalamic/pituitary control, not a UMN.

items.stem: The collection of upper-motor-neuron axons that travels from the cortex down to lower motor neurons in the spinal cord is the:
items.explanation: Corticospinal tract = UMN axons to the spinal cord. Corticobulbar tract = UMN axons to the brainstem. Takeaway: Corticospinal = UMN → spinal cord. Corticobulbar = UMN → brainstem. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The corticospinal tract carries UMN axons to the spinal cord (most decussate at the medulla). The corticobulbar tract instead goes to the brainstem. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The corticobulbar tract goes to the brainstem, not the spinal cord.
distractor_rationales.C: The dorsal column is a sensory (fine-touch) pathway.
distractor_rationales.D: The spinothalamic tract is a sensory (pain/temp) pathway.

items.stem: Damage to an UPPER motor neuron produces which pattern of signs?

choices.text: Hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response

items.explanation: UMN signs = 'up': hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia, Babinski. LMN signs = 'down': atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia. Takeaway: UMN = up (hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia, Babinski). LMN = down (atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. UMN lesions cause 'up' signs: hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia/spasticity, and a Babinski (extensor plantar) response. LMN lesions cause the 'down' signs (atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Those are LOWER motor neuron signs — the opposite pattern.
distractor_rationales.B: UMN damage clearly produces motor signs.
distractor_rationales.D: UMN lesions cause motor, not purely sensory, deficits.

items.stem: Rhythmic, involuntary contractions (e.g., the foot beating up and down when the ankle is dorsiflexed) — an upper-motor-neuron sign driven by hyperreflexia — are called:
items.explanation: Clonus = rhythmic involuntary contractions from hyperreflexia — an UMN sign. Takeaway: Clonus = rhythmic contractions from hyperreflexia (UMN sign). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Clonus is rhythmic involuntary contraction from an exaggerated stretch reflex (hyperreflexia), a UMN sign. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fasciculations are small twitches seen in LOWER motor neuron damage.
distractor_rationales.B: A resting tremor is characteristic of Parkinson's (basal ganglia), not clonus.
distractor_rationales.D: Ataxia is uncoordinated movement, often cerebellar, not clonus.

items.stem: When the sole of the foot is scraped, the normal adult response is toe flexion (curling down). An extensor response — the big toe going UP — (the Babinski sign) indicates:
items.explanation: An extensor plantar (Babinski) response in an adult = upper motor neuron damage (normal response is toe flexion). Takeaway: Babinski (toe up) in an adult = UMN damage. Normal adult = toes flex down. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. An extensor plantar (Babinski) response is abnormal in adults and signals UMN pathology (it's normal only in infants). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Toe flexion is the normal adult response; extension is abnormal.
distractor_rationales.B: The Babinski sign points to UMN, not specifically LMN, damage.
distractor_rationales.D: It reflects motor-pathway (UMN) damage, not a purely sensory issue.

items.stem: Increased skeletal-muscle tone and resistance to stretch — an upper-motor-neuron sign — is called:
items.explanation: Hypertonia (increased tone/spasticity) = UMN sign. Hypotonia (decreased tone) = LMN sign. Takeaway: Hypertonia = increased tone (UMN). Hypotonia = decreased tone (LMN). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hypertonia (increased tone/spasticity) is a UMN sign; hypotonia (decreased tone) is a LMN sign. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Hypotonia (decreased tone) is a LOWER motor neuron sign.
distractor_rationales.B: Anhedonia is loss of pleasure, unrelated to muscle tone.
distractor_rationales.C: Hyporeflexia (reduced reflexes) is a LMN sign.

items.stem: The four lobes of the cerebral cortex (mnemonic F-POT) are the:

choices.text: Frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes
Frontal, pontine, occipital, and thalamic lobes
Frontal, parietal, olfactory, and temporal lobes
Cerebellar, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes

items.explanation: Four cortical lobes: Frontal, Parietal, Occipital, Temporal (F-POT). Takeaway: Cortical lobes: Frontal, Parietal, Occipital, Temporal (F-POT). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. F-POT = Frontal, Parietal, Occipital, Temporal. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The pons and thalamus are not cortical lobes.
distractor_rationales.C: There is no 'olfactory lobe' among the four; it's occipital.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum is not a cortical lobe.

items.stem: The frontal lobe houses the motor cortex, the prefrontal cortex (executive function), and:
items.explanation: Frontal lobe = motor cortex + prefrontal cortex (executive) + Broca's area (speech production). Takeaway: Frontal = motor cortex, prefrontal (executive), Broca's (speech production). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The frontal lobe contains the motor cortex, prefrontal cortex, and Broca's area (speech production). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The primary visual cortex is in the occipital lobe.
distractor_rationales.C: Wernicke's area is in the temporal lobe.
distractor_rationales.D: The somatosensory cortex is in the parietal lobe.

items.stem: The lobe containing the somatosensory cortex (touch, pressure, pain from the skin) and handling spatial manipulation is the:
items.explanation: Parietal lobe = somatosensory cortex (skin sensation) + spatial manipulation. Takeaway: Parietal = somatosensory cortex + spatial processing. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The parietal lobe contains the somatosensory cortex and processes spatial orientation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The occipital lobe processes vision.
distractor_rationales.C: The temporal lobe processes hearing.
distractor_rationales.D: The frontal lobe handles motor/executive function, not somatosensation.

items.stem: Vision, including the primary visual ('striate') cortex, is processed in the:
items.explanation: Occipital lobe = vision (primary visual / striate cortex). Takeaway: Occipital = vision (striate cortex). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The occipital lobe houses the primary visual (striate) cortex. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The temporal lobe processes hearing.
distractor_rationales.C: The parietal lobe processes somatosensation/space.
distractor_rationales.D: The frontal lobe handles motor/executive function.

items.stem: Sound processing (auditory cortex) and Wernicke's area (language comprehension) are located in the:
items.explanation: Temporal lobe = hearing (auditory cortex) + Wernicke's area (comprehension). Takeaway: Temporal = auditory cortex + Wernicke's (comprehension). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The temporal lobe contains the auditory cortex and Wernicke's area. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The occipital lobe processes vision.
distractor_rationales.B: The parietal lobe processes somatosensation.
distractor_rationales.C: The frontal lobe handles motor/executive function and Broca's area.

items.stem: The motor cortex and the somatosensory cortex sit on opposite sides of the central sulcus. Which pairing is correct?

choices.text: Motor cortex in the parietal lobe; somatosensory cortex in the frontal lobe
Motor cortex in the frontal lobe; somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe

items.explanation: Motor cortex = frontal (precentral gyrus); somatosensory cortex = parietal (postcentral gyrus). They flank the central sulcus. Takeaway: Motor cortex = frontal. Somatosensory cortex = parietal (across the central sulcus). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The motor cortex (precentral gyrus) is frontal; the somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) is parietal — they flank the central sulcus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — motor is frontal, somatosensory is parietal.
distractor_rationales.B: Both are near the central sulcus (frontal/parietal), not occipital.
distractor_rationales.C: Neither is in the temporal lobe.

items.stem: The bumps and grooves (gyri and sulci) that fold the cerebral cortex serve to:

choices.text: Increase the cortical surface area (and cellular mass) that fits in the skull

items.explanation: Cortical folding (gyri/sulci) increases surface area — more cortex/neurons in the same skull volume. Takeaway: Cortical folds = more surface area (more neurons) in the skull. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cortical folding packs more surface area (and neurons) into the limited skull volume. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Folding increases, not decreases, neuronal capacity.
distractor_rationales.B: The folds aren't CSF reservoirs.
distractor_rationales.D: Folding isn't a myelin-generating structure.

items.stem: For movement and most senses, each cerebral hemisphere controls:

choices.text: The same (ipsilateral) side of the body
The opposite (contralateral) side of the body

items.explanation: The brain is contralateral: left hemisphere ↔ right body (and vice versa). Smell is the ipsilateral exception. Takeaway: Contralateral control: left brain ↔ right body. Smell = ipsilateral exception. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The brain is contralaterally organized — the left hemisphere controls the right body and vice versa (smell is the ipsilateral exception). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Control is contralateral, not ipsilateral (except smell).
distractor_rationales.B: Each hemisphere serves the opposite side, not both equally.
distractor_rationales.C: Hemispheric control extends to the whole contralateral body, not just head/neck.

items.stem: For the vast majority of people, the dominant hemisphere — handling language, math, and logic — is the:
items.explanation: Left hemisphere is dominant for most people: language, math, logic. Takeaway: Left hemisphere (dominant) = language, math, logic. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The left hemisphere is dominant for most people, specializing in language, math, and logical analysis. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The right hemisphere handles prosody, music, and spatial/holistic processing.
distractor_rationales.B: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not language dominance.
distractor_rationales.D: The brainstem handles vital functions, not language.

items.stem: The non-dominant (usually right) hemisphere specializes in:

choices.text: Emotional tone (prosody), music, spatial processing, and big-picture/holistic thinking

items.explanation: Right (non-dominant) hemisphere: emotional prosody, music, spatial, big-picture/holistic thinking. Takeaway: Right hemisphere = prosody, music, spatial, big-picture. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The right hemisphere handles the emotional tone of language (prosody), music, spatial processing, and holistic 'big-picture' thinking. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Grammar/vocabulary are left-hemisphere (language) functions.
distractor_rationales.B: Calculation is more left-hemisphere.
distractor_rationales.C: Speech production (Broca's) is left-hemisphere.

items.stem: Contralateral organization applies to most senses, but the exception — processed on the SAME (ipsilateral) side — is:
items.explanation: Smell is the ipsilateral exception (same-side); vision/hearing/touch are contralateral. Takeaway: Smell = ipsilateral exception. Vision/hearing/touch = contralateral. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Olfaction is ipsilateral — each nostril projects to the same-side hemisphere (it also bypasses the thalamus). Vision, hearing, and touch are contralateral. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Vision is contralaterally organized.
distractor_rationales.B: Hearing is largely contralateral.
distractor_rationales.D: Touch is contralateral.

items.stem: The two cerebral hemispheres communicate and share information through the:
items.explanation: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, letting them communicate. Takeaway: Corpus callosum = connects/communicates between hemispheres. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The corpus callosum is the large fiber bundle connecting the left and right hemispheres. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The internal capsule carries tracts like the corticospinal, not interhemispheric fibers.
distractor_rationales.B: The reticular formation governs arousal, not hemisphere connection.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement.

items.stem: The brainstem — which connects the brain to the spinal cord and carries the cranial nerves — consists of the:
items.explanation: The brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla. Takeaway: Brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla (mnemonic for the lower brainstem: Pons, Reticular formation, Medulla). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Those are higher structures, not the brainstem.
distractor_rationales.B: Those are cortical lobes, not the brainstem.
distractor_rationales.C: Those are limbic structures, not the brainstem.

items.stem: The lower brainstem structure that controls vital involuntary functions — heartbeat and breathing — and is the crossover (decussation) point for many nerve tracts is the:
items.explanation: The medulla controls heartbeat and breathing (vital autonomic functions) and is a tract crossover point. Takeaway: Medulla = heartbeat + breathing (vital); tract crossover point. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The medulla regulates heart rate and breathing and is a major decussation point for tracts. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not heartbeat/breathing.
distractor_rationales.C: The thalamus is a sensory relay, not the vital-function center.
distractor_rationales.D: The hippocampus handles memory.

items.stem: The network of neurons running through the brainstem that governs arousal, alertness, and the sleep–wake cycle — and filters incoming sensory information — is the:
items.explanation: The reticular formation governs arousal, alertness, and the sleep–wake cycle (and filters sensory input). Takeaway: Reticular formation = arousal/alertness + sleep–wake + sensory filtering. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The reticular formation controls arousal/alertness and the sleep–wake cycle, filtering sensory input to the thalamus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The corpus callosum connects hemispheres, unrelated to arousal.
distractor_rationales.C: The basal ganglia handle motor control.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement.

items.stem: The brainstem structure that acts as a bridge relaying signals, and plays a role in arousal and the sleep/REM cycle, is the:
items.explanation: The pons ('bridge') relays signals and contributes to arousal and the sleep/REM cycle. Takeaway: Pons = bridge/relay; arousal + sleep/REM. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The pons ('bridge') relays signals between brain regions and participates in arousal and sleep (including REM). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The medulla controls heartbeat/breathing specifically.
distractor_rationales.B: The cerebellum coordinates movement.
distractor_rationales.D: The amygdala handles fear/emotion.

items.stem: The structure that coordinates voluntary movement and balance — receiving proprioceptive feedback, and notably impaired by alcohol — is the:
items.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and balance (alcohol impairs it → poor coordination). Takeaway: Cerebellum = coordination + balance (alcohol impairs it). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and balance; alcohol impairs it (why intoxication disrupts coordination/balance). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The medulla controls vital autonomic functions.
distractor_rationales.B: The thalamus is a sensory relay.
distractor_rationales.D: The corpus callosum connects hemispheres.

items.stem: Your notes describe the brain as 'building on itself.' In general, the deeper/older structures handle ______, while the superficial cortex handles ______.

choices.text: Basic survival functions (breathing, sleep); higher-order functions (cognition)

items.explanation: Deep/old brain = survival basics (breathing, sleep); superficial cortex = higher-order cognition. Takeaway: Old/deep brain = survival (breathing, sleep). New/superficial cortex = higher cognition. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Older, deeper structures manage survival basics (breathing, heartbeat, sleep); the newer, superficial cortex handles higher-order cognition. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — deep/old = survival, superficial/new = higher cognition.
distractor_rationales.B: The old/new distinction isn't vision vs. hearing.
distractor_rationales.D: It isn't a simple motor vs. sensory split.

items.stem: Within the old brain, the structure that acts as the sensory relay station — routing eye/ear and other sensory info onward — is the:
items.explanation: The thalamus is the sensory relay station (all senses except smell). Takeaway: Thalamus = sensory relay (all senses but smell). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The thalamus relays incoming sensory information (all senses except smell) to the appropriate cortical areas. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not sensory relay.
distractor_rationales.C: The pons is a bridge/relay for arousal and cross-signals, but the sensory relay station is the thalamus.
distractor_rationales.D: The medulla controls vital autonomic functions.

items.stem: The subcortical nuclei that help refine and smooth voluntary movement (and also contribute to cognition and emotion), but contain NO upper motor neurons themselves, are the:
items.explanation: The basal ganglia refine/smooth voluntary movement (and aid cognition/emotion) — they modulate motor output, without UMNs of their own. Takeaway: Basal ganglia = smooth/refine movement (also cognition/emotion); no UMNs. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The basal ganglia help motor areas produce smooth, proper movements (and aid cognition/emotion); they modulate rather than directly command via UMNs. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The corpus callosum connects hemispheres, not a motor-refining nucleus.
distractor_rationales.C: The reticular formation governs arousal.
distractor_rationales.D: The olfactory bulb processes smell.

items.stem: The subcortical white-matter structure that carries many important pathways — including the corticospinal tract — down from the cortex is the:
items.explanation: The internal capsule carries major pathways (including the corticospinal tract) from the cortex downward. Takeaway: Internal capsule = white-matter bundle carrying the corticospinal tract. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The internal capsule is a compact white-matter bundle carrying tracts (like the corticospinal) between the cortex and lower structures. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, a different bundle.
distractor_rationales.B: The basal ganglia are gray-matter nuclei, not the tract-carrying capsule.
distractor_rationales.D: The cerebellum coordinates movement.

items.stem: Among the subcortical structures, the one connecting the right and left cerebral hemispheres is the:
items.explanation: The corpus callosum connects the right and left hemispheres. Takeaway: Corpus callosum = joins the two hemispheres. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The corpus callosum is the large commissure joining the two hemispheres. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The internal capsule carries corticospinal and other tracts, not the interhemispheric bridge.
distractor_rationales.C: The basal ganglia handle motor refinement.
distractor_rationales.D: The thalamus is the sensory relay.

items.stem: The subcortical structure that controls the pituitary gland — the 'master gland' that regulates other endocrine glands — is the:
items.explanation: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary (master gland), bridging the nervous and endocrine systems. Takeaway: Hypothalamus controls the pituitary (master gland). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary (master gland), linking the nervous and endocrine systems (and regulating hunger, thirst, temperature, etc.). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The basal ganglia handle motor refinement, not endocrine control.
distractor_rationales.B: The cerebellum coordinates movement.
distractor_rationales.D: The corpus callosum connects hemispheres.

items.stem: Because the basal ganglia refine movement, dysfunction there is associated with movement disorders such as:
items.explanation: Basal-ganglia dysfunction → movement disorders (e.g., Parkinson's disease: resting tremor, rigidity). Takeaway: Basal ganglia dysfunction → movement disorders (Parkinson's). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Basal-ganglia dysfunction (e.g., dopamine loss) produces movement disorders like Parkinson's disease. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Wernicke's aphasia is a temporal-lobe language disorder.
distractor_rationales.B: Anterograde amnesia is a hippocampal/memory disorder.
distractor_rationales.C: Anosmia is loss of smell.

items.stem: Learning is split into two broad types. Learning a link between two stimuli or between a behavior and its consequence is ______ learning; learning from repeated exposure to a single stimulus is ______ learning.
items.explanation: Associative learning links stimuli/behaviors (classical, operant); non-associative learning is response change to one repeated stimulus (habituation, sensitization). Takeaway: Associative = link stimuli/consequences. Non-associative = single repeated stimulus. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Associative learning (classical/operant conditioning) links stimuli or behaviors to outcomes; non-associative learning (habituation, sensitization) is a change in response to a single repeated stimulus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — associative links stimuli, non-associative is single-stimulus.
distractor_rationales.C: Latent and observational aren't the associative/non-associative split.
distractor_rationales.D: Insight/procedural aren't this dichotomy.

items.stem: Growing less responsive to a repeated, harmless stimulus — like ceasing to notice a ticking clock — is:
items.explanation: Habituation = decreased response to a repeated harmless stimulus (you tune it out). Takeaway: Habituation = tune out a repeated harmless stimulus (response decreases). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Habituation is a decreased response to a repeated, non-threatening stimulus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Sensitization is an INCREASED response, the opposite.
distractor_rationales.C: Acquisition is the initial learning of a conditioned association.
distractor_rationales.D: Generalization is responding to stimuli similar to a conditioned one.

items.stem: After you've habituated to a stimulus, a sudden change or new stimulus can restore the original response. This recovery is:
items.explanation: Dishabituation = a habituated response returns when a new or changed stimulus is introduced. Takeaway: Dishabituation = habituated response comes back when the stimulus changes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Dishabituation is the return of a habituated response when a new/changed stimulus appears. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Sensitization is a heightened response to a strong stimulus, a different process.
distractor_rationales.C: Extinction is the fading of a conditioned response, a classical-conditioning term.
distractor_rationales.D: Discrimination is distinguishing a specific conditioned stimulus.

items.stem: After a painful or intense stimulus, you become MORE responsive even to mild stimuli (jumpy after a scare). This is:
items.explanation: Sensitization = increased responsiveness after a strong/aversive stimulus (heightened reactivity). Takeaway: Sensitization = more responsive after an intense stimulus (opposite of habituation). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sensitization is an increased response following a strong or noxious stimulus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Habituation is a DECREASED response, the opposite.
distractor_rationales.C: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response.
distractor_rationales.D: Shaping is reinforcing steps toward a target behavior (operant).

items.stem: Habituation differs from sensory adaptation in that habituation is:

choices.text: Purely a change in the sensory receptors
The same thing as sensory adaptation
A change in the central nervous system's response (learning), not a change in the sensory receptors themselves
A conscious decision to ignore a stimulus

items.explanation: Habituation = a learned CNS-level drop in response; sensory adaptation = receptor-level drop in sensitivity. Different mechanisms. Takeaway: Habituation = learned (CNS) response drop. Sensory adaptation = receptor-level. Not the same. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Habituation is a learned, CNS-level decrease in behavioral response; sensory adaptation is a receptor-level decrease in sensory signaling. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's sensory adaptation (receptor-level), not habituation.
distractor_rationales.B: They're distinct: adaptation is receptor-level, habituation is a learned CNS response.
distractor_rationales.D: Habituation isn't a deliberate choice; it's a form of non-associative learning.

items.stem: In Pavlov's work, food automatically makes a dog salivate. The food is the ______ and the salivation to food is the ______.
items.explanation: UCS = stimulus that naturally triggers a response (food); UCR = the automatic response (salivation to food). No learning required. Takeaway: UCS = natural trigger (food). UCR = automatic response (salivate to food). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Food naturally triggers salivation with no learning: food = unconditioned stimulus (UCS), salivation-to-food = unconditioned response (UCR). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The food triggers salivation automatically (unconditioned), before any learning.
distractor_rationales.B: Food is not neutral — it naturally elicits the response.
distractor_rationales.C: Food is the unconditioned (not conditioned) stimulus.

items.stem: A bell initially produces no salivation. After being repeatedly paired with food, the bell alone makes the dog salivate. The bell has changed from a ______ into a ______.
items.explanation: A neutral stimulus (NS) becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) after repeated pairing with the UCS. Takeaway: Bell: neutral stimulus → conditioned stimulus (after pairing with food). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The bell starts neutral (no response), then through pairing with the UCS becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) that elicits the response. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — it goes from neutral to conditioned, not the other way.
distractor_rationales.B: The bell is a stimulus that becomes conditioned, not a UCS/UCR pair.
distractor_rationales.C: The bell is a stimulus (CS), not a response.

items.stem: After conditioning, the dog salivates to the bell alone. Salivation to the bell is the:
items.explanation: The conditioned response (CR) = the learned response to the conditioned stimulus (salivation to the bell). Takeaway: CR = learned response to the CS (salivate to the bell). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Salivation triggered by the bell (the learned trigger) is the conditioned response (CR). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The UCR is the response to the natural stimulus (food), not the bell.
distractor_rationales.C: The UCS is the natural stimulus (food), not a response.
distractor_rationales.D: A neutral stimulus is a stimulus, not a response.

items.stem: The initial stage of classical conditioning — when the neutral stimulus and unconditioned stimulus are repeatedly paired until the association is learned — is:
items.explanation: Acquisition = the phase of learning the CS–UCS association (CS ideally just before UCS). Takeaway: Acquisition = learning the CS–UCS pairing. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Acquisition is the phase where the CS–UCS association is established (works best when the CS slightly precedes the UCS). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Extinction is the weakening of the response, not its establishment.
distractor_rationales.C: Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished response.
distractor_rationales.D: Shaping is an operant-conditioning procedure, not classical acquisition.

items.stem: Classical conditioning is best characterized as learning that involves:

choices.text: Voluntary behaviors shaped by their consequences
Automatic, involuntary responses (reflexive) linked to a new stimulus
A single repeated stimulus with no pairing

items.explanation: Classical conditioning = automatic/reflexive responses linked to a new (conditioned) stimulus. Operant = voluntary behavior driven by consequences. Takeaway: Classical = involuntary/reflexive responses. Operant = voluntary behavior + consequences. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Classical conditioning associates a new stimulus with an automatic, reflexive response (salivation, fear). Voluntary behaviors driven by consequences are operant conditioning. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Voluntary behavior shaped by consequences is operant conditioning.
distractor_rationales.C: Learning by watching is observational learning.
distractor_rationales.D: A single repeated stimulus is non-associative learning.

items.stem: Classical conditioning is generally most effective when the neutral stimulus:

choices.text: Comes just BEFORE the unconditioned stimulus (forward conditioning)
Comes well AFTER the unconditioned stimulus
Is never paired with the unconditioned stimulus

items.explanation: Conditioning is strongest when the CS precedes the UCS (the CS predicts the UCS). Takeaway: Best conditioning: CS just before UCS (CS predicts UCS). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Learning is strongest when the CS reliably precedes (predicts) the UCS — forward conditioning. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Presenting the NS after the UCS (backward conditioning) is weak/ineffective.
distractor_rationales.C: Pairing is required for classical conditioning to occur.
distractor_rationales.D: The NS becomes a signal for the UCS; it doesn't replace the response.

items.stem: If the bell (CS) is repeatedly presented WITHOUT the food (UCS), the dog gradually stops salivating to the bell. This weakening of the conditioned response is:
items.explanation: Extinction = the conditioned response fades when the CS is presented without the UCS. Takeaway: Extinction = CR fades when CS is shown without the UCS. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Extinction is the fading of the CR when the CS is presented repeatedly without the UCS. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Spontaneous recovery is the RETURN of the response after a rest, not its fading.
distractor_rationales.B: Acquisition is the initial learning of the association.
distractor_rationales.C: Generalization is responding to similar stimuli.

items.stem: After a conditioned response has been extinguished, it suddenly reappears (weaker) following a rest period. This is:
items.explanation: Spontaneous recovery = an extinguished CR returns after a rest (the association was suppressed, not erased). Takeaway: Spontaneous recovery = extinguished response comes back after a break. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished CR after a pause — showing the association wasn't fully erased. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Extinction is the fading of the response, not its return.
distractor_rationales.C: Discrimination is distinguishing the specific CS from similar stimuli.
distractor_rationales.D: Habituation is a non-associative decrease in response.

items.stem: After being conditioned to salivate to a specific tone, the dog also salivates to similar tones. This is:
items.explanation: Stimulus generalization = the CR is elicited by stimuli similar to the original CS. Takeaway: Generalization = respond to stimuli SIMILAR to the CS. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Generalization is responding to stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Discrimination is the opposite — responding only to the specific CS.
distractor_rationales.C: Extinction is the fading of the response.
distractor_rationales.D: Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.

items.stem: With further training, the dog salivates only to the exact tone that was paired with food, not to different tones. This is:
items.explanation: Stimulus discrimination = responding only to the specific CS, not to similar stimuli. Takeaway: Discrimination = respond ONLY to the specific CS (opposite of generalization). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Discrimination is learning to respond only to the specific CS and not to similar stimuli — the opposite of generalization. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Generalization is responding to similar stimuli, the opposite.
distractor_rationales.C: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response.
distractor_rationales.D: Acquisition is the initial learning phase.

items.stem: Once a bell is a conditioned stimulus, pairing a NEW neutral stimulus (a light) with the bell can make the light elicit the response too. This is:
items.explanation: Higher-order conditioning: an established CS conditions a new neutral stimulus (light paired with an already-conditioned bell). Takeaway: Higher-order conditioning = an existing CS conditions a new stimulus. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Higher-order conditioning uses an established CS to condition a new neutral stimulus, without the original UCS. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Extinction is the fading of a conditioned response.
distractor_rationales.C: Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.
distractor_rationales.D: Shaping is an operant procedure.

items.stem: Operant conditioning (Skinner, building on Thorndike's law of effect) is learning in which:

choices.text: Reflexive responses are paired with a new stimulus
Voluntary behavior is strengthened or weakened by its consequences
Behavior changes from watching a model
Response to a single stimulus declines with repetition

items.explanation: Operant conditioning: voluntary behavior is shaped by its consequences (Thorndike's law of effect; Skinner). Takeaway: Operant = voluntary behavior shaped by consequences (reinforcement/punishment). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Operant conditioning changes voluntary behavior through consequences (reinforcement increases it; punishment decreases it). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's classical conditioning (reflexive responses + new stimulus).
distractor_rationales.C: That's observational learning.
distractor_rationales.D: That's habituation (non-associative).

items.stem: In operant terms, reinforcement always ______ a behavior, and punishment always ______ a behavior.
items.explanation: Reinforcement increases a behavior; punishment decreases it (independent of add/remove). Takeaway: Reinforcement ↑ behavior. Punishment ↓ behavior. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Reinforcement increases the likelihood of a behavior; punishment decreases it — regardless of whether a stimulus is added or removed. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — reinforcement increases, punishment decreases.
distractor_rationales.B: Punishment decreases behavior, not increases.
distractor_rationales.C: Reinforcement increases behavior, not decreases.

items.stem: In operant conditioning, 'positive' and 'negative' refer to:

choices.text: Whether a stimulus is added (positive) or removed (negative) — not good vs. bad
Whether the outcome is pleasant or unpleasant
Whether the behavior increases or decreases
Whether the learning is conscious or unconscious

items.explanation: In operant terms, positive = add a stimulus, negative = remove a stimulus (not good vs. bad). Takeaway: Positive = add stimulus. Negative = remove stimulus. (Not good/bad.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Positive = add a stimulus; negative = remove a stimulus. 'Good/bad' is captured by reinforcement vs. punishment, not by positive/negative. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Pleasant/unpleasant maps to reinforcement/punishment, not positive/negative.
distractor_rationales.C: Increase/decrease maps to reinforcement/punishment.
distractor_rationales.D: It refers to add/remove, not conscious/unconscious.

items.stem: Giving a dog a treat when it sits, which makes it sit more often, is:

choices.text: Positive reinforcement (add a pleasant stimulus → behavior increases)

items.explanation: Positive reinforcement = add a pleasant stimulus → behavior increases (treat for sitting). Takeaway: Positive reinforcement = add something good → behavior increases. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A pleasant stimulus is ADDED and the behavior INCREASES → positive reinforcement. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus, not adds a treat.
distractor_rationales.B: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus to decrease behavior.
distractor_rationales.C: Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior.

items.stem: A car beeps until you fasten your seatbelt; buckling STOPS the beep, so you buckle more. This is:

choices.text: Negative reinforcement (remove an aversive stimulus → behavior increases)

items.explanation: Negative reinforcement = remove an aversive stimulus → behavior increases (buckle to stop the beep). Not punishment! Takeaway: Negative reinforcement = remove something aversive → behavior increases (NOT punishment). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. An aversive stimulus (beep) is REMOVED and the behavior (buckling) INCREASES → negative reinforcement. It is NOT punishment. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus to reduce behavior.
distractor_rationales.B: Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus to reduce behavior.
distractor_rationales.D: Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus.

items.stem: Adding a shock when a rat presses a lever, which makes it press less, is:

choices.text: Positive punishment (add an aversive stimulus → behavior decreases)

items.explanation: Positive punishment = add an aversive stimulus → behavior decreases (shock for lever-press). Takeaway: Positive punishment = add something aversive → behavior decreases. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. An aversive stimulus is ADDED and the behavior DECREASES → positive punishment. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus.
distractor_rationales.B: Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior.
distractor_rationales.D: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behavior.

items.stem: Taking away a teen's phone for breaking curfew, which reduces curfew-breaking, is:

choices.text: Negative punishment (remove a pleasant stimulus → behavior decreases)

items.explanation: Negative punishment = remove a pleasant stimulus → behavior decreases (take the phone). Takeaway: Negative punishment = remove something good → behavior decreases. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A pleasant stimulus (phone) is REMOVED and the behavior DECREASES → negative punishment. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus.
distractor_rationales.B: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to INCREASE behavior.
distractor_rationales.D: Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior.

items.stem: Teaching a complex behavior by reinforcing successive approximations — steps that get closer and closer to the target — is:
items.explanation: Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior. Takeaway: Shaping = reinforce successive approximations toward the goal behavior. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a goal behavior. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Extinction is the fading of a response.
distractor_rationales.C: Generalization is responding to similar stimuli (classical).
distractor_rationales.D: Latent learning is learning that isn't shown until there's a reason to.

items.stem: A behavior reinforced only SOME of the time (partial/intermittent reinforcement), compared with every time (continuous), is:

choices.text: Faster to acquire but quickly extinguished

items.explanation: Partial (intermittent) reinforcement → more resistant to extinction (continuous → faster initial learning). Takeaway: Partial reinforcement = harder to extinguish. Continuous = faster to learn. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Continuous reinforcement produces faster initial learning, but partial (intermittent) reinforcement makes the behavior more resistant to extinction. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Continuous reinforcement gives faster acquisition; partial gives extinction resistance.
distractor_rationales.C: Partial reinforcement resists but doesn't prevent extinction entirely.
distractor_rationales.D: Reinforcement schedules are an operant, not classical, concept.

items.stem: A factory worker paid for every 10 units produced is on which reinforcement schedule?

choices.text: Fixed-ratio (FR) — reinforcement after a set number of responses

items.explanation: Fixed-ratio (FR) = reinforcement after a set NUMBER of responses (high rate, post-reinforcement pause). Takeaway: Fixed-ratio = set number of responses (e.g., pay per 10 units). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fixed-ratio delivers reinforcement after a set number of responses (every 10 units) — producing a high response rate with a brief post-reinforcement pause. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fixed-interval reinforces the first response after a set TIME, not a set count.
distractor_rationales.B: Variable-ratio reinforces after an unpredictable NUMBER of responses.
distractor_rationales.C: Variable-interval reinforces after an unpredictable TIME.

items.stem: A slot machine that pays out after an unpredictable number of pulls is which schedule — the one that produces the highest, steadiest response rate and greatest resistance to extinction?
items.explanation: Variable-ratio (VR) = reinforcement after an unpredictable NUMBER of responses → highest, steadiest rate, most resistant to extinction (gambling). Takeaway: Variable-ratio = unpredictable # of responses → highest rate, hardest to extinguish (gambling). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Variable-ratio reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses — the highest, steadiest rate and most extinction-resistant (why gambling is so persistent). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fixed-ratio uses a set number of responses and has a post-reinforcement pause.
distractor_rationales.C: Fixed-interval reinforces after a set time (scalloped pattern).
distractor_rationales.D: Variable-interval reinforces after unpredictable time (slow, steady).

items.stem: Reinforcing the first response after a set amount of TIME (e.g., a weekly paycheck) — producing a 'scalloped' pattern where responding speeds up near the deadline — is:
items.explanation: Fixed-interval (FI) = first response after a set TIME → scalloped pattern (responding accelerates near the deadline). Takeaway: Fixed-interval = set time → scalloped pattern (speed up near the deadline). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fixed-interval reinforces the first response after a fixed time; responding dips after reinforcement and accelerates as the interval ends (scalloped). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Variable-interval uses unpredictable time and gives a slow, steady rate.
distractor_rationales.C: Fixed-ratio is based on a set number of responses, not time.
distractor_rationales.D: Variable-ratio is based on an unpredictable number of responses.

items.stem: Checking your phone for a text that could arrive at any unpredictable time produces slow, steady responding. This is which schedule?
items.explanation: Variable-interval (VI) = first response after an unpredictable TIME → slow, steady responding. Takeaway: Variable-interval = unpredictable time → slow, steady responding. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Variable-interval reinforces the first response after an unpredictable time, producing a slow, steady response rate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Fixed-interval uses a set (predictable) time and gives a scalloped pattern.
distractor_rationales.C: Variable-ratio is based on an unpredictable number of responses (high rate).
distractor_rationales.D: Fixed-ratio is based on a set number of responses.

items.stem: Two general rules about schedules of reinforcement are:

choices.text: Interval schedules always beat ratio schedules for response rate
Ratio schedules produce higher response rates than interval schedules; variable schedules resist extinction better than fixed ones
Fixed schedules always resist extinction better than variable ones
Schedule type has no effect on behavior

items.explanation: Rules: ratio > interval for response rate; variable > fixed for extinction resistance. Takeaway: Ratio > interval (response rate). Variable > fixed (extinction resistance). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ratio (response-based) schedules drive higher rates than interval (time-based) schedules; variable (unpredictable) schedules resist extinction better than fixed ones. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ratio schedules produce HIGHER rates than interval schedules.
distractor_rationales.C: VARIABLE schedules resist extinction better than fixed ones.
distractor_rationales.D: Schedule type strongly shapes response rate and persistence.

items.stem: Learning a behavior by watching and imitating others, rather than through direct reinforcement, is:
items.explanation: Observational learning = learning by watching/imitating a model (Bandura's social cognitive theory). Takeaway: Observational learning = learn by watching/imitating a model. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Observational learning (modeling) is acquiring behavior by watching others — the basis of Bandura's social cognitive theory. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Classical conditioning pairs a stimulus with a reflexive response.
distractor_rationales.C: Operant conditioning shapes behavior through direct consequences.
distractor_rationales.D: Habituation is a non-associative decrease in response.

items.stem: The classic experiment showing children imitate aggression after watching an adult model attack a doll was conducted by:
items.explanation: Bandura's Bobo doll experiment demonstrated observational learning — children imitated modeled aggression. Takeaway: Bobo doll = Bandura, observational learning of aggression. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Bandura's Bobo doll study demonstrated observational learning of aggression through modeling. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Pavlov studied classical conditioning (salivation), not modeling.
distractor_rationales.C: Skinner studied operant conditioning (reinforcement schedules).
distractor_rationales.D: Watson studied classical conditioning (Little Albert).

items.stem: In observational learning, the person whose behavior is watched and imitated is called the:
items.explanation: The model is the person observed and imitated in observational learning. Takeaway: Model = the person you observe and imitate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The model is the individual being observed; imitating them is modeling. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A conditioned stimulus is a classical-conditioning term.
distractor_rationales.C: A reinforcer is a consequence that increases behavior (operant).
distractor_rationales.D: A discriminative stimulus signals that reinforcement is available (operant).

items.stem: Seeing someone else get rewarded for a behavior makes you more likely to do it yourself. This is:
items.explanation: Vicarious reinforcement = you're influenced by seeing a model rewarded (or punished) for a behavior. Takeaway: Vicarious reinforcement = learning from what happens to the model (reward/punishment). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Vicarious reinforcement is learning from the consequences experienced by a model — a reward to the model makes the observer more likely to imitate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Direct reinforcement is a consequence delivered to you, not observed in another.
distractor_rationales.B: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase your own behavior.
distractor_rationales.D: Extinction is the fading of a learned response.

items.stem: Bandura proposed observational learning requires attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. A neural system often linked to imitation is the:
items.explanation: Observational learning needs attention, retention, reproduction, motivation; mirror neurons are linked to imitation. Takeaway: Observational learning: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation. Mirror neurons = imitation. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Mirror neurons — which fire both when performing and when observing an action — are often linked to imitation/observational learning. Bandura's four processes: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The reticular activating system governs arousal, not imitation.
distractor_rationales.C: The vestibular system handles balance.
distractor_rationales.D: The endocrine system releases hormones.

items.stem: The finding that animals learn some associations far more easily than others — because of evolved predispositions — is called:
items.explanation: Biological constraints / preparedness: evolution makes some associations far easier to learn than others. Takeaway: Biological constraints (preparedness) = some associations learned much more easily (evolved). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Biological constraints (preparedness) mean evolution readies organisms to learn certain associations more readily than others. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Latent learning is learning not shown until it's useful.
distractor_rationales.C: Higher-order conditioning uses an established CS to condition a new stimulus.
distractor_rationales.D: Shaping reinforces successive approximations.

items.stem: Getting sick hours after eating a food, then avoiding that food after a SINGLE pairing (even with a long delay), is:

choices.text: Standard classical conditioning requiring many trials

items.explanation: Conditioned taste aversion (Garcia effect) = one-trial learning with a long delay — evolved preparedness, breaking usual conditioning rules. Takeaway: Taste aversion (Garcia) = one-trial, long-delay learning (biological preparedness). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Conditioned taste aversion (Garcia) is learned in one trial despite a long delay — a biologically prepared exception to normal conditioning rules. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ordinary classical conditioning needs repeated, closely-timed pairings; taste aversion needs neither.
distractor_rationales.B: It's a learned aversion (classical), not operant punishment.
distractor_rationales.D: Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.

items.stem: When trained animals drift back toward innate, instinctive behaviors that interfere with a conditioned response (the Brelands' raccoons), this is:
items.explanation: Instinctive drift = trained animals revert to instinctive behaviors — a biological limit on conditioning. Takeaway: Instinctive drift = revert to instinctive behavior (biological constraint). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Instinctive drift is the tendency to revert to instinctive behaviors, limiting what conditioning can achieve — another biological constraint. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished CR.
distractor_rationales.B: Generalization is responding to similar stimuli.
distractor_rationales.C: Latent learning is unexpressed learning.

items.stem: Learning to TERMINATE an aversive stimulus already present is escape learning; learning to PREVENT it before it starts is:
items.explanation: Escape learning ends an ongoing aversive stimulus; avoidance learning prevents it beforehand. Takeaway: Escape = end an ongoing aversive stimulus. Avoidance = prevent it beforehand. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Escape learning ends an ongoing aversive stimulus; avoidance learning prevents it from occurring at all (typically via a warning signal). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Escape learning terminates an ongoing aversive stimulus, not prevents it.
distractor_rationales.B: Latent learning is unexpressed learning shown later.
distractor_rationales.C: Habituation is non-associative.

items.stem: A rat that explores a maze with no reward shows it learned the layout only later, when a reward is introduced and its performance jumps. This is:
items.explanation: Latent learning = learning that occurs without reinforcement and isn't shown until it's useful (Tolman's cognitive maps). Takeaway: Latent learning = learned without reward, revealed later when useful. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Latent learning is learning that occurs without reinforcement and stays hidden until there's a reason to demonstrate it (Tolman's cognitive maps). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Observational learning is learning by watching a model.
distractor_rationales.B: Shaping reinforces successive approximations.
distractor_rationales.D: Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.

items.stem: An innate, fixed behavior pattern present without learning (e.g., a spider spinning a web) is an instinct, whereas a conditioned response is:
items.explanation: Instinct = innate, unlearned behavior; a conditioned response is acquired through experience. Takeaway: Instinct = innate/unlearned. Conditioned response = learned through experience. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Instincts are innate, unlearned fixed action patterns; conditioned responses are acquired through experience. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: A conditioned response is learned, not innate.
distractor_rationales.C: Conditioned responses can be modified (e.g., extinguished).
distractor_rationales.D: Instincts and conditioned responses differ in origin (innate vs. learned).

items.stem: The theory that behavior is driven by innate, fixed, unlearned patterns (like a bird building a nest) is:
items.explanation: Instinct theory: behavior is motivated by innate, fixed, unlearned patterns. Takeaway: Instinct theory = innate, fixed, unlearned behavior patterns. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Instinct theory attributes motivation to innate, species-typical fixed action patterns. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Drive-reduction theory is about reducing physiological need states, not innate instincts.
distractor_rationales.B: Incentive theory explains motivation by external rewards.
distractor_rationales.D: Cognitive theory explains motivation by expectations and value.

items.stem: Drive-reduction theory proposes that a physiological need creates an aroused tension (a drive) that motivates us to:

choices.text: Act to reduce the drive and restore homeostasis

items.explanation: Drive-reduction theory: a need → a drive (tension) → behavior that reduces it, restoring homeostasis. Takeaway: Drive-reduction = need creates a drive → act to reduce it (restore homeostasis). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A need (e.g., hunger) produces a drive that pushes behavior to satisfy the need and return the body to homeostatic balance. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Drive-reduction is about reducing tension, not seeking novelty for its own sake.
distractor_rationales.C: It seeks to reduce, not endlessly increase, arousal.
distractor_rationales.D: Imitating a model is observational learning, not drive reduction.

items.stem: In drive-reduction theory, hunger and thirst are ______ drives, while the desire for money or approval are ______ drives.
items.explanation: Primary drives = innate biological (hunger, thirst); secondary drives = learned (money, approval). Takeaway: Primary drives = biological (hunger). Secondary drives = learned (money). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Primary drives are innate biological needs (hunger, thirst); secondary drives are learned (money, approval). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — biological needs are primary, learned ones secondary.
distractor_rationales.B: Extrinsic/intrinsic describe reward source, not primary/secondary drives.
distractor_rationales.D: Those aren't the drive categories here.

items.stem: Arousal theory of motivation states that we are motivated to:

choices.text: Maintain an optimal level of arousal — seeking stimulation when under-aroused and calm when over-aroused

items.explanation: Arousal theory: motivation to reach an optimal arousal level (moderate) — performance peaks there (inverted-U). Takeaway: Arousal theory = seek an optimal (moderate) arousal level. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Arousal theory: people seek an optimal (moderate) arousal level; performance peaks there (Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: We don't seek zero arousal — too little prompts stimulation-seeking.
distractor_rationales.C: We don't endlessly maximize arousal — too much impairs performance.
distractor_rationales.D: Arousal theory isn't limited to biological drives.

items.stem: Incentive theory explains motivation as behavior driven by:

choices.text: External rewards that pull us toward a goal (rather than internal drives pushing us)
Only the reduction of biological needs

items.explanation: Incentive theory: external rewards pull behavior toward goals (vs. drives that push). Takeaway: Incentive theory = external rewards pull behavior (drives push, incentives pull). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Incentive theory emphasizes external incentives (rewards) that 'pull' behavior, complementing the internal 'push' of drives. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That's instinct theory, not incentive theory.
distractor_rationales.C: That's drive-reduction; incentive theory adds external rewards.
distractor_rationales.D: That describes cognitive dissonance, not motivation by incentives.

items.stem: Doing an activity for its own inherent satisfaction is ______ motivation; doing it for an external reward or to avoid punishment is ______ motivation.
items.explanation: Intrinsic motivation = for its own sake; extrinsic = for external reward/consequences. Takeaway: Intrinsic = internal satisfaction. Extrinsic = external reward. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Intrinsic motivation comes from internal satisfaction; extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards/consequences. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — intrinsic is internal, extrinsic is external.
distractor_rationales.C: Primary/secondary are drive types, not the intrinsic/extrinsic split.
distractor_rationales.D: Central/peripheral are persuasion routes, not motivation types.

items.stem: Rewarding someone for an activity they already enjoy can REDUCE their intrinsic motivation for it. This is the:
items.explanation: Overjustification effect: an external reward can undermine existing intrinsic motivation. Takeaway: Overjustification = rewarding an already-enjoyed activity lowers intrinsic motivation. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The overjustification effect: an external reward can undermine pre-existing intrinsic motivation (the person re-attributes their behavior to the reward). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Yerkes-Dodson relates arousal to performance, not reward undermining interest.
distractor_rationales.C: Foot-in-the-door is a compliance technique, not about intrinsic motivation.
distractor_rationales.D: Drive-reduction is about need states, not reward undermining interest.

items.stem: Maslow's hierarchy of needs, from the base upward, is:
items.explanation: Maslow (base→top): physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization. Takeaway: Maslow: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The pyramid rises: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That's the reverse order.
distractor_rationales.C: Physiological needs are the base, below esteem and love.
distractor_rationales.D: Physiological needs come before safety, and love before esteem.

items.stem: A central claim of Maslow's hierarchy is that:

choices.text: Higher needs must be met before lower ones
Lower (more basic) needs must be reasonably met before higher needs strongly motivate behavior
All needs are pursued equally at once
Only physiological needs ever motivate people

items.explanation: Maslow: lower needs are generally satisfied first, then higher needs motivate behavior. Takeaway: Maslow: meet basic needs first, then higher needs motivate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Maslow proposed a prepotent hierarchy: basic needs generally take priority until reasonably satisfied, then higher needs emerge. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — basic needs generally come first.
distractor_rationales.C: The hierarchy implies a general priority order, not equal simultaneous pursuit.
distractor_rationales.D: Higher needs (esteem, self-actualization) also motivate once basics are met.

items.stem: The need at the top of Maslow's pyramid — realizing one's full potential and becoming the most one can be — is:
items.explanation: Self-actualization = the top need: realizing your full potential. Takeaway: Self-actualization = realize your full potential (top of the pyramid).
