items.stem: Chargaff observed that in any double-stranded DNA sample, the amount of adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine. This reflects:

choices.text: Complementary base pairing (A pairs with T, G with C)
Equal amounts of all four bases always

items.explanation: Chargaff's rules: %A=%T and %G=%C (from complementary base pairing). Takeaway: Chargaff: %A=%T, %G=%C (complementary pairing). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Because A pairs with T and G with C, %A=%T and %G=%C in double-stranded DNA (Chargaff's rules). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Base composition isn't random; pairing constrains it.
distractor_rationales.C: %A=%T and %G=%C, but the four bases aren't necessarily equal to each other.
distractor_rationales.D: Chargaff's rules apply to double-stranded DNA.

items.stem: The backbone of a DNA strand is formed by covalent phosphodiester bonds linking:

choices.text: The nitrogenous bases of adjacent nucleotides
The 2' hydroxyl groups of adjacent sugars
The 3' carbon of one sugar to the 5' phosphate of the next

items.explanation: The backbone = phosphodiester bonds from the 3'-OH of one sugar to the 5'-phosphate of the next. Takeaway: Backbone = 3'→5' phosphodiester bonds (sugar-phosphate). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Phosphodiester bonds connect the 3'-OH of one deoxyribose to the 5'-phosphate of the next, giving the strand 5'→3' polarity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Bases pair across strands; they don't form the backbone linkages.
distractor_rationales.B: The backbone is sugar–phosphate–sugar, not phosphate–phosphate.
distractor_rationales.C: DNA's deoxyribose lacks a 2'-OH; linkage is 3'–5'.

items.stem: DNA's sugar (deoxyribose) differs from RNA's sugar (ribose) in that deoxyribose:

choices.text: Lacks a hydroxyl group at the 2' carbon

items.explanation: Deoxyribose lacks the 2'-OH that ribose has (H instead) → DNA is more stable than RNA. Takeaway: Deoxyribose = no 2'-OH (RNA's ribose has it). DNA more stable. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Deoxyribose is missing the 2'-OH present in ribose (it has H instead), making DNA more chemically stable than RNA. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The sugar difference is at the 2' position, not phosphate count.
distractor_rationales.C: Uracil is a base, not part of the sugar difference.
distractor_rationales.D: Both are five-carbon (pentose) sugars.

items.stem: The Meselson–Stahl experiment showed DNA replication is semiconservative, meaning each daughter molecule consists of:

choices.text: A random mix of old and new fragments in each strand
One parental (template) strand and one newly synthesized strand

items.explanation: Replication is semiconservative: each daughter DNA = one old + one new strand. Takeaway: Semiconservative = each new DNA has 1 old + 1 new strand. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Semiconservative replication: each new duplex has one conserved parental strand and one new strand. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That would be conservative replication, which was ruled out.
distractor_rationales.B: That would leave no new synthesis; both duplexes gain a new strand.
distractor_rationales.C: That describes the dispersive model, which was ruled out.

items.stem: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the ______ end of the growing strand, so synthesis always proceeds:
items.explanation: DNA polymerase adds to the 3'-OH → synthesis is always 5'→3'. Takeaway: DNA synthesis is always 5'→3' (adds to the 3' end). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the free 3'-OH, so the new strand grows 5'→3' (reading the template 3'→5'). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Polymerase adds to the 3' end, synthesizing 5'→3'.
distractor_rationales.C: Synthesis is 5'→3', not 3'→5'.
distractor_rationales.D: Nucleotides are added to the 3' end, not the 5' end.

items.stem: At the replication fork, the enzyme that unwinds and separates the two parental DNA strands is:
items.explanation: Helicase unwinds/separates the parental strands at the replication fork. Takeaway: Helicase = unwinds/separates DNA at the fork. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Helicase unwinds the double helix at the fork; single-strand binding proteins then keep the strands apart. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ligase seals nicks between fragments, it doesn't unwind DNA.
distractor_rationales.B: Primase lays down RNA primers.
distractor_rationales.D: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork but doesn't separate the strands at the fork.

items.stem: Because synthesis is only 5'→3', the lagging strand is made discontinuously as short segments called:
items.explanation: The lagging strand is built discontinuously as Okazaki fragments (leading strand is continuous). Takeaway: Lagging strand = Okazaki fragments (discontinuous); leading = continuous. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The lagging strand is synthesized in short Okazaki fragments (away from the fork), later joined by DNA ligase; the leading strand is continuous. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Introns are non-coding sequences removed from pre-mRNA.
distractor_rationales.B: Codons are mRNA base triplets.
distractor_rationales.C: Telomeres are repetitive sequences at chromosome ends.

items.stem: DNA polymerase needs a starting point, so ______ lays down an RNA primer; after synthesis, ______ seals the gaps between fragments.
items.explanation: Primase makes the RNA primer; DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments. Takeaway: Primase = RNA primer. Ligase = seals fragments. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Primase synthesizes RNA primers to provide a 3'-OH; DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments after primers are replaced. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — primase makes primers, ligase seals gaps.
distractor_rationales.B: Helicase/topoisomerase handle unwinding/supercoiling, not priming or sealing.
distractor_rationales.C: Telomerase extends chromosome ends, not the primer/sealing roles here.

items.stem: Many DNA polymerases improve fidelity by removing a mismatched nucleotide just added, using their:
items.explanation: Proofreading = 3'→5' exonuclease activity removes a just-added mismatched base. Takeaway: Proofreading = 3'→5' exonuclease (removes mismatches). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Proofreading uses 3'→5' exonuclease activity to excise a wrongly incorporated base, greatly lowering the error rate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The 5'→3' polymerase activity adds nucleotides; it doesn't remove mismatches.
distractor_rationales.B: Helicase unwinds DNA; it isn't a proofreading function.
distractor_rationales.C: Ligase seals nicks; it doesn't excise mismatches.

items.stem: Because DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the very ends of linear chromosomes, the enzyme that extends these repetitive ends (in germ/stem cells) is:
items.explanation: Telomerase extends telomeres (repetitive chromosome ends) to offset end-replication shortening. Takeaway: Telomerase = extends telomere ends (counters shortening). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase with an RNA template, extends telomeres to counter end-replication shortening. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling, not end-shortening.
distractor_rationales.C: Ligase seals nicks; it doesn't extend telomeres.
distractor_rationales.D: Primase makes primers; it doesn't extend chromosome ends.

items.stem: Transcription is carried out by RNA polymerase, which — unlike DNA polymerase — :

choices.text: Does not require a primer to begin synthesis

items.explanation: RNA polymerase needs no primer, synthesizes 5'→3', and uses uracil instead of thymine. Takeaway: RNA pol: no primer needed; 5'→3'; uses uracil. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. RNA polymerase can initiate synthesis de novo (no primer needed) and synthesizes RNA 5'→3' using uracil in place of thymine. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: RNA polymerase also synthesizes 5'→3'.
distractor_rationales.C: RNA uses uracil, not thymine.
distractor_rationales.D: Unlike DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase needs no primer.

items.stem: RNA polymerase reads the ______ strand to build an mRNA that is identical (except U for T) to the ______ strand.
items.explanation: mRNA is built from the template (antisense) strand and matches the coding (sense) strand (U for T). Takeaway: Template strand is read; mRNA = coding strand sequence (U for T). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The template (antisense) strand is read 3'→5'; the resulting mRNA matches the coding (sense) strand sequence with U replacing T. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the template is read, and mRNA matches the coding strand.
distractor_rationales.C: Leading/lagging are replication terms, not transcription strands.
distractor_rationales.D: Leading/lagging are replication terms, not transcription strands.

items.stem: Transcription begins when RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind a DNA sequence upstream of the gene called the:

choices.text: Promoter (which often contains a TATA box)

items.explanation: The promoter (often with a TATA box) is where RNA polymerase binds to start transcription. Takeaway: Promoter (TATA box) = transcription start site for RNA pol. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The promoter is the upstream binding site (eukaryotic promoters often contain a TATA box) that positions RNA polymerase to start transcription. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The terminator signals the END of transcription.
distractor_rationales.B: The poly-A tail is added post-transcriptionally to the mRNA 3' end.
distractor_rationales.D: The anticodon is on tRNA, unrelated to transcription initiation.

items.stem: In eukaryotes, the immediate product of transcription — before processing — is:
items.explanation: Eukaryotic transcription first makes pre-mRNA (hnRNA), later processed into mature mRNA. Takeaway: Transcription → pre-mRNA (hnRNA), then processed to mRNA. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Transcription yields pre-mRNA (hnRNA), which must be processed (cap, tail, splicing) before becoming mature mRNA. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Mature mRNA results only after processing the pre-mRNA.
distractor_rationales.C: A polypeptide is the product of translation, not transcription.
distractor_rationales.D: tRNA is a separate transcript; the mRNA precursor here is pre-mRNA.

items.stem: In eukaryotes, the RNA polymerase responsible for transcribing protein-coding genes into mRNA is:
items.explanation: RNA polymerase II transcribes mRNA. (Pol I = rRNA; Pol III = tRNA.) Takeaway: RNA Pol II = mRNA. Pol I = rRNA. Pol III = tRNA. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. RNA polymerase II transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes); Pol I makes rRNA and Pol III makes tRNA (and small RNAs). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: RNA polymerase I transcribes most rRNA.
distractor_rationales.C: RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
distractor_rationales.D: DNA polymerase III is a replication enzyme, not for transcription.

items.stem: Before a eukaryotic mRNA leaves the nucleus, it receives a 5' 7-methylguanosine cap and a 3' poly-A tail, which together:

choices.text: Protect the mRNA from degradation and aid export/translation

items.explanation: The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail protect mRNA and aid export/translation. Takeaway: 5' cap + poly-A tail = stability + export + translation. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail increase mRNA stability and promote nuclear export and ribosome binding. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The start codon (AUG) is within the mRNA sequence, not the cap/tail.
distractor_rationales.B: Splicing removes introns; the cap/tail don't.
distractor_rationales.D: The ribosome is made of rRNA and protein, not the mRNA cap/tail.

items.stem: During splicing, the non-coding sequences that are removed from pre-mRNA are ______, and the sequences that remain and are expressed are ______.
items.explanation: Introns are removed (intervening); exons are expressed (retained). Takeaway: Introns OUT, exons EXpressed. Splicing removes introns. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Introns are intervening sequences spliced OUT; exons are EXpressed sequences retained in the mature mRNA. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — introns are removed, exons are expressed.
distractor_rationales.B: Codons/anticodons are translation terms, not spliced sequences.
distractor_rationales.D: Promoters/terminators are transcription signals, not spliced sequences.

items.stem: Intron removal in eukaryotes is carried out by a complex of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) called the:
items.explanation: The spliceosome (snRNPs) removes introns from pre-mRNA. Takeaway: Spliceosome = removes introns (snRNPs). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The spliceosome (snRNPs + associated proteins) recognizes splice sites and excises introns. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The ribosome translates mRNA into protein.
distractor_rationales.B: The proteasome degrades proteins.
distractor_rationales.C: A nucleosome is DNA wrapped around histones.

items.stem: By joining different combinations of exons, a single gene can produce multiple distinct proteins. This is:
items.explanation: Alternative splicing: one gene → multiple proteins by combining exons differently. Takeaway: Alternative splicing = one gene → many proteins (different exon combos). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alternative splicing lets one gene encode several protein isoforms by including/excluding particular exons. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A point mutation changes a single base, not exon combinations.
distractor_rationales.C: Semiconservative replication describes DNA copying.
distractor_rationales.D: Wobble refers to flexible codon–anticodon pairing.

items.stem: The genetic code is read in units of three mRNA nucleotides, each specifying one amino acid. Each triplet is a:
items.explanation: A codon = 3 mRNA nucleotides coding one amino acid. Takeaway: Codon = 3-nucleotide mRNA unit → one amino acid. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A codon is a three-nucleotide mRNA unit that specifies an amino acid (or a start/stop signal). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The anticodon is the complementary triplet on tRNA.
distractor_rationales.B: An exon is a coding mRNA segment, not a single triplet.
distractor_rationales.C: An operon is a cluster of prokaryotic genes.

items.stem: With 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, most amino acids are specified by more than one codon. This property is called:
items.explanation: The code is degenerate: many codons → same amino acid (but each codon is unambiguous). Takeaway: Degenerate = multiple codons per amino acid (but each codon unambiguous). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The code is degenerate/redundant: multiple codons can encode the same amino acid (yet each codon is unambiguous — it codes for only one). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The code is unambiguous, not ambiguous — each codon has one meaning.
distractor_rationales.B: The code is non-overlapping; codons don't share nucleotides.
distractor_rationales.C: The code is nearly universal, which is a separate property.

items.stem: Translation begins at the start codon AUG (methionine) and ends at one of three stop codons:
items.explanation: Start = AUG (Met); stops = UAA, UAG, UGA. Takeaway: Start = AUG (Met). Stops = UAA, UAG, UGA. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The stop (nonsense) codons UAA, UAG, UGA terminate translation; AUG is the start codon coding methionine. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Those are alternative start-related codons, not the stop codons.
distractor_rationales.B: Those code amino acids, not stop signals.
distractor_rationales.D: Those include thymine (DNA); mRNA uses uracil, and these aren't the stop codons.

items.stem: Flexibility in base pairing at the THIRD codon position — allowing one tRNA to recognize multiple codons — is explained by the:
items.explanation: Wobble: flexible pairing at the 3rd codon position lets one tRNA read several codons. Takeaway: Wobble = flexible 3rd-position pairing (one tRNA, multiple codons). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Wobble allows non-standard pairing at the third codon (first anticodon) position, so fewer tRNAs are needed — and it underlies much of the code's degeneracy. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The central dogma is DNA→RNA→protein, not third-position pairing.
distractor_rationales.C: Chargaff's rules concern DNA base ratios.
distractor_rationales.D: The lock-and-key model describes enzyme–substrate specificity.

items.stem: The genetic code is described as nearly universal and non-overlapping, and it is read:

choices.text: In a fixed reading frame, three bases at a time without gaps
With codons overlapping by one base

items.explanation: The code is read 5'→3' in a fixed reading frame, three non-overlapping, commaless bases at a time. Takeaway: Code is read 5'→3', triplets, non-overlapping, no commas, fixed frame. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The code is read continuously (commaless) in a set reading frame, 5'→3', three non-overlapping bases at a time. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: mRNA is read 5'→3', not 3'→5'.
distractor_rationales.C: The code is non-overlapping; codons don't share bases.
distractor_rationales.D: The code is commaless; there are no separators between codons.

items.stem: Each transfer RNA carries a specific amino acid and recognizes an mRNA codon through its complementary:
items.explanation: tRNA's anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon to deliver the right amino acid. Takeaway: tRNA anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The tRNA anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon, ensuring the correct amino acid is delivered. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The codon is on the mRNA; tRNA carries the anticodon.
distractor_rationales.C: The promoter is a transcription start site.
distractor_rationales.D: The poly-A tail is an mRNA modification, not on tRNA.

items.stem: The ribosome, which catalyzes peptide bond formation, is composed of:

choices.text: rRNA and proteins (with rRNA providing the catalytic activity)

items.explanation: The ribosome = rRNA + protein; rRNA catalyzes peptide bonds (a ribozyme). Takeaway: Ribosome = rRNA + protein; rRNA is catalytic (ribozyme). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ribosomes are made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins; the rRNA is the catalytic component (a ribozyme) forming peptide bonds. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ribosomes contain no DNA or lipids.
distractor_rationales.B: Ribosomes contain rRNA in addition to protein.
distractor_rationales.C: mRNA is the message translated, not the ribosome's structure.

items.stem: The enzyme that attaches the correct amino acid to its matching tRNA ("charging" the tRNA) is:
items.explanation: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges each tRNA with its correct amino acid (uses ATP). Takeaway: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase = charges tRNA with the right amino acid. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge each tRNA with its correct amino acid, using ATP — a key fidelity step. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Peptidyl transferase (rRNA) forms peptide bonds in the ribosome.
distractor_rationales.C: RNA polymerase transcribes DNA to RNA.
distractor_rationales.D: Helicase unwinds DNA during replication.

items.stem: During elongation, an incoming charged tRNA enters the ______ site, the growing peptide is held at the ______ site, and the empty tRNA leaves from the E site.
items.explanation: Ribosome sites: A = incoming aminoacyl-tRNA, P = peptidyl (growing chain), E = exit. Takeaway: A = arrival (aminoacyl), P = peptide (growing), E = exit. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A site = incoming aminoacyl-tRNA; P site = peptidyl-tRNA (growing chain); E site = exit for the deacylated tRNA. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — incoming tRNA enters the A site, the chain is at the P site.
distractor_rationales.C: The incoming tRNA enters A, not E; the chain is held at P.
distractor_rationales.D: The growing chain is at P, but the incoming tRNA enters A, not P again.

items.stem: A polypeptide is synthesized from its ______ terminus to its ______ terminus as the ribosome reads mRNA 5'→3'.
items.explanation: Proteins are built N→C terminus as mRNA is read 5'→3'. Takeaway: Protein synthesis: N→C terminus (mRNA read 5'→3'). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Translation proceeds N-terminus → C-terminus while the ribosome reads mRNA 5'→3'. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — synthesis goes N→C, not C→N.
distractor_rationales.C: 5'/3' describe nucleic acids, not polypeptide termini.
distractor_rationales.D: 5'/3' describe nucleic acids; and the direction would be reversed.

items.stem: A point mutation that changes a codon but still specifies the SAME amino acid (thanks to code degeneracy) is a:
items.explanation: Silent mutation: codon changes but the amino acid stays the same (code degeneracy). Takeaway: Silent = codon changes, same amino acid. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A silent mutation alters the DNA/codon without changing the encoded amino acid — usually at the wobble position. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A missense mutation changes the amino acid.
distractor_rationales.C: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon.
distractor_rationales.D: A frameshift results from insertions/deletions, not a same-amino-acid substitution.

items.stem: A point mutation that changes one amino acid to a DIFFERENT amino acid is ______; one that changes an amino-acid codon into a STOP codon is ______.
items.explanation: Missense = different amino acid; nonsense = premature stop codon. Takeaway: Missense = wrong amino acid. Nonsense = premature STOP. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Missense = different amino acid; nonsense = premature stop codon (truncated protein). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — missense changes the amino acid, nonsense makes a stop.
distractor_rationales.C: Silent (no change) and frameshift (indel) are different categories.
distractor_rationales.D: Frameshift and silent aren't the substitution types described.

items.stem: An insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides NOT divisible by three causes a ______, which alters every codon downstream.
items.explanation: Frameshift = insertion/deletion not a multiple of 3 → all downstream codons altered. Takeaway: Frameshift = indel not divisible by 3 → downstream codons ruined. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A frameshift shifts the reading frame, garbling all downstream codons (often producing a premature stop). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A silent mutation doesn't shift the frame or change the protein.
distractor_rationales.B: A point substitution changes one base without shifting the frame.
distractor_rationales.C: A transition is a type of substitution, not a frameshift.

items.stem: A substitution of one purine for the other purine (or one pyrimidine for the other pyrimidine) is a ______; a purine↔pyrimidine swap is a ______.
items.explanation: Transition = same base type (purine↔purine / pyrimidine↔pyrimidine); transversion = purine↔pyrimidine. Takeaway: Transition = same type swap. Transversion = purine↔pyrimidine. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Transition = purine↔purine or pyrimidine↔pyrimidine (same type); transversion = purine↔pyrimidine (type switch). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — same-type swap is a transition.
distractor_rationales.B: Missense/nonsense describe effects on the protein, not base-type swaps.
distractor_rationales.D: Insertions/deletions are indels, not substitutions.

items.stem: A thymine dimer caused by UV light is removed and replaced by which repair pathway?
items.explanation: Nucleotide excision repair removes UV-induced thymine dimers (defective in xeroderma pigmentosum). Takeaway: Thymine dimers (UV) → fixed by nucleotide excision repair. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions like UV-induced thymine dimers, then resynthesizes the strand (defective in xeroderma pigmentosum). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Replication copies DNA; it isn't the dimer-repair pathway.
distractor_rationales.B: Wobble concerns codon–anticodon pairing.
distractor_rationales.C: Alternative splicing is an RNA-processing mechanism, not DNA repair.

items.stem: An organism's genetic makeup (its alleles) is its ______; the observable trait that results is its ______.
items.explanation: Genotype = alleles present; phenotype = the observable trait. Takeaway: Genotype = the alleles. Phenotype = the observable trait. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Genotype = the alleles present; phenotype = the expressed, observable characteristic. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — genotype is the genetic makeup, phenotype the observable trait.
distractor_rationales.C: Allele/locus describe a gene variant and its position, not this pair.
distractor_rationales.D: Dominant/recessive describe allele behavior, not genotype vs. phenotype.

items.stem: An individual with two identical alleles for a gene is ______; one with two different alleles is ______.
items.explanation: Homozygous = two identical alleles; heterozygous = two different alleles. Takeaway: Homozygous = same alleles (AA/aa). Heterozygous = different (Aa). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Homozygous = two identical alleles (AA or aa); heterozygous = two different alleles (Aa). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — identical alleles = homozygous.
distractor_rationales.B: Dominant/recessive describe how alleles are expressed, not zygosity.
distractor_rationales.C: Haploid/diploid describe chromosome number, not allele identity.

items.stem: Mendel's law of segregation states that the two alleles for a trait:

choices.text: Separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one
Are inherited only from the father

items.explanation: Law of segregation: the two alleles separate during gamete formation (one per gamete). Takeaway: Segregation = alleles separate into gametes (one each). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The two alleles segregate during meiosis so each gamete carries just one allele per gene. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Alleles separate, not stay together, during gamete formation.
distractor_rationales.C: Alleles remain discrete (particulate inheritance), not blended.
distractor_rationales.D: Each parent contributes one allele; inheritance isn't paternal-only.

items.stem: Mendel's law of independent assortment states that alleles of different genes:

choices.text: Assort into gametes independently of one another (if unlinked)

items.explanation: Independent assortment: unlinked genes sort into gametes independently → new combinations. Takeaway: Independent assortment = unlinked genes sort independently (meiosis). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Genes on different chromosomes assort independently during meiosis, producing new allele combinations (linked genes are an exception). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Independent assortment produces new combinations, not fixed co-inheritance.
distractor_rationales.B: It specifically enables new combinations.
distractor_rationales.D: Assortment occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.

items.stem: To determine whether an organism showing a dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous, you cross it with an individual that is:
items.explanation: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive partner to reveal a dominant individual's genotype. Takeaway: Test cross = cross with homozygous recessive to find the genotype. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A test cross with a homozygous recessive individual reveals the unknown genotype: any recessive offspring means the parent was heterozygous. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A homozygous dominant partner would mask the recessive allele, hiding the answer.
distractor_rationales.B: A heterozygous partner complicates interpretation of the ratios.
distractor_rationales.C: Diploid organisms are crossed; 'haploid' isn't the test-cross partner.

items.stem: When a heterozygote shows a BLENDED, intermediate phenotype (red × white → pink flowers), the inheritance pattern is:
items.explanation: Incomplete dominance = blended intermediate heterozygote (red × white → pink). Takeaway: Incomplete dominance = blended intermediate (pink). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is an intermediate blend of the two homozygous phenotypes. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: In codominance BOTH alleles are fully and separately expressed, not blended.
distractor_rationales.B: Complete dominance masks the recessive allele entirely.
distractor_rationales.D: Epistasis is one gene masking another gene's expression.

items.stem: When BOTH alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed in the heterozygote (e.g., AB blood type), the pattern is:
items.explanation: Codominance = both alleles fully expressed (AB blood type). Takeaway: Codominance = both alleles fully shown (AB blood). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In codominance both alleles are expressed distinctly and fully (the AB blood phenotype shows both A and B antigens). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Incomplete dominance blends the phenotypes; codominance shows both fully.
distractor_rationales.C: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.
distractor_rationales.D: Polygenic inheritance is many genes affecting one trait.

items.stem: The human ABO blood group, controlled by three alleles (I^A, I^B, i) in the population, illustrates:

choices.text: Multiple alleles (with codominance and complete dominance combined)

items.explanation: ABO = multiple alleles: I^A and I^B codominant, both dominant over i. Takeaway: ABO = 3 alleles; I^A/I^B codominant, both dominant over i. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. ABO has three alleles: I^A and I^B are codominant to each other and both dominant over the recessive i. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: ABO is governed by three alleles, not one.
distractor_rationales.C: I^A and I^B are codominant, not blended (incomplete).
distractor_rationales.D: ABO is autosomal, not sex-linked.

items.stem: One gene influencing MANY different traits is ______; MANY genes contributing to ONE trait (e.g., height) is ______.
items.explanation: Pleiotropy = one gene → many traits; polygenic = many genes → one trait. Takeaway: Pleiotropy = 1 gene, many traits. Polygenic = many genes, 1 trait. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pleiotropy = one gene, many effects; polygenic = many genes, one (often continuous) trait. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.
distractor_rationales.B: Epistasis/codominance describe different phenomena.
distractor_rationales.D: Codominance/epistasis aren't the one-gene-many-traits pair.

items.stem: When the expression of one gene MASKS or modifies the expression of a DIFFERENT gene (e.g., an albinism gene hiding coat-color genes), this is:
items.explanation: Epistasis: one gene masks/modifies the expression of a different gene. Takeaway: Epistasis = one gene masks another gene. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Epistasis is a gene–gene interaction in which one gene's alleles mask the phenotypic effect of another gene. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Incomplete dominance is an allele interaction within one gene.
distractor_rationales.C: Codominance is both alleles of one gene expressed.
distractor_rationales.D: Independent assortment is how genes sort into gametes.

items.stem: In humans, biological females are typically ______ and biological males are typically ______.
items.explanation: Females = XX; males = XY (Y carries SRY). Takeaway: Female = XX, Male = XY (Y has SRY). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Females are XX (two X chromosomes); males are XY. The Y carries the SRY gene that triggers male development. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — females are XX, males XY.
distractor_rationales.B: Males are XY, not XX.
distractor_rationales.D: Typical human males are XY, not XO.

items.stem: X-linked recessive disorders (e.g., hemophilia, red-green color blindness) affect males more often than females because males:

choices.text: Have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
Cannot inherit the X from their mother
Carry the allele on the Y chromosome

items.explanation: Males are hemizygous for X — one recessive X allele is expressed (no masking) → X-linked recessive affects males more. Takeaway: X-linked recessive hits males more: only 1 X, so no masking allele. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes — one recessive allele on their single X is enough to show the trait (no second X to mask it). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Males have one X and one Y, not two X chromosomes.
distractor_rationales.C: Males inherit their single X from their mother.
distractor_rationales.D: X-linked genes are on the X, not the Y.

items.stem: A phenotypically normal mother who carries one copy of an X-linked recessive allele is a ______, and she passes the allele to about half her sons, who will be:
items.explanation: A carrier mother (heterozygous) passes an X-linked recessive allele to ~half her sons, who are affected. Takeaway: Carrier mom → ~50% of sons affected (X-linked recessive). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A heterozygous carrier mother is unaffected but transmits the allele to ~50% of sons, who (being hemizygous) are affected. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The heterozygous mother is a carrier, not affected.
distractor_rationales.C: Sons receiving the allele are affected, not unaffected.
distractor_rationales.D: The carrier mother is heterozygous, not homozygous, and her affected sons show the trait.

items.stem: Meiosis produces gametes that are ______ and genetically ______ from the parent cell.
items.explanation: Meiosis → haploid, genetically varied gametes (halves chromosome number). Takeaway: Meiosis = haploid + varied gametes (halves 2n→n). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Meiosis halves the chromosome number (diploid → haploid) and generates genetic variation via crossing over and independent assortment. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Gametes are haploid, not diploid, and vary genetically.
distractor_rationales.C: Meiosis creates variation; gametes aren't genetically identical.
distractor_rationales.D: Gametes are haploid (n), not diploid (2n).

items.stem: During prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata. This process is:
items.explanation: Crossing over (prophase I): homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata → recombination. Takeaway: Crossing over = homologs swap segments in prophase I. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Crossing over swaps segments between homologous chromosomes in prophase I, creating recombinant chromosomes and genetic variation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Independent assortment is the random orientation of homolog pairs, a separate variation source.
distractor_rationales.B: Nondisjunction is failure of chromosomes to separate properly.
distractor_rationales.D: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm.

items.stem: Meiosis I separates ______, reducing the chromosome number (reductional); meiosis II separates ______ (equational), like mitosis.
items.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (reductional); meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Takeaway: Meiosis I = homologs (reductional). Meiosis II = sister chromatids. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Meiosis I (reductional) separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II (equational) separates sister chromatids. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — homologs separate in meiosis I, sister chromatids in II.
distractor_rationales.B: Meiosis I separates homologs, not chromatids.
distractor_rationales.D: The two divisions separate different structures (homologs, then chromatids).

items.stem: Meiosis increases genetic diversity through crossing over and:
items.explanation: Meiotic variation = crossing over + independent assortment. Takeaway: Meiosis variation = crossing over + independent assortment. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Independent assortment (random orientation of homolog pairs at metaphase I) plus crossing over generate genetic variation in gametes. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Semiconservative replication copies DNA faithfully; it doesn't create variation.
distractor_rationales.B: Proofreading reduces errors; it doesn't generate diversity.
distractor_rationales.C: Binary fission is asexual prokaryotic division.

items.stem: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during meiosis — producing gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers (e.g., trisomy 21) — is:
items.explanation: Nondisjunction = chromosomes fail to separate → abnormal chromosome number (e.g., trisomy 21). Takeaway: Nondisjunction = failed separation → aneuploidy (e.g., trisomy 21). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Nondisjunction is improper chromosome separation, yielding aneuploid gametes (e.g., Down syndrome, trisomy 21). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Crossing over exchanges segments; it doesn't cause aneuploidy by itself.
distractor_rationales.B: A translocation moves a segment to a nonhomologous chromosome.
distractor_rationales.C: Independent assortment is normal random orientation, not a separation failure.

items.stem: Genes located close together on the SAME chromosome tend to be inherited together and are called:
items.explanation: Linked genes sit close on the same chromosome and are usually inherited together. Takeaway: Linked genes = close on same chromosome, inherited together. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Linked genes are near each other on one chromosome, so they're usually inherited together (violating independent assortment unless crossing over separates them). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Unlinked genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
distractor_rationales.B: Homologous refers to matching chromosome pairs, not linkage.
distractor_rationales.D: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.

items.stem: The farther apart two genes are on a chromosome, the ______ the frequency of crossing over between them, which is used to build genetic maps.
items.explanation: Recombination frequency increases with distance between genes (basis of genetic maps). Takeaway: Farther apart genes → higher recombination frequency (map distance). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Greater distance → more chance a crossover occurs between the genes → higher recombination frequency (measured in map units/centimorgans). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Closer genes have LOWER recombination frequency; farther apart is higher.
distractor_rationales.C: Distance changes recombination frequency; it isn't constant.
distractor_rationales.D: Recombination frequency is only ~zero for very tightly linked genes.

items.stem: Two genes that assort essentially independently (far apart or on different chromosomes) show a maximum recombination frequency of about:
items.explanation: Max recombination frequency ≈ 50% = independent assortment. Takeaway: 50% recombination = independent assortment (the ceiling). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A recombination frequency of ~50% indicates independent assortment — the maximum, because you can't exceed a 1:1 parental-to-recombinant ratio. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Recombination frequency cannot exceed ~50%.
distractor_rationales.B: 0% would mean complete linkage (never separated).
distractor_rationales.D: 25% indicates linkage, not independent assortment.

items.stem: In the Hardy-Weinberg model, if p and q are the frequencies of two alleles, then:
items.explanation: Hardy-Weinberg allele frequencies: p + q = 1. Takeaway: H-W: p + q = 1 (allele frequencies). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Allele frequencies for a two-allele gene sum to 1: p + q = 1. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The frequencies sum to 1, not 2.
distractor_rationales.B: They sum to 1; their product isn't fixed at 1.
distractor_rationales.D: p and q are generally unequal, so p − q isn't necessarily 0.

items.stem: The Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies are given by:
items.explanation: H-W genotypes: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (homo dominant + hetero + homo recessive). Takeaway: H-W genotypes: p² + 2pq + q² = 1. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. p² (homozygous dominant) + 2pq (heterozygous) + q² (homozygous recessive) = 1. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: This omits the 2pq heterozygote term.
distractor_rationales.C: That isn't the genotype-frequency equation.
distractor_rationales.D: Genotype frequencies sum (not multiply) to 1.

items.stem: A population stays in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (allele frequencies unchanging) only if there is:

choices.text: No mutation, no migration, no selection, random mating, and a large population

items.explanation: H-W equilibrium needs: no mutation, no migration, no selection, random mating, large population. Takeaway: H-W: no mutation/migration/selection, random mating, large N. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Equilibrium requires no mutation, no gene flow, no selection, random mating, and a large (no genetic drift) population — rarely all met, so deviations signal evolution. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Selection changes allele frequencies, breaking equilibrium.
distractor_rationales.B: Mutation introduces new alleles, breaking equilibrium.
distractor_rationales.C: Nonrandom mating disrupts genotype frequencies.

items.stem: If a recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 people (q² = 0.0001), the frequency of the recessive allele (q) is:
items.explanation: q = √(q²); here √0.0001 = 0.01. Takeaway: q = √(affected frequency). √0.0001 = 0.01. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. q = √(q²) = √0.0001 = 0.01. (Then p = 0.99 and carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 0.0198.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: 0.0001 is q² (the affected frequency), not q.
distractor_rationales.D: 0.5 doesn't follow from q² = 0.0001.

items.stem: Every standard amino acid has a central (alpha) carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and:
items.explanation: Amino acid = alpha carbon + amino group + carboxyl group + H + a variable R group. Takeaway: Amino acid: alpha C bonded to -NH2, -COOH, H, and R group. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The alpha carbon carries an amino group, a carboxyl group, an H, and a distinctive R group (side chain) that defines each amino acid. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Only acidic amino acids have a second carboxyl; it's not universal.
distractor_rationales.B: Phosphate groups are found in nucleotides, not the amino acid core.
distractor_rationales.C: Nitrogenous bases belong to nucleotides, not amino acids.

items.stem: Amino acids are grouped by their side chains as nonpolar (hydrophobic), polar, acidic, or basic. Amino acids with hydrophobic side chains tend to be found:

choices.text: On the surface interacting with water
Buried in the interior of a folded protein, away from water

items.explanation: Hydrophobic (nonpolar) side chains bury in the protein interior; polar/charged face the water. Takeaway: Hydrophobic R groups bury inside; polar/charged face water. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hydrophobic (nonpolar) side chains cluster in the protein's interior, away from the aqueous environment; polar/charged residues face the water. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Polar and charged residues, not hydrophobic ones, face the aqueous surface.
distractor_rationales.B: Hydrophobic residues aren't restricted to the active site.
distractor_rationales.C: Side chains aren't generally phosphate-bonded.

items.stem: At physiological pH, an amino acid exists predominantly as a zwitterion, meaning it has:

choices.text: A positively charged amino group and a negatively charged carboxyl group (net neutral)
A phosphate and a hydroxyl charge

items.explanation: A zwitterion: protonated amino group (+) and deprotonated carboxyl (−) → net neutral. Takeaway: Zwitterion = +NH3 and -COO− (net neutral, at physiological pH). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Near neutral pH the amino group is protonated (+) and the carboxyl is deprotonated (−), giving a net-neutral zwitterion. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The zwitterion has one + and one −, not two positives.
distractor_rationales.C: It carries charges (one + and one −) that cancel; it's not uncharged.
distractor_rationales.D: The charges are on the amino and carboxyl groups, not phosphate/hydroxyl.

items.stem: The pH at which an amino acid carries no net charge (exists mainly as the zwitterion) is its:
items.explanation: The isoelectric point (pI) = pH at which the amino acid has no net charge. Takeaway: pI = pH of zero net charge (zwitterion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH of zero net charge — useful in techniques like electrophoresis. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The pKa of water isn't the amino acid's neutral-charge pH.
distractor_rationales.C: Optimal temperature relates to enzyme activity, not charge.
distractor_rationales.D: Melting point isn't the pH of zero net charge.

items.stem: Amino acids are joined into proteins by peptide bonds, which form between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next via a:
items.explanation: Peptide bonds form by dehydration (condensation), releasing water (a covalent amide bond). Takeaway: Peptide bond = dehydration reaction (amide bond, releases water). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Peptide bond formation is a dehydration/condensation reaction linking a carboxyl to an amino group and releasing water. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds; it doesn't form them.
distractor_rationales.C: Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides, not amino acids.
distractor_rationales.D: A peptide bond is a covalent amide bond, not a hydrogen bond.

items.stem: The specific linear sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, determined by the gene, is its ______ structure.
items.explanation: Primary structure = the amino acid sequence (peptide bonds). Takeaway: Primary = amino acid sequence. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held together by peptide bonds. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Secondary structure is local folding (helices/sheets).
distractor_rationales.B: Tertiary structure is the overall 3D shape of one chain.
distractor_rationales.C: Quaternary structure is the assembly of multiple chains.

items.stem: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets — local folded patterns stabilized by hydrogen bonds along the backbone — make up a protein's ______ structure.
items.explanation: Secondary structure = alpha helices & beta sheets (backbone hydrogen bonds). Takeaway: Secondary = alpha helix + beta sheet (backbone H-bonds). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Secondary structure (alpha helix, beta sheet) arises from hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Primary structure is the linear sequence.
distractor_rationales.C: Tertiary structure is the overall 3D fold.
distractor_rationales.D: Quaternary structure involves multiple subunits.

items.stem: The overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide — stabilized by side-chain interactions (hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges) — is its ______ structure.
items.explanation: Tertiary structure = the 3D shape of one chain (side-chain interactions, disulfide bonds). Takeaway: Tertiary = 3D shape of one chain (R-group interactions). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Tertiary structure is the 3D conformation of one chain, driven largely by R-group interactions (notably hydrophobic packing and disulfide bonds). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Secondary structure is local (helices/sheets), not the whole 3D fold.
distractor_rationales.C: Primary structure is the sequence.
distractor_rationales.D: Quaternary structure requires multiple polypeptide chains.

items.stem: When two or more separate polypeptide subunits assemble into a functional protein (e.g., hemoglobin's four chains), that arrangement is the ______ structure.
items.explanation: Quaternary structure = multiple polypeptide subunits assembled (e.g., hemoglobin). Takeaway: Quaternary = multiple subunits assembled (hemoglobin). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Quaternary structure is the assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits into one functional complex. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Tertiary structure concerns a single chain's 3D shape.
distractor_rationales.C: Secondary structure is local folding within a chain.
distractor_rationales.D: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence.

items.stem: Heat, extreme pH, or chemicals can disrupt a protein's shape without breaking peptide bonds, causing loss of function. This is:
items.explanation: Denaturation = loss of 3D shape/function (heat, pH, chemicals) with the peptide bonds intact. Takeaway: Denaturation = protein unfolds/loses function (primary sequence intact). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Denaturation unfolds a protein (disrupting secondary/tertiary/quaternary structure) while leaving the primary sequence intact — often irreversibly abolishing function. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Translation builds a protein; it doesn't unfold one.
distractor_rationales.B: Transcription makes RNA from DNA.
distractor_rationales.C: Replication copies DNA.

items.stem: Enzymes speed up reactions by:

choices.text: Lowering the activation energy of the reaction

items.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy (they don't change ΔG or equilibrium, and aren't consumed). Takeaway: Enzymes lower activation energy (not ΔG, not equilibrium). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Enzymes are catalysts that lower activation energy, increasing rate without altering the reaction's thermodynamics (ΔG or equilibrium). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Enzymes don't shift the equilibrium; they speed both directions equally.
distractor_rationales.B: Enzymes don't change ΔG; they only lower the activation barrier.
distractor_rationales.C: Catalysts are not consumed — they're regenerated.

items.stem: An enzyme's specificity comes from the shape and chemistry of its ______, where the substrate binds.
items.explanation: Enzyme specificity comes from the active site (complementary shape/chemistry). Takeaway: Active site = where substrate binds; source of specificity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The active site's complementary shape/chemistry determines which substrate binds, giving enzymes their specificity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: An allosteric site is a regulatory site elsewhere, not the substrate-binding pocket.
distractor_rationales.B: The hydrophobic core stabilizes folding, not substrate binding specificity.
distractor_rationales.D: A signal peptide targets a protein for transport.

items.stem: The model in which the enzyme's active site changes shape slightly to wrap around the substrate upon binding is the:
items.explanation: Induced fit: the active site adjusts its shape to embrace the substrate on binding. Takeaway: Induced fit = active site molds around the substrate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In induced fit, substrate binding induces a conformational change that optimizes catalysis (a refinement of the rigid lock-and-key idea). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The lock-and-key model assumes a rigid, pre-fit active site.
distractor_rationales.C: Michaelis-Menten describes kinetics, not the binding conformational change.
distractor_rationales.D: The second-messenger model is about signal transduction.

items.stem: Many enzymes require non-protein helpers for activity: inorganic ions are ______, while organic molecules (often vitamin-derived) are ______.
items.explanation: Cofactors = inorganic ions; coenzymes = organic helpers (often vitamin-derived). Takeaway: Cofactor = inorganic ion. Coenzyme = organic (vitamin-derived). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cofactors are inorganic (e.g., Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺); coenzymes are organic (e.g., NAD⁺, FAD, from vitamins). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — inorganic = cofactor, organic = coenzyme.
distractor_rationales.B: Substrates/products are reactants, not enzyme helpers.
distractor_rationales.C: Inhibitors/activators regulate enzymes; they aren't the cofactor/coenzyme pair.

items.stem: Enzyme activity is highest at an optimal temperature and pH; beyond these, activity drops sharply because the enzyme:
items.explanation: Beyond optimal temperature/pH, enzymes denature and lose activity. Takeaway: Extreme temp/pH → enzyme denatures → activity drops. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Outside optimal temperature/pH, the enzyme denatures (unfolds), disrupting the active site and reducing activity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Enzyme activity change isn't due to transcription rate.
distractor_rationales.B: Denaturation destroys, not creates, the active site.
distractor_rationales.C: The enzyme isn't converted into a substrate.

items.stem: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Vmax is the maximum reaction rate, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration at which the rate is:
items.explanation: Km = substrate concentration at ½ Vmax (low Km → high affinity). Takeaway: Km = [S] at half Vmax. Low Km = high affinity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Km is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity (½ Vmax); a low Km indicates high substrate affinity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The rate reaches Vmax only at saturating (very high) substrate.
distractor_rationales.B: Km is a positive substrate concentration where the rate is ½ Vmax, not zero.
distractor_rationales.C: Reaction rate cannot exceed Vmax.

items.stem: As substrate concentration increases, the reaction rate rises then plateaus at Vmax because:

choices.text: All enzyme active sites become saturated (occupied)

items.explanation: Rate plateaus at Vmax when all active sites are saturated. Takeaway: Vmax plateau = enzyme active sites saturated. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. At high substrate, active sites are saturated, so adding more substrate can't increase the rate — it levels off at Vmax. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Enzymes are catalysts and aren't consumed.
distractor_rationales.C: Substrate doesn't denature; the plateau is from saturation.
distractor_rationales.D: Km is a constant for a given enzyme–substrate pair, not ever-increasing.

items.stem: An enzyme with a LOW Km for its substrate has:

choices.text: A low affinity for that substrate
A high affinity for that substrate (reaches half-max at low substrate)

items.explanation: Low Km → high affinity (half-max reached at low substrate). Takeaway: Low Km = high substrate affinity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Low Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at low substrate concentration — i.e., it binds substrate tightly (high affinity). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Low Km indicates HIGH affinity, not low.
distractor_rationales.B: Km doesn't indicate lack of activity.
distractor_rationales.C: Km and Vmax are independent parameters; low Km doesn't set Vmax.

items.stem: A competitive inhibitor binds the ______, and its effect can be overcome by adding more substrate — raising the apparent Km while Vmax is unchanged.
items.explanation: Competitive inhibitor: binds the active site; ↑ apparent Km, Vmax unchanged (overcome by more substrate). Takeaway: Competitive: active site; ↑Km, same Vmax (beaten by more substrate). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Competitive inhibitors bind the active site, competing with substrate; excess substrate outcompetes them, so Vmax is unchanged but apparent Km rises. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Binding an allosteric site describes noncompetitive inhibition.
distractor_rationales.C: A competitive inhibitor binds the enzyme, not the substrate.
distractor_rationales.D: It competes at the active site, not by acting as a coenzyme.

items.stem: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds a site OTHER than the active site (an allosteric site) and:

choices.text: Lowers Vmax and cannot be overcome by adding substrate

items.explanation: Noncompetitive inhibitor: binds allosterically; ↓Vmax, not overcome by more substrate. Takeaway: Noncompetitive: allosteric site; ↓Vmax, more substrate won't help. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind allosterically, reducing Vmax; adding substrate doesn't relieve them (Km typically unchanged). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Noncompetitive inhibition lowers, not raises, Vmax.
distractor_rationales.C: It binds the enzyme's allosteric site, not the substrate.
distractor_rationales.D: Its reversibility isn't determined by heating.

items.stem: Allosteric enzymes are regulated by molecules that bind a site distinct from the active site, causing a conformational change that:

choices.text: Either activates or inhibits the enzyme

items.explanation: Allosteric regulation: a regulator binds a separate site → conformational change that activates OR inhibits. Takeaway: Allosteric = regulator at a separate site, can activate or inhibit. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Allosteric regulators (activators or inhibitors) bind a regulatory site and shift the enzyme's conformation, tuning activity up or down. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Allosteric regulation can inhibit as well as activate.
distractor_rationales.B: It changes conformation, not peptide bonds.
distractor_rationales.C: It alters shape/activity, not the primary sequence.

items.stem: In many pathways, the final product inhibits an enzyme early in its own pathway. This self-regulation is:
items.explanation: Feedback inhibition: the end product inhibits an early pathway enzyme (prevents overproduction). Takeaway: Feedback inhibition = end product shuts off its own pathway. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Feedback inhibition uses the pathway's end product as an allosteric inhibitor of an upstream enzyme, preventing overproduction. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Feedforward activation is the opposite direction of control.
distractor_rationales.C: 'Competitive activation' isn't a standard regulatory mechanism.
distractor_rationales.D: Denaturation is loss of protein shape, not pathway self-regulation.

items.stem: A reaction with a NEGATIVE change in Gibbs free energy (ΔG 0 is ______.
items.explanation: ΔG = exergonic (spontaneous); ΔG > 0 = endergonic (needs energy). Takeaway: Exergonic = ΔG0. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. ΔG 0 = endergonic (nonspontaneous, requires energy input). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — negative ΔG is exergonic.
distractor_rationales.C: Catabolic/anabolic describe breakdown/build-up, not the ΔG sign directly.
distractor_rationales.D: Oxidized/reduced describe electron transfer, not spontaneity.

items.stem: ATP powers cellular work because hydrolysis of its terminal phosphate bond is:
items.explanation: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic — its released energy is coupled to drive endergonic reactions. Takeaway: ATP hydrolysis = exergonic (drives endergonic reactions via coupling). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. ATP hydrolysis (ATP → ADP + Pi) is exergonic; cells couple it to endergonic reactions to drive them. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: ATP hydrolysis releases (not stores) energy.
distractor_rationales.C: It is strongly exergonic, not neutral.
distractor_rationales.D: ATP hydrolysis occurs throughout the cell, not only the nucleus.

items.stem: Cells drive an unfavorable (endergonic) reaction by coupling it to:

choices.text: An exergonic reaction such as ATP hydrolysis

items.explanation: Energy coupling: an exergonic reaction (ATP hydrolysis) drives an endergonic one. Takeaway: Coupling = exergonic (ATP) drives endergonic reaction. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Energy coupling links an exergonic process (e.g., ATP hydrolysis) to an endergonic one so the combined ΔG is negative. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Coupling two endergonic reactions can't make the pair spontaneous.
distractor_rationales.C: Denaturation destroys enzymes; it isn't an energy source.
distractor_rationales.D: Passive diffusion releases little usable free energy for coupling.

items.stem: In redox reactions central to metabolism, a molecule that LOSES electrons is ______; one that GAINS electrons is ______.
items.explanation: Oxidation = lose electrons; reduction = gain electrons (LEO says GER). Takeaway: Oxidation = lose e⁻. Reduction = gain e⁻ (LEO GER). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. LEO the lion says GER: Lose Electrons = Oxidation; Gain Electrons = Reduction. Electron carriers like NAD⁺ are reduced to NADH. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — losing electrons is oxidation.
distractor_rationales.C: Hydrolysis/condensation involve water, not electron transfer.
distractor_rationales.D: Phosphorylation adds a phosphate, not electrons.

items.stem: Glycolysis splits one glucose (6 carbons) into two molecules of ______, occurring in the ______.
items.explanation: Glycolysis: glucose → 2 pyruvate in the cytoplasm (anaerobic-capable). Takeaway: Glycolysis = glucose → 2 pyruvate (cytoplasm). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Glycolysis converts glucose into two pyruvate in the cytoplasm (no oxygen required). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Pyruvate is later converted to acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrion; glycolysis makes pyruvate.
distractor_rationales.C: Lactate forms only during fermentation, and glycolysis is cytoplasmic, not nuclear.
distractor_rationales.D: Ethanol forms in alcoholic fermentation, not standard glycolysis.

items.stem: Glycolysis has a net yield per glucose of:
items.explanation: Glycolysis net: 2 ATP + 2 NADH per glucose. Takeaway: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP + 2 NADH. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and produces 4 (net 2 ATP), plus 2 NADH per glucose. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: ~30–36 ATP is the total from full aerobic respiration, not glycolysis alone.
distractor_rationales.B: Glycolysis has a positive net ATP yield (2).
distractor_rationales.D: It nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH, not 4 NADH with no ATP.

items.stem: Glycolysis itself:

choices.text: Does not require oxygen (occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions)

items.explanation: Glycolysis needs no oxygen — it runs in the cytoplasm aerobically or anaerobically. Takeaway: Glycolysis is oxygen-independent (cytoplasm). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Glycolysis is oxygen-independent; oxygen is needed later (in the ETC), not for glycolysis itself. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glycolysis proceeds without oxygen.
distractor_rationales.B: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, not the mitochondria.
distractor_rationales.D: No CO2 is released during glycolysis (that happens in later steps).

items.stem: Before the citric acid cycle, each pyruvate is oxidized and decarboxylated to form ______, releasing CO2 and generating NADH.
items.explanation: Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (+ CO2 + NADH) by pyruvate dehydrogenase (the link reaction). Takeaway: Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (+CO2, +NADH) before the Krebs cycle. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing one CO2 and producing NADH (the link reaction). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Lactate forms in fermentation, not the link to the citric acid cycle.
distractor_rationales.C: Glucose is the starting fuel, not a product of pyruvate oxidation.
distractor_rationales.D: Oxaloacetate combines WITH acetyl-CoA to start the cycle; it isn't made from pyruvate here.

items.stem: The citric acid (Krebs) cycle occurs in the ______ and, per acetyl-CoA, produces NADH, FADH2, and:

choices.text: Mitochondrial matrix; GTP (or ATP) and CO2

items.explanation: Krebs cycle (matrix): per acetyl-CoA → 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, 2 CO2. Takeaway: Krebs (matrix): NADH, FADH2, GTP, CO2 per acetyl-CoA. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Each acetyl-CoA in the matrix yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (≈ATP), and 2 CO2. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Pyruvate is a glycolysis product; the cycle is in the matrix, not cytoplasm.
distractor_rationales.C: The cycle occurs in the matrix and doesn't make DNA.
distractor_rationales.D: The ETC is on the inner membrane and consumes O2; the cycle doesn't produce O2.

items.stem: The main purpose of the citric acid cycle for ATP production is to generate ______, which then feed the electron transport chain.
items.explanation: The Krebs cycle mainly makes NADH & FADH2 to feed the electron transport chain. Takeaway: Krebs cycle's key job: make NADH/FADH2 for the ETC. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The cycle's chief energetic role is producing NADH and FADH2, which deliver electrons to the ETC where most ATP is made. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The cycle makes only 1 GTP per acetyl-CoA directly; most ATP comes later.
distractor_rationales.B: The cycle oxidizes fuel; it doesn't synthesize glucose for storage.
distractor_rationales.D: The cycle consumes carbon fuel; it doesn't produce oxygen.

items.stem: In the electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane), electrons from NADH and FADH2 are passed down carriers, and the energy released is used to:

choices.text: Directly phosphorylate ADP at each step
Pump protons (H+) across the membrane, creating a gradient

items.explanation: The ETC pumps H+ across the inner membrane, storing energy as a proton gradient. Takeaway: ETC pumps H+ → proton gradient (inner membrane). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The ETC uses electron energy to pump H+ into the intermembrane space, building the proton-motive force used by ATP synthase. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: ATP is made by ATP synthase using the gradient, not directly at each carrier.
distractor_rationales.B: The ETC consumes O2 (forming water); it doesn't split water.
distractor_rationales.D: Glucose synthesis is not a function of the ETC.

items.stem: ATP is produced when protons flow back down their gradient through ______, a process called:
items.explanation: Protons flow through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis) → ATP. Takeaway: ATP synthase + proton flow = chemiosmosis → ATP. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Protons flow through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), driving phosphorylation of ADP to ATP — oxidative phosphorylation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glycolysis is a separate cytoplasmic pathway, not proton flow through ATP synthase.
distractor_rationales.B: Aquaporins conduct water, not the ATP-generating proton flow.
distractor_rationales.D: Pyruvate dehydrogenase makes acetyl-CoA; fermentation is anaerobic.

items.stem: In aerobic respiration, the FINAL electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain is:
items.explanation: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is oxygen (→ water). Takeaway: O2 = final electron acceptor (forms water). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the ETC and combines with H+ to form water; without O2, the chain backs up and stops. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: CO2 is a waste product of earlier steps, not the final electron acceptor.
distractor_rationales.C: NAD+ is an electron carrier that gets reduced earlier, not the terminal acceptor.
distractor_rationales.D: Pyruvate is a fermentation electron acceptor, not the aerobic terminal acceptor.

items.stem: Complete aerobic respiration of one glucose yields approximately how much ATP?
items.explanation: Aerobic respiration ≈ 30–38 ATP per glucose (mostly from oxidative phosphorylation). Takeaway: Aerobic respiration ≈ 30–38 ATP/glucose (most from oxphos). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Aerobic respiration yields roughly 30–38 ATP per glucose (estimates vary), most from oxidative phosphorylation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: 2 ATP is the net from glycolysis alone.
distractor_rationales.C: 4 ATP is not the full aerobic yield.
distractor_rationales.D: The yield is far below 100 ATP per glucose.

items.stem: When oxygen is unavailable, fermentation allows glycolysis to continue by:

choices.text: Regenerating NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can keep running
Producing large amounts of ATP directly

items.explanation: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen. Takeaway: Fermentation = regenerate NAD+ to keep glycolysis going (no O2). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fermentation reoxidizes NADH to NAD+, replenishing the NAD+ that glycolysis needs — its main purpose (little extra ATP). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Fermentation yields no extra ATP beyond glycolysis's net 2.
distractor_rationales.C: Fermentation doesn't produce oxygen.
distractor_rationales.D: It doesn't synthesize glucose; it sustains glycolysis.

items.stem: In humans (and muscle during intense exercise), fermentation converts pyruvate to ______; in yeast, pyruvate is converted to ethanol and ______.
items.explanation: Human/muscle: pyruvate → lactate. Yeast: pyruvate → ethanol + CO2. Takeaway: Lactic acid ferm (humans) → lactate. Alcoholic (yeast) → ethanol + CO2. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Human/muscle cells perform lactic acid fermentation (pyruvate → lactate); yeast perform alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate → ethanol + CO2). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Humans make lactate, not ethanol; the pairing is reversed.
distractor_rationales.B: Fermentation doesn't produce acetyl-CoA/water as its products here.
distractor_rationales.D: Fermentation doesn't regenerate glucose or oxygen.

items.stem: Excess glucose is stored in the liver and muscle as the branched polysaccharide ______; its breakdown to release glucose is glycogenolysis.
items.explanation: Animals store glucose as glycogen (liver/muscle); glycogenolysis releases it. Takeaway: Glycogen = animal glucose storage (liver/muscle). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Animals store glucose as glycogen (glycogenesis); glycogenolysis breaks it down to release glucose. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Starch is the plant storage polysaccharide, not the animal one.
distractor_rationales.C: Cellulose is a structural plant polysaccharide, indigestible to humans.
distractor_rationales.D: Triglycerides store energy as fat, not as a glucose polymer.

items.stem: During prolonged fasting, the body synthesizes new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (lactate, amino acids, glycerol). This pathway is:
items.explanation: Gluconeogenesis = making new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (fasting). Takeaway: Gluconeogenesis = make glucose from non-carbs (fasting).
