The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (mainly in the liver) to maintain blood glucose during fasting. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glycolysis breaks glucose down; it doesn't synthesize it.
distractor_rationales.B: Beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids, not glucose synthesis.
distractor_rationales.D: Glycogenesis stores glucose as glycogen; it doesn't make new glucose from non-carbs.

items.stem: After a meal, high blood glucose triggers ______, which promotes glucose uptake and storage; during fasting, ______ raises blood glucose.
items.explanation: Insulin lowers blood glucose (fed); glucagon raises it (fasting). Takeaway: Insulin = lower glucose (fed). Glucagon = raise glucose (fasting). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose (uptake/storage); glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — insulin lowers glucose after a meal, glucagon raises it when fasting.
distractor_rationales.B: Cortisol raises glucose but isn't the post-meal lowering hormone; insulin is.
distractor_rationales.C: Both glucagon and epinephrine raise glucose, but the post-meal hormone is insulin.

items.stem: Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl-CoA (which enters the Krebs cycle) through the process of:
items.explanation: Beta-oxidation breaks fatty acids into acetyl-CoA for the Krebs cycle. Takeaway: Beta-oxidation = fatty acids → acetyl-CoA. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Beta-oxidation cleaves fatty acids two carbons at a time into acetyl-CoA (yielding NADH/FADH2) for the Krebs cycle. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glycolysis breaks down glucose, not fatty acids.
distractor_rationales.B: Transamination transfers amino groups in amino acid metabolism.
distractor_rationales.D: Gluconeogenesis synthesizes glucose.

items.stem: The cell membrane is described by the fluid mosaic model as a:

choices.text: Phospholipid bilayer with embedded, mobile proteins

items.explanation: Fluid mosaic: a fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded, mobile proteins. Takeaway: Membrane = fluid phospholipid bilayer + embedded proteins. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer with proteins (and cholesterol, carbohydrates) embedded and able to move laterally. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The membrane is fluid, not a rigid wall.
distractor_rationales.C: It's a bilayer (two leaflets), not a single layer.
distractor_rationales.D: Cholesterol modulates fluidity but doesn't form the sheet itself.

items.stem: Phospholipids form a bilayer because each molecule is amphipathic, with:

choices.text: A charged core and neutral surface
A hydrophilic (phosphate) head and hydrophobic (fatty acid) tails

items.explanation: Phospholipids are amphipathic: hydrophilic head + hydrophobic tails → bilayer. Takeaway: Phospholipid = polar head + nonpolar tails (amphipathic). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The hydrophilic heads face the aqueous exterior/interior and the hydrophobic tails face inward, self-assembling into a bilayer. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A molecule with two hydrophilic ends wouldn't form a stable bilayer.
distractor_rationales.B: Two hydrophobic ends wouldn't orient toward water.
distractor_rationales.C: The heads (surface) are charged/polar and tails (core) are nonpolar — the opposite of this option.

items.stem: In animal cell membranes, cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer, meaning it:

choices.text: Keeps the membrane fluid at low temperatures and stable at high temperatures

items.explanation: Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity (fluid when cold, stable when hot). Takeaway: Cholesterol = fluidity buffer (fluid when cold, firm when hot). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cholesterol buffers fluidity: at high temperature it restrains movement (stabilizes), at low temperature it prevents tight packing (keeps fluid). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Its effect depends on temperature; it doesn't only increase fluidity.
distractor_rationales.C: It moderates fluidity rather than making the membrane rigid.
distractor_rationales.D: Cholesterol regulates fluidity; it isn't an ion transporter.

items.stem: Movement of a solute DOWN its concentration gradient without energy is ______ transport; movement AGAINST the gradient using ATP is ______ transport.
items.explanation: Passive = down gradient, no energy; active = against gradient, uses ATP. Takeaway: Passive = down gradient (free). Active = against gradient (ATP). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Passive transport (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis) needs no energy; active transport uses ATP to move against the gradient. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — down-gradient is passive, against-gradient is active.
distractor_rationales.C: 'Bulk/simple' aren't the passive/active pair.
distractor_rationales.D: Osmotic/oncotic describe pressures, not this distinction.

items.stem: Osmosis is the passive movement of ______ across a semipermeable membrane from a region of ______ solute concentration to ______ solute concentration.
items.explanation: Osmosis: water moves from low→high solute (toward the more concentrated side). Takeaway: Osmosis = water moves toward higher solute concentration. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Water moves toward the higher solute concentration (lower water concentration) to equalize — i.e., from low to high solute. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Osmosis is the movement of water, not solute.
distractor_rationales.C: Water moves toward higher solute (this reverses it).
distractor_rationales.D: Osmosis specifically refers to water movement, not ions.

items.stem: A red blood cell placed in a HYPOTONIC solution (lower solute outside) will:

choices.text: Swell and possibly lyse as water moves in

items.explanation: In a hypotonic solution, water enters the cell → it swells/lyses. Takeaway: Hypotonic = cell swells (water in). Hypertonic = shrinks. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In a hypotonic solution, water flows into the cell (toward higher internal solute), causing it to swell and potentially burst (lyse). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Shriveling (crenation) happens in a hypertonic solution, where water leaves.
distractor_rationales.B: In a hypotonic solution the cell gains water and changes size.
distractor_rationales.C: Water movement here is passive osmosis, not active pumping.

items.stem: The Na+/K+ ATPase is a form of active transport that, per cycle, pumps:

choices.text: 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, using ATP

items.explanation: Na+/K+ ATPase: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP (sets up gradients). Takeaway: Na+/K+ pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in (uses ATP). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The Na+/K+ pump uses ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+, maintaining gradients essential for membrane potential. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The ratio is 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, not the reverse.
distractor_rationales.B: It moves Na+ out and K+ in (opposite directions), not both out.
distractor_rationales.C: It transports ions, not water.

items.stem: The organelle that houses the cell's DNA and controls gene expression is the nucleus; within it, the site of ribosome assembly is the:
items.explanation: The nucleolus (in the nucleus) assembles ribosomes (rRNA synthesis). Takeaway: Nucleolus = ribosome assembly (inside nucleus). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The nucleolus (inside the nucleus) is where rRNA is transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The Golgi modifies and packages proteins, outside the nucleus.
distractor_rationales.B: Lysosomes digest cellular material.
distractor_rationales.D: Centrioles organize the mitotic spindle.

items.stem: The rough endoplasmic reticulum (studded with ribosomes) synthesizes ______, while the smooth ER synthesizes ______ and detoxifies.
items.explanation: Rough ER = protein synthesis; smooth ER = lipid synthesis + detox. Takeaway: Rough ER = proteins. Smooth ER = lipids + detox. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rough ER makes and processes proteins (has ribosomes); smooth ER synthesizes lipids/steroids and detoxifies drugs. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — rough ER makes proteins, smooth ER makes lipids.
distractor_rationales.C: The ER doesn't synthesize DNA/RNA (that's the nucleus).
distractor_rationales.D: ATP is made in mitochondria, not the ER.

items.stem: The organelle that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery (like a cellular post office) is the:
items.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins/lipids for shipping. Takeaway: Golgi = modify + package + ship (cellular post office). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The Golgi apparatus modifies (e.g., glycosylation), sorts, and packages molecules into vesicles for their destinations. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The mitochondrion produces ATP, not protein packaging.
distractor_rationales.C: Ribosomes synthesize polypeptides; they don't sort/package.
distractor_rationales.D: The nucleus stores DNA; it isn't the packaging center.

items.stem: The organelle where most cellular ATP is produced via the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation is the:
items.explanation: The mitochondrion makes most ATP (Krebs + oxphos); has its own DNA. Takeaway: Mitochondrion = ATP powerhouse (Krebs + oxphos). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The mitochondrion (with its own DNA and double membrane) is the site of aerobic ATP production — the 'powerhouse' of the cell. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Lysosomes digest macromolecules.
distractor_rationales.C: Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and detoxify peroxides.
distractor_rationales.D: Vacuoles store water and materials.

items.stem: The membrane-bound organelles filled with hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes that break down waste, debris, and worn organelles are:
items.explanation: Lysosomes = digestive organelles (hydrolytic enzymes) for waste and recycling. Takeaway: Lysosome = digestive enzymes (breaks down waste). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lysosomes contain acidic hydrolytic enzymes that digest macromolecules and recycle cellular components (autophagy). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ribosomes synthesize proteins; they don't digest.
distractor_rationales.C: Centrosomes organize microtubules for cell division.
distractor_rationales.D: Golgi vesicles transport materials; the digestive organelle is the lysosome.

items.stem: The cytoskeleton is built from microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, and the largest fibers, which form spindle fibers and the tracks for organelle transport:
items.explanation: Microtubules = largest cytoskeletal fibers (spindle, cilia/flagella, transport tracks). Takeaway: Microtubules = spindle + cilia/flagella + transport tracks. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Microtubules (tubulin) are the largest cytoskeletal fibers; they form the mitotic spindle, cilia/flagella cores, and vesicle-transport tracks. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ribosomes synthesize proteins; they aren't cytoskeletal fibers.
distractor_rationales.B: Cilia are made OF microtubules; the fiber type is microtubules.
distractor_rationales.D: Phospholipids build membranes, not the cytoskeleton.

items.stem: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella move using a characteristic microtubule arrangement described as:
items.explanation: Motile cilia/flagella = 9+2 microtubule arrangement (axoneme). Takeaway: Cilia/flagella = 9+2 microtubule arrangement. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Motile cilia/flagella have a 9+2 axoneme: nine outer microtubule doublets surrounding two central microtubules. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: 9+0 describes non-motile primary cilia and basal bodies/centrioles, not motile flagella.
distractor_rationales.C: 2+2 is not the axoneme arrangement.
distractor_rationales.D: Cilia/flagella contain many microtubules in the 9+2 pattern, not one.

items.stem: The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2) and the mitotic phase. DNA is replicated during:
items.explanation: DNA is replicated in S phase (G1 = growth, G2 = growth, M = division). Takeaway: S phase = DNA replication. G1/G2 = growth. M = division. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. DNA synthesis (replication) occurs in S phase; G1 and G2 are growth phases, and M phase is mitosis/division. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: G1 is a growth phase before DNA synthesis.
distractor_rationales.B: G2 is growth after replication, preparing for mitosis.
distractor_rationales.D: M phase is when the cell divides, after replication.

items.stem: The correct order of the phases of mitosis is:
items.explanation: Mitosis order: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase (PMAT). Takeaway: Mitosis = PMAT (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. PMAT: Prophase (condense), Metaphase (align at the middle), Anaphase (sister chromatids separate), Telophase (nuclei re-form). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Prophase precedes metaphase.
distractor_rationales.B: That order is scrambled.
distractor_rationales.C: That is the reverse order.

items.stem: Chromosomes line up along the cell's equator during ______; sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles during ______.
items.explanation: Metaphase = chromosomes align at the equator; anaphase = sister chromatids separate. Takeaway: Metaphase = line up. Anaphase = pull apart. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Metaphase = alignment at the metaphase plate; anaphase = sister chromatids separate toward opposite poles. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — alignment is metaphase, separation is anaphase.
distractor_rationales.B: Prophase is condensation; telophase is nuclear reassembly.
distractor_rationales.D: That pairing is incorrect.

items.stem: Progression through the cell cycle is controlled at checkpoints by regulatory proteins called ______ and their partner kinases (CDKs).
items.explanation: Cyclins + CDKs drive the cell through checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M). Takeaway: Cyclins + CDKs = cell cycle checkpoint control. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cyclins bind cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) to drive the cell past checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M); loss of control can lead to cancer. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Histones package DNA; they aren't the checkpoint regulators.
distractor_rationales.C: Telomeres are chromosome-end sequences, not cycle regulators.
distractor_rationales.D: Ribozymes are catalytic RNAs, not cell-cycle proteins.

items.stem: The tumor suppressor protein that halts the cycle for DNA repair (or triggers apoptosis) at the G1/S checkpoint — and is mutated in many cancers — is:
items.explanation: p53 = tumor suppressor that arrests the cycle for repair or triggers apoptosis (mutated in many cancers). Takeaway: p53 = 'guardian of the genome' (arrest/repair or apoptosis). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. p53 arrests the cycle to allow repair or induces apoptosis if damage is severe; its loss of function permits damaged cells to divide (cancer). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Cyclin D promotes progression; it isn't the guardian tumor suppressor.
distractor_rationales.C: Telomerase extends telomeres; it isn't the checkpoint guardian.
distractor_rationales.D: Actin is a cytoskeletal protein, not a cell-cycle regulator.

items.stem: Programmed cell death — an orderly, regulated dismantling of a cell (important in development and removing damaged cells) — is:
items.explanation: Apoptosis = programmed, orderly cell death (vs. necrosis = uncontrolled). Takeaway: Apoptosis = programmed cell death (orderly). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Apoptosis is controlled, programmed cell death (unlike necrosis, which is uncontrolled injury-induced death). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death from injury, causing inflammation.
distractor_rationales.C: Mitosis is cell division, not death.
distractor_rationales.D: Binary fission is prokaryotic asexual reproduction.

items.stem: The defining feature that distinguishes prokaryotic cells from eukaryotic cells is that prokaryotes:

choices.text: Lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles

items.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Takeaway: Prokaryote = no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus (DNA sits in the nucleoid) and lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Prokaryotes have DNA — it just isn't enclosed in a nucleus.
distractor_rationales.B: Prokaryotes are typically single-celled.
distractor_rationales.C: Prokaryotes are smaller and lack mitochondria.

items.stem: Gram-positive bacteria stain purple because they have a THICK peptidoglycan cell wall; Gram-negative bacteria stain pink because they have:

choices.text: A thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane

items.explanation: Gram-positive = thick peptidoglycan (purple); Gram-negative = thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane (pink). Takeaway: Gram+ = thick wall (purple). Gram− = thin wall + outer membrane (pink). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gram-negatives have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an additional outer membrane (with LPS), so they retain less crystal violet and appear pink. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Gram-negatives do have a (thin) peptidoglycan wall.
distractor_rationales.B: Gram-positives, not negatives, have the thicker wall.
distractor_rationales.C: Bacteria are prokaryotes and have no nucleus.

items.stem: Prokaryotes reproduce asexually by ______, producing two genetically identical daughter cells.
items.explanation: Prokaryotes divide by binary fission (asexual, two identical cells). Takeaway: Binary fission = asexual prokaryotic division (2 identical cells). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Binary fission is the asexual division of a prokaryote into two identical cells (no spindle, no mitosis). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Meiosis produces gametes in sexually reproducing eukaryotes.
distractor_rationales.C: Mitosis is eukaryotic nuclear division.
distractor_rationales.D: Spore budding isn't the standard prokaryotic division mechanism.

items.stem: Besides the main circular chromosome, many bacteria carry small circular DNA molecules — often bearing antibiotic-resistance genes — called:
items.explanation: Plasmids = small circular bacterial DNA (often antibiotic-resistance genes). Takeaway: Plasmid = extra circular DNA (often resistance genes). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Plasmids are small, independently replicating circular DNA molecules that can carry advantageous genes (e.g., antibiotic resistance) and be transferred between cells. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ribosomes synthesize protein; they aren't DNA molecules.
distractor_rationales.C: Lysosomes are eukaryotic digestive organelles.
distractor_rationales.D: A centromere is a chromosome region, not a separate DNA molecule.

items.stem: The transfer of DNA (often a plasmid) directly between two bacterial cells through a physical bridge (pilus) is:
items.explanation: Conjugation = DNA transfer between bacteria via a pilus (direct contact). Takeaway: Conjugation = bacteria transfer DNA through a pilus bridge. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Conjugation transfers DNA via direct cell-to-cell contact through a sex pilus — a form of horizontal gene transfer. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transformation is uptake of naked DNA from the environment.
distractor_rationales.C: Transduction is DNA transfer by a bacteriophage.
distractor_rationales.D: Binary fission is asexual reproduction, not gene transfer between cells.

items.stem: When a bacterium takes up free (naked) DNA fragments directly from its environment, this is:
items.explanation: Transformation = uptake of naked DNA from the environment. Takeaway: Transformation = bacterium grabs free DNA from surroundings. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Transformation is uptake and incorporation of exogenous DNA from the surroundings. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact via a pilus.
distractor_rationales.C: Transduction uses a virus to move DNA.
distractor_rationales.D: Translation is protein synthesis, not gene transfer.

items.stem: The transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another via a bacteriophage (virus) is:
items.explanation: Transduction = bacterial DNA moved by a bacteriophage (virus). Takeaway: Transduction = virus carries bacterial DNA to a new cell. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In transduction, a bacteriophage accidentally packages host bacterial DNA and injects it into a new host. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transformation is uptake of naked environmental DNA.
distractor_rationales.B: Conjugation is direct transfer via a pilus.
distractor_rationales.C: Fermentation is an anaerobic metabolic process, not gene transfer.

items.stem: A bacterial growth curve typically follows the order:
items.explanation: Bacterial growth: lag → log → stationary → death. Takeaway: Growth curve: lag → log → stationary → death. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Growth proceeds through lag (adjusting), log/exponential (rapid division), stationary (nutrients limiting), and death phases. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Lag precedes log; the order is scrambled.
distractor_rationales.C: Lag comes first, not stationary.
distractor_rationales.D: That is roughly the reverse order.

items.stem: A microbe that REQUIRES oxygen to survive is an obligate ______; one that is KILLED by oxygen is an obligate ______.
items.explanation: Obligate aerobe requires O2; obligate anaerobe is killed by O2. Takeaway: Obligate aerobe = needs O2. Obligate anaerobe = killed by O2. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Obligate aerobes need O2; obligate anaerobes are poisoned by it (facultative organisms can use either). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the oxygen-requiring microbe is the aerobe.
distractor_rationales.C: Halophile/thermophile describe salt/heat preferences, not oxygen.
distractor_rationales.D: Autotroph/heterotroph describe carbon source, not oxygen use.

items.stem: Some bacteria (e.g., Clostridium, Bacillus) survive extreme heat, radiation, and drought by forming dormant, highly resistant structures called:
items.explanation: Endospores = dormant, resistant bacterial survival structures. Takeaway: Endospores = tough dormant survival forms (Clostridium, Bacillus). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Endospores are dormant, tough survival structures that let certain bacteria persist through harsh conditions and later germinate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Plasmids are DNA molecules, not survival structures.
distractor_rationales.B: Flagella are for motility.
distractor_rationales.C: Ribosomes synthesize protein.

items.stem: A virus consists at minimum of genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat called a:
items.explanation: A virus = nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) in a protein capsid (± envelope). Takeaway: Virus = genome + protein capsid (± envelope). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The capsid is the protein shell surrounding the viral genome; some viruses also have a lipid envelope from the host membrane. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Viruses lack a cell wall.
distractor_rationales.B: Viruses are acellular and have no plasma membrane of their own (some have a host-derived envelope).
distractor_rationales.D: The nucleoid is a bacterial DNA region, not a viral coat.

items.stem: Viruses are not considered fully living cells primarily because they:

choices.text: Have their own ribosomes and metabolism
Cannot reproduce without hijacking a host cell's machinery

items.explanation: Viruses are acellular obligate parasites — they need a host cell to replicate. Takeaway: Viruses can't reproduce alone — they hijack host cells. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites — they lack ribosomes and metabolism and must use a host cell to replicate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Viruses do contain genetic material (DNA or RNA).
distractor_rationales.B: Viruses lack their own ribosomes and metabolism.
distractor_rationales.D: Viruses can't divide on their own; they require a host.

items.stem: A bacteriophage that immediately replicates and bursts (lyses) the host cell follows the ______ cycle; one that integrates its DNA into the host genome and lies dormant follows the ______ cycle.
items.explanation: Lytic = replicate + burst the cell; lysogenic = integrate + lie dormant (prophage). Takeaway: Lytic = burst now. Lysogenic = integrate + hide (prophage). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lytic = immediate replication and cell lysis; lysogenic = viral DNA integrates (as a prophage) and replicates passively until induced. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — immediate lysis is the lytic cycle.
distractor_rationales.C: Lag/log are bacterial growth phases, not phage cycles.
distractor_rationales.D: Aerobic/anaerobic describe metabolism, not phage cycles.

items.stem: Retroviruses like HIV carry RNA and an enzyme that copies their RNA into DNA for host integration. That enzyme is:
items.explanation: Reverse transcriptase copies retroviral RNA → DNA (e.g., HIV). Takeaway: Retrovirus (HIV): reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Reverse transcriptase transcribes viral RNA into DNA (reversing the usual flow), which integrates into the host genome. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Helicase unwinds DNA; it doesn't copy RNA into DNA.
distractor_rationales.C: RNA polymerase II makes mRNA from DNA, the opposite direction.
distractor_rationales.D: DNA ligase seals DNA nicks; it isn't a reverse transcriptase.

items.stem: A typical neuron at rest has a membrane potential of about −70 mV, meaning the inside of the cell is:

choices.text: Equal in charge to the outside

items.explanation: Resting potential ≈ −70 mV: inside negative relative to outside. Takeaway: Resting potential ≈ −70 mV (inside negative). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. At rest the interior is negative (~−70 mV) relative to the exterior, maintained by ion gradients and membrane permeability. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The interior is negative, not positive, at rest.
distractor_rationales.C: There is a charge separation (potential difference), not equality.
distractor_rationales.D: There is a measurable potential difference; the membrane is polarized.

items.stem: At rest, the concentration of ______ is high OUTSIDE the neuron, and ______ is high INSIDE, gradients set up by the Na+/K+ pump.
items.explanation: At rest: Na+ high outside, K+ high inside (set by the Na+/K+ pump). Takeaway: Resting gradients: Na+ out, K+ in (Na+/K+ pump). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The Na+/K+ pump keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside; the resting membrane is most permeable to K+. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — Na+ is high outside, K+ is high inside.
distractor_rationales.B: Ca2+/Cl− aren't the primary resting-potential gradient pair.
distractor_rationales.D: That reverses the relevant ions.

items.stem: The resting membrane potential is close to the equilibrium potential for potassium because at rest the membrane is:

choices.text: Most permeable to K+ (K+ leak channels are open)

items.explanation: At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+ (leak channels) → potential near E_K. Takeaway: Resting membrane = mostly K+ permeable (leak channels). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Open K+ leak channels make the resting membrane most permeable to K+, so the resting potential sits near K+'s equilibrium potential. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Na+ permeability is low at rest; it rises during an action potential.
distractor_rationales.C: The membrane is selectively permeable, not impermeable.
distractor_rationales.D: Ca2+ isn't the dominant resting permeability.

items.stem: During the rising phase of an action potential, voltage-gated ______ channels open, and ______ rushes IN, making the inside more positive.
items.explanation: Depolarization: voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ rushes in (inside becomes positive). Takeaway: Depolarization = Na+ in (voltage-gated Na+ channels). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Depolarization is driven by voltage-gated Na+ channels opening and Na+ flowing into the cell. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: K+ efflux causes repolarization, not the depolarizing rise.
distractor_rationales.C: Ca2+ influx triggers neurotransmitter release at the terminal, not the main depolarization.
distractor_rationales.D: Cl− movement is inhibitory, not the depolarizing current.

items.stem: After the peak, the neuron repolarizes as voltage-gated ______ channels open and ______ flows OUT.
items.explanation: Repolarization: voltage-gated K+ channels open, K+ flows out. Takeaway: Repolarization = K+ out (voltage-gated K+ channels). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Repolarization occurs as voltage-gated K+ channels open and K+ exits, restoring the negative interior (often overshooting to hyperpolarization). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Na+ influx causes depolarization, not repolarization.
distractor_rationales.C: Ca2+ is not the repolarizing current in the axon.
distractor_rationales.D: Cl− isn't the main repolarizing ion here.

items.stem: Once a stimulus reaches threshold, an action potential fires at full amplitude; a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger spike. This is the:
items.explanation: All-or-none: reaching threshold fires a full-amplitude spike (intensity = frequency, not size). Takeaway: All-or-none = full spike at threshold; intensity coded by frequency. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Action potentials are all-or-none: threshold triggers a full-sized spike; stimulus strength is encoded by firing FREQUENCY, not amplitude. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Summation is the adding of graded potentials, not the fixed spike size.
distractor_rationales.B: The refractory period concerns the interval before another spike can fire.
distractor_rationales.D: Wobble is a genetics/codon concept.

items.stem: Immediately after firing, a neuron cannot fire a second action potential no matter how strong the stimulus. This interval — due to inactivated Na+ channels — is the:
items.explanation: Absolute refractory period: no new spike possible (Na+ channels inactivated). Takeaway: Absolute refractory = can't fire again (Na+ channels inactivated). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. During the absolute refractory period, inactivated Na+ channels make another action potential impossible, ensuring one-way propagation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: In the relative refractory period a stronger-than-usual stimulus CAN fire a spike.
distractor_rationales.C: 'Latent period' isn't the standard term for Na+ channel inactivation.
distractor_rationales.D: The resting period is the baseline state, not the post-spike block.

items.stem: In myelinated axons, the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, greatly speeding conduction. This is:
items.explanation: Saltatory conduction: the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons (fast). Takeaway: Saltatory conduction = impulse jumps node to node (myelin, fast). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Saltatory conduction: myelin insulates the axon so the impulse regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier, jumping node to node (fast). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Continuous conduction occurs in unmyelinated axons (slower).
distractor_rationales.B: Retrograde transport moves materials back toward the soma, not the impulse.
distractor_rationales.C: The impulse is an active, regenerating signal, not passive diffusion.

items.stem: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, it opens voltage-gated ______ channels, and the influx triggers neurotransmitter vesicle fusion and release.
items.explanation: At the terminal, Ca2+ influx triggers neurotransmitter vesicle release. Takeaway: Ca2+ influx → neurotransmitter release at the terminal. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ca2+ influx at the terminal triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: K+ efflux repolarizes the membrane; it doesn't trigger release.
distractor_rationales.C: Cl− is inhibitory and not the release trigger.
distractor_rationales.D: Although Na+ carries the axonal impulse, Ca2+ specifically triggers vesicle release at the terminal.

items.stem: Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds ______ on the postsynaptic membrane, altering its membrane potential.
items.explanation: Neurotransmitter crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors (often ligand-gated channels). Takeaway: Neurotransmitter binds postsynaptic receptors across the cleft. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Neurotransmitters bind postsynaptic receptors (often ligand-gated ion channels), producing excitatory or inhibitory potentials. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ribosomes synthesize protein; they don't receive neurotransmitters.
distractor_rationales.C: The nucleolus assembles ribosomes in the nucleus.
distractor_rationales.D: Myelin insulates axons; it isn't the neurotransmitter receptor.

items.stem: A neurotransmitter that DEPOLARIZES the postsynaptic cell (making it more likely to fire) produces an ______; one that HYPERPOLARIZES it produces an ______.
items.explanation: EPSP = depolarizing (excitatory); IPSP = hyperpolarizing (inhibitory). Takeaway: EPSP = depolarize (excite). IPSP = hyperpolarize (inhibit). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) depolarizes; an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) hyperpolarizes. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — depolarizing is excitatory (EPSP).
distractor_rationales.C: EPSP/IPSP are graded potentials, not full action/resting potentials.
distractor_rationales.D: Both EPSPs and IPSPs are graded signals.

items.stem: The neurotransmitter signal is stopped by enzymatic breakdown or by ______, in which the neurotransmitter is transported back into the presynaptic neuron.
items.explanation: The synaptic signal ends via enzymatic breakdown or reuptake into the presynaptic neuron. Takeaway: Signal ends by enzyme breakdown or reuptake. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Reuptake (via transporters) recycles neurotransmitter back into the presynaptic terminal, terminating the signal (the target of many antidepressants). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Depolarization initiates signaling; it doesn't terminate it.
distractor_rationales.C: Summation combines multiple inputs; it isn't signal termination.
distractor_rationales.D: Transduction is converting a stimulus to a neural signal, not termination.

items.stem: Water-soluble peptide hormones bind ______ receptors and act via second messengers; lipid-soluble steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind ______ receptors.
items.explanation: Peptide hormones → surface receptors + second messengers; steroid hormones → intracellular receptors. Takeaway: Peptide = surface receptor (2nd messenger). Steroid = intracellular receptor. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Peptide hormones (hydrophilic) bind membrane receptors and use second messengers (fast, short-acting); steroids (lipophilic) diffuse in and bind intracellular/nuclear receptors (slow, long-acting). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — peptides bind surface receptors, steroids bind intracellular ones.
distractor_rationales.C: Peptide receptors are on the surface, not ribosomal.
distractor_rationales.D: Both hormone types have receptors; the difference is their location.

items.stem: Because peptide hormones can't cross the membrane, they trigger intracellular signaling molecules such as cyclic AMP (cAMP). These relay molecules are:
items.explanation: Peptide hormones act through second messengers (e.g., cAMP) inside the cell. Takeaway: Second messengers (cAMP) relay peptide-hormone signals intracellularly. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Second messengers (e.g., cAMP, IP3, Ca2+) relay the signal inside the cell after the hormone (first messenger) binds a surface receptor. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The hormone itself is the first messenger; cAMP is the second.
distractor_rationales.B: Steroid hormones act directly on intracellular receptors, not via surface-triggered second messengers.
distractor_rationales.D: Neurotransmitters act at synapses; here the relay molecule is a second messenger.

items.stem: Compared with steroid hormones, peptide hormones generally act:
items.explanation: Peptide hormones: fast onset, short duration. Steroids: slow onset, long duration. Takeaway: Peptide = fast + short. Steroid = slow + long. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Peptide hormones act quickly via second messengers but their effects are short-lived; steroids act slowly (altering gene transcription) with longer-lasting effects. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That describes steroid hormones, not peptides.
distractor_rationales.B: Peptides act fast but not long-lasting.
distractor_rationales.D: Peptides act fast, not slow.

items.stem: The 'master gland' that releases hormones controlling many other endocrine glands — and is itself directed by the hypothalamus — is the:
items.explanation: The pituitary = master gland (directed by the hypothalamus). Takeaway: Pituitary = master gland (run by hypothalamus). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The pituitary (anterior and posterior) is the master gland, regulated by the hypothalamus, controlling downstream glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The thyroid regulates metabolism but is downstream of the pituitary.
distractor_rationales.B: The adrenal gland is regulated by pituitary ACTH.
distractor_rationales.D: The pancreas regulates glucose but isn't the master gland.

items.stem: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine (T4/T3), which primarily regulates:
items.explanation: Thyroid hormone (T3/T4) raises basal metabolic rate. Takeaway: Thyroid (T3/T4) = sets metabolic rate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Thyroid hormones (T3/T4) raise the body's basal metabolic rate; TSH from the pituitary stimulates their release. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Blood glucose is controlled by insulin/glucagon, not thyroxine.
distractor_rationales.B: Blood calcium is controlled by calcitonin/PTH, not thyroxine (calcitonin is also from the thyroid but is a different hormone).
distractor_rationales.D: Water reabsorption is controlled by ADH.

items.stem: The adrenal ______ releases cortisol (a steroid) for longer-term stress; the adrenal ______ releases epinephrine for the rapid fight-or-flight response.
items.explanation: Adrenal cortex = cortisol (steroid, slow); adrenal medulla = epinephrine (fast). Takeaway: Adrenal cortex = cortisol. Medulla = epinephrine (COTisol from CORTex). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The adrenal cortex secretes cortisol (steroid, slower); the adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine/norepinephrine (fast). Mnemonic: COTisol from the CORTex. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — cortisol is from the cortex, epinephrine from the medulla.
distractor_rationales.C: Anterior/posterior describe the pituitary, not the adrenal gland.
distractor_rationales.D: Alpha/beta describe receptors or pancreatic cells, not adrenal regions.

items.stem: Most hormone axes are regulated by negative feedback, so that rising hormone levels:

choices.text: Inhibit further release of the stimulating hormones upstream

items.explanation: Endocrine axes use negative feedback: high hormone → suppress upstream release. Takeaway: Negative feedback = high hormone shuts off its own upstream signals. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Negative feedback: high levels of a downstream hormone suppress the hypothalamic/pituitary signals that drive it, keeping levels in range. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That would be positive feedback, which is rarer (e.g., oxytocin in labor).
distractor_rationales.C: Hormone levels do feed back to regulate their own secretion.
distractor_rationales.D: Feedback modulates output; it doesn't permanently disable the gland.

items.stem: Deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle, and is pumped to the:
items.explanation: Right heart → lungs (pulmonary); left heart → body (systemic). Takeaway: Right side → lungs. Left side → body. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circuit); the left side then pumps oxygenated blood to the body (systemic circuit). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the LEFT ventricle to the body.
distractor_rationales.C: Blood reaches the left atrium only after returning from the lungs.
distractor_rationales.D: Blood goes to the lungs for oxygenation before systemic distribution.

items.stem: After returning from the lungs, oxygenated blood enters the LEFT atrium, then the left ventricle, which pumps it to the body through the:
items.explanation: Left ventricle → aorta → body (oxygenated, systemic circuit). Takeaway: Left ventricle → aorta → body. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The left ventricle (the most muscular chamber) pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for systemic distribution. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
distractor_rationales.C: The vena cava returns deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.
distractor_rationales.D: The pulmonary vein delivers oxygenated blood TO the left atrium; the aorta carries it out.

items.stem: The heart's intrinsic pacemaker, which initiates each heartbeat, is the:
items.explanation: The SA node is the heart's pacemaker (SA → AV → bundle of His → Purkinje). Takeaway: SA node = pacemaker (then AV → His → Purkinje). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The SA node sets the rhythm; the impulse then travels to the AV node, down the bundle of His, and out the Purkinje fibers. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The AV node delays and relays the impulse; it isn't the primary pacemaker.
distractor_rationales.C: The bundle of His conducts the impulse to the ventricles.
distractor_rationales.D: Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricles.

items.stem: The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart muscle CONTRACTS to eject blood is ______; the phase when it RELAXES and fills is ______.
items.explanation: Systole = contraction (eject); diastole = relaxation (fill). Takeaway: Systole = squeeze. Diastole = fill. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Systole = contraction (ejection); diastole = relaxation (filling). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — contraction is systole.
distractor_rationales.B: Depolarization/repolarization describe the electrical events, not the mechanical phases.
distractor_rationales.D: Inspiration/expiration are breathing phases, not cardiac phases.

items.stem: Vessels that carry blood AWAY from the heart (usually oxygenated, under high pressure) are ______; vessels that return blood TO the heart are ______.
items.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it. Takeaway: Arteries = away from heart. Veins = back to heart. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick, muscular, high pressure); veins return blood to the heart (thinner, with valves). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — arteries carry blood away from the heart.
distractor_rationales.C: Capillaries/arterioles aren't the away/toward pair.
distractor_rationales.D: Venules are small veins, not the full away/toward contrast.

items.stem: Although arteries usually carry oxygenated blood, the ______ carries DEOXYGENATED blood, and the pulmonary VEIN carries oxygenated blood.
items.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood (pulmonary vein carries oxygenated) — the exception. Takeaway: Pulmonary artery = deoxygenated (exception to the rule). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The pulmonary artery (heart → lungs) carries deoxygenated blood — the classic exception to 'arteries carry oxygenated blood.' Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The aorta carries oxygenated blood.
distractor_rationales.B: Coronary arteries carry oxygenated blood to the heart muscle.
distractor_rationales.C: The carotid artery carries oxygenated blood to the head.

items.stem: Gas, nutrient, and waste exchange between blood and tissues occurs across the thin walls of the:
items.explanation: Capillaries (thin walls) are the site of gas/nutrient/waste exchange. Takeaway: Capillaries = exchange site (thin walls). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Capillaries have single-cell-thick walls enabling exchange of O2, CO2, nutrients, and wastes with tissues. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Arteries are thick-walled distribution vessels, not exchange sites.
distractor_rationales.C: Veins return blood; they aren't the main exchange vessels.
distractor_rationales.D: The aorta is the largest artery, for distribution, not exchange.

items.stem: Oxygen is carried in the blood mainly bound to ______ inside red blood cells.
items.explanation: O2 is transported bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells. Takeaway: Hemoglobin (in RBCs) carries oxygen. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hemoglobin (four subunits, each with an iron-containing heme) binds O2 in red blood cells for transport. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Albumin maintains oncotic pressure and carries some molecules, not the main O2 carrier.
distractor_rationales.B: Fibrinogen is a clotting protein.
distractor_rationales.D: Platelets are cell fragments for clotting, not O2 carriers.

items.stem: During exercise, increased CO2, lower pH, and higher temperature shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT, which:

choices.text: Promotes oxygen unloading to active tissues (the Bohr effect)

items.explanation: Right shift (↑CO2, ↓pH, ↑temp) = Bohr effect → more O2 released to tissues. Takeaway: Right shift = Bohr effect = O2 unloaded to active tissues. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A rightward shift (Bohr effect) lowers hemoglobin's O2 affinity, releasing more O2 where metabolically active tissues need it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: A right shift DECREASES affinity, aiding unloading.
distractor_rationales.C: The shift enhances, not prevents, O2 release.
distractor_rationales.D: It occurs in active tissues, where CO2/H+ are high.

items.stem: The formed elements of blood include oxygen-carrying red blood cells, clot-forming platelets, and immune ______.
items.explanation: Blood formed elements: red cells (O2), platelets (clotting), white cells (immunity). Takeaway: Blood cells: RBC (O2), platelets (clot), WBC (immunity). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Leukocytes (white blood cells) are the immune formed elements; red cells carry O2 and platelets aid clotting. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Hepatocytes are liver cells, not blood cells.
distractor_rationales.B: Neurons are nerve cells.
distractor_rationales.D: Osteocytes are bone cells.

items.stem: In the lungs, gas exchange between air and blood occurs across the thin walls of the tiny air sacs called:
items.explanation: Gas exchange occurs in the alveoli (thin-walled air sacs). Takeaway: Alveoli = gas exchange site in the lungs. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alveoli provide a huge, thin surface for O2 and CO2 to diffuse between air and the surrounding capillaries. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Bronchi are conducting airways, not the exchange surface.
distractor_rationales.B: The trachea conducts air to the bronchi.
distractor_rationales.C: Bronchioles conduct air to the alveoli but aren't the exchange surface themselves.

items.stem: Gas exchange is driven by partial-pressure gradients: oxygen diffuses from ______ into the blood, and CO2 diffuses from the blood into the ______.
items.explanation: In the lungs: O2 diffuses alveoli → blood; CO2 diffuses blood → alveoli (down partial-pressure gradients). Takeaway: Lungs: O2 in (alveoli→blood), CO2 out (blood→alveoli). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In the lungs, O2 moves from high-PO2 alveolar air into blood, and CO2 moves from high-PCO2 blood into the alveoli to be exhaled — each down its partial-pressure gradient. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: O2 moves INTO the blood, and CO2 moves OUT of it, in the lungs.
distractor_rationales.C: Tissue exchange runs the opposite direction (O2 out of blood).
distractor_rationales.D: The gradient is between alveolar air and capillary blood, described by the alveoli.

items.stem: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, which ______ thoracic volume and ______ intrapulmonary pressure, drawing air in.
items.explanation: Inhalation: diaphragm down → ↑ volume, ↓ pressure → air in (Boyle's law). Takeaway: Inhale: diaphragm down → volume up, pressure down → air in. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Diaphragm contraction increases chest volume, lowering the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric, so air flows in (Boyle's law). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That describes exhalation (volume down, pressure up).
distractor_rationales.C: Increased volume lowers pressure, not raises it.
distractor_rationales.D: Volume increases during inhalation, not decreases.

items.stem: The immune defenses that are NONspecific, present from birth, and act as a rapid first response (skin, phagocytes, inflammation) make up the ______ immune system.
items.explanation: Innate immunity = nonspecific, fast, no memory (barriers, phagocytes, inflammation). Takeaway: Innate = nonspecific, fast, first line (no memory). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Innate immunity is nonspecific, immediate, and lacks memory (barriers, phagocytes, complement, inflammation); adaptive immunity is specific and slower. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Adaptive immunity is specific and develops memory over time.
distractor_rationales.C: Humoral immunity is a branch of adaptive immunity.
distractor_rationales.D: 'Memory' is a feature of adaptive, not innate, immunity.

items.stem: Innate immune cells such as macrophages and neutrophils defend the body by:
items.explanation: Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils) engulf and digest pathogens. Takeaway: Phagocytes = engulf/digest pathogens (innate). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils) engulf and destroy pathogens and debris — a core innate defense. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Antibody production is done by B cells/plasma cells (adaptive immunity).
distractor_rationales.B: Oxygen storage is a red-cell/myoglobin function, not phagocyte activity.
distractor_rationales.C: Clot formation is a platelet/coagulation function.

items.stem: The redness, heat, swelling, and pain at a site of infection or injury — caused by increased blood flow and vascular permeability (mediated by histamine) — is:
items.explanation: Inflammation = innate response with ↑ blood flow/permeability (redness, heat, swelling, pain). Takeaway: Inflammation = innate response (redness, heat, swelling, pain). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Inflammation is an innate response: vasodilation and increased permeability bring immune cells and fluid to the site (histamine is a key mediator). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not the inflammatory response.
distractor_rationales.C: Clonal selection is an adaptive-immunity process.
distractor_rationales.D: Opsonization is the tagging of pathogens for phagocytosis, a component but not the whole response.

items.stem: In the humoral (antibody-mediated) branch of adaptive immunity, ______ differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.
items.explanation: B cells → plasma cells → antibodies (humoral immunity). Takeaway: B cells = antibodies (humoral immunity). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. B cells mediate humoral immunity, maturing into plasma cells that secrete antibodies specific to an antigen. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: T cells mediate cell-mediated immunity; they don't secrete antibodies.
distractor_rationales.C: Red blood cells carry oxygen, not immunity.
distractor_rationales.D: Platelets aid clotting, not antibody production.

items.stem: In cell-mediated immunity, ______ T cells coordinate the immune response by activating other cells, while ______ T cells directly kill infected cells.
items.explanation: Helper T (CD4+) coordinate; cytotoxic T (CD8+) kill infected cells. Takeaway: Helper T (CD4) = coordinate. Cytotoxic T (CD8) = kill infected cells. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Helper T cells (CD4+) orchestrate the response; cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) destroy virus-infected or abnormal cells directly. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — helper (CD4+) coordinate, cytotoxic (CD8+) kill.
distractor_rationales.B: Plasma/memory are B-cell fates, not the T-cell subsets described.
distractor_rationales.C: NK cells are innate; B cells make antibodies.

items.stem: Adaptive immunity produces long-lived ______ cells, so a second exposure to the same pathogen triggers a faster, stronger response (the basis of vaccination).
items.explanation: Adaptive immunity forms memory cells → faster secondary response (vaccination). Takeaway: Memory cells = faster/stronger second response (vaccines). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Memory B and T cells persist after an infection, enabling a rapid, robust secondary response — the principle behind vaccines. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Stem cells are undifferentiated precursors, not immune-memory cells.
distractor_rationales.C: Phagocytic cells are innate; they don't provide antigen-specific memory.
distractor_rationales.D: Mast cells release histamine in allergy/inflammation, not adaptive memory.

items.stem: Chemical digestion of carbohydrates begins in the mouth via salivary ______, while protein digestion begins in the stomach.
items.explanation: Carb digestion starts in the mouth (salivary amylase); protein digestion starts in the stomach (pepsin). Takeaway: Mouth = amylase (carbs). Stomach = pepsin (protein). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Salivary amylase starts carbohydrate (starch) digestion in the mouth; pepsin begins protein digestion in the acidic stomach. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach, not carbohydrates in the mouth.
distractor_rationales.C: Lipase digests fats (mainly in the small intestine).
distractor_rationales.D: Trypsin digests protein in the small intestine, not carbs in the mouth.

items.stem: The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid, creating a low pH that activates ______, the enzyme that begins protein digestion.
items.explanation: Stomach HCl activates pepsin (from pepsinogen) to start protein digestion. Takeaway: Stomach acid → activates pepsin (protein digestion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gastric HCl converts pepsinogen to active pepsin (optimal at low pH), which begins breaking down proteins. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Amylase digests carbohydrates and is inactivated by stomach acid.
distractor_rationales.B: Bile emulsifies fats; it isn't a stomach protein enzyme.
distractor_rationales.D: Insulin is a blood-glucose hormone, not a digestive enzyme.

items.stem: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the ______, whose surface area is hugely increased by villi and microvilli.
items.explanation: Most nutrient absorption is in the small intestine (villi + microvilli → huge surface area). Takeaway: Small intestine = main absorption (villi/microvilli). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The small intestine is the main absorption site; villi and microvilli create an enormous surface area for nutrient uptake. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The stomach mainly digests and stores; little absorption occurs there.
distractor_rationales.C: The large intestine mainly absorbs water and forms feces.
distractor_rationales.D: The esophagus is a conducting tube; no absorption occurs there.

items.stem: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, aids fat digestion by ______, while the pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate.
items.explanation: Bile (liver/gallbladder) emulsifies fats; the pancreas supplies enzymes + bicarbonate. Takeaway: Bile emulsifies fat (not an enzyme); pancreas = enzymes + bicarbonate. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Bile emulsifies fats (mechanically increasing surface area for lipase), but it is not an enzyme; the pancreas provides enzymes and neutralizing bicarbonate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Bile emulsifies fat physically; it doesn't cleave peptide bonds.
distractor_rationales.C: Bile doesn't absorb glucose.
distractor_rationales.D: Stomach acid is made by the stomach, not bile.

items.stem: The functional unit of the kidney, where blood is filtered and urine is formed, is the:
items.explanation: The nephron is the kidney's functional unit (filtration + urine formation). Takeaway: Nephron = functional unit of the kidney. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The nephron (glomerulus + tubule) filters blood and processes the filtrate into urine. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The alveolus is the gas-exchange unit of the lung.
distractor_rationales.B: The sarcomere is the contractile unit of muscle.
distractor_rationales.C: The villus is an intestinal absorptive projection.

items.stem: Urine formation involves filtration at the glomerulus, ______ of useful substances back into the blood, and ______ of wastes into the tubule.
items.explanation: Nephron processes: filtration → reabsorption → secretion. Takeaway: Kidney: filter, reabsorb (keep), secrete (dump wastes). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The three processes are filtration (glomerulus), reabsorption (tubule → blood, recovering water/glucose/ions), and secretion (blood → tubule, adding wastes). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — useful substances are reabsorbed, wastes are secreted.
distractor_rationales.C: Digestion/absorption are gastrointestinal, not renal, processes.
distractor_rationales.D: Diffusion/osmosis are mechanisms, not the three named renal processes.

items.stem: When the body is dehydrated, the posterior pituitary releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which causes the kidney to:

choices.text: Excrete more water, producing dilute urine
Reabsorb more water, producing concentrated urine

items.explanation: ADH → more water reabsorption → concentrated urine (conserves water). Takeaway: ADH = reabsorb water → concentrated urine (when dehydrated). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct (more aquaporins), conserving water and concentrating the urine. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: ADH conserves water; excreting more water is the opposite effect.
distractor_rationales.B: ADH doesn't halt filtration.
distractor_rationales.C: ADH regulates water, not glucose secretion.

items.stem: The adrenal hormone that increases sodium (and thus water) reabsorption in the kidney, raising blood pressure, is:
items.explanation: Aldosterone → Na+ (and water) reabsorption → ↑ blood pressure. Takeaway: Aldosterone = reabsorb Na+/water → raise BP. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Aldosterone (from the adrenal cortex) promotes Na+ reabsorption (water follows), increasing blood volume and pressure. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Insulin regulates blood glucose, not renal sodium.
distractor_rationales.B: Thyroxine sets metabolic rate.
distractor_rationales.C: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium.

items.stem: The production of gametes by meiosis is called gametogenesis: sperm form via spermatogenesis, and eggs form via:
items.explanation: Oogenesis = egg production (meiosis); spermatogenesis = sperm production. Takeaway: Oogenesis = eggs. Spermatogenesis = sperm (both meiosis). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Oogenesis is the meiotic production of eggs (ova); spermatogenesis produces sperm. Both are forms of gametogenesis. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Mitosis produces identical body cells, not haploid gametes.
distractor_rationales.C: Fertilization is the fusion of gametes, not their production.
distractor_rationales.D: Ovulation is the release of an egg, not its formation.

items.stem: A surge in ______ from the anterior pituitary triggers ovulation around the middle of the menstrual cycle.
items.explanation: A mid-cycle LH surge triggers ovulation. Takeaway: LH surge = ovulation trigger (mid-cycle). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A mid-cycle LH surge triggers ovulation (release of the egg from the follicle); FSH drives follicle maturation earlier. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Progesterone (from the corpus luteum) dominates the luteal phase after ovulation; it doesn't trigger it.
distractor_rationales.B: ADH regulates water balance, not ovulation.
distractor_rationales.C: Insulin regulates blood glucose.

items.stem: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes ______ to maintain the uterine lining.
items.explanation: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone to maintain the uterine lining. Takeaway: Corpus luteum → progesterone (maintains endometrium). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and estrogen), maintaining the endometrium; if no pregnancy occurs, it degenerates and progesterone falls, triggering menstruation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Testosterone is the principal male androgen, not the corpus luteum's product.
distractor_rationales.C: Amylase is a digestive enzyme.
distractor_rationales.D: Adrenaline is a fight-or-flight hormone.

items.stem: The fusion of a haploid sperm and a haploid egg produces a diploid ______, which then begins dividing.
items.explanation: Sperm + egg → diploid zygote (fertilization restores 2n). Takeaway: Fertilization: sperm + egg → diploid zygote. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fertilization forms a diploid zygote, restoring the full chromosome number; it then undergoes cleavage. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Gametes are the haploid sex cells that fuse, not the product.
distractor_rationales.C: The gastrula is a later stage after gastrulation.
distractor_rationales.D: The blastocyst is a later hollow-ball stage.

items.stem: The rapid series of mitotic divisions immediately after fertilization — increasing cell number without increasing overall size — is:
items.explanation: Cleavage = rapid mitotic divisions after fertilization (more cells, same total size). Takeaway: Cleavage = fast early divisions (more cells, no size gain). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cleavage divides the zygote into many smaller cells (blastomeres) with little growth, forming a morula then a blastula/blastocyst. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Gastrulation forms the germ layers, later than cleavage.
distractor_rationales.B: Differentiation is cells becoming specialized.
distractor_rationales.D: Implantation is the embryo embedding in the uterine wall.

items.stem: Gastrulation produces three primary germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The nervous system and epidermis derive from the:
items.explanation: Ectoderm → nervous system + epidermis (mesoderm → muscle/bone; endoderm → gut lining). Takeaway: Ectoderm = nervous system + skin. (Meso = muscle/bone; Endo = gut.) The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ectoderm → nervous system and epidermis; mesoderm → muscle, bone, blood, kidneys; endoderm → gut and respiratory linings. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Mesoderm gives rise to muscle, bone, and the circulatory system.
distractor_rationales.C: Endoderm forms the gut lining and associated organs.
distractor_rationales.D: The blastocoel is the fluid cavity of the blastula, not a germ layer.

items.stem: The three types of muscle tissue are skeletal (voluntary, striated), cardiac (involuntary, striated), and:
items.explanation: Muscle types: skeletal (voluntary/striated), cardiac (involuntary/striated), smooth (involuntary/non-striated). Takeaway: 3 muscle types: skeletal, cardiac, smooth. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated (lines organs/vessels); skeletal is voluntary/striated; cardiac is involuntary/striated. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Tendons connect muscle to bone; they aren't a muscle-tissue type.
distractor_rationales.B: Ligaments connect bone to bone; they aren't muscle.
distractor_rationales.D: Adipose is fat tissue, not muscle.

items.stem: Muscle contracts when ______ filaments slide past ______ filaments, shortening the sarcomere (the sliding filament model).
items.explanation: Sliding filament: myosin (thick) pulls actin (thin) → sarcomere shortens. Takeaway: Contraction = actin slides along myosin (sarcomere shortens). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In the sliding filament model, myosin (thick) heads pull actin (thin) filaments inward, shortening each sarcomere and contracting the muscle. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Actin is the thin filament and myosin the thick one (this reverses them).
distractor_rationales.C: Collagen/keratin are structural proteins, not sarcomere filaments.
distractor_rationales.D: Tubulin forms microtubules, not the contractile filaments.

items.stem: Muscle contraction is triggered when ______ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and binds troponin, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin.
items.explanation: Ca2+ binds troponin → exposes actin sites → myosin binds → contraction. Takeaway: Ca2+ binds troponin → exposes actin → contraction. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, shifting tropomyosin to expose actin's binding sites so myosin can attach and pull. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Na+ influx drives the action potential but isn't what binds troponin.
distractor_rationales.B: K+ efflux repolarizes membranes; it doesn't trigger the cross-bridge.
distractor_rationales.D: Cl− isn't the trigger for the actin–myosin interaction.

items.stem: Bone is continuously remodeled by ______, which build bone, and osteoclasts, which resorb (break down) bone.
items.explanation: Osteoblasts build bone; osteoclasts break it down. Takeaway: OsteoBlasts Build, osteoClasts Carve (break down). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Osteoblasts build/deposit bone matrix; osteoclasts resorb bone. (Mnemonic: osteoBlasts Build; osteoClasts Carve/Chew.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Osteoclasts resorb bone; the bone-building cells are osteoblasts.
distractor_rationales.B: Chondrocytes maintain cartilage, not bone deposition.
distractor_rationales.C: Myocytes are muscle cells.

items.stem: At physiological pH, the amino acids with NEGATIVELY charged (acidic) side chains are:
items.explanation: Acidic (−): aspartate, glutamate. Basic (+): lysine, arginine, histidine. Takeaway: Acidic = Asp, Glu. Basic = Lys, Arg, His. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Aspartate and glutamate have carboxylate side chains (negative at pH 7). Lysine, arginine, histidine are the basic (positive) ones. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Lysine and arginine are basic (positively charged), not acidic.
distractor_rationales.C: Serine and threonine are polar but uncharged.
distractor_rationales.D: Valine and leucine are nonpolar/hydrophobic.

items.stem: The three amino acids with basic (positively charged or ionizable-basic) side chains are:
items.explanation: Basic amino acids: lysine, arginine, histidine. Takeaway: Basic = Lys, Arg, His (His pKa ~6 → active sites). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lysine, arginine, and histidine have basic side chains (histidine's pKa near physiological pH makes it a common active-site residue). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Aspartate and glutamate are acidic; serine is polar uncharged.
distractor_rationales.C: Those are nonpolar/hydrophobic amino acids.
distractor_rationales.D: Those are the aromatic amino acids.

items.stem: 'Essential' amino acids are those that:

choices.text: Cannot be synthesized by the body and must come from the diet
Are made only in the liver

items.explanation: Essential amino acids can't be made by the body — they must come from the diet. Takeaway: Essential = must eat them (body can't synthesize). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Essential amino acids (9 in humans) can't be synthesized de novo and must be obtained from food. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: 'Essential' refers to dietary necessity, not universal presence in proteins.
distractor_rationales.C: Essentiality is about synthesis, not charge.
distractor_rationales.D: Nonessential amino acids are synthesized by the body; essential ones must be eaten.

items.stem: The amino acids with aromatic (ring-containing) side chains — which absorb UV light at 280 nm — are:
items.explanation: Aromatic: phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan (absorb UV at 280 nm). Takeaway: Aromatic = Phe, Tyr, Trp (UV 280 nm). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan have aromatic rings; their UV absorbance at 280 nm is used to quantify protein. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Those are small/nonpolar amino acids without aromatic rings.
distractor_rationales.C: Those are charged amino acids.
distractor_rationales.D: Those are polar uncharged amino acids.

items.stem: The smallest amino acid, with just a hydrogen as its side chain (making it achiral and conformationally flexible), is:
items.explanation: Glycine: side chain = H → smallest, achiral, flexible. Takeaway: Glycine = just H side chain (small, flexible, achiral). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Glycine's side chain is a single H, so it is achiral and provides flexibility in protein backbones (common in turns). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Proline is a rigid ring (imino acid), the opposite of flexible.
distractor_rationales.B: Cysteine has a thiol side chain that forms disulfides.
distractor_rationales.C: Tryptophan is the largest, aromatic amino acid.

items.stem: The amino acid whose side chain loops back to bond the backbone nitrogen — forming a rigid ring that disrupts alpha helices and creates kinks — is:
items.explanation: Proline: rigid ring (imino acid) → kinks, disrupts alpha helices. Takeaway: Proline = rigid ring → kinks/helix breaker. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Proline's cyclic (imino) structure restricts backbone rotation, introducing kinks and disrupting regular secondary structure. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glycine adds flexibility; it doesn't create rigid kinks.
