items.explanation: Storage polysaccharides (starch, glycogen) use digestible α linkages. Takeaway: Starch/glycogen = α linkages (digestible). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Starch and glycogen use α-1,4 (and α-1,6 branch) linkages, which human enzymes can hydrolyze. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: β linkages (as in cellulose) can't be digested by humans.
distractor_rationales.B: Peptide bonds link amino acids, not sugars.
distractor_rationales.C: Ester bonds appear in fats, not the glucose–glucose sugar linkage.

items.stem: Humans cannot digest cellulose (dietary fiber) even though it is made of glucose, because cellulose uses ______ glycosidic linkages.
items.explanation: Cellulose = β linkages → indigestible to humans (fiber); starch = α (digestible). Takeaway: Cellulose = β (indigestible fiber); starch = α (digestible). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cellulose's β-1,4 linkages resist human digestive enzymes (which only cleave α linkages), so it passes as fiber. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: α linkages (starch/glycogen) ARE digestible; cellulose is β.
distractor_rationales.C: Peptide bonds are in proteins.
distractor_rationales.D: Phosphodiester bonds are in nucleic acids.

items.stem: A fatty acid with NO carbon-carbon double bonds (straight chains that pack tightly, solid at room temp) is ______; one with double bonds (kinked, liquid) is ______.
items.explanation: Saturated = no double bonds (solid); unsaturated = double bonds/kinks (liquid). Takeaway: Saturated = no double bonds (solid); unsaturated = kinked (liquid). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Saturated fatty acids (no double bonds) pack tightly and are solid (fats); unsaturated ones have kinks and are liquid (oils). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — no double bonds = saturated.
distractor_rationales.B: Fatty acid tails are nonpolar regardless; this isn't the saturation distinction.
distractor_rationales.D: Essential/nonessential concerns dietary need, not double bonds.

items.stem: The main form of long-term energy storage in animals, consisting of glycerol bonded to three fatty acids via ester bonds, is a:
items.explanation: Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids (main energy storage). Takeaway: Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids (energy storage). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids) are the primary energy-storage lipids, yielding more energy per gram than carbohydrates. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Phospholipids have two fatty acids + a phosphate head (membranes), not three fatty acids.
distractor_rationales.B: Steroids have a four-ring structure, not glycerol + fatty acids.
distractor_rationales.D: Proteins are amino acid polymers.

items.stem: Phospholipids form cell membranes because they are amphipathic: a phosphate head plus ______ fatty acid tail(s).
items.explanation: Phospholipids = phosphate head + 2 fatty acid tails (amphipathic → bilayer). Takeaway: Phospholipid = phosphate head + 2 tails (membrane). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails, driving bilayer formation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Three fatty acids describes a triglyceride (a storage lipid), not a phospholipid.
distractor_rationales.B: Four rings describes steroids, not phospholipid tails.
distractor_rationales.C: Phospholipids do have fatty acid tails (two of them).

items.stem: Cholesterol and the steroid hormones share a characteristic structure of:

choices.text: A glycerol backbone with three tails

items.explanation: Steroids = four fused carbon rings (cholesterol, steroid hormones). Takeaway: Steroids = four fused rings (cholesterol → steroid hormones). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Steroids (cholesterol, cortisol, testosterone, estrogen) share a four-fused-ring core; cholesterol is the precursor of steroid hormones. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A single long chain describes fatty acids, not steroids.
distractor_rationales.B: Glycerol + 3 tails is a triglyceride.
distractor_rationales.C: A phosphate head describes phospholipids.

items.stem: Unlike carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids, lipids are:

choices.text: Not true polymers (not built from repeating monomer units)

items.explanation: Lipids are defined by hydrophobicity, not by being polymers (unlike carbs/proteins/nucleic acids). Takeaway: Lipids = hydrophobic, NOT polymers. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lipids are a diverse group defined by hydrophobicity, not by being polymers of a repeating monomer. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glycerol is a component of some lipids but they aren't glycerol polymers.
distractor_rationales.C: Nucleotide polymers are nucleic acids.
distractor_rationales.D: Amino acid polymers are proteins.

items.stem: Natural selection acts on heritable variation so that individuals with traits better suited to the environment leave more offspring. The measure of an individual's reproductive success is its:
items.explanation: Fitness = reproductive success; natural selection favors higher-fitness heritable traits. Takeaway: Fitness = reproductive success (what selection acts on). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Fitness quantifies reproductive success; natural selection increases the frequency of alleles that raise fitness. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Genetic drift is random allele-frequency change, not a measure of reproductive success.
distractor_rationales.B: Mutation rate is the rate of new variation, not reproductive success.
distractor_rationales.C: Ploidy is the number of chromosome sets.

items.stem: Selection that favors one extreme phenotype, shifting the population mean, is ______ selection; selection favoring the average and against extremes is ______ selection.
items.explanation: Directional = favors one extreme; stabilizing = favors the average; disruptive = both extremes. Takeaway: Directional = one extreme; stabilizing = the middle; disruptive = both ends. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Directional selection shifts toward one extreme; stabilizing selection favors intermediate phenotypes; disruptive selection favors both extremes. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — favoring one extreme is directional.
distractor_rationales.B: Artificial/natural describes the selector, not the phenotype pattern.
distractor_rationales.D: Sexual/kin selection are different concepts.

items.stem: Random change in allele frequencies due to chance — which has a larger effect in SMALL populations (e.g., bottleneck, founder effects) — is:
items.explanation: Genetic drift = random allele-frequency change (strongest in small populations). Takeaway: Genetic drift = random change (big effect in small populations). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Genetic drift is random (non-adaptive) allele-frequency change, most pronounced in small populations. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Natural selection is non-random, based on fitness.
distractor_rationales.B: Gene flow is allele movement between populations (migration).
distractor_rationales.D: Directional selection is a non-random, fitness-based process.

items.stem: The formation of a new species generally requires ______ between populations, preventing gene flow so they diverge genetically.
items.explanation: Speciation requires reproductive isolation (blocks gene flow → divergence). Takeaway: Speciation = reproductive isolation → divergence. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Reproductive isolation (geographic or otherwise) stops gene flow, allowing populations to diverge into separate species. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Increased gene flow homogenizes populations, opposing speciation.
distractor_rationales.C: Mutation alone doesn't produce a new species without isolation.
distractor_rationales.D: Population size isn't the defining requirement for speciation.

items.stem: A population that is EVOLVING at a given gene will show allele/genotype frequencies that:
items.explanation: Deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium signals evolution is occurring. Takeaway: Evolving population = deviates from Hardy-Weinberg. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hardy-Weinberg describes a NON-evolving population; deviation from its predicted frequencies is evidence of evolutionary change (selection, drift, migration, etc.). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Matching H-W predictions indicates no evolution at that locus.
distractor_rationales.C: p = q is a special case, not a signature of evolution.
distractor_rationales.D: Populations have alleles; evolution changes their frequencies.

items.stem: Gel electrophoresis with SDS (SDS-PAGE) separates proteins primarily by:
items.explanation: SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size (SDS gives uniform charge). Takeaway: SDS-PAGE = separate proteins by size. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. SDS coats proteins with uniform negative charge and denatures them, so migration through the gel depends on size (smaller = faster). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: SDS masks native charge so size, not charge, drives separation.
distractor_rationales.C: SDS denatures proteins, removing native shape as the variable.
distractor_rationales.D: Electrophoresis separates by physical properties, not function.

items.stem: A technique that separates proteins along a pH gradient, with each protein migrating until it reaches the pH equal to its ______, is isoelectric focusing.
items.explanation: Isoelectric focusing separates proteins by pI (each stops where pH = pI). Takeaway: Isoelectric focusing = separate by pI (pH gradient). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In isoelectric focusing, a protein stops migrating where the pH equals its pI (net charge zero). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Size-based separation is SDS-PAGE, not isoelectric focusing.
distractor_rationales.B: Optimal temperature is an enzyme-activity parameter.
distractor_rationales.C: Km is an enzyme-kinetics constant.

items.stem: A separation method in which a protein mixture passes through a column and components separate based on properties like size, charge, or affinity is:
items.explanation: Chromatography separates proteins by size, charge, or affinity (column methods). Takeaway: Chromatography = separate by size/charge/affinity (column). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Column chromatography (size-exclusion, ion-exchange, affinity) separates proteins by differential interaction with the stationary phase. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Centrifugation separates by density/mass under spinning force, not column interaction.
distractor_rationales.C: Titration measures acid-base quantities.
distractor_rationales.D: PCR amplifies DNA.

items.stem: Cell junctions that form a watertight seal between adjacent cells, preventing molecules from leaking between them (e.g., in the gut lining), are:
items.explanation: Tight junctions = watertight seal between cells (no leakage). Takeaway: Tight junction = seal (no leakage between cells). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Tight junctions seal neighboring cells to block paracellular leakage, controlling what crosses an epithelial layer. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Gap junctions form communication channels, not watertight seals.
distractor_rationales.B: Desmosomes provide mechanical anchoring, not sealing.
distractor_rationales.C: Plasmodesmata connect plant cells, not animal epithelia.

items.stem: Channels that directly connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, allowing ions and small molecules to pass for communication (e.g., coordinating heart-muscle contraction), are:
items.explanation: Gap junctions = channels connecting cytoplasm for communication (ions/small molecules). Takeaway: Gap junction = communication channel (ions/molecules pass). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gap junctions are intercellular channels enabling rapid electrical/chemical communication (important in cardiac and smooth muscle). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Tight junctions seal cells rather than connect their cytoplasm.
distractor_rationales.B: Desmosomes anchor cells mechanically, without a communicating channel.
distractor_rationales.C: Peroxisomes are organelles, not cell junctions.

items.stem: Junctions that act like rivets, anchoring adjacent cells together to resist mechanical stress (e.g., in skin), are:
items.explanation: Desmosomes = anchoring junctions (mechanical strength, like rivets). Takeaway: Desmosome = anchor/rivet (mechanical strength). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Desmosomes provide strong mechanical adhesion between cells, distributing tension across a tissue. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Gap junctions communicate; they don't primarily anchor.
distractor_rationales.C: Tight junctions seal; desmosomes anchor.
distractor_rationales.D: Ribosomes synthesize protein, not a junction.

items.stem: The four basic tissue types in animals are epithelial, connective, nervous, and:
items.explanation: Four tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous. Takeaway: 4 tissues: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The four primary tissue types are epithelial (covering/lining), connective (support), muscle (movement), and nervous (signaling). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Bone is a TYPE of connective tissue, not a separate primary category.
distractor_rationales.C: Blood is a specialized connective tissue, not a fourth primary type.
distractor_rationales.D: Adipose is a connective tissue, not a primary category.

items.stem: A stem cell that can give rise to ANY cell type in the body plus extra-embryonic tissue (placenta) is ______; one that can become any body cell but not placenta is ______.
items.explanation: Totipotent = any cell + placenta; pluripotent = any body cell; multipotent = limited. Takeaway: Toti = everything+placenta; pluri = any body cell; multi = limited. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Totipotent (e.g., zygote) → any cell + placenta; pluripotent (embryonic stem cells) → any body cell; multipotent → a limited range; unipotent → one type. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — totipotent is the most versatile (includes placenta).
distractor_rationales.B: Multipotent/unipotent are more restricted than the stem-cell types described.
distractor_rationales.C: That reverses the restriction order.

items.stem: As a cell differentiates into a specialized type, it does so mainly by:

choices.text: Selectively expressing different genes (not by losing DNA)
Losing its nucleus in all cases

items.explanation: Differentiation = selective gene expression, not loss of DNA. Takeaway: Differentiation = different genes expressed (same DNA). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Differentiated cells keep the same genome but express different subsets of genes; DNA is generally not lost (with rare exceptions). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Cells retain their full genome; they don't delete unused genes.
distractor_rationales.B: Differentiation doesn't add new chromosomes.
distractor_rationales.D: Most differentiated cells keep their nucleus (red blood cells are an exception).

items.stem: The stage at which a cell becomes committed to a particular fate — even before it visibly specializes — is:
items.explanation: Determination = commitment to a cell fate (before visible differentiation). Takeaway: Determination = committed to a fate (before specializing). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Determination is commitment to a fate; differentiation is the subsequent visible specialization. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Denaturation is loss of protein structure.
distractor_rationales.C: Translation is protein synthesis.
distractor_rationales.D: Transduction is signal conversion (or viral gene transfer).

items.stem: Dense bone forming the hard outer shell is ______ bone; the porous inner bone containing red marrow is ______ bone.
items.explanation: Compact bone = dense outer shell; spongy bone = porous inner (marrow). Takeaway: Compact = dense outer; spongy = porous inner (marrow). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Compact (cortical) bone is the dense outer layer; spongy (trabecular) bone is the porous interior housing marrow. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — the dense outer layer is compact bone.
distractor_rationales.C: Cartilage is a separate connective tissue, not the outer shell here.
distractor_rationales.D: Tendons/ligaments connect tissues; they aren't bone types.

items.stem: The flexible, avascular connective tissue that cushions joints and forms structures like the ear and nose is:
items.explanation: Cartilage = flexible, avascular connective tissue (joints, ear, nose). Takeaway: Cartilage = flexible, avascular (cushions joints). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cartilage is a flexible, avascular (no direct blood supply) connective tissue; it cushions joints and serves as a template for bone. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Compact bone is rigid and vascularized, unlike cartilage.
distractor_rationales.B: A tendon connects muscle to bone.
distractor_rationales.D: Nerve tissue conducts signals.

items.stem: Bone is continuously remodeled: ______ deposit new bone matrix, while osteoclasts resorb it, and mature ______ maintain the tissue.
items.explanation: Osteoblasts build, osteoclasts resorb, osteocytes maintain bone. Takeaway: Osteoblast = build, osteoclast = break, osteocyte = maintain. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts break it down, and osteocytes (mature, embedded cells) maintain it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Osteoclasts resorb; the builders are osteoblasts.
distractor_rationales.C: Chondrocytes/myocytes maintain cartilage/muscle, not bone.
distractor_rationales.D: Neurons/glia are nervous-tissue cells.

items.stem: Beyond structure, the skeleton serves as the body's main reservoir for:
items.explanation: The skeleton is the body's main calcium/phosphate reservoir (hormone-regulated). Takeaway: Bone = calcium/phosphate reservoir (PTH/calcitonin). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Bone stores most of the body's calcium and phosphate, releasing or storing it under hormonal control (PTH, calcitonin, vitamin D). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Glucose is stored as glycogen in liver/muscle, not bone.
distractor_rationales.B: Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin, not stored in bone.
distractor_rationales.C: Sodium is regulated mainly by the kidney, not bone reservoir.

items.stem: From outermost to innermost, the layers of the skin are the epidermis, the ______ (containing blood vessels, nerves, glands), and the hypodermis.
items.explanation: Skin layers: epidermis → dermis → hypodermis. Takeaway: Skin: epidermis (barrier), dermis (vessels/nerves), hypodermis (fat). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The skin's layers are epidermis (outer barrier), dermis (vessels, nerves, glands, follicles), and hypodermis (fat/insulation). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: 'Cortex' refers to outer regions of organs like kidney/adrenal, not skin.
distractor_rationales.B: 'Medulla' is an inner region of organs, not a skin layer.
distractor_rationales.C: An alveolus is a lung air sac.

items.stem: To COOL the body when overheated, the skin responds by ______ and increasing sweat production.

choices.text: Vasodilating (widening) blood vessels near the surface

items.explanation: Cooling: skin vasodilates + sweats. Warming: vasoconstrict, shiver, piloerection. Takeaway: Cool = vasodilate + sweat; warm = vasoconstrict + shiver. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Cooling: surface vasodilation radiates heat away and sweating evaporates heat. Warming responses are the opposite (vasoconstriction, shivering, piloerection). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Vasoconstriction conserves heat (a warming response), not cooling.
distractor_rationales.C: Shivering generates heat to warm the body.
distractor_rationales.D: Piloerection traps insulating air to warm the body.

items.stem: A primary function of the skin in the immune system is to serve as:

choices.text: A physical barrier (first line of innate defense) against pathogens

items.explanation: The skin is a physical barrier — innate immunity's first line of defense. Takeaway: Skin = physical barrier (innate first line of defense). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The skin is a physical/chemical barrier — part of innate immunity's first line of defense against pathogen entry. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Antibodies are made by plasma cells (B cells), not the skin.
distractor_rationales.C: Gas exchange occurs in the lungs.
distractor_rationales.D: The pituitary, not skin, is the endocrine master gland.

items.stem: A key function of the lymphatic system is to collect excess interstitial fluid that leaks from capillaries and return it to the:
items.explanation: The lymphatic system returns excess interstitial fluid to the bloodstream (prevents edema). Takeaway: Lymphatics return interstitial fluid to blood (prevent edema). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The lymphatic system returns filtered interstitial fluid (lymph) to the venous blood, maintaining fluid balance; blockage causes edema. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Lymph returns to the venous blood, not directly to the kidneys.
distractor_rationales.C: It doesn't drain into the digestive tract.
distractor_rationales.D: It doesn't return fluid via the lungs.

items.stem: As lymph passes through lymph nodes, it is filtered and screened for pathogens by resident:
items.explanation: Lymph nodes filter lymph using immune cells (lymphocytes, macrophages). Takeaway: Lymph nodes = filter lymph + immune screening. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lymph nodes house immune cells that filter lymph and mount responses against pathogens/antigens. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Red blood cells carry oxygen; they don't screen lymph.
distractor_rationales.C: Osteocytes are bone cells.
distractor_rationales.D: Nephrons are kidney filtration units, not lymph filters.

items.stem: In the small intestine, specialized lymphatic vessels called ______ absorb dietary fats (as chylomicrons).
items.explanation: Lacteals = intestinal lymphatic vessels that absorb dietary fat (chylomicrons). Takeaway: Lacteals = absorb dietary fat (chylomicrons) via lymph. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries in intestinal villi that absorb fats (chylomicrons), which enter lymph before the bloodstream. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Nephrons are kidney units, not fat absorbers.
distractor_rationales.C: Alveoli are lung air sacs.
distractor_rationales.D: Fat absorption uses lacteals (lymphatic), not arteries.

items.stem: Distance and speed are scalars (magnitude only); displacement and velocity are ______ because they also include direction.
items.explanation: Vectors (displacement, velocity) have direction; scalars (distance, speed) don't. Takeaway: Displacement/velocity = vectors; distance/speed = scalars. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Displacement and velocity are vectors (magnitude + direction); distance and speed are scalars (magnitude only). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Displacement and velocity carry direction, making them vectors, not scalars.
distractor_rationales.C: 'Units' aren't a category of quantity type.
distractor_rationales.D: They aren't constants; they can vary.

items.stem: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of:
items.explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity over time (Δv/Δt). Takeaway: Acceleration = Δvelocity / Δtime. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Acceleration = Δvelocity / Δtime; it is nonzero whenever speed OR direction changes. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Rate of change of position is velocity, not acceleration.
distractor_rationales.B: Rate of change of force isn't the definition of acceleration.
distractor_rationales.C: Mass is generally constant and isn't part of the definition.

items.stem: Near Earth's surface, in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration of approximately:

choices.text: A value proportional to their mass

items.explanation: Free-fall acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s², the same for all masses. Takeaway: g ≈ 9.8 m/s², independent of mass. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gravitational acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² is the same for all masses in free fall (a heavy and light object fall together in a vacuum). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Free-fall acceleration is independent of mass.
distractor_rationales.B: Objects in free fall accelerate; g is not zero.
distractor_rationales.D: g is an acceleration (m/s²), not a velocity (m/s).

items.stem: In projectile motion (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal and vertical components of motion are:

choices.text: Independent of each other (horizontal velocity constant, vertical accelerates at g)

items.explanation: Projectile motion: horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (accelerates at g) are independent. Takeaway: Projectile: horizontal constant, vertical accelerates — independent. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Horizontal and vertical motions are independent: horizontal velocity is constant (no horizontal force), while vertical motion accelerates due to gravity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The components are generally not equal.
distractor_rationales.C: There is no horizontal acceleration (ignoring air resistance).
distractor_rationales.D: The vertical component accelerates, so both aren't constant.

items.stem: Newton's second law states that the net force on an object equals:
items.explanation: Newton's 2nd law: F_net = ma. Takeaway: F = ma (net force = mass × acceleration). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. F_net = ma; net force and acceleration are directly proportional (and in the same direction). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Mass times velocity is momentum (p), not force.
distractor_rationales.B: That inverts the relationship incorrectly.
distractor_rationales.D: Weight times height relates to potential energy, not this law.

items.stem: Newton's third law states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force, acting on:

choices.text: A different object (the two forces act on different bodies)

items.explanation: Newton's 3rd law: equal and opposite forces on two different objects. Takeaway: 3rd law: equal/opposite forces on DIFFERENT objects. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Action-reaction pairs are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on DIFFERENT objects (so they don't cancel on one object). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The pair acts on two different objects, not the same one — that's why they don't cancel.
distractor_rationales.B: Both objects experience the force regardless of size.
distractor_rationales.C: The forces are real and act on the two interacting bodies.

items.stem: Mass is the amount of matter (constant everywhere); weight is the ______ on that mass and changes with location.
items.explanation: Weight = mg (a force that varies with g); mass is constant. Takeaway: Mass = matter (constant); weight = mg (force, varies). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Weight = mg (a force, in newtons) and varies with g; mass (in kg) is invariant. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Weight and mass are different quantities (force vs. amount of matter).
distractor_rationales.B: Volume is space occupied, not weight.
distractor_rationales.D: Density is mass per volume, not weight.

items.stem: The friction force that must be overcome to START a stationary object moving is generally ______ the friction once it is already sliding.

choices.text: Greater than (static friction max > kinetic friction)

items.explanation: Max static friction > kinetic friction (harder to start than to keep moving). Takeaway: Static friction (max) > kinetic friction. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Maximum static friction is typically greater than kinetic friction, which is why it takes more force to start motion than to maintain it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Static (max) friction is greater, not less, than kinetic.
distractor_rationales.B: They differ; static max generally exceeds kinetic.
distractor_rationales.C: Static friction isn't zero — it can be substantial.

items.stem: In physics, work is done on an object only when a force causes:

choices.text: Any force to be applied, even without motion
Displacement in the direction of the force (W = Fd·cosθ)

items.explanation: Work = F·d·cosθ — requires displacement along the force. Takeaway: Work = force × displacement × cosθ (needs motion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Work = F·d·cosθ; if there is no displacement (or force is perpendicular to motion), no work is done. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Holding an object still (no displacement) does zero physical work.
distractor_rationales.C: Work relates to force and displacement, not mass change.
distractor_rationales.D: Work is energy transfer via force×displacement, not defined by temperature.

items.stem: The kinetic energy of a moving object is given by:
items.explanation: Kinetic energy = ½ mv² (scales with speed squared). Takeaway: KE = ½ mv² (double speed → 4× KE). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Kinetic energy = ½ mv²; it scales with the SQUARE of speed (doubling speed quadruples KE). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: mgh is gravitational potential energy.
distractor_rationales.C: mv is momentum, not kinetic energy.
distractor_rationales.D: ½ kx² is spring (elastic) potential energy.

items.stem: In a closed system with only conservative forces, as an object falls, its gravitational potential energy is:

choices.text: Converted into kinetic energy (total mechanical energy conserved)

items.explanation: Falling: PE → KE, total mechanical energy conserved (no friction). Takeaway: Energy conserved: PE converts to KE as it falls. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Energy is conserved: PE converts to KE as the object falls, keeping total mechanical energy constant (without friction). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Energy is conserved, not destroyed.
distractor_rationales.C: Energy isn't converted to mass in classical mechanics problems.
distractor_rationales.D: Gravitational PE decreases as the object falls, not increases.

items.stem: Power is the rate at which work is done, given by:
items.explanation: Power = Work / time (rate of doing work). Takeaway: Power = work / time (watts). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Power = work/time (watts); it measures how quickly energy is transferred. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Power is work per unit time, not work times time.
distractor_rationales.C: Force times displacement is work, not power.
distractor_rationales.D: Mass times acceleration is force.

items.stem: The momentum of an object is defined as:
items.explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity (p = mv), a vector. Takeaway: Momentum p = mv (vector). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Momentum p = mv is a vector quantity (direction matters); it's conserved in isolated systems. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: ½ mv² is kinetic energy, not momentum.
distractor_rationales.C: Mass times acceleration is force.
distractor_rationales.D: Force times distance is work.

items.stem: Impulse equals the change in momentum, and also equals:

choices.text: Force times the time it acts (J = F·Δt)

items.explanation: Impulse = F·Δt = Δp (longer time → smaller force). Takeaway: Impulse = F·Δt = change in momentum. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Impulse = F·Δt = Δp; extending the time of a collision (e.g., airbags) reduces the force for a given momentum change. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Force times distance is work, not impulse.
distractor_rationales.C: That isn't the impulse relationship.
distractor_rationales.D: Work times time isn't impulse.

items.stem: In an isolated system (no external forces), the total momentum before a collision:

choices.text: Equals the total momentum after the collision

items.explanation: Momentum is conserved: total before = total after (isolated system). Takeaway: Momentum conserved: p(before) = p(after). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Momentum is conserved in isolated systems: total p before = total p after, whether the collision is elastic or inelastic. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Total momentum is conserved, not increased.
distractor_rationales.C: Total momentum need not be zero; it's simply conserved.
distractor_rationales.D: Kinetic energy (not momentum) can convert to heat in inelastic collisions.

items.stem: In a perfectly ELASTIC collision, both momentum and ______ are conserved; in an INELASTIC collision, only momentum is.
items.explanation: Elastic: momentum + kinetic energy conserved. Inelastic: only momentum. Takeaway: Elastic = KE conserved too; inelastic = KE lost. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy; inelastic collisions conserve momentum but lose kinetic energy (to heat/deformation). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Mass is conserved in both, so it doesn't distinguish them.
distractor_rationales.B: Force isn't a conserved quantity here.
distractor_rationales.D: Temperature isn't the conserved quantity that defines elastic collisions.

items.stem: An object is in translational equilibrium (not accelerating) when:

choices.text: The net force on it is zero (ΣF = 0)

items.explanation: Translational equilibrium: net force = 0 (ΣF = 0). Takeaway: Translational equilibrium = ΣF = 0 (rest or constant velocity). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Translational equilibrium requires ΣF = 0; the object may be at rest OR moving at constant velocity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Equilibrium includes constant-velocity motion, not only rest.
distractor_rationales.B: Zero net torque is ROTATIONAL equilibrium, a separate condition.
distractor_rationales.D: Mass isn't zero; the forces simply balance.

items.stem: Torque, the rotational equivalent of force, is calculated as:
items.explanation: Torque = rF·sinθ (force × lever arm). Takeaway: Torque = r × F × sinθ (lever arm matters). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Torque = rF·sinθ; a longer lever arm or perpendicular force produces more rotational effect. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Force times mass isn't torque.
distractor_rationales.B: Torque is force times distance, not divided by it.
distractor_rationales.C: Mass times velocity is momentum.

items.stem: For an object to be in complete equilibrium, the net force AND the net ______ must both be zero.
items.explanation: Complete equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0. Takeaway: Full equilibrium = net force AND net torque both zero. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Complete (static) equilibrium requires ΣF = 0 AND Στ = 0 (no linear or rotational acceleration). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Mass isn't a balance condition for equilibrium.
distractor_rationales.B: Velocity can be constant (nonzero) in equilibrium.
distractor_rationales.C: Density isn't an equilibrium condition.

items.stem: The restoring force of an ideal spring is proportional to its displacement from equilibrium, given by:
items.explanation: Hooke's law: F = −kx (restoring force proportional to displacement). Takeaway: Hooke's law: F = −kx (spring restoring force). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hooke's law: F = −kx; the negative sign shows the force opposes (restores toward) the displacement. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: F = ma is Newton's second law, not the spring force law.
distractor_rationales.C: ½ kx² is spring potential energy, not force.
distractor_rationales.D: mgh is gravitational potential energy.

items.stem: For a simple pendulum (small angles), the period depends on the length and gravity but is INDEPENDENT of:

choices.text: The string material's rigidity aside, everything
The mass of the bob and the amplitude

items.explanation: Pendulum period depends on length and g, NOT mass or amplitude. Takeaway: Pendulum T = 2π√(L/g): independent of mass & amplitude. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Period T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length and g — not on the bob's mass or (for small swings) the amplitude. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Period DOES depend on length.
distractor_rationales.B: Period DOES depend on g.
distractor_rationales.C: Period specifically depends on L and g; it's mass/amplitude that don't matter.

items.stem: In simple harmonic motion (like a mass on a spring), speed is MAXIMUM at the ______ and zero at the ______.
items.explanation: SHM: speed max at equilibrium, zero at turning points. Takeaway: SHM: fastest at equilibrium, stops at the extremes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In SHM, speed peaks at equilibrium (max KE) and is zero at the extremes (max PE), where the object momentarily stops. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — speed is zero at the turning points, max at equilibrium.
distractor_rationales.B: SHM speed varies with position along the whole path, not just top/bottom.
distractor_rationales.C: Speed changes continuously in SHM.

items.stem: Pressure is defined as:
items.explanation: Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A). Takeaway: Pressure = F/A (force per area). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pressure = F/A; the same force over a smaller area produces greater pressure. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Pressure is force divided by area, not multiplied.
distractor_rationales.C: Force times distance is work.
distractor_rationales.D: Mass per volume is density, not pressure.

items.stem: The pressure in a static fluid increases with depth according to P = ρgh, so pressure depends on:

choices.text: Fluid density and depth (not the container's shape)
The surface area of the fluid

items.explanation: Hydrostatic P = ρgh: depends on density and depth, not container shape. Takeaway: Fluid pressure = ρgh (density × g × depth). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hydrostatic pressure P = ρgh depends on density and depth; container shape and total volume don't affect pressure at a given depth. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Container shape doesn't change pressure at a given depth.
distractor_rationales.C: Surface area alone doesn't set the pressure at depth.
distractor_rationales.D: Depth, not total volume, determines the pressure.

items.stem: Pascal's principle — the basis of hydraulic lifts — states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is:

choices.text: Transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid

items.explanation: Pascal's principle: applied pressure transmits equally throughout an enclosed fluid. Takeaway: Pascal: pressure transmits equally through a fluid (hydraulics). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Pascal's principle: applied pressure transmits equally throughout an enclosed fluid, letting a small force on a small area lift a large load on a large area. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The pressure transmits fully, not lost as heat.
distractor_rationales.C: It is felt throughout the fluid, not only at the top.
distractor_rationales.D: It isn't determined by container weight.

items.stem: The buoyant force on a submerged or floating object equals:

choices.text: The weight of the fluid displaced

items.explanation: Buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes). Takeaway: Buoyancy = weight of displaced fluid. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Archimedes' principle: buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid (F_b = ρ_fluid · V_displaced · g). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The buoyant force equals the displaced fluid's weight, not the object's weight (unless floating).
distractor_rationales.C: Volume isn't a force.
distractor_rationales.D: Atmospheric pressure isn't the buoyant force.

items.stem: An object floats if its average density is ______ the fluid's density, and sinks if it is ______.
items.explanation: Float if density fluid. Takeaway: Less dense = float; more dense = sink. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Less dense than the fluid → floats; more dense → sinks; equal → neutrally buoyant (suspended). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — lower density floats.
distractor_rationales.B: Equal density gives neutral buoyancy, not the float/sink pair.
distractor_rationales.D: Density isn't zero; it's compared to the fluid's density.

items.stem: For an incompressible fluid in a pipe, the continuity equation (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) means that where the pipe NARROWS, the fluid:
items.explanation: Continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂): narrower pipe → faster flow. Takeaway: Continuity: narrow pipe = faster flow (A·v constant). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Continuity: flow rate (A·v) is constant, so a smaller cross-sectional area forces a higher velocity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Fluid speeds up, not slows down, in a narrower section.
distractor_rationales.C: It doesn't stop; it accelerates.
distractor_rationales.D: Incompressible fluid density stays constant.

items.stem: Bernoulli's principle states that in a flowing fluid, where the velocity is HIGH, the pressure is:
items.explanation: Bernoulli: high fluid velocity → low pressure. Takeaway: Bernoulli: fast flow = low pressure. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Bernoulli: faster-moving fluid exerts lower pressure (energy conservation) — the basis of lift and the Venturi effect. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: High velocity corresponds to LOW pressure, not high.
distractor_rationales.C: Pressure changes with velocity per Bernoulli.
distractor_rationales.D: Pressure is lower but not necessarily zero.

items.stem: The ideal gas law relating pressure, volume, moles, and temperature is:
items.explanation: Ideal gas law: PV = nRT. Takeaway: PV = nRT (P, V, moles, temperature). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. PV = nRT relates pressure, volume, moles (n), and absolute temperature; R is the gas constant. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It uses moles (n), not mass (m), with R.
distractor_rationales.B: That form isn't the ideal gas law.
distractor_rationales.D: That arrangement isn't correct.

items.stem: At constant temperature, if the volume of a gas DECREASES, its pressure will:

choices.text: Increase (P and V are inversely proportional)

items.explanation: Boyle's law: at constant T, P and V are inversely related. Takeaway: Boyle: ↓volume → ↑pressure (constant T). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Boyle's law: at constant T, P ∝ 1/V — compressing a gas raises its pressure. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Pressure rises when volume falls, not decreases.
distractor_rationales.C: Pressure changes; it doesn't stay constant.
distractor_rationales.D: Pressure increases but doesn't go to zero.

items.stem: According to kinetic molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to:
items.explanation: Average kinetic energy of gas molecules ∝ absolute temperature. Takeaway: Gas KE ∝ Kelvin temperature. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Average molecular kinetic energy ∝ absolute temperature; heavier molecules move slower at the same temperature but have the same average KE. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Pressure alone doesn't set average kinetic energy.
distractor_rationales.C: Volume alone doesn't set it.
distractor_rationales.D: At a given temperature, KE is the same regardless of molar mass.

items.stem: In a mixture of non-reacting gases, the total pressure equals:

choices.text: The pressure of the largest gas only
The sum of the partial pressures of each gas

items.explanation: Dalton's law: total pressure = sum of partial pressures. Takeaway: Dalton: P_total = sum of partial pressures. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Dalton's law: total pressure = sum of each gas's partial pressure (each contributes independently). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Every gas contributes, not just the largest.
distractor_rationales.C: It's the sum, not the average.
distractor_rationales.D: It's the sum, not the product.

items.stem: The electrostatic force between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to:

choices.text: The square of the distance between them

items.explanation: Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r² (inverse-square with distance). Takeaway: Coulomb: F ∝ q₁q₂/r² (inverse square). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r² — an inverse-square relationship with distance (like gravity). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The dependence is on distance SQUARED, not distance to the first power.
distractor_rationales.B: It depends on the product of charges, not their sum, and on r².
distractor_rationales.C: It's an inverse-square (r²), not inverse-cube, law.

items.stem: Two charges of the SAME sign will ______, while opposite charges will ______.
items.explanation: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Takeaway: Like repel, opposite attract. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy. Neighbouring options fail because they name a different relation, drop a required conversion, or contradict a number given in the stem. Those traps are not a second live key. This row stays unverified and is not an official percentile item.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — same-sign charges repel.
distractor_rationales.C: Same-sign charges repel, so not both attract.
distractor_rationales.D: Opposite charges attract, so not both repel.

items.stem: Electric potential difference (voltage) is the ______ per unit charge between two points.
items.explanation: Voltage = work (energy) per unit charge (V = W/q). Takeaway: Voltage = energy per charge (W/q). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Voltage = work (energy) per unit charge (V = W/q); it drives charge flow in a circuit. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Force per charge is the electric field, not voltage.
distractor_rationales.C: Current is charge flow rate, not energy per charge.
distractor_rationales.D: Resistance opposes current; it isn't energy per charge.

items.stem: Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance as:
items.explanation: Ohm's law: V = IR. Takeaway: V = IR (voltage = current × resistance). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ohm's law: V = IR (voltage = current × resistance). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That inverts the relationship incorrectly.
distractor_rationales.C: That inverts it incorrectly.
distractor_rationales.D: The quantities multiply (I×R), they don't add.

items.stem: Resistors connected in SERIES have a total resistance equal to:

choices.text: The reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals
The sum of the individual resistances (R_total = R₁ + R₂ + ...)
Always less than the smallest resistor

items.explanation: Resistors in series add: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + ... Takeaway: Series resistors add (R_total = R₁+R₂+...). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Series resistances add directly; total resistance is greater than any single resistor. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reciprocal-of-reciprocals is the PARALLEL formula, not series.
distractor_rationales.C: Series total is larger than the largest resistor, not smaller than the smallest.
distractor_rationales.D: Series resistance isn't zero.

items.stem: Adding resistors in PARALLEL causes the total resistance to:
items.explanation: Resistors in parallel: total resistance DECREASES (more current paths). Takeaway: Parallel resistors: total R decreases (more paths). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Parallel resistors provide more paths for current, lowering total resistance below the smallest branch (1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Parallel resistance decreases, not increases.
distractor_rationales.C: It changes as branches are added.
distractor_rationales.D: It doesn't simply double.

items.stem: The power dissipated by an electrical device can be calculated as:
items.explanation: Electrical power P = IV (= I²R = V²/R). Takeaway: P = IV (electrical power). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Electrical power P = IV (also I²R or V²/R); it's the rate of energy transfer. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That isn't the power relationship.
distractor_rationales.C: That isn't correct either.
distractor_rationales.D: Power is a product (IV), not a sum.

items.stem: A capacitor is a device that stores ______ in the electric field between two separated conductors.
items.explanation: A capacitor stores charge/energy in an electric field (Q = CV). Takeaway: Capacitor = stores charge/energy (Q = CV). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A capacitor stores charge/energy (Q = CV) in the field between its plates; it opposes changes in voltage. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Capacitors store charge, not a flow of current itself.
distractor_rationales.B: Resistance is stored by resistors, not capacitors.
distractor_rationales.D: Magnetic flux is associated with inductors, not capacitors.

items.stem: A magnetic field is produced by ______, and a magnetic force acts on a charge only when the charge is:
items.explanation: Magnetic fields come from moving charges; magnetic force acts only on moving charges. Takeaway: Magnetism = moving charges (force only on moving charge). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Moving charges (currents) create magnetic fields, and magnetic force acts only on charges that are MOVING (F = qvB·sinθ). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Stationary charges create electric, not magnetic, fields and feel no magnetic force.
distractor_rationales.C: Neutral atoms and heating aren't the source described.
distractor_rationales.D: Magnetism relates to moving charge, not insulators specifically.

items.stem: The speed of a wave equals its:
items.explanation: Wave speed v = fλ (frequency × wavelength). Takeaway: v = fλ (speed = frequency × wavelength). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. v = fλ; for a fixed wave speed, frequency and wavelength are inversely related. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Speed is the product of f and λ, not the quotient.
distractor_rationales.B: Amplitude relates to energy/intensity, not wave speed.
distractor_rationales.C: That isn't the wave-speed relationship.

items.stem: Sound waves are ______ waves, in which particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy propagation.
items.explanation: Sound = longitudinal (parallel oscillation); light = transverse. Takeaway: Sound = longitudinal; light = transverse. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sound is a longitudinal (compression) wave — particle motion is parallel to propagation; light is transverse. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to propagation (e.g., light), unlike sound.
distractor_rationales.B: Sound is mechanical, not electromagnetic.
distractor_rationales.D: Standing waves are a special pattern, not the basic sound-wave type.

items.stem: Unlike light, sound cannot travel through:

choices.text: A vacuum (it requires a material medium)

items.explanation: Sound requires a medium — it can't travel through a vacuum (light can). Takeaway: Sound needs a medium (no sound in vacuum). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sound is a mechanical wave requiring a medium (air, water, solids); it can't propagate through a vacuum. Light (EM) can. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Sound travels through air.
distractor_rationales.B: Sound travels through water (even faster than air).
distractor_rationales.D: Sound travels through solids (fastest of the three).

items.stem: As an ambulance siren approaches you, the perceived pitch (frequency) is ______; as it moves away, the pitch is ______.
items.explanation: Doppler: approaching → higher pitch; receding → lower pitch. Takeaway: Doppler: approaching = higher pitch, receding = lower. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The Doppler effect: approaching source → waves compressed → higher perceived frequency; receding → stretched → lower. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — approaching raises the pitch.
distractor_rationales.B: The perceived pitch changes with relative motion.
distractor_rationales.D: Pitch shifts up or down, not to zero/maximum.

items.stem: Visible light, X-rays, radio waves, and microwaves are all forms of electromagnetic radiation that travel through a vacuum at:
items.explanation: All EM radiation travels at c in a vacuum (differing in frequency/wavelength). Takeaway: All EM waves travel at c in vacuum (differ in λ/f). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum; they differ in frequency/wavelength (and thus energy), not vacuum speed. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: All EM radiation travels at c in a vacuum, regardless of type.
distractor_rationales.B: EM waves travel far faster than sound.
distractor_rationales.D: EM waves travel at c, not zero.

items.stem: When light passes into a denser medium (higher index of refraction), it slows down and bends:
items.explanation: Into a denser medium: light slows and bends toward the normal. Takeaway: Denser medium → light bends toward the normal (slows). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Entering a denser (higher-n) medium, light slows and bends toward the normal; entering a less dense medium, it bends away. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Bending away from the normal occurs going to a LESS dense medium.
distractor_rationales.B: Refraction is transmission with bending, not reflection.
distractor_rationales.C: The bending angle depends on the indices, not always 90°.

items.stem: A converging (convex) lens focuses parallel light rays to a point and can form a ______ image of a distant object.
items.explanation: A converging lens focuses light and forms a real, inverted image of a distant object. Takeaway: Converging lens = focuses rays; real inverted image (distant object). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A converging lens brings parallel rays to a real focal point and forms a real, inverted image of an object beyond its focal length. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It forms real inverted images for distant objects (virtual upright only when object is within f).
distractor_rationales.C: It does form images.
distractor_rationales.D: The image isn't always magnified or upright.

items.stem: When light travels from a denser to a less dense medium beyond the critical angle, it undergoes:

choices.text: Total internal reflection (the basis of fiber optics)

items.explanation: Total internal reflection: beyond the critical angle, light fully reflects (fiber optics). Takeaway: TIR = full reflection beyond critical angle (fiber optics). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Beyond the critical angle, light hitting a boundary to a less dense medium is entirely reflected back — total internal reflection (used in fiber optics). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Beyond the critical angle, light is reflected, not transmitted.
distractor_rationales.C: This is reflection, not diffraction.
distractor_rationales.D: This is reflection, not polarization.

items.stem: The atomic number of an element equals its number of ______, while the mass number equals protons plus ______.
items.explanation: Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons. Takeaway: Atomic # = protons; mass # = protons + neutrons. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Atomic number = number of protons (defines the element); mass number = protons + neutrons. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — atomic number counts protons.
distractor_rationales.B: Atomic number counts protons, not electrons.
distractor_rationales.D: Mass number adds neutrons, not electrons (electrons have negligible mass).

items.stem: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but DIFFERENT numbers of neutrons are:
items.explanation: Isotopes = same protons, different neutrons. Takeaway: Isotopes = same element, different neutron count. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Isotopes differ in neutron number (and thus mass number) but share the same atomic number (element identity). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Ions differ in electron number (charge), not neutrons.
distractor_rationales.C: Isomers are molecules with the same formula but different structure.
distractor_rationales.D: Allotropes are different structural forms of an element (e.g., graphite vs. diamond).

items.stem: An atom that has LOST electrons becomes a ______ (positive ion), while one that has GAINED electrons becomes a ______ (negative ion).
items.explanation: Cation = lost electrons (positive); anion = gained electrons (negative). Takeaway: Cation = + (lost e−); anion = − (gained e−). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Losing electrons → net positive = cation; gaining electrons → net negative = anion. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — losing electrons makes a cation (positive).
distractor_rationales.C: Those are neutron-count/structure terms, not charge.
distractor_rationales.D: Protons/neutrons are nuclear particles, not ion types.

items.stem: Electronegativity generally INCREASES as you move ______ across a period and ______ up a group.
items.explanation: Electronegativity increases toward the upper-right (max at fluorine). Takeaway: Electronegativity: increases right and up (F highest). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Electronegativity increases toward the upper right of the periodic table (fluorine is the most electronegative). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It increases toward the right and up, not left and down.
distractor_rationales.B: It increases going up, not down.
distractor_rationales.D: It increases going right, not left.

items.stem: Atomic radius generally ______ across a period (left to right) and ______ down a group.
items.explanation: Atomic radius: decreases across a period, increases down a group. Takeaway: Radius: shrinks left→right, grows top→bottom. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Across a period, more protons pull electrons in tighter (smaller radius); down a group, added shells make atoms larger. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — radius decreases across a period, increases down a group.
distractor_rationales.C: It decreases across a period.
distractor_rationales.D: It increases down a group.

items.stem: Ionization energy (the energy to remove an electron) generally follows the ______ trend as electronegativity.

choices.text: Same (increases up and to the right)

items.explanation: Ionization energy increases up and to the right (same direction as electronegativity). Takeaway: Ionization energy increases up/right (like electronegativity). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ionization energy increases toward the upper right (like electronegativity) — electrons are held more tightly there. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: It follows the same, not opposite, trend as electronegativity.
distractor_rationales.C: The trends are related, both reflecting nuclear pull.
distractor_rationales.D: The trend is systematic, not random.

items.stem: In radioactive decay, an ______ particle is a helium nucleus (heavy, low penetration), while a ______ particle is a high-energy electron.
items.explanation: Alpha = helium nucleus; beta = electron; gamma = photon. Takeaway: Alpha = He nucleus; beta = electron; gamma = photon. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alpha = helium nucleus (2p + 2n); beta = electron (or positron); gamma = high-energy photon (most penetrating). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the helium nucleus is the alpha particle.
distractor_rationales.B: Gamma is a photon, not the helium nucleus.
distractor_rationales.C: Gamma is a photon, not an electron.

items.stem: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time required for:

choices.text: Half of the radioactive nuclei to decay

items.explanation: Half-life = time for half the radioactive nuclei to decay. Takeaway: Half-life = time for half the sample to decay. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Each half-life reduces the remaining radioactive quantity by half (exponential decay), regardless of the starting amount. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: One half-life decays half, not all, of the sample.
distractor_rationales.B: Radioactive decay reduces the quantity; it doesn't double the mass.
distractor_rationales.D: Half-life concerns quantity decayed, not halving the atomic number.

items.stem: Ranked from LEAST to MOST penetrating, the three types of radiation are:
items.explanation: Penetration: alpha (gamma most penetrating). Takeaway: Penetration: alpha < beta < gamma. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alpha (stopped by paper) < beta (stopped by aluminum) < gamma (needs lead/concrete). Heavier, more-charged particles penetrate less. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That's the reverse — gamma is most penetrating.
distractor_rationales.C: Alpha is the least penetrating, not in the middle.
distractor_rationales.D: Gamma is most penetrating, so it comes last, not middle.

items.stem: Water is an excellent solvent for ionic and polar substances because the water molecule is:
items.explanation: Water is polar (bent + partial charges) → dissolves ions/polar solutes. Takeaway: Water = polar (bent) → great solvent for ionic/polar. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Water's bent geometry and O–H electronegativity difference make it polar, so it dissolves ions and polar molecules ('like dissolves like'). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Water is bent, not linear, and it is polar.
distractor_rationales.B: Water has distinct partial charges (δ− on O, δ+ on H), not a uniform sphere.
distractor_rationales.C: Water has partial charges that make it polar.

items.stem: Many of water's unusual properties (high boiling point, high specific heat, cohesion) arise from:
items.explanation: Water's special properties come from hydrogen bonding between molecules. Takeaway: Water's properties = hydrogen bonding (high specific heat, cohesion). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules give water high specific heat, high boiling point, surface tension, and cohesion/adhesion. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The bonds WITHIN a water molecule are covalent; between molecules they're hydrogen bonds.
distractor_rationales.B: Water molecules aren't held together by ionic bonds.
distractor_rationales.C: Hydrogen bonding (not just weak dispersion) dominates water's behavior.

items.stem: By the Brønsted-Lowry definition, an acid is a proton (H+) ______ and a base is a proton ______.
items.explanation: Brønsted-Lowry: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. Takeaway: B-L acid = H+ donor; base = H+ acceptor. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Brønsted-Lowry: acid donates H+, base accepts H+. (Lewis definition uses electron pairs instead.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the acid donates the proton.
distractor_rationales.B: Electron donor/acceptor is the Lewis definition, not Brønsted-Lowry.
distractor_rationales.C: Those aren't the Brønsted-Lowry roles.

items.stem: When an acid donates a proton, what remains is its:
items.explanation: An acid minus H+ = its conjugate base (differ by one proton). Takeaway: Acid − H+ = conjugate base. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. An acid loses H+ to become its conjugate base; a base gains H+ to become its conjugate acid (they differ by one proton). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Gaining a proton (base → conjugate acid) is the reverse relationship.
distractor_rationales.C: The product is the conjugate base, not necessarily a neutral salt.
distractor_rationales.D: It's the same species minus a proton, not a different element.

items.stem: A STRONG acid differs from a weak acid in that a strong acid:
items.explanation: A strong acid dissociates completely; a weak acid only partially. Takeaway: Strong acid = fully dissociates; weak = partial (Ka). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Strong acids ionize ~100% in water; weak acids only partially dissociate (described by Ka). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Partial dissociation describes a WEAK acid.
distractor_rationales.C: Acids by definition donate H+; strong ones do so completely.
distractor_rationales.D: Strength refers to degree of dissociation, not concentration.

items.stem: pH is defined as:

choices.text: The negative log of the hydrogen ion concentration (pH = −log[H+])

items.explanation: pH = −log[H+] (log scale; each unit = 10×). Takeaway: pH = −log[H+] (each unit = 10× change). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. pH = −log[H+]; each unit change in pH is a 10-fold change in [H+]. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: It's the NEGATIVE log, so lower pH = higher [H+].
distractor_rationales.C: pH is a log scale, not the raw concentration.
distractor_rationales.D: pH tracks [H+], not directly [OH−].

items.stem: At 25°C, for any aqueous solution, pH + pOH equals:
items.explanation: At 25°C, pH + pOH = 14. Takeaway: pH + pOH = 14 (at 25°C). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Because Kw = [H+][OH−] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C, pH + pOH = 14. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: 7 is neutral pH, not the sum of pH and pOH.
distractor_rationales.C: The sum is 14, not 0.
distractor_rationales.D: The sum is 14, not 100.

items.stem: A solution with pH 7 is ______.
items.explanation: pH acidic; pH = 7 neutral; pH > 7 = basic. Takeaway: pH7 basic. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. pH below 7 = acidic (more H+); pH above 7 = basic (more OH−); 7 = neutral. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — below 7 is acidic.
distractor_rationales.B: Only pH exactly 7 is neutral.
distractor_rationales.D: Saturated/dilute describe concentration, not pH.

items.stem: A buffer solution, which resists changes in pH, is typically made of:

choices.text: A strong acid and a strong base
A weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base + conjugate acid)

items.explanation: A buffer = weak acid + its conjugate base (resists pH change). Takeaway: Buffer = weak acid + conjugate base. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Buffers pair a weak acid with its conjugate base, neutralizing added acid or base to hold pH nearly constant. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Strong acid + strong base neutralize to a salt; that isn't a buffer.
distractor_rationales.B: Pure water has negligible buffering capacity.
distractor_rationales.D: Two strong acids don't form a buffer.

items.stem: When a buffer contains equal concentrations of weak acid and conjugate base, the pH equals:
items.explanation: When [acid] = [conjugate base], pH = pKa (Henderson-Hasselbalch). Takeaway: Equal acid/base → pH = pKa (best buffering). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]); when [base] = [acid], the log term is 0, so pH = pKa (maximum buffering). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: pH equals pKa here, not necessarily 7.
distractor_rationales.C: pH isn't zero.
distractor_rationales.D: It equals the pKa, not the pKb.

items.stem: In an acid-base titration, the equivalence point is where:

choices.text: Moles of added base exactly neutralize the moles of acid

items.explanation: Equivalence point: moles of titrant = moles of analyte (fully neutralized). Takeaway: Equivalence point = moles acid = moles base. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. At the equivalence point, added titrant has reacted stoichiometrically with the analyte (moles acid = moles base). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The indicator is added at the start, not the equivalence point.
distractor_rationales.C: Equivalence pH is 7 only for strong acid + strong base; weak systems differ.
distractor_rationales.D: The endpoint is detected, not spontaneous.

items.stem: On a weak-acid titration curve, at the half-equivalence point (half the acid neutralized), the pH equals:

choices.text: The pKa of the weak acid

items.explanation: At the half-equivalence point, pH = pKa (buffer region). Takeaway: Half-equivalence: pH = pKa. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. At half-equivalence, [acid] = [conjugate base], so pH = pKa — a useful way to read pKa from a titration curve. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: pH = pKa here, not necessarily 7.
distractor_rationales.C: pH isn't zero at half-equivalence.
distractor_rationales.D: The half-equivalence pH (pKa) differs from the equivalence-point pH.

items.stem: For a titration of a STRONG acid with a STRONG base, the pH at the equivalence point is:
items.explanation: Strong acid + strong base: equivalence pH = 7. Takeaway: Strong-strong titration: equivalence pH = 7. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Strong acid + strong base yields a neutral salt and water, so the equivalence point is pH 7. (Weak-acid titrations give equivalence pH > 7.) Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Equivalence pH > 7 applies to weak acid + strong base, not strong-strong.
distractor_rationales.C: Equivalence pH < 7 applies to strong acid + weak base.
distractor_rationales.D: It's 7, not 0.

items.stem: The solubility product constant (Ksp) describes the equilibrium for:

choices.text: A slightly soluble ionic solid dissolving into its ions

items.explanation: Ksp = equilibrium constant for a sparingly soluble salt dissolving into ions. Takeaway: Ksp = dissolution equilibrium of a solid (bigger Ksp = more soluble). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ksp is the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a sparingly soluble salt into its constituent ions; a larger Ksp means greater solubility. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Gas solubility is described by Henry's law, not Ksp.
distractor_rationales.C: Proton donation is described by Ka.
distractor_rationales.D: Redox equilibria use cell potentials, not Ksp.

items.stem: Adding an ion already present in a saturated salt solution will ______ the solubility of that salt.
items.explanation: Common ion effect: a shared ion decreases a salt's solubility (Le Chatelier). Takeaway: Common ion → less soluble (equilibrium shifts back). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The common ion effect shifts the dissolution equilibrium backward (Le Chatelier), decreasing solubility. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A common ion decreases, not increases, solubility.
distractor_rationales.C: It shifts equilibrium and changes solubility.
distractor_rationales.D: It suppresses dissolution, it doesn't remove the ion.
