items.stem: A bond formed by the TRANSFER of electrons (typically metal + nonmetal) is ______; a bond formed by SHARING electrons (nonmetal + nonmetal) is ______.
items.explanation: Ionic = electron transfer; covalent = electron sharing. Takeaway: Ionic = transfer e−; covalent = share e−. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Ionic bonds transfer electrons (forming cations/anions); covalent bonds share electron pairs. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — electron transfer is ionic, sharing is covalent.
distractor_rationales.C: Metallic bonding is a different type (delocalized electrons), not electron transfer here.
distractor_rationales.D: Hydrogen 'bonds' are intermolecular attractions, not the electron-sharing bond type.

items.stem: A covalent bond between atoms of DIFFERENT electronegativities, creating partial charges, is a:
items.explanation: Polar covalent = unequal sharing (electronegativity difference → partial charges). Takeaway: Polar covalent = unequal e− sharing (δ+/δ−). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Unequal sharing (electronegativity difference) makes a bond polar covalent, with δ+ and δ− ends. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Nonpolar covalent bonds share electrons equally (similar electronegativity).
distractor_rationales.B: A large enough difference becomes ionic; a moderate difference is polar covalent.
distractor_rationales.C: Metallic bonds involve delocalized electrons among metal atoms.

items.stem: A molecule is nonpolar overall if its bond dipoles ______, even if individual bonds are polar (e.g., CO2).
items.explanation: A molecule is nonpolar if symmetric geometry makes bond dipoles cancel (e.g., CO2). Takeaway: Symmetric molecule = dipoles cancel = nonpolar (CO2). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Symmetric geometry can cancel bond dipoles, making the whole molecule nonpolar (CO2 is linear/symmetric despite polar C=O bonds). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Symmetric dipoles cancel rather than adding.
distractor_rationales.C: Polar covalent bonds aren't ionic.
distractor_rationales.D: In a nonpolar molecule the dipoles oppose/cancel, not point the same way.

items.stem: VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on the idea that electron pairs around a central atom:

choices.text: Repel and arrange to maximize their separation

items.explanation: VSEPR: electron pairs repel and spread out to set molecular geometry. Takeaway: VSEPR = electron pairs repel → determine shape. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. VSEPR: electron pairs (bonding and lone) repel, arranging to minimize repulsion (maximize separation), which sets the molecular geometry. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Electron pairs repel, they don't cluster.
distractor_rationales.B: Electron-pair arrangement determines shape.
distractor_rationales.C: Angles vary by geometry (e.g., 109.5° tetrahedral, 120° trigonal), not always 90°.

items.stem: Ranked from WEAKEST to STRONGEST, the intermolecular forces are:
items.explanation: IMF strength: London dispersion . Takeaway: IMF: dispersion < dipole-dipole < H-bonding. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. London dispersion (weakest, present in all) < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding (strongest IMF, a special strong dipole force). Ion-dipole is even stronger. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That's reversed — hydrogen bonding is strongest.
distractor_rationales.B: London dispersion is weakest, not in the middle.
distractor_rationales.C: The forces differ substantially in strength.

items.stem: Hydrogen bonding (the strongest normal IMF) occurs when H is bonded to:

choices.text: N, O, or F (highly electronegative atoms)

items.explanation: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F. Takeaway: H-bonding = H on N, O, or F. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hydrogen bonds form when H is bonded to N, O, or F and interacts with a lone pair on another N, O, or F. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: C–H bonds are not polar enough for true hydrogen bonding.
distractor_rationales.C: H bonded to a metal isn't the hydrogen-bonding scenario.
distractor_rationales.D: H2 has no hydrogen bonding.

items.stem: A substance with STRONGER intermolecular forces will generally have a ______ boiling point.
items.explanation: Stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling point. Takeaway: Stronger IMFs = higher boiling point. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Stronger IMFs require more energy to separate molecules into the gas phase, raising the boiling point. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Stronger IMFs raise, not lower, the boiling point.
distractor_rationales.B: Boiling point varies with IMF strength.
distractor_rationales.D: Boiling points aren't zero for molecules with IMFs.

items.stem: A reaction that RELEASES heat has a ______ enthalpy change (ΔH < 0); one that ABSORBS heat has ΔH ______.
items.explanation: Exothermic: ΔH (releases heat); endothermic: ΔH > 0 (absorbs heat). Takeaway: Exothermic ΔH0 (absorbs). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH 0). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — releasing heat is ΔH < 0 (exothermic).
distractor_rationales.C: ΔH isn't zero for these reactions.
distractor_rationales.D: Endothermic ΔH is positive, not negative.

items.stem: Entropy (S) is a measure of ______, and it tends to INCREASE when a solid melts or a gas forms.
items.explanation: Entropy (S) = disorder; increases with melting, vaporization, dissolving. Takeaway: Entropy = disorder (increases: solid→liquid→gas). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Entropy measures disorder; it increases as substances become more dispersed/random (solid → liquid → gas, dissolving). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Heat content relates to enthalpy, not entropy.
distractor_rationales.C: Rate is a kinetics concept, not entropy.
distractor_rationales.D: Mass is conserved and isn't entropy.

items.stem: A reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favorable) when its Gibbs free energy change is:
items.explanation: Spontaneous when ΔG (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS). Takeaway: Spontaneous = ΔG < 0 (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG 0 nonspontaneous, ΔG = 0 at equilibrium. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: ΔG > 0 is nonspontaneous.
distractor_rationales.C: ΔG = 0 is equilibrium, not spontaneity.
distractor_rationales.D: ΔG equals ΔH only if TΔS = 0.

items.stem: For a reaction that is endothermic (ΔH > 0) but increases entropy (ΔS > 0), spontaneity is favored at:
items.explanation: ΔH>0, ΔS>0 → spontaneous at high temperature (−TΔS dominates). Takeaway: ΔH>0, ΔS>0: spontaneous at high T. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. When ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, raising T makes the −TΔS term more negative, eventually making ΔG < 0 (spontaneous at high T). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Low temperatures keep ΔG positive here.
distractor_rationales.C: Spontaneity depends on temperature in this case.
distractor_rationales.D: It becomes spontaneous once T is high enough.

items.stem: The minimum energy required for a reaction to proceed (the barrier reactants must overcome) is the:
items.explanation: Activation energy (Ea) = the barrier reactants must overcome to react. Takeaway: Activation energy = reaction barrier (lower = faster). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Activation energy (Ea) is the energy barrier for a reaction; a lower Ea means a faster rate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity, not the kinetic barrier.
distractor_rationales.B: Bond dissociation energy is for breaking a specific bond, not the overall barrier.
distractor_rationales.C: Entropy measures disorder, not the reaction barrier.

items.stem: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by ______ without being consumed, and it does NOT change:

choices.text: Lowering the activation energy; the equilibrium position or ΔG
Raising the activation energy; the rate

items.explanation: A catalyst lowers activation energy (faster rate) but doesn't change ΔG/equilibrium. Takeaway: Catalyst = lower Ea (faster), no change to ΔG/equilibrium. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A catalyst provides a lower-Ea pathway (faster rate) but doesn't alter ΔG, the equilibrium position, or the reaction's thermodynamics. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: A catalyst LOWERS activation energy and speeds the rate.
distractor_rationales.C: It doesn't supply net energy or change the products.
distractor_rationales.D: It doesn't change ΔG.

items.stem: Increasing the temperature of a reaction generally ______ the reaction rate because molecules collide more frequently and energetically.
items.explanation: Higher temperature → faster rate (more energetic, frequent collisions). Takeaway: ↑Temperature = ↑rate (more/harder collisions). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Higher temperature raises molecular speed and collision energy/frequency, increasing the fraction of collisions that exceed Ea → faster rate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Higher temperature increases, not decreases, rate.
distractor_rationales.B: Temperature strongly affects rate.
distractor_rationales.C: Reactions speed up, not stop, at higher temperature.

items.stem: Le Chatelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium, when disturbed, will shift to:
items.explanation: Le Chatelier: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to counteract the change. Takeaway: Le Chatelier: system shifts to oppose the stress. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Le Chatelier: an equilibrium responds to a stress (concentration, pressure, temperature) by shifting in the direction that relieves it. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The system counteracts, not amplifies, the stress.
distractor_rationales.C: It re-establishes equilibrium; it doesn't stop.
distractor_rationales.D: The shift direction depends on the stress, not always toward products.

items.stem: If more reactant is added to a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium will shift:
items.explanation: Adding reactant shifts equilibrium toward products. Takeaway: Add reactant → shift toward products. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Adding reactant stresses the system, so it shifts toward products to consume the excess (Le Chatelier). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Adding reactant pushes toward products, not back toward reactants.
distractor_rationales.C: It does shift to relieve the added reactant.
distractor_rationales.D: The shift is toward products, not necessarily a solid.

items.stem: A large equilibrium constant (Keq >> 1) indicates that at equilibrium the reaction favors:
items.explanation: Large Keq (>>1) → products favored at equilibrium. Takeaway: Keq >> 1 = products favored. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Keq = [products]/[reactants]; a large Keq means products dominate at equilibrium. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A small Keq (<< 1) would favor reactants.
distractor_rationales.B: A large Keq clearly favors one side (products).
distractor_rationales.C: Keq magnitude reflects product/reactant ratio, not precipitation specifically.

items.stem: In a redox reaction, the species that LOSES electrons is ______ and the species that GAINS electrons is ______.
items.explanation: Oxidation = lose electrons; reduction = gain (OIL RIG). Takeaway: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). The oxidized species is the reducing agent. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — losing electrons is oxidation.
distractor_rationales.B: Redox is about electron transfer, not acid-base neutralization.
distractor_rationales.C: Those describe solubility changes, not redox.

items.stem: In any electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the ______ and reduction occurs at the ______.
items.explanation: Oxidation at the anode; reduction at the cathode (An Ox, Red Cat). Takeaway: Anode = oxidation; cathode = reduction. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Oxidation always occurs at the anode; reduction always at the cathode ('An Ox' and 'Red Cat'). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — oxidation is at the anode.
distractor_rationales.C: An electrolyte isn't where a half-reaction occurs; electrodes are.
distractor_rationales.D: The salt bridge balances charge; it isn't a reduction site.

items.stem: A ______ (voltaic) cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to GENERATE electricity, while an ______ cell uses electricity to DRIVE a nonspontaneous reaction.
items.explanation: Galvanic = spontaneous (makes current); electrolytic = driven by electricity. Takeaway: Galvanic = spontaneous (battery); electrolytic = forced by power. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Galvanic cells: spontaneous (ΔG < 0, produces current). Electrolytic cells: nonspontaneous (require an external power source). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the spontaneous, current-generating cell is galvanic.
distractor_rationales.C: Anode/cathode are electrodes, not cell types.
distractor_rationales.D: Series/parallel describe circuit wiring, not cell types.

items.stem: A carbon double-bonded to one oxygen AND single-bonded to a hydroxyl (–COOH) is the ______ group, found in carboxylic acids.
items.explanation: Carboxyl (–COOH) = carboxylic acids (acidic). Takeaway: Carboxyl = –COOH (carboxylic acid, acidic). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The carboxyl group (–COOH) defines carboxylic acids; it's acidic because the conjugate base is resonance-stabilized. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A hydroxyl is just –OH (alcohol).
distractor_rationales.B: An amino group is –NH2.
distractor_rationales.C: A lone carbonyl (C=O) without the –OH is an aldehyde/ketone, not a carboxyl.

items.stem: The –OH group defines an ______, while a C=O group defines a ______ (aldehyde or ketone).
items.explanation: –OH = alcohol; C=O = carbonyl (aldehyde/ketone). Takeaway: Hydroxyl (–OH) = alcohol; carbonyl (C=O) = aldehyde/ketone. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hydroxyl (–OH) = alcohol; carbonyl (C=O) = aldehyde (terminal) or ketone (internal). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Amino defines amines; carboxyl (not carbonyl alone) defines carboxylic acids.
distractor_rationales.B: Ester/ether are other oxygen groups, not –OH and C=O.
distractor_rationales.C: Alkane/alkene describe C–C saturation, not these functional groups.

items.stem: A carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one HYDROGEN (carbonyl at the end of a chain) is an ______; a carbonyl bonded to two carbons (internal) is a ______.
items.explanation: Aldehyde = terminal carbonyl (–CHO); ketone = internal carbonyl. Takeaway: Aldehyde = end carbonyl; ketone = middle carbonyl. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Aldehydes have the carbonyl at a chain END (–CHO); ketones have it between two carbons. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — the terminal carbonyl is an aldehyde.
distractor_rationales.C: Ester/ether aren't the carbonyl-position distinction.
distractor_rationales.D: Alcohol/acid aren't defined by carbonyl position.

items.stem: Molecules with the same molecular formula but DIFFERENT connectivity (bonding order) are ______ isomers; those with the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement are ______.
items.explanation: Structural = different connectivity; stereoisomers = same connectivity, different 3D. Takeaway: Structural = different bonds; stereo = same bonds, different 3D. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Structural (constitutional) isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers share connectivity but differ in 3D arrangement. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — different connectivity is structural isomerism.
distractor_rationales.B: Enantiomers/diastereomers are subtypes of stereoisomers, not the top-level pair.
distractor_rationales.D: Cis/trans are a subtype of stereoisomers.

items.stem: Two stereoisomers that are non-superimposable MIRROR IMAGES of each other are:
items.explanation: Enantiomers = non-superimposable mirror images. Takeaway: Enantiomers = mirror images (non-superimposable). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images (like left/right hands); they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images.
distractor_rationales.C: Structural isomers differ in connectivity, not mirror-image relationship.
distractor_rationales.D: Conformers interconvert by bond rotation; they aren't distinct configurations.

items.stem: A carbon atom bonded to FOUR different groups — giving the molecule handedness — is a:
items.explanation: A chiral center = carbon with four different groups (source of handedness). Takeaway: Chiral center = C with 4 different groups. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A chiral center is a carbon with four different substituents; it makes the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: A carbonyl carbon is C=O, not necessarily chiral.
distractor_rationales.C: The anomeric carbon is a specific sugar case, not the general definition.
distractor_rationales.D: An achiral carbon lacks four different groups.

items.stem: A solution of a single enantiomer is 'optically active,' meaning it:
items.explanation: Optically active = rotates plane-polarized light (chiral, single enantiomer). Takeaway: Optical activity = rotates polarized light (chiral). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Chiral molecules (single enantiomers) rotate plane-polarized light; a racemic (50/50) mixture shows no net rotation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Optical activity is about rotating polarized light, not absorbing all light.
distractor_rationales.C: Optical activity is unrelated to water solubility.
distractor_rationales.D: Optical activity requires a stereocenter, not the absence of one.

items.stem: In organic reactions, an electron-RICH species that attacks is a ______; an electron-POOR species that accepts electrons is an ______.
items.explanation: Nucleophile = electron-rich (attacks); electrophile = electron-poor (accepts). Takeaway: Nucleophile = electron-rich; electrophile = electron-poor. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Nucleophiles ('nucleus-loving,' electron-rich) donate electrons to electrophiles (electron-poor). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — the electron-rich attacker is the nucleophile.
distractor_rationales.C: Acid/base (proton transfer) isn't the same framing as nucleophile/electrophile.
distractor_rationales.D: Oxidant/reductant concern electron transfer in redox, a different context.

items.stem: An SN2 reaction occurs in a single concerted step with backside attack (causing inversion) and is fastest with ______ substrates; SN1 goes through a carbocation and is favored by ______ substrates.
items.explanation: SN2 favors primary (backside attack, inversion); SN1 favors tertiary (carbocation). Takeaway: SN2 = primary (inversion); SN1 = tertiary (carbocation). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. SN2 needs an accessible carbon (primary, less steric hindrance); SN1 forms a carbocation, stabilized best at tertiary carbons. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — SN2 favors primary, SN1 favors tertiary.
distractor_rationales.C: Aromatic/aliphatic isn't the SN1/SN2 substrate distinction.
distractor_rationales.D: Polar/nonpolar describes solvents/bonds, not the substrate order here.

items.stem: Oxidizing a PRIMARY alcohol gives an aldehyde and then a ______; oxidizing a SECONDARY alcohol gives a ______.
items.explanation: Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid; secondary → ketone (oxidation). Takeaway: 1° alcohol → acid; 2° alcohol → ketone (oxidation). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; secondary alcohol → ketone; tertiary alcohols resist oxidation. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — secondary alcohols give ketones, primary give acids.
distractor_rationales.B: Oxidation here adds oxygen/removes hydrogen, not forming ethers/esters.
distractor_rationales.C: These are oxygenation products, not alkane/alkene.

items.stem: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is used primarily to identify ______ by the characteristic vibrations of their bonds (e.g., a broad O–H peak, a strong C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹).
items.explanation: IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups (bond vibrations). Takeaway: IR = functional groups (C=O ~1700, broad O–H). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. IR detects bond vibrations, revealing functional groups (O–H broad, C=O ~1700 cm⁻¹, etc.). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Molecular mass is determined by mass spectrometry.
distractor_rationales.C: Proton counting/environments is NMR.
distractor_rationales.D: Optical rotation is measured by a polarimeter.

items.stem: Nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR) spectroscopy provides information about:

choices.text: The number and environment of hydrogen atoms (molecular structure)

items.explanation: NMR reveals hydrogen number/environment → molecular structure. Takeaway: NMR = H environments (structure). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. ¹H NMR reveals how many hydrogens are present and their chemical environments (via shifts, splitting, integration), building up the structure. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Molecular weight is from mass spectrometry.
distractor_rationales.B: Boiling point isn't determined by NMR.
distractor_rationales.C: Optical rotation is measured by polarimetry.

items.stem: Mass spectrometry determines a compound's ______ by ionizing it and measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of the fragments.
items.explanation: Mass spectrometry gives molecular mass (and fragments) via m/z. Takeaway: Mass spec = molecular mass + fragments (m/z). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Mass spec ionizes and fragments molecules, measuring m/z to give molecular mass and structural clues from the fragments. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Bond-vibration identification of functional groups is IR.
distractor_rationales.C: Hydrogen environments come from NMR.
distractor_rationales.D: pH is an acid-base property, not a mass-spec output.

items.stem: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating because its ______ is constantly changing, and the net force points:

choices.text: Velocity (direction); toward the center of the circle

items.explanation: Uniform circular motion: velocity direction changes; net force points toward the center (centripetal). Takeaway: Circular motion: centripetal force points to the center. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In uniform circular motion, speed is constant but velocity's DIRECTION changes, so there is centripetal acceleration and a net (centripetal) force toward the center. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Speed is constant; it's the velocity direction that changes, and the force points inward.
distractor_rationales.B: Mass doesn't change; the force is centripetal (inward), not tangential.
distractor_rationales.D: Speed is constant here; the changing quantity is velocity direction.

items.stem: The centripetal force required to keep an object of mass m moving at speed v in a circle of radius r is:
items.explanation: Centripetal force F = mv²/r. Takeaway: F_centripetal = mv²/r. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Centripetal force F = mv²/r (from a = v²/r); it increases sharply with speed and decreases with larger radius. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: That omits the square on v.
distractor_rationales.C: That isn't the centripetal force relationship.
distractor_rationales.D: That inverts the relationship.

items.stem: The outward 'centrifugal force' you seem to feel in a turning car is:

choices.text: A fictitious (apparent) force — really your inertia resisting the inward acceleration

items.explanation: Centrifugal force is fictitious — it's inertia; the real force is centripetal (inward). Takeaway: Centrifugal = fictitious (inertia); real force is inward. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Centrifugal force is a fictitious force in a rotating frame; the only real force is the inward (centripetal) one, and inertia makes you feel pushed outward. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: It is not a real force; it's an inertial effect.
distractor_rationales.C: It isn't gravity.
distractor_rationales.D: It's the opposite of the (real, inward) centripetal force.

items.stem: The centripetal force keeping a planet in orbit or a car turning is not a new force — it is PROVIDED by:

choices.text: An existing force (gravity, friction, tension, etc.) directed toward the center

items.explanation: Centripetal force is a ROLE filled by gravity, friction, or tension (whatever points inward). Takeaway: Centripetal = role played by gravity/friction/tension (inward). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. 'Centripetal' names the ROLE, not a new force — gravity (orbits), friction (turning car), or tension (whirled object) supplies the inward force. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: There is no separate 'centripetal force' — an ordinary force plays that role.
distractor_rationales.B: Centrifugal force is fictitious and points outward.
distractor_rationales.D: Air resistance opposes motion; it isn't the centripetal source.

items.stem: The gravitational force between two masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to:

choices.text: The square of the distance between them (F = Gm₁m₂/r²)

items.explanation: Gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r² (inverse-square). Takeaway: Gravity: F ∝ m₁m₂/r² (inverse square). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Universal gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r² is an inverse-square law (like Coulomb's law for charges). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The dependence is on r squared, not r.
distractor_rationales.C: It depends on the PRODUCT of masses, not their sum.
distractor_rationales.D: It's inverse-square, not inverse-cube.

items.stem: A satellite stays in circular orbit because the gravitational force acts as the ______ force, continuously pulling it toward the planet.
items.explanation: In orbit, gravity is the centripetal force pulling the satellite inward. Takeaway: Orbit: gravity = centripetal force. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Gravity supplies the centripetal force for orbital motion, constantly redirecting the satellite toward the planet's center. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Centrifugal force is fictitious.
distractor_rationales.C: There is no normal (contact) force in orbit.
distractor_rationales.D: There is no friction in the vacuum of orbit.

items.stem: Astronauts in orbit feel 'weightless' not because gravity is absent, but because they are:

choices.text: In continuous free fall around the Earth
Moving too fast for gravity to act
Shielded from gravity by the spacecraft

items.explanation: Orbital 'weightlessness' = continuous free fall (gravity is still present). Takeaway: Weightless in orbit = free fall (gravity still acts). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Orbiting astronauts (and their craft) are in free fall together, so there's no normal force — producing apparent weightlessness though gravity is still substantial. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Gravity is still strong in low orbit; it hasn't disappeared.
distractor_rationales.C: Speed doesn't turn off gravity; free fall causes weightlessness.
distractor_rationales.D: Spacecraft don't shield gravity.

items.stem: Viscosity is a fluid's:
items.explanation: Viscosity = a fluid's resistance to flow (internal friction). Takeaway: Viscosity = resistance to flow (honey > water). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Viscosity measures a fluid's internal resistance to flow; honey is more viscous than water. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Floating is buoyancy, not viscosity.
distractor_rationales.C: Density is mass per volume, a separate property.
distractor_rationales.D: Pressure transmission is Pascal's principle, not viscosity.

items.stem: Smooth, orderly fluid flow in parallel layers is ______ flow; chaotic, mixing flow (at high velocity) is ______ flow.
items.explanation: Laminar = smooth layered flow; turbulent = chaotic (high velocity). Takeaway: Laminar = smooth; turbulent = chaotic (fast). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Laminar flow is smooth and layered; turbulent flow is chaotic and occurs at high velocity/high Reynolds number. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — smooth layered flow is laminar.
distractor_rationales.B: Ideal/viscous describe fluid types, not this flow pattern.
distractor_rationales.C: Static/dynamic isn't the laminar/turbulent distinction.

items.stem: In laminar flow through a tube, the flow rate is extremely sensitive to the tube's radius — proportional to the radius raised to the:
items.explanation: Poiseuille: flow rate ∝ r⁴ (tiny radius changes hugely affect flow). Takeaway: Flow ∝ r⁴ (radius dominates; Poiseuille). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Poiseuille's law: flow rate ∝ r⁴, so even a small narrowing of a vessel drastically reduces flow (clinically important for blood vessels). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The dependence is r⁴, far stronger than linear.
distractor_rationales.C: It's r⁴, not r².
distractor_rationales.D: Flow strongly depends on radius, not independent of it.

items.stem: The electric field at a point is the force per unit ______ that a small positive test charge would experience there.
items.explanation: Electric field E = F/q (force per unit charge). Takeaway: E = F/q (field = force per charge). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Electric field E = F/q (force per unit charge); it points away from positive charges and toward negative charges. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Force per mass is a gravitational field, not electric.
distractor_rationales.C: Field isn't force per distance.
distractor_rationales.D: Field isn't force per area.

items.stem: Electric field lines point ______ from a positive charge and ______ a negative charge.
items.explanation: Field lines: away from +, toward −. Takeaway: Field lines: out of +, into −. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. By convention, field lines emanate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges (direction a positive test charge would move). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — lines point away from positive charges.
distractor_rationales.C: Lines point toward negative charges, not away.
distractor_rationales.D: Lines point away from positive charges, not toward.

items.stem: Electric potential (voltage) is potential energy per unit ______; it exists in space whether or not a charge is present.
items.explanation: Electric potential = potential energy per charge (V = PE/q). Takeaway: Potential (V) = PE per charge. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Electric potential = potential energy per unit charge (V = PE/q); a charge placed at that potential then has PE = qV. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Per mass would relate to gravitation, not electric potential.
distractor_rationales.C: Potential isn't energy per distance.
distractor_rationales.D: Potential isn't energy per time (that's power).

items.stem: The decibel scale for sound intensity is ______, so a 10 dB increase represents a ______ increase in intensity.
items.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic: +10 dB = 10× intensity. Takeaway: dB is logarithmic: +10 dB = 10× intensity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Decibels are logarithmic: every +10 dB is a 10× increase in intensity (so +20 dB is 100×). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The dB scale is logarithmic, not linear.
distractor_rationales.B: +10 dB is a 10×, not 2×, change.
distractor_rationales.C: The scale is logarithmic; +10 dB is 10×, not a doubling.

items.stem: When a driving frequency matches an object's natural frequency, the amplitude grows dramatically. This is:
items.explanation: Resonance: driving at the natural frequency → large amplitude. Takeaway: Resonance = drive at natural frequency → big amplitude. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Resonance is the large-amplitude response when a system is driven at its natural frequency (e.g., a pushed swing, a shattered glass). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Refraction is the bending of waves entering a new medium.
distractor_rationales.C: Diffraction is bending around obstacles/openings.
distractor_rationales.D: Attenuation is the loss of amplitude, the opposite of resonance.

items.stem: On a string fixed at both ends, only certain wavelengths produce standing waves; these allowed frequencies are the:
items.explanation: Standing waves occur at harmonics (fundamental × integer multiples). Takeaway: Standing waves = harmonics (integer multiples of fundamental). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A fixed string supports standing waves at the fundamental frequency and integer multiples (harmonics), set by the string's length. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Beats arise from two close frequencies interfering, not from a single string's modes.
distractor_rationales.C: Allowed frequencies are set by length, not unrelated.
distractor_rationales.D: Only specific (quantized) frequencies are allowed, not random ones.

items.stem: A converging (convex) lens has a ______ focal length; a diverging (concave) lens has a ______ focal length.
items.explanation: Converging = positive f; diverging = negative f. Takeaway: Converging f > 0; diverging f < 0. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sign convention: converging lenses/mirrors have positive focal length; diverging ones have negative focal length. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — converging is positive.
distractor_rationales.B: Focal lengths are finite nonzero values here.
distractor_rationales.C: Those values are incorrect for these lens types.

items.stem: The thin lens (and mirror) equation relating focal length f, object distance o, and image distance i is:
items.explanation: Thin lens/mirror equation: 1/f = 1/o + 1/i. Takeaway: 1/f = 1/o + 1/i. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. 1/f = 1/o + 1/i governs image formation for thin lenses and mirrors. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That isn't the thin lens equation.
distractor_rationales.B: That isn't correct either.
distractor_rationales.D: The terms add (1/o + 1/i), not subtract.

items.stem: A real image (which can be projected on a screen) forms where light rays actually converge and has a ______ image distance; a virtual image has a ______ image distance.
items.explanation: Real image = positive i (projectable, inverted); virtual = negative i (upright). Takeaway: Real image = +i (projectable); virtual = −i (upright). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Real images (rays actually meet) have positive image distance and are inverted; virtual images (rays only appear to diverge from) have negative image distance and are upright. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — real images have positive image distance.
distractor_rationales.C: Real images have positive, not zero, image distance.
distractor_rationales.D: Those values are incorrect.

items.stem: Electrons fill orbitals from lowest to highest energy, one orbital type at a time. This is the:
items.explanation: Aufbau principle: electrons fill lowest-energy orbitals first. Takeaway: Aufbau = fill lowest-energy orbitals first. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The Aufbau ('building up') principle: electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals first. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The uncertainty principle concerns position/momentum, not filling order.
distractor_rationales.C: Le Chatelier concerns equilibrium shifts.
distractor_rationales.D: Pauli exclusion limits electrons per orbital (2, opposite spins), a related but different rule.

items.stem: The Pauli exclusion principle states that a single orbital can hold at most ______ electrons, which must have ______.
items.explanation: Pauli exclusion: max 2 electrons per orbital, opposite spins. Takeaway: Pauli: 2 e− per orbital, opposite spins. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons with opposite (paired) spins. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Paired electrons must have OPPOSITE spins, not the same.
distractor_rationales.B: An orbital holds two electrons, not eight (a shell may hold more).
distractor_rationales.D: An orbital can hold two electrons, not just one.

items.stem: The electrons in the outermost shell, which determine an atom's chemical bonding behavior, are the:
items.explanation: Valence electrons (outermost shell) determine bonding. Takeaway: Valence electrons = outer shell (drive bonding). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Valence electrons (outermost shell) govern bonding and reactivity; core electrons are shielded and generally inert. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Core electrons are inner and don't drive bonding.
distractor_rationales.C: 'Free electrons' describes conduction, not the general bonding electrons.
distractor_rationales.D: Delocalized electrons are a special (metallic/aromatic) case.

items.stem: When filling degenerate (equal-energy) orbitals, electrons occupy them singly with parallel spins before pairing up. This is:
items.explanation: Hund's rule: fill degenerate orbitals singly (parallel spins) before pairing. Takeaway: Hund's rule: one electron per orbital first (then pair). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hund's rule: electrons spread out singly across equal-energy orbitals (minimizing repulsion) before doubling up. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Aufbau sets the order of orbital energies, not single-filling within a subshell.
distractor_rationales.B: Ohm's law concerns circuits.
distractor_rationales.D: Raoult's law concerns vapor pressure of solutions.

items.stem: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency, given by:
items.explanation: Photon energy E = hf (higher frequency = higher energy). Takeaway: E = hf (photon energy ∝ frequency). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Photon energy E = hf (h = Planck's constant); higher frequency (e.g., UV) means higher energy per photon. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: E = mc² is mass-energy equivalence, not photon energy.
distractor_rationales.B: ½ mv² is kinetic energy of a mass.
distractor_rationales.D: That isn't Planck's relation.

items.stem: Atoms emit light at specific discrete wavelengths (line spectra) because their electrons can only occupy:
items.explanation: Line spectra arise from quantized energy levels (discrete electron transitions). Takeaway: Emission lines = quantized energy-level transitions. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Electrons occupy quantized energy levels; light is emitted at discrete wavelengths when an electron drops between levels (line spectrum). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Energies are quantized (discrete), not continuous.
distractor_rationales.B: Electrons occupy multiple discrete levels, not a single one.
distractor_rationales.C: Electrons occupy orbitals around, not within, the nucleus.

items.stem: In the photoelectric effect, electrons are ejected from a metal only when the light exceeds a threshold ______, demonstrating light's particle (photon) nature.
items.explanation: Photoelectric effect: ejection needs a threshold frequency (photon nature of light). Takeaway: Photoelectric: needs threshold frequency (not just intensity). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A minimum photon FREQUENCY (energy) is needed to eject electrons; increasing intensity below threshold frequency does nothing — evidence for photons. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Below the threshold frequency, more intensity still ejects no electrons.
distractor_rationales.C: It's a minimum frequency (maximum wavelength) threshold, framed by frequency.
distractor_rationales.D: Temperature isn't the threshold variable in the photoelectric effect.

items.stem: Molarity, the most common concentration unit, is defined as:

choices.text: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L)

items.explanation: Molarity (M) = moles solute / liters solution. Takeaway: Molarity = mol solute / L solution. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Molarity (M) = moles solute / liters of solution. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Grams per liter is a mass concentration, not molarity.
distractor_rationales.B: Moles per kilogram of solvent is MOLALITY, not molarity.
distractor_rationales.C: That inverts the definition.

items.stem: To calculate concentrations when diluting a stock solution, use:
items.explanation: Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ (moles conserved). Takeaway: Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. In dilution, moles of solute are conserved, so M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That isn't the dilution relationship.
distractor_rationales.C: Concentrations and volumes don't add in dilution.
distractor_rationales.D: The subscripts must match (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂).

items.stem: Unlike molarity (per liter of solution), molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent and is preferred when ______ matters.

choices.text: Temperature (mass doesn't change with temperature; volume does)

items.explanation: Molality (mol/kg solvent) is temperature-independent (mass, not volume). Takeaway: Molality = mol/kg solvent (temp-independent). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Molality uses mass (temperature-independent), so it's preferred for temperature-dependent work like colligative properties; molarity's volume changes with temperature. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Color is irrelevant to the concentration unit choice.
distractor_rationales.B: Molality's advantage is temperature independence, not pressure.
distractor_rationales.C: Catalysis isn't the reason to choose molality.

items.stem: Colligative properties (like freezing point depression) depend on the ______ of solute particles, not their chemical identity.
items.explanation: Colligative properties depend on the NUMBER of particles, not identity. Takeaway: Colligative = depends on particle count (not identity). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Colligative properties depend only on the NUMBER of dissolved particles, not what they are. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: It's particle number, not mass, that matters.
distractor_rationales.B: Color is irrelevant to colligative behavior.
distractor_rationales.D: Shape/identity don't matter — only particle count.

items.stem: Dissolving a solute (like salt in water) ______ the freezing point and ______ the boiling point.
items.explanation: Solute: lowers freezing point, raises boiling point. Takeaway: Solute: ↓freezing point, ↑boiling point. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Solutes depress freezing point and elevate boiling point (why salt melts ice and pasta water boils hotter). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — solute lowers freezing point, raises boiling point.
distractor_rationales.B: Boiling point rises, not falls.
distractor_rationales.C: Freezing point falls, not rises.

items.stem: The pressure needed to stop water from flowing across a semipermeable membrane into a more concentrated solution is the ______, a colligative property.
items.explanation: Osmotic pressure = pressure resisting water flow into a concentrated solution. Takeaway: Osmotic pressure = colligative (drives water across membranes). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Osmotic pressure is the colligative property driving water across membranes toward higher solute concentration (key in cell biology). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Vapor pressure concerns evaporation, not osmosis.
distractor_rationales.C: Atmospheric pressure is the ambient air pressure.
distractor_rationales.D: Partial pressure concerns gas mixtures.

items.stem: The direct transition of a solid to a gas, without passing through the liquid phase (e.g., dry ice), is:
items.explanation: Sublimation = solid → gas directly (deposition is the reverse). Takeaway: Sublimation = solid → gas (dry ice). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Sublimation is solid → gas directly; deposition is the reverse (gas → solid). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Condensation is gas → liquid.
distractor_rationales.B: Vaporization is liquid → gas.
distractor_rationales.C: Deposition is gas → solid (the reverse of sublimation).

items.stem: On a heating curve, temperature stays CONSTANT during a phase change (a plateau) because added energy goes into:

choices.text: Breaking intermolecular forces (latent heat), not raising temperature

items.explanation: Phase-change plateaus: energy breaks IMFs (latent heat), temperature constant. Takeaway: Phase change = latent heat (temp constant, breaks IMFs). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. During a phase change, absorbed energy (latent heat) breaks intermolecular attractions rather than increasing kinetic energy, so temperature is constant. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Temperature is constant during the plateau, not rising.
distractor_rationales.C: Phase changes break intermolecular forces, not chemical bonds.
distractor_rationales.D: The energy goes into the phase change, not pressure.

items.stem: On a phase diagram, a substance with stronger intermolecular forces will require ______ to boil.
items.explanation: Stronger IMFs → higher boiling temperature. Takeaway: Stronger IMFs = higher boiling point. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Stronger IMFs hold molecules together more tightly, so more thermal energy (higher temperature) is needed to vaporize them. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Stronger IMFs raise, not lower, the boiling temperature.
distractor_rationales.B: Boiling still requires heat energy.
distractor_rationales.D: Temperature (not only pressure) determines boiling for a given pressure.

items.stem: The heat absorbed or released when a substance changes temperature (without a phase change) is:
items.explanation: q = mcΔT (heat = mass × specific heat × temperature change). Takeaway: q = mcΔT (heating without phase change). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. q = mcΔT, where m is mass, c is specific heat, and ΔT is the temperature change. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: mgh is gravitational potential energy.
distractor_rationales.C: ½ mv² is kinetic energy.
distractor_rationales.D: Pt is electrical energy (power × time).

items.stem: Water resists temperature change and stabilizes climate/organisms because it has an unusually ______ specific heat.
items.explanation: Water has a high specific heat (resists temperature change). Takeaway: Water = high specific heat (temperature buffer). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Water's high specific heat (from hydrogen bonding) means it absorbs a lot of heat for a small temperature change — buffering temperature. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Water's specific heat is high, not low.
distractor_rationales.B: Specific heat isn't zero.
distractor_rationales.C: Specific heat is a positive quantity.

items.stem: Because enthalpy is a state function, the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same regardless of the pathway taken. This is:
items.explanation: Hess's law: ΔH is path-independent (enthalpy is a state function). Takeaway: Hess's law: ΔH independent of path (sum the steps). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hess's law: ΔH is path-independent, so reaction enthalpies can be summed from steps. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Le Chatelier concerns equilibrium shifts.
distractor_rationales.B: Hund's rule concerns orbital filling.
distractor_rationales.C: Raoult's law concerns vapor pressure of solutions.

items.stem: A rate law such as rate = k[A]²[B] expresses the reaction rate as a function of:

choices.text: Reactant concentrations (each raised to an experimentally determined order)

items.explanation: Rate laws depend on reactant concentrations to experimentally determined orders. Takeaway: Rate law orders = experimental (not the coefficients). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Rate laws are determined experimentally; the exponents (orders) are NOT necessarily the stoichiometric coefficients. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Orders are found experimentally, not simply read from coefficients.
distractor_rationales.B: Rate depends on concentrations (and k, which depends on temperature), not temperature alone.
distractor_rationales.D: The equilibrium constant describes equilibrium, not the rate law.

items.stem: In the rate law rate = k[A]²[B], the OVERALL reaction order is:
items.explanation: Overall order = sum of exponents (2 + 1 = 3). Takeaway: Overall order = sum of exponents. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Overall order = sum of the exponents = 2 + 1 = 3. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: 2 is the order in A alone, not the overall order.
distractor_rationales.B: 1 is the order in B alone.
distractor_rationales.C: The exponents are summed (2+1=3), not multiplied.

items.stem: In a multi-step reaction, the overall rate is controlled by the:
items.explanation: The rate-determining step is the slowest step (the bottleneck). Takeaway: Rate-determining step = slowest step. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The slowest step is the bottleneck (rate-determining step) that sets the overall reaction rate. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The fastest step doesn't limit the rate.
distractor_rationales.B: The slowest step limits it, which isn't always the first.
distractor_rationales.D: Exothermicity (thermodynamics) doesn't set the kinetic bottleneck.

items.stem: One mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number of particles, which is approximately:
items.explanation: One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number). Takeaway: 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. A mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number); it links the atomic and macroscopic scales. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light, not Avogadro's number.
distractor_rationales.C: 9.8 is g (m/s²).
distractor_rationales.D: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the elementary charge.

items.stem: In a reaction, the limiting reagent is the reactant that:

choices.text: Is present in the greatest amount
Runs out first, limiting how much product can form

items.explanation: The limiting reagent runs out first and caps product formation. Takeaway: Limiting reagent = runs out first (caps yield). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The limiting reagent is completely consumed first and caps the amount of product; the others are in excess. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The most abundant reactant is usually in excess, not limiting.
distractor_rationales.B: Cost is irrelevant to which reagent limits.
distractor_rationales.D: The limiting reagent sets the yield, not necessarily the rate.

items.stem: Percent yield is calculated as:
items.explanation: Percent yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100%. Takeaway: % yield = actual/theoretical × 100. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Percent yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100%; it's usually below 100% due to side reactions and losses. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: That inverts the ratio.
distractor_rationales.C: Yields aren't multiplied.
distractor_rationales.D: Percent yield is a ratio, not a difference.

items.stem: The formula giving the SIMPLEST whole-number ratio of atoms (e.g., CH₂O) is the ______ formula; the actual number of atoms (e.g., C₆H₁₂O₆) is the ______ formula.
items.explanation: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual atom counts. Takeaway: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual counts. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual counts (a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Reversed — the simplest ratio is the empirical formula.
distractor_rationales.C: Structural/condensed describe how formulas are drawn, not this ratio distinction.
distractor_rationales.D: Ionic/covalent describe bonding, not formula types here.

items.stem: Hydrocarbons with only single C–C bonds are ______; those with a carbon-carbon double bond are ______; those with a triple bond are alkynes.
items.explanation: Alkanes = single bonds; alkenes = double; alkynes = triple. Takeaway: Alkane (single), alkene (double), alkyne (triple). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Alkanes (single bonds, saturated), alkenes (C=C), alkynes (C≡C). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Reversed — single-bond hydrocarbons are alkanes.
distractor_rationales.C: Aromatic/aliphatic is a different classification.
distractor_rationales.D: Esters/ethers are oxygen-containing groups, not hydrocarbons.

items.stem: A 'saturated' hydrocarbon is one that:
items.explanation: Saturated hydrocarbon = only single bonds (max hydrogens). Takeaway: Saturated = single bonds only (max H). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Saturated = only single C–C bonds (holding the maximum number of hydrogens); unsaturated hydrocarbons have double/triple bonds. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Double/triple bonds make a hydrocarbon UNsaturated.
distractor_rationales.B: 'Saturated' here refers to bonding, not a saturated solution.
distractor_rationales.C: A benzene ring is unsaturated (aromatic).

items.stem: Benzene is unusually stable because its ring of alternating double bonds forms a delocalized system described as:
items.explanation: Benzene is aromatic — delocalized pi electrons give special stability. Takeaway: Benzene = aromatic (delocalized, resonance-stabilized). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Benzene's delocalized pi electrons (aromaticity) confer special stability and distinctive reactivity. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Benzene is aromatic and unusually STABLE, not simply reactive aliphatic.
distractor_rationales.C: Benzene is covalent/aromatic, not ionic.
distractor_rationales.D: The electrons are delocalized around the ring, not a single localized bond.

items.stem: A carboxylic acid reacting with an alcohol (losing water) forms an:
items.explanation: Carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water (esterification). Takeaway: Acid + alcohol → ester + water (esterification). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water (a condensation/dehydration reaction). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: An amide forms from a carboxylic acid + amine.
distractor_rationales.B: An ether is R–O–R, formed differently.
distractor_rationales.C: An alkane has no oxygen functional group.

items.stem: The reverse of a condensation reaction — breaking a bond (e.g., an ester or peptide bond) by ADDING water — is:
items.explanation: Hydrolysis = breaking a bond by adding water (reverse of condensation). Takeaway: Hydrolysis = add water to break a bond. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Hydrolysis uses water to cleave bonds (esters, amides, peptides); dehydration synthesis is the reverse (removing water to form bonds). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Dehydration synthesis forms bonds by removing water — the opposite.
distractor_rationales.C: Oxidation involves electron loss, not water-mediated cleavage.
distractor_rationales.D: Sublimation is a phase change, not a bond reaction.

items.stem: The bond linking a carboxylic acid derivative to an amine — the same linkage found between amino acids in proteins — is an:
items.explanation: An amide (peptide) bond links a carbonyl to nitrogen (protein backbone). Takeaway: Amide bond = carbonyl–N (peptide bond in proteins). The keyed choice holds because: Correct. An amide bond joins a carbonyl to a nitrogen; in proteins this is the peptide bond. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: An ester bond links a carbonyl to an oxygen (acid + alcohol).
distractor_rationales.B: An ether bond is C–O–C.
distractor_rationales.D: A glycosidic bond links sugars.

passages.title: Aesthetics — why originals matter
passages.body:
Suppose a forger produces a copy of a painting so exact that no expert, however equipped, could tell it from the original. Most of us would still prefer to own the original, and would pay vastly more for it. This preference is easy to mock as mere snobbery — a fetish for provenance that adds nothing to what the eye receives. If two canvases are visually identical, the skeptic asks, how can one be aesthetically superior to the other? Whatever we are paying for, it cannot be the look of the thing.

The skeptic assumes that the value of a painting must reside entirely in its present visual surface. But this assumption is far from obvious. When I stand before a canvas that Rembrandt himself touched, I am in physical, causal contact with the very object his hand shaped. The forgery, however exquisite, offers no such contact; it is the terminus of a different causal chain, one that runs back not to Rembrandt but to a clever imitator in a rented studio. To value the original is to value that lineage, and there is nothing irrational about caring where a thing comes from.

An analogy makes the point. A letter in a beloved's handwriting is treasured over a flawless photocopy, though the copy conveys every word. We do not think the person who keeps the original has made a perceptual error, as though they had failed to notice that the words are the same. They are responding to something the photocopy lacks: a direct trace of the writer's presence. Paintings, on this view, are less like texts, whose value is exhausted by their content, and more like relics, whose value depends on their history.

Yet the analogy should not be pressed too far. Relics are valued almost wholly for contact and hardly at all for how they look; the point of a saint's bone is not its appearance. Great paintings are not like this. Their history matters, but so, undeniably, does what they show — the very composition and color the forger has reproduced. A defender of originals need not deny that appearance carries much of a painting's worth. The claim is only that appearance does not carry all of it, and that the remainder, however hard to name, is not nothing.

This more modest thesis is also the more defensible one. It grants the skeptic everything plausible in the skeptical position — that the visible work is most of what we prize — while denying the further, unargued step from "most" to "all." The forger's triumph, if it is one, is to have captured the larger share of a painting's value. It is not to have shown that the smaller share was an illusion all along.

questions.stem: The author's central thesis is that:

choices.text: a flawless forgery is aesthetically equal to the original it copies
a painting's worth lies partly in its history and not solely in its appearance
the higher price paid for originals reflects snobbery rather than reason
the visible appearance of a painting contributes nothing to its true value

questions.explanation: The passage builds to the "modest thesis" of the last two paragraphs: appearance carries most of a painting's value, but not all — the remainder comes from historical, causal contact. Takeaway: The CARS main idea is usually the qualified thesis the author settles on, not the strongest-sounding claim in the passage. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Appearance carries "much"/"most," but history supplies a real remainder (¶4–5). Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: This is the skeptic's position, which the author spends the passage arguing against.
distractor_rationales.C: The author explicitly rejects the charge that the preference is "mere snobbery."
distractor_rationales.D: Overstated — the author concedes appearance carries "the larger share" of the value.

questions.stem: The discussion of relics in the fourth paragraph functions primarily to:

choices.text: qualify the earlier analogy and narrow the author's own claim
establish that paintings are, strictly speaking, a kind of relic
concede that the skeptic was correct all along
raise an objection the author is ultimately unable to answer

questions.explanation: The paragraph opens "Yet the analogy should not be pressed too far" and distinguishes paintings (whose appearance matters) from relics (whose appearance does not), refining the thesis to "appearance does not carry all" of the value. Takeaway: A "Yet/But" paragraph following an analogy typically qualifies it — its job is refinement, not reversal. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. It checks the letter/relic analogy and refines the claim to its modest form. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The opposite — the paragraph argues paintings are not simply relics.
distractor_rationales.C: Only a partial concession is made (appearance carries much), not the whole skeptical claim.
distractor_rationales.D: The author does resolve it; it is a self-correction, not an unanswered objection.

questions.stem: Regarding the person who prefers an original letter to a photocopy, the author would most likely agree that this preference is:

choices.text: a reasonable response to the letter's history rather than its wording
a perceptual mistake about the letter's actual content
proof that, for texts, content is the only thing that matters
stronger than the preference most people feel for original paintings

questions.explanation: In the third paragraph the author says such a person has not "made a perceptual error"; they respond to "a direct trace of the writer's presence" — the letter's history, not its (identical) words. Takeaway: Distractors often reverse the author's point or smuggle in a comparison the text never makes. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The preference tracks presence/history, not the wording, which is the same in both. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The passage explicitly denies this is a perceptual error.
distractor_rationales.C: Backwards — the example is meant to show that something beyond content matters.
distractor_rationales.D: The passage never ranks the two preferences; it uses the letter to illuminate the painting.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most seriously WEAKEN the author's thesis?

choices.text: At auction, verified originals sell for far more than acknowledged copies.
After being truthfully told which of two visually identical canvases is the authentic original, viewers assign the two exactly equal value.
Experts are sometimes unable to distinguish a skilled forgery from an original.
A relic is prized by believers regardless of how unremarkable it looks.

questions.explanation: The thesis is that a real remainder of value survives once appearance is held constant. If people value two identical canvases equally even after learning which is authentic, then appearance carries all the value and the "remainder" is nothing — directly contradicting the claim. passages.title: History — the press and the Reformation
passages.body:
It is often said that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Luther's theses, the story goes, would have died as a local academic dispute had the new technology not broadcast them across Europe within weeks. There is something to this. Print did carry Luther's words farther and faster than any scribe could, and the reformers themselves marveled at the machine — one called it "God's highest act of grace." But "the press caused the Reformation" claims more than the evidence will bear.

Consider what the same presses were printing. In the decades before Luther, Europe's workshops turned out indulgences, devotional manuals, and papal bulls in enormous numbers; the technology served the old church at least as eagerly as it later served its critics. A tool that amplifies whatever message it is given cannot, by itself, explain why one message rather than another swept the continent. To credit the press with the Reformation is to mistake a multiplier for a cause.

The point can be sharpened. Earlier reformers — Wyclif in England, Hus in Bohemia — had advanced doctrines close to Luther's a full century before movable type, and had won substantial followings without it. Their movements were contained, but by armies and inquisitions, not by any shortage of copyists. What differed in Luther's case was not merely the speed of transmission but a constellation of circumstances: a fractured German political landscape in which sympathetic princes could shield him, a literate urban public primed by grievance, and a message pitched to that public's discontents.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. Technologies shape the movements that use them, and a Reformation conducted by pamphlet was bound to differ from one conducted by sermon and manuscript. The press lowered the cost of dissent and widened the circle of those who could join it. But "shaped" is not "caused," and "made easier" is not "made inevitable." The most we can say is that print was among the conditions that allowed the Reformation to spread as it did — a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation.

The appeal of the simpler story is easy to understand. Causes that can be named and dated — a machine, an invention — are more satisfying than a tangle of politics, literacy, and timing. But history rarely obliges us with single causes, and the historian's task is often to resist the tidy explanation in favor of the true one.

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose is to:

choices.text: argue that the printing press played no role in the Reformation
defend the claim that Luther would certainly have failed without printing
show that the press was a contributing condition of the Reformation rather than its cause

Paragraphs 4–5 land on print as one condition among several, not the cause. Takeaway: Purpose questions want the author's argumentative aim, not an incidental detail like technical history. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The thesis is condition-not-cause: "a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation." Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The author undercuts single-cause stories and notes Wyclif and Hus gained followings without print.

distractor_rationales.C: Indulgences are cited as an example of what presses printed, not as a cause.

The invention of the wheel is the cause of all later transportation.

The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Neutral multiplier + earlier occurrences without it + "enabling condition" mirrors the passage exactly. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. choices.text: contemptuous of anyone who finds it appealing
indifferent to whether it is true

Takeaway: When an author calls a view "understandable" and then pivots on "but," expect sympathy for its appeal and rejection of its substance. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. The author acknowledges the appeal while rejecting the accuracy. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: "Easy to understand" is empathetic, not contemptuous.
distractor_rationales.B: The author spends the passage arguing against it.
distractor_rationales.C: The closing lines show the author cares a great deal about getting the truth right.

passages.title: Philosophy — can we learn from fiction?
passages.body:
Can a novel teach us anything true about the world? The doubt is old and not unserious. A novel, after all, is by definition a made-up story; its characters never lived, its events never happened. Whatever a novelist asserts through the tale is unsupported by evidence — the author simply stipulates that things are so within the fiction. If I want to know how grief works, or how power corrupts, it seems I should consult a psychologist or a historian, not a storyteller who has invented her data.

This objection has force against one kind of knowledge but not another. It is true that fiction cannot establish general facts: no number of novels about ambitious men could prove that ambition corrupts, since the novelist controls the outcome. But not all knowledge is knowledge of general facts. There is also knowing what something is like — what it would be to face a certain choice, to bear a certain loss. And here fiction has resources the treatise lacks: it can place us, in imagination, inside a situation and let us try it on.

Consider the difference between being told that jealousy distorts perception and following, page by page, a character's jealous misreadings of an innocent scene. The first hands us a proposition to file away; the second rehearses the experience, and may leave us better able to recognize the distortion in ourselves. The novelist need not prove that jealousy works this way. It is enough that she renders it so vividly that we recognize it — the recognition, not the proof, is the point.

A skeptic may reply that this "knowledge" is merely emotional, not cognitive — that we have been moved, not taught. But the line is not so clean. To grasp what a situation is like is often a precondition for judging it well; the person who cannot imagine another's suffering will reason poorly about how to treat them. If fiction cultivates that imaginative grasp, it is doing cognitive work, even if it proves no theorems.

The modest conclusion is that fiction and science divide the labor of understanding rather than compete for it. Science tells us that things are so and why; fiction shows us what their being so is like from the inside. To ask a novel to furnish general laws is to misunderstand the kind of knowledge it offers — and to conclude, from its failure to do so, that it offers none, is to make the same mistake twice.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

choices.text: novels can prove general truths about human psychology
fiction and science are ultimately in competition
fiction offers a kind of understanding — of what experiences are like — distinct from the general facts science provides
emotional responses to fiction carry no cognitive value

questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2–5 distinguish "knowing that" (general facts, science's domain) from "knowing what something is like" (fiction's domain), and the last paragraph frames this as a division of labor. Takeaway: The main idea is the distinction the author builds, not either extreme claim the passage sets up in order to reject. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. This is the "knowing what it is like" thesis, complementary to science. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The final paragraph says the two "divide the labor... rather than compete."

questions.stem: The passage implies that a person who dismisses novels as sources of knowledge because they cannot establish general laws has:

distractor_rationales.C: The author argues fiction does cognitive work, not that it is mere entertainment.
distractor_rationales.D: The critique concerns misjudging fiction, not misunderstanding science.

Unverified personal study copy.
