distractor_rationales.C: Measures a general frequency — again "knowing that."
distractor_rationales.D: Establishes a general truth by proof, the opposite of experiential knowledge.

passages.title: Anthropology — the invention of tradition
passages.body:
Many customs that present themselves as immemorial are surprisingly young. The Scottish clan tartan, worn as a badge of ancient lineage, was largely codified in the nineteenth century; the elaborate ceremonial of certain monarchies, apparently the residue of centuries, was substantially devised within living memory of those who first performed it. Historians have given such practices a name: invented traditions — rituals that claim continuity with a distant past to which their actual connection is tenuous or fabricated.

Why manufacture a past? Invented traditions tend to appear, scholars note, at moments of rapid change, when older bonds have frayed and new institutions must secure loyalty quickly. A ritual that feels ancient lends the present an air of inevitability; what looks as though it has always been done is harder to question than what is admittedly new. The invention, in other words, does work: it stabilizes, legitimizes, binds.

It would be easy to draw a cynical moral — that such traditions are frauds, and that exposing their recent origins deflates them. But this conclusion moves too fast. That a practice was invented at a datable moment does not show that it is meaningless to those who observe it. A wedding ritual devised a century ago may bind a community as tightly as one a millennium old; the bonds are real even if the pedigree is not. To confuse the falsity of a tradition's origin story with the falsity of its present function is to misjudge what such traditions are for.

Nor is the category as tidy as it first appears. Few traditions are either wholly ancient or wholly invented; most are refashioned inheritances — old materials put to new use. The nineteenth-century codifiers of tartan did not conjure it from nothing: they systematized and embellished a genuine, if looser, prior practice. "Invented" is thus better read as a matter of degree than as a verdict of pure fabrication.

The value of the concept, then, is not that it unmasks tradition as a lie. It is that it dissolves a false assumption: that the authority of a practice depends on the antiquity of its origins. Once we see how readily a sense of the ancient can be manufactured, we are freed to ask a better question — not how old a tradition is, but what work it does, and for whom.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: exposing invented traditions as frauds that ought to be abandoned
proving that all traditions are in fact recent inventions
arguing that a tradition's meaning and function do not depend on the antiquity of its origins
tracing the specific history of the Scottish tartan

questions.explanation: The third and fifth paragraphs make the core point: invented origins do not negate present function, and a practice's authority rests not on antiquity but on "what work it does." Takeaway: A passage's subject is the thesis it argues, not the illustrative example it happens to open with. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Origin-age is severed from present meaning and function. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: The third paragraph explicitly rejects the cynical "frauds" reading.
distractor_rationales.B: The fourth paragraph says most traditions are "refashioned inheritances," not pure inventions.
distractor_rationales.D: Tartan is one recurring example, not the subject of the passage.

questions.stem: The author raises the "cynical moral" in the third paragraph in order to:

choices.text: introduce it and then reject it, refining the view of invented traditions
endorse it as the passage's conclusion
prove that invented traditions are meaningless
show that exposing a tradition's origins always deflates it

questions.explanation: The paragraph states the cynical reading ("frauds," "deflates them") and immediately answers that "this conclusion moves too fast," separating false origins from real present function. Takeaway: A view introduced with wording like "it would be easy to conclude" is usually being set up for rejection. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. It is raised in order to be refuted, which sharpens the thesis. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: The author rejects the cynical moral rather than endorsing it.
distractor_rationales.C: This is the opposite of what the author concludes.
distractor_rationales.D: The author denies exactly this: the bonds can be "real even if the pedigree is not."

questions.stem: The tartan example in the fourth paragraph is used to support the claim that:

choices.text: invented traditions are always total fabrications
the line between ancient and invented traditions is a matter of degree
the nineteenth-century codifiers invented tartan from nothing

questions.explanation: Tartan, "systematized and embellished" from "a genuine, if looser, prior practice," is offered to show that "invented" is "a matter of degree than... pure fabrication." Takeaway: An example placed late in a passage usually supports the immediate surrounding claim — here, "degree, not pure fabrication." The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Tartan exemplifies refashioned inheritance, i.e., a matter of degree. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: Directly contradicted — the codifiers "did not conjure it from nothing."
distractor_rationales.C: No claim of uniqueness is made; tartan is a general example.
distractor_rationales.D: The text asserts the opposite.

questions.stem: Which situation would the author most likely classify as an "invented tradition" in the refined sense of the fourth paragraph?

choices.text: A university's "centuries-old" graduation hymn that was in fact written in 1900 by adapting an older folk melody.
A festival documented continuously since antiquity and unchanged in form.
A brand-new corporate slogan that makes no claim to any past.
A law passed last year that everyone openly knows is recent.

questions.explanation: The refined sense is old material refashioned and presented as ancient. The hymn — adapted around 1900 from an older melody yet treated as "centuries-old" — is a refashioned inheritance claiming continuity. Takeaway: Apply the refined definition, not the loose one: an invented tradition reworks old material and passes it off as ancient. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Recent codification of older material, dressed up as long-standing. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.B: Genuinely continuous and ancient, so not invented.
distractor_rationales.C: Makes no claim to a past, so it is not a tradition claiming continuity.
distractor_rationales.D: Openly recent; invented traditions specifically claim antiquity.

questions.stem: The "better question" the author endorses in the final paragraph implies that judgments about a tradition's authority should rest on:

choices.text: how far back its origins can be traced
whether its origin story is literally true
how many people currently observe it
its present function and whom it serves

questions.explanation: The closing lines urge us to ask "not how old a tradition is, but what work it does, and for whom." Takeaway: When an author reframes toward "a better question," the answer is whatever that new question foregrounds — here, function rather than antiquity. The keyed choice holds because: Correct. Function and beneficiaries, per the final sentence. Source: Open-MCAT (CC BY-NC 4.0, © 2026 Makenzi L. McDermott). Unverified personal study copy.

distractor_rationales.A: This is precisely the criterion the author is displacing.
distractor_rationales.B: The author separates the truth of an origin story from present authority.
distractor_rationales.C: Popularity is not the proposed criterion; "what work it does, for whom" is.
